topic: Classical & Axiomatic Probability, Consequences
subtopic: Classical & Axiomatic Probability, Consequences
stem: Let $A_1,A_2,A_3,A_4$ be independent events with $P(A_1)=\dfrac12,\ P(A_2)=\dfrac14,\ P(A_3)=\dfrac18,\ P(A_4)=\dfrac{1}{16}$. What is $P(A_1\cup A_2\cup A_3\cup A_4)$?
shortcut: For independent events never expand inclusion-exclusion. Use $\operatorname{P}\!\left(\text{none occurs}\right)$ = product of the complements: $(1/2)(3/4)(7/8)(15/16) = 315/1024$, so the union is $1 - 315/1024 = 709/1024$. Ten seconds.
tips: Option $(d) 315/1024$ is the planted trap: it is $\operatorname{P}\!\left(\text{no event occurs}\right)$, i.e. the answer you get if you forget to subtract from 1.

Denominator check: $2 \times 4 \times 8 \times 16 = 1024$, so any correct answer must have 1024 (or a divisor of it) as denominator. That instantly kills $(a) 15/16$ unless it reduces, and it does not.
$1023/1024$ in option (b) equals $1 - 1/1024$, the value you would get if all four probabilities were $1/2$ each - another distractor built from a plausible slip.
Memorise: $\operatorname{P}\!\left(\text{union of independent events}\right) = 1 - \prod(1 - p_{i})$. It is the single most reused one-line identity in this part of the paper.
solution: The events A1, A2, A3, A4 are independent, therefore their complements $A_{1}', A_{2}', A_{3}', A_{4}'$ are also independent.
P(no $A_{i}$ occurs) = $\operatorname{P}(A_{1}' \cap A_{2}' \cap A_{3}' \cap A_{4}') = (1/2)(3/4)(7/8)(15/16) = (1 \times 3 \times 7 \times 15)/(2 \times 4 \times 8 \times 16) = 315/1024$.
The union is the complement of that event: $\operatorname{P}(A_{1} \cup A_{2} \cup A_{3} \cup A_{4}) = 1 - 315/1024 = (1024 - 315)/1024 = 709/1024$.
Hence option (c) is correct.

topic: Classical & Axiomatic Probability, Consequences
subtopic: Classical & Axiomatic Probability, Consequences
stem: A lot of 15 mobiles has 4 defectives. Mobiles are examined one by one without replacement. The probability that the 9th mobile examined is the last defective is
shortcut: Split the event: 'exactly 3 defectives among the first 8' AND 'the 9th is the 4th defective'. Hypergeometric x conditional = $[\binom{4}{3}\binom{11}{5}/\binom{15}{8}] x (1/7) = (56/195)(1/7) = 8/195$.
tips: Option $(a) 56/195$ is exactly the first factor alone - the trap for candidates who stop after the hypergeometric step and forget the 9th draw.
After 8 draws, 7 mobiles remain and exactly 1 of them is defective, so the conditional probability of a defective on draw 9 is $1/7$ - no new combinatorics needed.
'The k-th item is the LAST defective' always factors as $\operatorname{P}\!\left(\text{exactly d-1 defectives in the first k-1}\right) x P$(defective on draw k | that). Learn this two-step template.
Sanity bound: the answer must be small (well under $1/7$), so $(c) 1/7$ and $(d) 24/65 = 0.37$ can be eliminated on size alone.
solution: Let the lot have $N = 15$ mobiles of which $D = 4$ are defective. We need P(the 9th mobile examined is the 4th and last defective).
This requires exactly 3 defectives among the first 8 mobiles, and then a defective on the 9th draw.
$\operatorname{P}\!\left(\text{exactly 3 defectives in the first 8}\right) = \binom{4}{3} \binom{11}{5} / \binom{15}{8} = (4)(462)/6435 = 1848/6435 = 56/195$.
Given that, $15 - 8 = 7$ mobiles remain and exactly $4 - 3 = 1$ of them is defective, so P(9th is defective | above) = $1/7$.
Hence option (b) is correct.

topic: Random Variables & Distribution Functions
subtopic: Random Variables & Distribution Functions
stem: $X$ has p.d.f. $$f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{x}{2}, & 0<x\le1\\[4pt] \dfrac12, & 1<x\le2\\[4pt] \dfrac{3-x}{3}, & 2<x\le3\end{cases}$$ What is $P(1.5<X\le2.5\mid X>1)$?
issue: SOURCE DEFECT - stem and options are mutually inconsistent. As printed, the third branch $(3-x)/3$ on $2<x \le 3$ contributes $1/6$, giving a total mass of $1/4 + 1/2 + 1/6 = 11/12$, so the printed function is not a density. With the third branch normalised to the only value that makes f a density, $(3-x)/2$, the exact answer is $\operatorname{P}(1.5<X \le 2.5 \mid X>1) = (7/16)/(3/4) = 7/12$, which is NOT among the four printed options; taking the branch exactly as printed gives $9/16$, which is also not among them. The source has therefore been preserved verbatim and this question is flagged and excluded from scoring rather than silently rewritten. No option has been invented.
shortcut: AI-derived: with the density normalised, $\operatorname{P}(X>1) = 3/4$ and $\operatorname{P}(1.5<X \le 2.5) = 1/2 \times 0.5$ + area of the trapezium under $(3-x)/2$ from 2 to $2.5 = 0.25 + 0.1875 = 7/16$, giving $7/12$.
tips: Always run the normalisation check FIRST on a piecewise density: integrate every branch and confirm the pieces sum to 1. Here they do not, which is the fastest way to spot the misprint.
For a linear branch, the integral is just the area of a trapezium: (average height) x (width). From 2 to 2.5 the heights are 0.5 and 0.25, so the area is $0.375 \times 0.5 = 0.1875$.
$\operatorname{P}(A\mid B)$ with B = {$X>1$}: the denominator is 1 minus the mass of the first branch, not 1 minus the value of the density.
In a real exam, a stem that fails the normalisation check and whose exact answer is absent from the options is a candidate for a UPSC key challenge - mark it and move on rather than forcing a fit.
solution: Step 0 (integrity check): $\int x/2$ over (0,1] = $1/4$; $\int 1/2$ over (1,2] = $1/2$; $\int (3-x)/3$ over (2,3] = $(1/3)(1/2) = 1/6$. Total = $11/12$, not 1, so the function as printed is not a probability density.
Reading the third branch as $(3-x)/2$ - the unique constant that normalises it - gives masses $1/4, 1/2, 1/4$ which sum to 1.
Denominator: $\operatorname{P}(X>1) = 1 - 1/4 = 3/4$.
Numerator: $\operatorname{P}(1.5 < X \le 2.5) = \int 1/2$ from 1.5 to 2 plus $\int (3-x)/2$ from 2 to $2.5 = 0.25 + 0.1875 = 0.4375 = 7/16$.
$7/12$ does not equal $3/8, 1/2, 5/8$ or $1/4$, so no printed option is correct and the question is flagged as a source defect.

topic: Conditional Probability, Law of Total Probability, Bayes' Theorem
subtopic: Conditional Probability, Law of Total Probability, Bayes' Theorem
stem: Urn 1 has 7 white, 10 black balls; urn 2 has 5 white, 12 black; urn 3 has 17 white only. An urn is chosen at random and a ball drawn is white. What are the probabilities it came from urn 1, 2, 3 respectively?
shortcut: All three urns hold 17 balls, so the denominators cancel. The posteriors are simply proportional to the white counts 7, 5, 17, whose total is 29. Answer: $7/29, 5/29, 17/29$ - read straight off the counts.
tips: Equal urn totals + equal prior selection probability = posterior proportional to the number of favourable balls. Look for this shortcut before writing Bayes' formula.
The three posteriors MUST sum to 1. Option (a) gives $(7+6+18)/29 = 31/29 > 1$ and option (b) gives $32/29 > 1$ - both are eliminated by inspection in about five seconds.
Urn 3 has 17 white and 0 black, so P(white | urn 3) = 1; its posterior weight is the full 17.

The generic form is $\operatorname{P}(U_{i} \mid W) = \operatorname{P}(U_{i})\operatorname{P}(W\mid U_{i})$ / SUM_j $\operatorname{P}(U_{j})\operatorname{P}(W\mid U_{j})$; the common prior $1/3$ cancels top and bottom.
solution: Each urn contains 17 balls: urn 1 has 7 white and 10 black, urn 2 has 5 white and 12 black, urn 3 has 17 white and 0 black.

Prior: $\operatorname{P}\!\left(\text{urn i}\right) = 1/3$ for each i. Likelihoods: $\operatorname{P}(W\mid U_{1}) = 7/17, \operatorname{P}(W\mid U_{2}) = 5/17, \operatorname{P}(W\mid U_{3}) = 17/17 = 1$.
Similarly $\operatorname{P}(U_{2}\mid W) = 5/29$ and $\operatorname{P}(U_{3}\mid W) = 17/29$. These sum to $29/29 = 1$, confirming the arithmetic.
Hence option (c) is correct.

topic: Random Vectors: Joint, Marginal & Conditional Distributions
subtopic: Random Vectors: Joint, Marginal & Conditional Distributions
stem: $X,Y$ have joint p.d.f. $$f(x,y)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{1+xy}{4}, & |x|<1,\ |y|<1\\[4pt] 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$ 1. $X$ and $Y$ are independent. 2. $X^2$ and $Y^2$ are independent.
shortcut: Both marginals are Uniform(-1,1) with density $1/2$, so the product $1/4$ does not equal $(1+xy)/4$ - statement 1 fails. But integrating the xy term over any symmetric rectangle kills it, so squares are independent - statement 2 holds. Answer: 2 only.
tips: The 'copula-style' density $(1 + xy)/4$ on the square is a classic: dependent variables whose squares (and whose signs) behave independently.
Marginal shortcut: integrating $(1+xy)/4$ in y over $(-1,1)$ kills the odd term xy, leaving $2/4 = 1/2$. Any odd-in-y term always vanishes on a symmetric interval.
$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)$ here is NOT zero $(\operatorname{E}(XY) = 1/9)$, so this is not the usual 'uncorrelated but dependent' example - do not answer from pattern memory.
For 1-only / 2-only / both / neither items, test the CHEAPER statement first. Here statement 1 takes one line, so start there and use it to eliminate two options immediately.
solution: Marginal of X: $f_{X}(x)$ = integral over y in $(-1,1)$ of $(1+xy)/4 dy = (1/4)[y + xy^{2}/2]$ from -1 to $1 = (1/4)(2) = 1/2$ for |x| < 1. By symmetry $f_{Y}(y) = 1/2$ for |y| < 1.
Statement 1: $f_{X}(x) f_{Y}(y) = 1/4$, but the joint density is $(1+xy)/4$. These differ whenever xy is not 0, so X and Y are NOT independent. Statement 1 is false.

Statement 2: take any $0 < a, b \le 1$. $\operatorname{P}(X^{2} \le a^{2}, Y^{2} \le b^{2}) = \operatorname{P}(\lvert X\rvert \le a, \lvert Y\rvert \le b)$ = double $\int (1+xy)/4$ over $[-a,a] x [-b,b]$.
The xy term is odd in x on a symmetric interval, so it integrates to 0; the remaining term gives $(1/4)(2a)(2b)$ = ab.

Also $\operatorname{P}(X^{2} \le a^{2}) = \operatorname{P}(\lvert X\rvert \le a) = a$ and $\operatorname{P}(Y^{2} \le b^{2}) = b$. Since ab = a x b, the joint CDF of $(X^{2}, Y^{2})$ factorises, so $X^{2}$ and $Y^{2}$ ARE independent. Statement 2 is true.
Only statement 2 is correct, so option (b) is right.

topic: Mathematical Expectation & Conditional Expectation
subtopic: Mathematical Expectation & Conditional Expectation
stem: $X$ has p.d.f. $f(x)=2/x^3,\ x\ge1$ (and $0$ for $x<1$). Which is correct?
options: Mean exists but variance does not.
Variance exists but mean does not.
shortcut: A Pareto-type tail $f(x) \sim 2/x^{3}$ has $\operatorname{E}(X^{k})$ finite only when $k < 2$. So $k = 1$ (mean) converges, $k = 2$ (second moment) diverges: mean exists, variance does not.
tips: Tail rule to memorise: if f(x) behaves like $c/x^{a+1}$ for large x, then $\operatorname{E}(X^{k})$ exists exactly when $k < a$. Here $a = 2$, so only the first moment survives.
The integrand for the mean is $2/x^{2}$, which converges; for $\operatorname{E}(X^{2})$ it is $2/x$, whose integral is $\log x$ and diverges. Reduce the power first, integrate second.
Distributions with heavy polynomial tails (Pareto, Cauchy, t with low d.f.) are the standard vehicle for 'which moments exist' questions - expect one every couple of papers.
Variance cannot exist while the mean fails to, so option (d) is logically impossible and can be struck out before any integration.
solution: The density is $f(x) = 2/x^{3}$ for $x \ge 1$ and 0 otherwise. Check: $\int_{1}^{\infty} 2x^{-3}\,dx = [-x^{-2}]$ from 1 to $\infty = 1$, so f is a valid density.
Mean: $\operatorname{E}(X) = \int_{1}^{\infty} x (2/x^{3})\,dx = \int 2x^{-2}\,dx = [-2/x]$ from 1 to $\infty = 0 - (-2) = 2$. Finite, so the mean exists and equals 2.
Second moment: $\operatorname{E}(X^{2}) = \int_{1}^{\infty} x^{2} (2/x^{3})\,dx = \int_{1}^{\infty} 2/x\,dx = [2 \log x]$ from 1 to $\infty$, which diverges.
Since $\operatorname{E}(X^{2})$ is infinite, $\operatorname{Var}(X) = \operatorname{E}(X^{2}) - [\operatorname{E}(X)]^{2}$ does not exist.
Mean exists but variance does not, so option (b) is correct.

topic: Standard Discrete Distributions
subtopic: Standard Discrete Distributions
stem: $X\sim\text{Binomial}(n=13,p=0.3)$. 1. The mode of $X$ is $3$. 2. The distribution is negatively skewed.
shortcut: Mode of Bin(n,p) = floor($(n+1)p$) = floor(14 x 0.3) = floor(4.2) = 4, not 3. Skewness sign = sign of $(1-2p)$ = sign of $0.4 > 0$, so positively skewed, not negatively. Both statements fail.
tips: Mode formula: floor($(n+1)p$); if $(n+1)p$ is an integer there are two modes, $(n+1)p$ and $(n+1)p - 1$. Here 4.2 is not an integer, so the mode is unique at 4.
Binomial skewness = $(1 - 2p)/sqrt$(npq). Its sign depends only on p: $p < 0.5$ gives positive skew, $p > 0.5$ gives negative skew, $p = 0.5$ is symmetric. You never need to compute the value.
Common trap: using np = 3.9 and rounding to 3. The mean is 3.9 but the mode is 4 - mean and mode are not interchangeable for a skewed discrete law.
When both statements in $a 1/2$/both/neither item look 'nearly right', suspect (d). Examiners build these from two near-misses.
solution: Here X ~ Binomial($n = 13, p = 0.3$), so $q = 0.7$.

Statement 1 (mode): the mode is floor($(n+1)p$) = floor(14 x 0.3) = floor(4.2) = 4. Confirm by ratio: $\operatorname{P}(X=4)/\operatorname{P}(X=3) = [(n-3)/4](p/q) = (10/4)(3/7) = 30/28 > 1$, so $\operatorname{P}(X=4) > \operatorname{P}(X=3)$ and 3 is not the mode. Statement 1 is FALSE.
Statement 2 (skewness): for the binomial, the coefficient of skewness is $(1 - 2p)/sqrt$(npq) = $(1 - 0.6)/\sqrt{13 \times 0.3 \times 0.7} = 0.4/\sqrt{2.73}$ = +0.242.
The skewness is positive, so the distribution is positively skewed, not negatively skewed. Statement 2 is FALSE.
Neither statement is correct, so option (d) is right.

topic: Distributions of Functions of Random Variables
subtopic: Distributions of Functions of Random Variables
stem: If $X\sim N(4,100)$, the distribution of $Y=\dfrac12\left(\dfrac{X-4}{10}\right)^2$ is
shortcut: $(X-4)/10 = Z \sim N(0,1)$, so $Z^{2} \sim \chi^{2}_{1} = \Gamma$(shape $1/2$, scale 2). Halving $a \Gamma$ scales the scale parameter to 1, leaving $\Gamma$ with parameter $1/2$ - option (c), not the $\chi^{2}$ in option (b).
tips: The factor $1/2$ is the whole question. $Z^{2}$ is $\chi^{2}_{1}$; $Z^{2}/2$ is NOT, because $\chi^{2}$ has a fixed scale of 2. Read the coefficient before answering.
Standard identity: $\chi^{2}_{v} = \Gamma$(shape $v/2$, scale 2). Dividing by 2 gives $\Gamma$(shape $v/2$, scale 1), the 'Gamma with parameter $v/2'$ of Indian textbook notation.
Variance 100 means $\sigma = 10$, so the standardising divisor is 10 and not 100. Mis-standardising is the second trap here.
Option (b) is the answer to the question the examiner did NOT ask - it is correct for $Y = Z^{2}$. Distinguishing (b) from (c) is precisely the discrimination being tested.
solution: $X \sim N(4, 100)$ means mean 4 and variance 100, so the standard deviation is 10 and $Z = (X - 4)/10 \sim N(0, 1)$.
The statistic is $Y = (1/2) Z^{2}$.
It is standard that $Z^{2} \sim \chi^{2}$ with 1 degree of freedom, and $\chi^{2}_{1}$ is the same as $\Gamma$(shape $1/2$, scale 2).
If $W \sim \Gamma$(shape a, scale b) then cW ~ $\Gamma$(shape a, scale cb). With $c = 1/2$ and $b = 2, Y = Z^{2}/2 \sim \Gamma$(shape $1/2$, scale 1).
Direct check: the density of Y is $f(y) = y^{-1/2} e^{-y}/\Gamma(1/2)$ for $y > 0$, which is exactly the standard $\Gamma$ density with parameter $1/2$.
Hence Y follows $a \Gamma$ distribution with parameter $1/2$, option (c).

topic: Distributions of Functions of Random Variables
subtopic: Distributions of Functions of Random Variables
stem: $X\sim G(\alpha_1,\beta)$, $Y\sim G(\alpha_2,\beta)$ independent. $\dfrac{X}{X+Y}$ is distributed as
shortcut: The $\Gamma$-Beta connection: for independent $G(a_{1},b)$ and $G(a_{2},b)$ with the SAME scale, $X/(X+Y)$ ~ Beta first kind $(a_{1}, a_{2})$, independent of the total X+Y. Read it straight off.
tips: Both Gammas must share the same scale parameter $\beta$ for this to hold - that is why the question states it. If the scales differed the ratio would not be Beta.
Companion results worth memorising together: $X + Y \sim G(a_{1} + a_{2}, b)$; X/Y ~ Beta second kind $(a_{1}, a_{2})$; and $X/(X+Y)$ is independent of X + Y.
Range check: $X/(X+Y)$ lies in $(0,1)$, which immediately rules out $(a) G(a_{1}+a_{2}, b)$ and $(d) G(a_{1},a_{2})$ since $\Gamma$ variables are unbounded above.
Option $(c) U(0,1)$ is only the special case $a_{1} = a_{2} = 1$, so it is too narrow to be the general answer.
solution: Let $X \sim \Gamma(a_{1}, b)$ and $Y \sim \Gamma(a_{2}, b)$ be independent, sharing the common scale parameter b.
Apply the transformation $U = X/(X+Y), V = X + Y$, so X = UV and $Y = \operatorname{V}(1-U)$. The Jacobian of the transformation is V.
The joint density becomes proportional to $[ (uv)^{a1-1} (v(1-u))^{a2-1} e^{-v/b} ] v = [ u^{a1-1} (1-u)^{a2-1} ] [ v^{a1+a_{2}-1} e^{-v/b} ]$.
This factorises into a function of u alone and a function of v alone, so U and V are independent.
The u-factor $u^{a1-1}(1-u)^{a2-1}$ on $(0,1)$ is exactly the Beta distribution of the first kind with parameters a1 and a2.
Hence $X/(X+Y)$ ~ Beta first kind $(a_{1}, a_{2})$, option (b).

topic: Standard Continuous Distributions
subtopic: Standard Continuous Distributions
stem: For $f(x)=\theta e^{-\theta x},\ x>0$: 1. Variance $>$ mean if $0<\theta<1$. 2. Variance $=$ mean if $\theta=1$. 3. Variance $<$ mean if $\theta>1$.
shortcut: For Exp($\theta$): mean = $1/\theta$, variance = $1/\theta^{2}$. Comparing $1/\theta^{2}$ with $1/\theta$ reduces to comparing $1/\theta$ with 1, i.e. comparing 1 with $\theta$. So all three statements are just $\theta < 1, \theta = 1, \theta > 1$ - all correct.
tips: $Var$/mean = $(1/\theta^{2})/(1/\theta) = 1/\theta$. The whole item collapses to 'is $1/\theta$ bigger, equal to, or smaller than 1?'.
Note that $\theta$ here is the RATE (the parameter in $\theta e^{-\theta x}$), not the mean. Mixing up rate and mean parameterisation inverts every inequality.

When three statements exhaustively cover $\theta < 1, \theta = 1$ and $\theta > 1$ and each is internally consistent, (d) 'all of them' is the natural answer - check one and the pattern usually confirms.
For any distribution, comparing mean and variance is fastest via the ratio (the index of dispersion), not by subtracting.
solution: For the exponential density $f(x) = \theta e^{-\theta x}, x > 0$, the mean is $\operatorname{E}(X) = 1/\theta$ and the variance is $\operatorname{Var}(X) = 1/\theta^{2}$.
Form the ratio $\operatorname{Var}(X)/\operatorname{E}(X) = (1/\theta^{2})/(1/\theta) = 1/\theta$.
Statement 1: variance > mean means $1/\theta > 1$, i.e. $\theta < 1$. Combined with $\theta > 0$ this is exactly $0 < \theta < 1$. TRUE.
Statement 2: variance = mean means $1/\theta = 1$, i.e. $\theta = 1$ (both equal 1). TRUE.
Statement 3: variance < mean means $1/\theta < 1$, i.e. $\theta > 1$. TRUE.
All three statements are correct, so option (d) is right.

topic: Mathematical Expectation & Conditional Expectation
subtopic: Mathematical Expectation & Conditional Expectation
stem: A rod of length $2l$ is broken at random into two pieces. The mean and variance of the length of the shorter piece are
shortcut: If the break point is U ~ Uniform(0, 2l), the shorter piece is $\min(U, 2l-U)$, which is Uniform(0, l). So mean = $l/2$ and variance = $l^{2}/12$ straight from the uniform formulas.
tips: Key insight: the minimum of U and 2l - U for U uniform on $(0,2l)$ is again uniform, on $(0,l)$. Prove it once, then reuse it - this 'broken rod' set-up recurs constantly.
Uniform(0,a) has mean $a/2$ and variance $a^{2}/12$. With $a = l$ that is $l/2$ and $l^{2}/12$ - no integration required.
The mean must be less than l (the shorter piece can never exceed half the rod), which kills options (b) and (d) immediately.
Variance $l^{2}/3$ in option (a) is the variance of Uniform(0, 2l) (namely $4l^{2}/12$), the value you get if you forget to take the shorter piece.
solution: Let the rod occupy the interval $(0, 2l)$ and let U, the break point, be uniformly distributed on $(0, 2l)$, so $f_{U}(u) = 1/(2l)$.
The two pieces have lengths U and 2l - U. The shorter piece is $S = \min(U, 2l - U)$, which takes values in $(0, l)$.
For $0 < s < l, \operatorname{P}(S \le s) = \operatorname{P}(U \le s) + \operatorname{P}(U \ge 2l - s) = s/(2l) + s/(2l) = s/l$.
That is the CDF of a Uniform(0, l) variable, so $S \sim U(0, l)$ with density $1/l$ on $(0, l)$.
Hence $\operatorname{E}(S) = l/2$ and $\operatorname{Var}(S) = l^{2}/12$.
So the mean and variance are $l/2$ and $l^{2}/12$, option (c).

topic: Random Vectors: Joint, Marginal & Conditional Distributions
subtopic: Random Vectors: Joint, Marginal & Conditional Distributions
stem: The joint distribution function of $X,Y$ is $F(x,y)=(1-e^{-x})(1-e^{-y})$ for $x,y>0$ (else $0$). What is $P(|X-Y|\le10)$?
shortcut: The joint CDF factorises into $(1-e^{-x})(1-e^{-y})$, so X and Y are i.i.d. Exp(1). For i.i.d. exponentials, |X - Y| is again Exp(1) by memorylessness, so $\operatorname{P}(\lvert X-Y\rvert \le 10) = 1 - e^{-10}$.
tips: A factorised joint CDF is the fastest possible independence certificate - no integration, no marginals.
Memorise: for i.i.d. Exp($\lambda$), the absolute difference |X - Y| ~ Exp($\lambda$). This turns a two-dimensional integral into a one-line lookup.
Intuition for that fact: condition on which variable is smaller; by the lack-of-memory property the excess of the larger over the smaller is again Exp($\lambda$).
Option (b) is what you get if you forget to double the two symmetric regions $X > Y$ and $Y > X$; option (c) mishandles the complement.
solution: The joint CDF $F(x,y) = (1 - e^{-x})(1 - e^{-y})$ for $x, y > 0$ factorises as $F_{X}(x) F_{Y}(y)$, so X and Y are independent, each Exponential with mean 1.
Let D = |X - Y|. For $d > 0, \operatorname{P}(D > d) = \operatorname{P}(X - Y > d) + \operatorname{P}(Y - X > d)$, and by symmetry this equals $2 \operatorname{P}(X - Y > d)$.
$\operatorname{P}(X - Y > d) = \int e^{-y} \operatorname{P}(X > y + d)\,dy = \int e^{-y} e^(-(y+d))\,dy = e^{-d} \int e^{-2y}\,dy = e^{-d}/2$.
Therefore $\operatorname{P}(D > d) = 2 x e^{-d}/2 = e^{-d}$, i.e. |X - Y| ~ Exponential(1).
Putting $d = 10$ gives $\operatorname{P}(\lvert X - Y\rvert > 10) = e^{-10}$, so $\operatorname{P}(\lvert X - Y\rvert \le 10) = 1 - e^{-10}$.
Hence option (a) is correct.

topic: Random Vectors: Joint, Marginal & Conditional Distributions
subtopic: Random Vectors: Joint, Marginal & Conditional Distributions
stem: $X,Y$ have joint p.d.f. $f(x,y)=2e^{-x}e^{-2y},\ 0<x,y<\infty$. What is $P(X<Y)$?
shortcut: The density factorises: X ~ Exp(rate 1), Y ~ Exp(rate 2), independent. For independent exponentials, $\operatorname{P}(X < Y)$ = rate_X/(rate_X + rate_Y) = $1/(1+2) = 1/3$.
tips: Memorise the competing-risks formula $\operatorname{P}(X < Y) = \lambda_{X}/(\lambda_{X} + \lambda_{Y})$ for independent exponentials. It converts this whole question into one division.
Read the rates off the exponents, not off the constants: $e^{-x}$ gives rate 1 and $e^{-2y}$ gives rate 2; the leading 2 is only the normalising constant.
Sanity check: Y has the larger rate, so Y is stochastically smaller and $X < Y$ should have probability less than $1/2$. That alone eliminates $(b) 1/2$.
The same formula answers 'which component fails first' reliability questions, a recurring ISS theme.
solution: The joint density $f(x,y) = 2 e^{-x} e^{-2y}$ on $x, y > 0$ factorises into $g(x) = e^{-x}$ and $h(y) = 2 e^{-2y}$, so X ~ Exp(1) and Y ~ Exp(2) independently.
$\operatorname{P}(X < Y) = \int f_{Y}(y) \operatorname{P}(X < y)\,dy$.
Now $\operatorname{P}(X < y) = 1 - e^{-y}$, so the integral is the $\int_{0}^{\infty} 2 e^{-2y} (1 - e^{-y})\,dy = \int 2e^{-2y}\,dy - \int 2e^{-3y}\,dy = 1 - 2/3 = 1/3$.
This agrees with the general rule $\operatorname{P}(X<Y) = \lambda_{X}/(\lambda_{X} + \lambda_{Y}) = 1/(1+2) = 1/3$.
Hence option (a) is correct.

topic: Mathematical Expectation & Conditional Expectation
subtopic: Mathematical Expectation & Conditional Expectation
stem: $X,Y$ have joint p.d.f. $f(x,y)=\dfrac13(x+y),\ 0<x<1,\ 0<y<2$. What is $E[3X(X+2Y)]$?
shortcut: Expand first: $\operatorname{E}[3X(X+2Y)] = 3\operatorname{E}(X^{2}) + 6\operatorname{E}(XY)$. With $f = (x+y)/3$ on $(0,1)x(0,2), \operatorname{E}(X^{2}) = 7/18$ and $\operatorname{E}(XY) = 2/3$, so the value is $7/6 + 4 = 31/6$.
tips: Always expand the bracket by linearity before integrating. Integrating $3x(x + 2y)$ directly is the same work but far more error-prone.
Normalisation check takes five seconds here: the double $\int (x+y)/3$ over the rectangle is $(1/3)(1 + 2) = 1$, so the density is valid and your set-up is right.
Integrate over y first (its range 0 to 2 is the wider one); the inner $\int (x + y)\,dy$ from 0 to 2 is 2x + 2, which is clean to carry forward.
The answer exceeds 4 because the 6E(XY) term alone contributes 4 - use that to eliminate any option below 4 at a glance.
solution: The density is $f(x,y) = (x + y)/3$ on $0 < x < 1, 0 < y < 2$. Check: $\int (x+y)/3\,dy$ from 0 to $2 = (2x + 2)/3$, and integrating that over x from 0 to 1 gives $(1 + 2)/3 = 1$. Valid density.
By linearity, $\operatorname{E}[3X(X + 2Y)] = 3 \operatorname{E}(X^{2}) + 6 \operatorname{E}(XY)$.
$\operatorname{E}(XY) = (1/3) \int_{0}^{1} x [ \int_{0}^{2} y(x + y)\,dy ]\,dx$. The inner integral is $[xy^{2}/2 + y^{3}/3]$ from 0 to $2 = 2x + 8/3$.

topic: Random Vectors: Joint, Marginal & Conditional Distributions
subtopic: Random Vectors: Joint, Marginal & Conditional Distributions
shortcut: A single zero cell settles independence: $\operatorname{P}(X=0, Y=1) = 0$ but $\operatorname{P}(X=0)\operatorname{P}(Y=1) = (1/3)(1/3)$ is non-zero, so they are dependent. $\operatorname{E}(X) = 0$ by symmetry and $\operatorname{E}(XY) = 1/6 - 1/6 - 1/6 + 1/6 = 0$, so $Cov = 0$. Only statement 2 holds.
tips: To DISPROVE independence, hunt for a zero entry whose marginal product is non-zero. It is a one-cell check and never requires the full table.
This is the textbook 'uncorrelated but dependent' table - the standard counterexample to 'zero covariance implies independence'.
Because X is symmetric about 0 with $\operatorname{E}(X) = 0, \operatorname{Cov}(X,Y) = \operatorname{E}(XY)$ alone; you can skip computing E(Y) entirely.
Marginals here are X: $1/3, 1/3, 1/3$ and Y: $2/3, 0, 1/3$. Compute marginals once and reuse them for both statements.
solution: Row sums give the marginal of Y: $\operatorname{P}(Y=-1) = 1/6 + 1/3 + 1/6 = 2/3, \operatorname{P}(Y=0) = 0, \operatorname{P}(Y=1) = 1/6 + 0 + 1/6 = 1/3$.

Column sums give the marginal of X: $\operatorname{P}(X=-1) = 1/6 + 0 + 1/6 = 1/3, \operatorname{P}(X=0) = 1/3 + 0 + 0 = 1/3, \operatorname{P}(X=1) = 1/6 + 0 + 1/6 = 1/3$. The grand total is 1, so the table is consistent.

Statement 1: $\operatorname{P}(X = 0, Y = 1) = 0$ from the table, but $\operatorname{P}(X=0) \operatorname{P}(Y=1) = (1/3)(1/3) = 1/9$, which is not 0. Hence X and Y are NOT independent; statement 1 is false.
So $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y) = \operatorname{E}(XY) - \operatorname{E}(X)\operatorname{E}(Y) = 0 - 0 = 0$; statement 2 is true. Only statement 2 holds, option (b).

topic: Mathematical Expectation & Conditional Expectation
subtopic: Mathematical Expectation & Conditional Expectation
stem: $X$ has p.d.f. $f(x)=1+x$ for $-1<x\le0$; $1-x$ for $0<x<1$ (else $0$). $U=X,\ V=X^2$. 1. $\text{Cov}(U,V)=0$. 2. $U,V$ are independent.
shortcut: The density is the symmetric triangular law on $(-1,1)$, so all odd moments vanish: $\operatorname{Cov}(X, X^{2}) = \operatorname{E}(X^{3}) - \operatorname{E}(X)\operatorname{E}(X^{2}) = 0 - 0 = 0$. But $V = U^{2}$ is a function of U, so they cannot be independent. Statement 1 only.
tips: $V = X^{2}$ is a deterministic function of $U = X$. A non-degenerate variable is never independent of a non-constant function of itself - answer statement 2 without any computation.
Symmetry about 0 makes every odd moment zero. Spot the symmetry of f (it satisfies $f(-x) = f(x)$) and $\operatorname{E}(X) = \operatorname{E}(X^{3}) = 0$ follow instantly.

This is the mirror image of the previous item: there, zero covariance with dependence in a table; here, zero covariance with functional dependence. Both illustrate that $Cov = 0$ does not imply independence.
If you are ever tempted by 'both 1 and 2', remember that independence is strictly stronger than uncorrelatedness - never the other way round.
solution: The density $f(x) = 1 + x$ on (-1, 0] and 1 - x on $(0, 1)$ is the symmetric triangular density; it satisfies $f(-x) = f(x)$.
By symmetry every odd moment vanishes: $\operatorname{E}(X) = 0$ and $\operatorname{E}(X^{3}) = 0$.

Statement 1: $\operatorname{Cov}(U, V) = \operatorname{Cov}(X, X^{2}) = E$(X . $X^{2}$) - $\operatorname{E}(X) \operatorname{E}(X^{2}) = \operatorname{E}(X^{3}) - 0$ . $\operatorname{E}(X^{2}) = 0 - 0 = 0$. Statement 1 is TRUE.

Statement 2: $V = X^{2}$ is a (non-constant) deterministic function of $U = X$. For instance $\operatorname{P}(\lvert U\rvert < 1/2, V > 1/2) = 0$ while both marginal probabilities are strictly positive, so the joint law does not factorise.
Hence U and V are dependent and statement 2 is FALSE.
Only statement 1 is correct, so option (a) is right.

topic: Characteristic Function, MGF & PGF; Inversion, Uniqueness, Continuity
subtopic: Characteristic Function, MGF & PGF; Inversion, Uniqueness, Continuity
stem: $X,Y$ independent normal, means $10,5$, variances $9,4$. $Z=4X-5Y$. The MGF $M_Z(t)$ is
shortcut: $Z = 4X - 5Y$ is normal with mean $4(10) - 5(5) = 15$ and variance $16(9) + 25(4) = 244$. The normal MGF is $\exp(mt + s^{2} t^{2}/2) = \exp(15t + 122 t^{2})$. Note the variance ADDS even though the coefficient is negative.
tips: $\operatorname{Var}(aX - bY) = a^{2} \operatorname{Var}(X) + b^{2} \operatorname{Var}(Y)$ for independent X, Y - the minus sign disappears when squared. Options (b) and (d) with a negative $t^{2}$ coefficient are impossible for any MGF.
The MGF exponent carries $\sigma^{2}/2$, not $\sigma^{2}$. Here $244/2 = 122$, which separates (c) from the 22 in option (a).
Option $(a)'s 22$ comes from $4(9) - 5(4) x$ ... i.e. from adding variances without squaring the coefficients - the single most common slip in this family.
A linear combination of independent normals is always normal, so you only ever need its mean and variance; never attempt a convolution integral.
solution: $X \sim N(10, 9)$ and $Y \sim N(5, 4)$ are independent, so $Z = 4X - 5Y$ is normally distributed.
Mean: $\operatorname{E}(Z) = 4 \operatorname{E}(X) - 5 \operatorname{E}(Y) = 4(10) - 5(5) = 40 - 25 = 15$.
Variance: $\operatorname{Var}(Z) = 4^{2} \operatorname{Var}(X) + (-5)^{2} \operatorname{Var}(Y) = 16(9) + 25(4) = 144 + 100 = 244$.
The MGF of $a N(\mu, \sigma^{2})$ variable is $M(t) = \exp(\mu t + \sigma^{2} t^{2} / 2)$.
Substituting $\mu = 15$ and $\sigma^{2} = 244$ gives $M_{Z}(t) = \exp(15t + 244 t^{2}/2) = \exp(15t + 122 t^{2})$.
Hence option (c) is correct.

topic: Characteristic Function, MGF & PGF; Inversion, Uniqueness, Continuity
subtopic: Characteristic Function, MGF & PGF; Inversion, Uniqueness, Continuity
stem: A fair die is thrown repeatedly until $3$ or $4$ appears. $X$ = number of throws. The p.g.f. of $X$ for $|s|<3/2$ is
shortcut: Success = 'a 3 or $a 4'$ has $p = 2/6 = 1/3$, so X is geometric on {1,2,3,...}. Its PGF is ps/$(1 - qs) = (s/3)/(1 - 2s/3) = s/(3 - 2s)$.
tips: Memorise the two geometric PGFs and keep them apart: counting TRIALS (support 1,2,3,...) gives ps/$(1-qs)$; counting FAILURES (support 0,1,2,...) gives $p/(1-qs)$.
Radius-of-convergence check: $1 - qs = 0$ at $s = 1/q = 3/2$, which matches the stated |s| < $3/2$. That single check confirms $q = 2/3$ and eliminates option (a), whose pole is at $s = 3$.
Every PGF must satisfy $\operatorname{P}(1) = 1$. Testing $s = 1$: option (b) gives $1/(3-2) = 1$ (valid); option (a) gives $2/2 = 1$ as well, so use the pole test to separate them.
Options (c) and (d) are reciprocals of the first two and blow up at $s = 0$, so they are not PGFs at all - strike them immediately.
solution: A 'success' is the appearance of a 3 or a 4, so $p = 2/6 = 1/3$ and $q = 1 - p = 2/3$.
X is the number of throws required for the first success, so X takes values 1, 2, 3, ... with $\operatorname{P}(X = k) = q^{k-1} p$.
The probability generating function is $\operatorname{P}(s) = \operatorname{E}(s^{X}) = \sum q^{k-1} p s^{k}$ = ps $\sum (qs)^{k-1}$ = ps/$(1 - qs)$, valid for |qs| < 1.
Substituting $p = 1/3$ and $q = 2/3$: $\operatorname{P}(s) = (s/3)/(1 - 2s/3)$.
Multiplying numerator and denominator by 3: $\operatorname{P}(s) = s/(3 - 2s)$.
The condition |qs| < 1 becomes |s| < $3/2$, exactly as stated. Hence option (b) is correct.

topic: Tchebycheff's & Kolmogorov's Inequalities
subtopic: Tchebycheff's & Kolmogorov's Inequalities
stem: Weekly automobile sales have $E=16$, $\text{Var}=9$. The probability that next week's sales are between 10 and 22 is at least
shortcut: The interval 10 to 22 is centred at the mean 16 with half-width 6, and $\sigma = 3$, so the half-width is exactly $k = 2$ standard deviations. Chebyshev gives at least $1 - 1/k^{2} = 1 - 1/4 = 0.75$.
tips: Chebyshev's inequality: $\operatorname{P}(\lvert X - \mu\rvert < k \sigma) \ge 1 - 1/k^{2}$. The words 'at least' in the stem are the signal to use it rather than a normal table.
Always find k as (half-width)/$\sigma$. Here $(22 - 16)/3 = 2$ and $(16 - 10)/3 = 2$ - the interval is symmetric, which is required for the standard form.
0.75 is the $k = 2$ bound and is worth memorising along with $k = 3$ giving $8/9 = 0.889$ and $k = 1.5$ giving $5/9 = 0.556$.
Do NOT use the normal 95% figure: option (d) 0.95 is the planted trap for candidates who assume normality where none is given.
solution: Let X be next week's sales, with $\mu = \operatorname{E}(X) = 16$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X) = 9$, so $\sigma = 3$.
The event is $10 < X < 22$, that is |X - 16| < 6.
Write the half-width as a multiple of $\sigma$: $6 = k \sigma = 3k$, so $k = 2$.
Chebyshev's inequality states $\operatorname{P}(\lvert X - \mu\rvert < k \sigma) \ge 1 - 1/k^{2}$.
With $k = 2$ this gives $\operatorname{P}(10 < X < 22) \ge 1 - 1/4 = 3/4 = 0.75$.
Hence the probability is at least 0.75, option (c).

topic: Distributions of Functions of Random Variables
subtopic: Distributions of Functions of Random Variables
stem: $X$ has p.d.f. $f(x)=\dfrac{kx^3}{(1+2x)^6},\ x>0$. $Y=\dfrac{2X}{1+2X}$ is a Beta distribution of the first kind with parameters:
shortcut: Substitute $y = 2x/(1+2x)$, so $1 + 2x = 1/(1-y)$ and $x = y/(2(1-y))$. The density picks up $x^{3} (1+2x)^{-6} \mid dx/dy$| ~ $y^{3} (1-y)^{1}$, i.e. Beta(4, 2). So $m = 4, n = 2$.
tips: Match exponents at the end: $y^{m-1}(1-y)^{n-1} = y^{3} (1-y)^{1}$ gives $m = 4$ and $n = 2$ by inspection. Never integrate to identify a Beta.
The transformation $y = 2x/(1+2x)$ is the standard Beta-second-kind to Beta-first-kind map; its inverse relation $1 - y = 1/(1+2x)$ is the piece that does all the work.
Check the parameter total: a density of the form $x^{m-1}/(1+2x)^{m+n}$ transforms to Beta(m,n). Here the exponent $6 = m + n$ and the numerator power $3 = m - 1$, giving $m = 4, n = 2$ in one line.
Do not forget the Jacobian $dx/dy = 1/(2(1-y)^{2})$ - omitting it changes n from 2 to 4 and lands you on a wrong option.
solution: Let $Y = 2X/(1 + 2X)$. Then $1 - Y = 1/(1 + 2X)$, so $1 + 2X = 1/(1 - Y)$ and $X = Y/(2(1 - Y))$, with Y in $(0,1)$ as X ranges over $(0, \infty)$.
Differentiating, $dx/dy = 1/(2(1 - y)^{2})$.
Comparing with the Beta first kind density proportional to $y^{m-1}(1-y)^{n-1}$: $m - 1 = 3$ and $n - 1 = 1$, so $m = 4$ and $n = 2$, option (a).

topic: Collection, Compilation & Presentation of Data; Frequency Distributions
subtopic: Collection, Compilation & Presentation of Data; Frequency Distributions
stem: Consider the following statements: 1. The weight of a strawberry box is measured on an interval scale. 2. The number of students admitted to each IIM in 2007 is cross-sectional data. 3. Barcodes for items in a departmental store are measured on a nominal scale.
shortcut: Weight has a true zero and meaningful ratios, so it is RATIO scale, not interval - statement 1 fails. Statements 2 and 3 are textbook-correct, so the answer is 2 and 3 only.
tips: Scale ladder: nominal (labels) < ordinal (ranks) < interval (equal gaps, arbitrary zero) < ratio (true zero). Weight, length, income and counts are ratio; temperature in Celsius and calendar dates are interval.
The single discriminator for interval vs ratio is 'is zero meaningful?'. Zero weight means no weight, so weight is ratio.
Cross-sectional = many units at ONE time point; time series = one unit over MANY time points; panel = both. 'Each IIM in $2007'$ is many units, one year, so cross-sectional.
Barcodes, PIN codes, jersey numbers and Aadhaar numbers are all nominal even though they look numeric - arithmetic on them is meaningless.
solution: Statement 1: the weight of a strawberry box is a physical measurement with an absolute zero point, and ratios such as 'twice as heavy' are meaningful. That is the definition of a RATIO scale, not an interval scale. FALSE.
Statement 2: the number of students admitted to each IIM in 2007 records many different units (the IIMs) at a single point in time. That is cross-sectional data. TRUE.
Statement 3: a barcode is only an identifying label; the numbers cannot be ordered or added meaningfully, so the measurement is on a nominal scale. TRUE.
Only statements 2 and 3 are correct, so option (c) is right.

topic: Correlation: Distribution of r, Partial, Multiple, Intraclass, Correlation Ratio
subtopic: Correlation: Distribution of r, Partial, Multiple, Intraclass, Correlation Ratio
stem: The minimum value of $\text{Var}(Y-aX)$ over all $a$ is
shortcut: $\operatorname{Var}(Y - aX)$ is a quadratic in a; minimising it is exactly least squares. The minimum is the residual variance of the regression of Y on X, which is $\operatorname{Var}(Y)(1 - \rho^{2})$.
tips: Remember the identity: minimum residual variance = $(1 - \rho^{2}) x \operatorname{Var}(Y)$. The factor $(1 - \rho^{2})$ is the proportion of variance NOT explained; $\rho^{2}$ is the proportion explained.
Dimensional check kills two options instantly: the answer must have the units of $\operatorname{Var}(Y)$. Options (a) and (b) are ratios of variances and are dimensionally wrong.
The minimising value is $a = \operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)/\operatorname{Var}(X)$, which is precisely the regression coefficient $b_{YX}$ - the question is least squares in disguise.
If $\rho = 0$ the minimum must equal $\operatorname{Var}(Y)$ (X is useless); if $\rho$ = +-1 it must be 0. Only option (d) satisfies both limits.
solution: Write $g(a) = \operatorname{Var}(Y - aX) = \operatorname{Var}(Y) - 2a \operatorname{Cov}(X,Y) + a^{2} \operatorname{Var}(X)$. This is an upward parabola in a.
Setting $g'(a)$ = -$2 \operatorname{Cov}(X,Y) + 2a \operatorname{Var}(X) = 0$ gives the minimising value a* = $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)/\operatorname{Var}(X)$.
Substituting back: $g(a*) = \operatorname{Var}(Y) - [\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)]^{2}/\operatorname{Var}(X)$.

Since $\rho = \operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)/(sd(X) sd(Y))$, we have $[\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)]^{2} = \rho^{2} \operatorname{Var}(X) \operatorname{Var}(Y)$, so $[\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)]^{2}/\operatorname{Var}(X) = \rho^{2} \operatorname{Var}(Y)$.
Therefore the minimum value is $\operatorname{Var}(Y) - \rho^{2} \operatorname{Var}(Y) = (1 - \rho^{2}) \operatorname{Var}(Y)$.
Hence option (d) is correct.

topic: Skewness & Kurtosis (Moments)
subtopic: Skewness & Kurtosis (Moments)
stem: For a frequency distribution: Mean $=62$, Median $=65$, Coefficient of skewness $=-0.3$. The standard deviation is
shortcut: Use the empirical (median) form of Pearson's skewness: Sk = 3(Mean - Median)/SD. So -$0.3 = 3(62 - 65)$/SD = -9/SD, giving SD = 30.
tips: Two forms of Pearson's coefficient: (Mean - Mode)/SD and 3(Mean - Median)/SD. When the MEDIAN is supplied, the factor 3 is compulsory - dropping it gives SD = 10, which is planted as option (a).
The sign works out automatically: mean below median gives a negative numerator and hence negative skewness, consistent with the given -0.3.
The relation comes from the empirical mode formula Mode = 3 Median - 2 Mean, which is worth memorising in its own right.
Sanity check the magnitude: |Mean - Median| = 3 and the coefficient is small $(0.3)$, so the SD must be an order of magnitude larger than 3 - that alone points to 30.
solution: Pearson's coefficient of skewness in its median form is Sk = 3(Mean - Median)/SD.
Substitute the given values: -$0.3 = 3(62 - 65)$/SD.
The numerator is $3 x (-3)$ = -9, so -0.3 = -9/SD.
Hence the standard deviation is 30, option (b).

topic: Bivariate & Multivariate Data; Association & Contingency
subtopic: Bivariate & Multivariate Data; Association & Contingency
stem: Smoking habits (father, son): 1. Father smoker, son smoker: 50 2. Father smoker, son not: 10 3. Father not, son smoker: 10 4. Neither smoker: 30 The coefficient of association between smoking habits of father and son is
tips: Yule's coefficient of association $Q = (ad - bc)/(ad + bc)$ always lies between -1 and +1; it is 0 exactly when ad = bc, i.e. under independence.

Set the 2x2 table out as a = both present, b and c = one present, d = both absent. Here the diagonal product ad = 1500 dominates the off-diagonal bc = 100, so the association must be strongly POSITIVE - that alone eliminates (c).
Do not confuse Yule's Q with the coefficient of colligation $Y = (\sqrt{ad} - \sqrt{bc})/(\sqrt{ad} + \sqrt{bc})$, which would give a different value here.
Sons of smokers smoking 50:10 while sons of non-smokers smoke 10:30 is a clear positive association - a quick common-sense check on the sign before computing.
solution: Arrange the 2x2 contingency table: $(AB) = 50$ (both smoke), $(A \beta) = 10$ (father smokes, son does not), $(\alpha B) = 10$ (father does not, son does), $(\alpha \beta) = 30$ (neither smokes).
Yule's coefficient of association is $Q = [(AB)(\alpha \beta) - (A \beta)(\alpha B)] / [(AB)(\alpha \beta) + (A \beta)(\alpha B)]$.
Diagonal product: $(AB)(\alpha \beta) = 50 \times 30 = 1500$.
Off-diagonal product: $(A \beta)(\alpha B) = 10 \times 10 = 100$.
The value is positive and close to 1, indicating strong positive association. Option (b) is correct.

topic: Bivariate & Multivariate Data; Association & Contingency
subtopic: Bivariate & Multivariate Data; Association & Contingency
stem: Consider the following statements: 1. Attributes $A,B$ are positively associated if the presence of $A$ is accompanied by the presence of $B$. 2. $A,B$ are negatively associated if the presence of $A$ ensures the absence of $B$ or vice versa. 3. $A,B$ are independent if the presence/absence of one has a linear relationship with the other.
shortcut: Statements 1 and 2 are the standard verbal definitions of positive and negative association. Statement 3 misdefines independence as a 'linear relationship' - independence means NO relationship at all. So 1 and 2 only.
tips: Independence of attributes means $(AB) = (A)(B)/N$, i.e. the observed joint frequency equals the product of the marginals. Nothing about linearity is involved - linearity belongs to correlation of variables, not association of attributes.
The examiner's favourite trap in this chapter is importing correlation language (linear, positive, negative) into attribute theory. Read every option for that swap.
Association compares (AB) with $(A)(B)/N$: greater means positive association, smaller means negative association, equal means independence. Three cases, one formula.
Whenever one statement in a set is a definition that has been subtly reworded, that is almost always the false one - here statement 3.
solution: Two attributes A and B are said to be INDEPENDENT when $(AB) = (A)(B)/N$, where N is the total frequency.
Statement 1: A and B are positively associated when the presence of A tends to be accompanied by the presence of B, i.e. $(AB) > (A)(B)/N$. This is the standard verbal definition. TRUE.
Statement 2: A and B are negatively associated (disassociated) when the presence of one tends to exclude the other, i.e. $(AB) < (A)(B)/N$. TRUE.

Statement 3: independence is defined by the frequency identity above, not by any 'linear relationship'. Linearity is a concept of correlation between quantitative variables, not of association between attributes. FALSE.
Only statements 1 and 2 are correct, so option (b) is right.

topic: Regression - Linear & Polynomial
subtopic: Regression - Linear & Polynomial
stem: If the joint p.d.f. of $(X,Y)$ is $f(x,y)=\dfrac13x^2e^{-y(1+x)},\ x\ge0,y\ge0$, the regression equation of $Y$ on $X$ is
shortcut: Fix x and look at the y-part: f is proportional to $e^(-y(1+x))$, which is an Exponential with RATE $(1+x)$. Its mean is the reciprocal, so $\operatorname{E}(Y\mid X=x) = 1/(1+x)$.
tips: The regression of Y on X IS the conditional mean $\operatorname{E}(Y\mid X=x)$. Whenever the joint density factorises as $g(x) e^(-y h(x))$, the conditional law of Y is Exponential(h(x)) and the answer is $1/h(x)$ - one line, no integration.

Any multiplicative function of x alone (here $x^{2}/3$) is absorbed into the normalising constant of the conditional density and cannot appear in $\operatorname{E}(Y\mid X)$. That rules out options (b) and (d) at a glance.
Option $(c) y = 1 + x$ inverts the relationship: it is the RATE, not the mean. Reciprocal errors are the standard trap in exponential conditionals.

Note that the printed joint density is not normalisable over the stated range (the $x-\int x^{2}/(1+x)$ diverges), but the conditional distribution of Y given X - and hence the answer - is unaffected.
solution: The joint density is $f(x,y) = (1/3) x^{2} e^(-y(1+x))$ for $x \ge 0, y \ge 0$.
For a fixed value $X = x$, the conditional density of Y is $f(y\mid x) = f(x,y)/f_{X}(x)$, which is proportional to $e^(-y(1+x))$ for $y \ge 0$.
Normalising, $f(y\mid x) = (1 + x) e^(-y(1+x))$, which is the Exponential density with rate parameter $(1 + x)$.
The mean of an Exponential distribution with rate $\lambda$ is $1/\lambda$, so $\operatorname{E}(Y \mid X = x) = 1/(1 + x)$.
The regression of Y on X is the curve $y = \operatorname{E}(Y\mid X = x) = 1/(1 + x)$.
Hence option (a) is correct.

topic: Bivariate Normal Distribution
subtopic: Bivariate Normal Distribution
stem: Let $(X,Y)\sim BVN(\mu_1,\mu_2,\sigma_1^2,\sigma_2^2,\rho)$. 1. $X,Y$ are independent iff $\rho=0$. 2. Every linear combination of $X,Y$ is a normal variate. 3. The regressions of $Y$ on $X$ and $X$ on $Y$ are linear and homoscedastic.
shortcut: All three are standard properties of the bivariate normal: zero correlation gives independence, every linear combination is normal, and both regression lines are linear with constant (homoscedastic) conditional variance. Answer: all three.
tips: 'rho = 0 implies independence' is TRUE for the bivariate normal and FALSE in general - the examiner exploits this asymmetry constantly. Check whether normality is stated.
The conditional variance of Y given X is $\sigma_{2}^{2}(1 - \rho^{2})$, which does not depend on x. That constancy is exactly what homoscedasticity means.
The conditional mean is $\operatorname{E}(Y\mid X=x) = \mu_{2} + \rho (\sigma_{2}/\sigma_{1})(x - \mu_{1})$ - linear in x, which gives the linear regression property.
In $a 1/2/3$ item where every statement is a bookwork property of the same distribution, (d) 'all of them' is very often the key - but confirm the one you are least sure of, here statement 3.
solution: Statement 1: for the bivariate normal, the joint density factorises into the product of the two marginal normal densities precisely when $\rho = 0$. So independence holds if and only if $\rho = 0$. TRUE. (Note this equivalence is special to the normal; in general $\rho = 0$ does not imply independence.)
Statement 2: if (X,Y) is bivariate normal then aX + bY is univariate normal for all constants a, b - this is a defining property of the multivariate normal family. TRUE.
Statement 3: the conditional distribution of Y given $X = x$ is $N(\mu_{2} + \rho (\sigma_{2}/\sigma_{1})(x - \mu_{1}), \sigma_{2}^{2}(1 - \rho^{2}))$.

The conditional mean is linear in x, so the regression of Y on X is linear; the conditional variance $\sigma_{2}^{2}(1 - \rho^{2})$ is free of x, so the regression is homoscedastic. By symmetry the same holds for X on Y. TRUE.
All three statements are correct, so option (d) is right.

topic: Correlation: Distribution of r, Partial, Multiple, Intraclass, Correlation Ratio
subtopic: Correlation: Distribution of r, Partial, Multiple, Intraclass, Correlation Ratio
stem: The correlation between Maths and Statistics marks for 60 students is $0.65$. After Maths marks are all increased by 3, the correlation between original Statistics marks and revised Maths marks is
shortcut: Correlation is invariant under a change of origin. Adding 3 to every Maths mark shifts the origin only, so r is unchanged at 0.65.
tips: r is invariant under any change of origin and under a change of scale by a POSITIVE constant; multiplying by a negative constant flips only the sign, never the magnitude.
The sample size 60 is deliberately irrelevant here - the examiner adds it purely as a distraction.
Formally, $\operatorname{Cov}(X + c, Y) = \operatorname{Cov}(X, Y)$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X + c) = \operatorname{Var}(X)$, so every ingredient of r is unchanged.
Option (d) 'almost 1' punishes the belief that a systematic adjustment somehow strengthens the relationship - the scatter pattern is simply translated.
solution: Let X be Maths marks and Y be Statistics marks, with $r(X,Y) = 0.65$.
The revised Maths marks are $X' = X + 3, a$ pure change of origin.
Covariance is unaffected by a shift: $\operatorname{Cov}(X + 3, Y) = \operatorname{Cov}(X, Y)$.
Variance is also unaffected: $\operatorname{Var}(X + 3) = \operatorname{Var}(X)$, so sd(X') = sd(X).
Therefore $r(X', Y) = \operatorname{Cov}(X',Y)/(sd(X') sd(Y)) = \operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)/(sd(X) sd(Y)) = r(X,Y) = 0.65$.
Hence option (b) is correct.

topic: Correlation: Distribution of r, Partial, Multiple, Intraclass, Correlation Ratio
subtopic: Correlation: Distribution of r, Partial, Multiple, Intraclass, Correlation Ratio
stem: If the zero-order correlation coefficients among 3 variates all equal $\rho$, the multiple correlation $R^2_{1.23}$ equals
tips: Memorise $R^{2}_{1.23} = (r_{12}^{2} + r_{13}^{2} - 2 r_{12} r_{13} r_{23})/(1 - r_{23}^{2})$. Every multiple-correlation numerical in this paper reduces to it.
The cancellation of $(1 - \rho)$ is the whole trick; factor $1 - \rho^{2}$ as $(1-\rho)(1+\rho)$ before simplifying rather than after.

Check the limits: $\rho = 0$ must give $R^{2} = 0$ (option (b) gives 0, correct) and $\rho = 1$ must give $R^{2} = 1$ (option (b) gives $2/2 = 1$, correct). Option (c) fails the $\rho = 1$ test, giving $1/2$.
$R^{2}$ is a squared quantity, so a bare $\rho$ as in option (a) cannot be right on dimensional grounds.
solution: The square of the multiple correlation of X1 on X2, X3 is $R^{2}_{1.23} = (r_{12}^{2} + r_{13}^{2} - 2 r_{12} r_{13} r_{23})/(1 - r_{23}^{2})$.
All three zero-order correlations equal $\rho$, so $r_{12} = r_{13} = r_{23} = \rho$.
Numerator: $\rho^{2} + \rho^{2} - 2 \rho$ . $\rho$ . $\rho = 2\rho^{2} - 2\rho^{3} = 2\rho^{2} (1 - \rho)$.
Denominator: $1 - \rho^{2} = (1 - \rho)(1 + \rho)$.
Cancelling the common factor $(1 - \rho)$ gives $R^{2}_{1.23} = 2\rho^{2}/(1 + \rho)$.
Hence option (b) is correct.

topic: Correlation: Distribution of r, Partial, Multiple, Intraclass, Correlation Ratio
subtopic: Correlation: Distribution of r, Partial, Multiple, Intraclass, Correlation Ratio
stem: If $r$ is the correlation coefficient of a sample of $N$ independent observations from a bivariate normal population with true correlation zero, then $E(1-r^2)^{-1}$ is
shortcut: Under $\rho = 0$ the density of r is proportional to $(1 - r^{2})^((N-4)/2)$. Multiplying by $(1-r^{2})^{-1}$ lowers the exponent by one, so the expectation is a ratio of Beta functions that collapses to $(N-3)/(N-4)$.
tips: Null density to memorise: $f(r) = (1 - r^{2})^((N-4)/2) / B(1/2, (N-2)/2)$ on $(-1, 1)$. Almost every 'distribution of r when $\rho = 0'$ item is solved by shifting its exponent.
The standard integral is: integral over $(-1,1)$ of $(1 - r^{2})^{a-1}$ dr = $B(1/2, a)$. Recognising the integrand as a Beta kernel converts the whole problem into $\Gamma$-function algebra.
Use $\Gamma(z+1) = z \Gamma(z)$ and $\Gamma(z + 3/2) = (z + 1/2) \Gamma(z + 1/2)$ - after those two substitutions everything cancels except $(N-3)/(N-4)$.
Sanity check with large N: the answer must tend to 1 because r tends to 0 and $(1-r^{2})^{-1}$ tends to 1. Only options (a) and (d) do that, and (d) ignores N entirely.
solution: When the population correlation is zero, the density of the sample correlation coefficient based on N observations is $f(r) = (1 - r^{2})^((N-4)/2) / B(1/2, (N-2)/2)$, for -$1 < r < 1$.
Hence $\operatorname{E}[(1 - r^{2})^{-1}] = [1/B(1/2, (N-2)/2)]$ times the integral over $(-1,1)$ of $(1 - r^{2})^((N-6)/2)$ dr.
Using the standard result integral over $(-1,1)$ of $(1 - r^{2})^{a-1}$ dr = $B(1/2, a)$, with $a - 1 = (N-6)/2$ so that $a = (N-4)/2$, the integral equals $B(1/2, (N-4)/2)$.

Writing $B(1/2, a) = \Gamma(1/2)\Gamma(a)/\Gamma(a + 1/2)$ and putting $a_{1} = (N-4)/2, a_{2} = a_{1} + 1$, the ratio becomes $[\Gamma(a_{1}) \Gamma(a_{1} + 3/2)] / [\Gamma(a_{1} + 1/2) \Gamma(a_{1} + 1)]$.

topic: Correlation: Distribution of r, Partial, Multiple, Intraclass, Correlation Ratio
subtopic: Correlation: Distribution of r, Partial, Multiple, Intraclass, Correlation Ratio
stem: If $ax_1+bx_2+cx_3=0$ holds identically for all $x_1,x_2,x_3$, the partial correlation coefficient $r_{12.3}$ is
shortcut: An exact linear relation makes the two residuals proportional. From $a x_{1} + b x_{2} + c x_{3} = 0$ we get x1 = -$(b/a)x_{2} - (c/a)x_{3}$, so after removing x3 the residual of x1 is a NEGATIVE multiple of that of x2 (for a, b of the same sign), giving r12.3 = -1.
tips: Exact linear dependence always forces a partial correlation of magnitude 1 - so the real question is only the sign, and options (a) and (d) can be struck out at once.
Sign rule: r12.3 = -sign($b/a$). With the usual textbook convention that a, b, c are positive constants (as in the classic $x_{1} + x_{2} + x_{3} = 0$), the value is -1.
The formula r12.$3 = (r_{12} - r_{13} r_{23})/sqrt((1 - r_{13}^{2})(1 - r_{23}^{2}))$ also gives +-1 here, but the residual argument reaches the sign far faster.
Partial correlation removes the linear effect of x3 from BOTH variables; what remains is the pure x1-x2 link, which is deterministic here.
solution: The relation $a x_{1} + b x_{2} + c x_{3} = 0$ holds identically, so the three variables are exactly linearly dependent.
Solve for x1: x1 = -$(b/a) x_{2} - (c/a) x_{3}$.
Regress each of x1 and x2 on x3 and take residuals. Because the relation above is exact, the residual of x1 after removing x3 equals -$(b/a)$ times the residual of x2 after removing x3.
A residual pair related by an exact multiplicative constant has correlation +1 if the constant is positive and -1 if it is negative.
Here the constant is -$(b/a)$, which is negative when a and b have the same sign - the standard convention in this classical result (e.g. the case $x_{1} + x_{2} + x_{3} = 0$).
Hence r12.3 = -1, option (c). (If a and b had opposite signs the value would be +1; the magnitude is always 1.)

topic: Correlation: Distribution of r, Partial, Multiple, Intraclass, Correlation Ratio
subtopic: Correlation: Distribution of r, Partial, Multiple, Intraclass, Correlation Ratio
stem: $X_1,X_2,X_3,X_4$ are four uncorrelated random variables, each with variance $\sigma^2$. What is the correlation between $U=X_1+X_2+X_3$ and $V=X_1+X_2+X_4$?
shortcut: U and V share X1 and X2. $\operatorname{Cov}(U,V) = \operatorname{Var}(X_{1}) + \operatorname{Var}(X_{2}) = 2 \sigma^{2}$, while $\operatorname{Var}(U) = \operatorname{Var}(V) = 3 \sigma^{2}$. So $r = 2 \sigma^{2}/(3 \sigma^{2}) = 2/3$.
tips: For sums of uncorrelated variables with a common variance, the correlation is simply (number of SHARED terms)/sqrt(count in U x count in V). Here $2/\sqrt{3 \times 3} = 2/3$.
Uncorrelated cross terms vanish, so the covariance counts only the overlap - never expand all nine products.
$\sigma^{2}$ cancels completely, which is why the answer is a pure number; if your working leaves $a \sigma$ you have slipped.
Extreme checks: no shared terms would give 0 and complete overlap would give 1, so a two-out-of-three overlap must land strictly between - eliminating (a) and (b).
solution: X1, X2, X3, X4 are uncorrelated, each with variance $\sigma^{2}$, so all cross-covariances are 0.
$\operatorname{Var}(U) = \operatorname{Var}(X_{1} + X_{2} + X_{3}) = 3 \sigma^{2}$, and similarly $\operatorname{Var}(V) = \operatorname{Var}(X_{1} + X_{2} + X_{4}) = 3 \sigma^{2}$.
$\operatorname{Cov}(U, V) = \operatorname{Cov}(X_{1} + X_{2} + X_{3}, X_{1} + X_{2} + X_{4})$. Every cross term between distinct variables is 0, so only the shared variables contribute.
$\operatorname{Cov}(U, V) = \operatorname{Var}(X_{1}) + \operatorname{Var}(X_{2}) = \sigma^{2} + \sigma^{2} = 2 \sigma^{2}$.
Therefore $r(U, V) = 2 \sigma^{2} / sqrt$($3 \sigma^{2}$ . $3 \sigma^{2}$) = $2 \sigma^{2}/(3 \sigma^{2}) = 2/3$.
Hence option (d) is correct.

topic: Laws of Large Numbers & Central Limit Theorems
subtopic: Laws of Large Numbers & Central Limit Theorems
stem: $(X_1,\ldots,X_n)$ is a random sample of size $n$ from $U[-3,3]$. The large-sample distribution of $\sqrt n\,\bar X$ is
shortcut: For $U[-3,3]$, mean = 0 and variance = $(6)^{2}/12 = 3$. By the CLT, $\sqrt{n} (\bar{X} - \mu)$ converges to $N(0, \sigma^{2}) = N(0, 3)$. No division by $\sigma$ appears, so the variance stays 3.
tips: Variance of U[a,b] is $(b-a)^{2}/12$. Here $(3 - (-3))^{2}/12 = 36/12 = 3$ - compute this before anything else.

Distinguish the two CLT forms: $\sqrt{n} \bar{X} / \sigma$ tends to $N(0,1)$ whereas $\sqrt{n} \bar{X}$ tends to $N(0, \sigma^{2})$. The stem has no $\sigma$ in the denominator, so option (b) not (a).
The limit is NORMAL, never uniform - the CLT destroys the parent shape. Options (c) and (d) are eliminated on principle without any arithmetic.
The mean of $U[-a,a]$ is 0 by symmetry, which is why the limiting mean is 0 and no centring constant is needed.
solution: For the Uniform distribution on $[-3, 3]$, the mean is $\mu = (-3 + 3)/2 = 0$ and the variance is $\sigma^{2} = (3 - (-3))^{2}/12 = 36/12 = 3$.
The Central Limit Theorem states that $\sqrt{n}(\bar{X} - \mu)/\sigma$ converges in distribution to $N(0, 1)$ as n grows.
Since $\mu = 0$, this reads $\sqrt{n} \bar{X} / \sigma$ tends to $N(0,1)$.
Multiplying by the constant $\sigma, \sqrt{n} \bar{X}$ converges in distribution to $N(0, \sigma^{2}) = N(0, 3)$.
Hence the large-sample distribution is $N(0, 3)$, option (b).

topic: Sampling Distributions: Sample Mean, Sample Variance, t, Chi-square, F
subtopic: Sampling Distributions: Sample Mean, Sample Variance, t, Chi-square, F
stem: A normal population has mean $0.1$, SD $2.1$. What is the probability that the mean of a sample of size $900$ is negative? [Given $P(0<Z<1.43)=0.4236$]
tips: $\sqrt{900} = 30$ is the only arithmetic that matters; $2.1/30 = 0.07$ makes the z-score a clean -1.43, which is exactly the value the examiner supplies.
The supplied figure $\operatorname{P}(0 < Z < 1.43) = 0.4236$ is a CENTRAL area, not a tail. The left tail is $0.5 - 0.4236 = 0.0764$ - subtracting from 0.5, never from 1.
Option $(b) 0.6408 = 0.5 + 0.1408$ and option (d) 0.7046 are built from misreading the table; option (c) 0.6074 is 0.5 + 0.1074. All assume the wrong tail.
Sanity check: the population mean 0.1 is positive and the sample is large, so a negative sample mean should be UNLIKELY - the answer must be well below 0.5, which only (a) is.
solution: The population has mean $\mu = 0.1$ and standard deviation $\sigma = 2.1$; the sample size is $n = 900$.
The standard error of the sample mean is $\sigma/\sqrt{n} = 2.1/30 = 0.07$.
We need $\operatorname{P}(\bar{X} < 0)$. Standardising: $z = (0 - 0.1)/0.07$ = -1.4286, which rounds to -1.43.
$\operatorname{P}(\bar{X} < 0) = \operatorname{P}(Z < -1.43) = \operatorname{P}(Z > 1.43)$ by symmetry.
Using the supplied value $\operatorname{P}(0 < Z < 1.43) = 0.4236$, we get $\operatorname{P}(Z > 1.43) = 0.5 - 0.4236 = 0.0764$.
Hence option (a) is correct.

topic: Sampling Distributions: Sample Mean, Sample Variance, t, Chi-square, F
subtopic: Sampling Distributions: Sample Mean, Sample Variance, t, Chi-square, F
stem: $(X_1,\ldots,X_5)$ are independent standard normal. The variable $\dfrac{C(X_1+X_2)}{(X_3^2+X_4^2+X_5^2)^{1/2}}$ has a $t$-distribution if $C$ equals
tips: The t-statistic template is ALWAYS standard normal divided by sqrt($\chi^{2}$/its own d.f.). Identify the two pieces and their d.f. before touching the algebra.
X1 + X2 has variance 2, so it must be divided by $\sqrt{2}$ to become standard normal. Forgetting this gives $\sqrt{3}$ and no matching option.
The d.f. is 3 (three squared normals), so the divisor inside the square root is 3 - that is where the $\sqrt{3}$ in the numerator comes from.
$\sqrt{3/2} = \sqrt{6}/2 = 1.2247$ while $\sqrt{3}/2 = 0.866$; option (a) is the trap for candidates who take the square root of 3 but not of 2.
solution: X1, ..., X5 are independent $N(0,1)$.
$X_{3}^{2} + X_{4}^{2} + X_{5}^{2} \sim \chi^{2}$ with 3 degrees of freedom, and it is independent of X1 + X2.
By definition, $t = Z / sqrt$($\chi$-square_3 / 3) follows Student's t with 3 d.f.

topic: Sampling Distributions: Sample Mean, Sample Variance, t, Chi-square, F
subtopic: Sampling Distributions: Sample Mean, Sample Variance, t, Chi-square, F
stem: If $X\sim F(m,n)$ with $m>2,n>2$, then $E(X)\,E(1/X)$ equals
shortcut: $\operatorname{E}(X) = n/(n-2)$ for $X \sim F(m,n)$. Since $1/X \sim F(n,m)$, swapping the roles gives $\operatorname{E}(1/X) = m/(m-2)$. The product is mn/$((m-2)(n-2))$.
tips: The reciprocal property $1/F(m,n) \sim F(n,m)$ is the key. Once you have it, $\operatorname{E}(1/X)$ needs no integration - just swap m and n in the mean formula.
Remember the mean of F(m,n) involves only the DENOMINATOR d.f.: $E = n/(n-2), n > 2$. Candidates who use $m/(m-2)$ for E(X) land on option (b), the mirror-image trap.
The conditions $m > 2$ and $n > 2$ in the stem exist precisely so that both expectations are finite - they are a hint about which formula to use.
By Jensen's inequality $\operatorname{E}(X)\operatorname{E}(1/X) \ge 1$ always. Option (c) gives mn/$((m-2)(n-2)) > 1$ for all admissible m, n, which is the only option guaranteed to satisfy this.
solution: For $X \sim F(m, n)$ with $n > 2$, the mean is $\operatorname{E}(X) = n/(n - 2)$.
A standard property of the F distribution is that $1/X \sim F(n, m)$, i.e. the degrees of freedom interchange.
Applying the mean formula to $1/X \sim F(n, m)$, whose denominator d.f. is now m, gives $\operatorname{E}(1/X) = m/(m - 2)$, valid since $m > 2$.
Multiplying: $\operatorname{E}(X) \operatorname{E}(1/X) = [n/(n-2)] [m/(m-2)]$ = mn/$((m-2)(n-2))$.
Hence option (c) is correct.

topic: Non-parametric Tests
subtopic: Non-parametric Tests
stem: Which non-parametric test is analogous to the chi-square goodness-of-fit test?
shortcut: Both the $\chi^{2}$ goodness-of-fit test and the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test compare an observed distribution with a completely specified theoretical one. K-S is the distribution-free analogue.
tips: Sort the non-parametric tests by what they compare: goodness of fit to a specified distribution = $\chi^{2}$ and K-S (one sample); two independent samples = Mann-Whitney and median test; paired/matched data = Wilcoxon signed-rank and sign test; randomness = run test.
$\chi^{2}$ needs GROUPED data with adequate expected frequencies; K-S works directly on the ungrouped empirical CDF and is therefore preferred for small samples and continuous data.
K-S uses the maximum absolute deviation $D = \sup \mid F_{n}(x) - F_{0}(x)$| - remember it as a 'largest vertical gap between two CDFs' test.
Mann-Whitney (option a) and Wilcoxon (option c) are location-comparison tests, and the median test (option d) compares medians - none of them tests fit to a specified distribution.
solution: The $\chi^{2}$ goodness-of-fit test compares observed frequencies with the frequencies expected under a fully specified theoretical distribution.
Among the listed non-parametric procedures, the Kolmogorov-Smirnov one-sample test performs the same task: it compares the empirical distribution function $F_{n}(x)$ with a hypothesised $F_{0}(x)$.
The K-S statistic is $D = \sup$ over x of |$F_{n}(x) - F_{0}(x)$|, the largest vertical distance between the two curves, and a large D leads to rejection of the hypothesised distribution.
The Mann-Whitney and Wilcoxon tests compare locations of samples, and the median test compares medians; none of them tests agreement with a specified distribution.
Hence the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test is the analogue of the $\chi^{2}$ goodness-of-fit test, option (b).

topic: Sampling Distributions: Sample Mean, Sample Variance, t, Chi-square, F
subtopic: Sampling Distributions: Sample Mean, Sample Variance, t, Chi-square, F
stem: Consider the following statements: 1. The normal distribution is a special case of the chi-square distribution with 1 degree of freedom. 2. All moments of order less than $n$ of the $t$-distribution with $n$ df exist. 3. If $t$ follows Student's $t$ with $n$ df, then $t^2$ follows $F(1,n)$.
shortcut: Statement 1 reverses the relationship - the SQUARE of a standard normal is $\chi^{2}_{1}$, not the other way round - so it is false. Statements 2 and 3 are standard results, giving 2 and 3 only.
tips: Correct direction: $Z \sim N(0,1)$ implies $Z^{2} \sim \chi^{2}_{1}$. The normal is not a special case of the $\chi^{2}$; the $\chi^{2}$ family is built FROM normals.
Moment rule for t with n d.f.: $\operatorname{E}(t^{k})$ exists only for $k < n$. The t with 1 d.f. is the Cauchy, which has no mean at all - a good anchor for remembering the rule.
$t_{n}^{2} \sim F(1, n)$ is worth memorising alongside $F(m,n) = 1/F(n,m)$ and $\chi^{2}_{n}/n$ as n grows tending to 1. These three identities cover most sampling-distribution items.
Where one statement asserts a containment between distribution families, check the DIRECTION of the containment - reversal is the single most common falsification device.
solution: Statement 1: the $\chi^{2}$ with 1 degree of freedom is the distribution of $Z^{2}$ where $Z \sim N(0,1)$. The normal itself is not $a \chi^{2}$; the $\chi^{2}$ is non-negative and skewed while the normal is symmetric on the whole line. FALSE.

Statement 2: for Student's t with n degrees of freedom, the tail behaves like |t|^(-$(n+1)$), so $\operatorname{E}(\lvert t\rvert ^{k})$ is finite exactly when $k < n$. Hence all moments of order less than n exist. TRUE.

Statement 3: write $t = Z/\sqrt{V/n}$ with $Z \sim N(0,1)$ and $V \sim \chi^{2}_{n}$ independent. Then $t^{2} = Z^{2}/(V/n) = (Z^{2}/1)/(V/n), a$ ratio of independent $\chi$-squares divided by their degrees of freedom, which is $F(1, n)$. TRUE.
Only statements 2 and 3 are correct, so option (c) is right.

topic: Order Statistics - Minimum, Maximum, Range, Median
subtopic: Order Statistics - Minimum, Maximum, Range, Median
stem: For a random sample of size 2 from $N(0,\sigma^2)$, what is $E[X_{(1)}]$ (first order statistic)?
shortcut: $\min(X_{1},X_{2}) = [(X_{1}+X_{2}) - \lvert X_{1}-X_{2}\rvert ]/2$. The first term has mean 0 and $X_{1} - X_{2} \sim N(0, 2 \sigma^{2})$, so $E\mid X_{1}-X_{2}$| = $\sigma \sqrt{2}$ . $\sqrt{2/pi} = 2 \sigma/\sqrt{pi}$. Hence $\operatorname{E}[X_{1}]$ = -$\sigma/\sqrt{pi}$.
tips: Identity worth memorising: $\min(a,b) = (a + b - \lvert a - b\rvert )/2$ and $\max(a,b) = (a + b + \lvert a - b\rvert )/2$. It converts order-statistic expectations into a mean-absolute-deviation computation.
For $W \sim N(0, \tau^{2}), E\mid W$| = $\tau \sqrt{2/pi}$. Here $\tau = \sigma \sqrt{2}$, so $E\mid X_{1} - X_{2}$| = $2 \sigma/\sqrt{pi}$.
Sign check first: the minimum of two symmetric mean-zero variables must have a NEGATIVE expectation, which immediately eliminates options (a) and (b).
For a sample of size 2 from any symmetric distribution, $\operatorname{E}[X_{1}]$ = -$\operatorname{E}[X_{2}]$; the two order statistics are mirror images about the mean.
solution: Let X1, X2 be independent $N(0, \sigma^{2})$ and let $X_{1} = \min(X_{1}, X_{2})$.
Use the identity $\min(X_{1}, X_{2}) = [(X_{1} + X_{2}) - \lvert X_{1} - X_{2}\rvert ]/2$.
$\operatorname{E}(X_{1} + X_{2}) = 0$ since both means are 0.

$X_{1} - X_{2} \sim N(0, 2 \sigma^{2})$, so with $\tau = \sigma \sqrt{2}$ and the half-normal mean formula E|W| = $\tau \sqrt{2/pi}$, we get $E\mid X_{1} - X_{2}$| = $\sigma \sqrt{2}$ . $\sqrt{2/pi} = 2 \sigma/\sqrt{pi}$.
Therefore $\operatorname{E}[X_{1}] = [0 - 2 \sigma/\sqrt{pi}]/2$ = -$\sigma/\sqrt{pi}$.
Hence option (c) is correct.

topic: Order Statistics - Minimum, Maximum, Range, Median
subtopic: Order Statistics - Minimum, Maximum, Range, Median
stem: If $X_i,\ i=1,\ldots,n$ are iid with c.d.f. $F(x)=x,\ 0\le x\le1$, the p.d.f. $g(r)$ of the range $R=X_{(n)}-X_{(1)}$ is
shortcut: For $a U(0,1)$ sample the range R ~ Beta(n-1, 2), whose density is $n(n-1) r^{n-2}(1-r)$ on $(0,1)$. Recognise the Beta and read the answer off.
tips: General range density: $g(r) = n(n-1)$ times the $\int f(x) f(x+r) [F(x+r) - F(x)]^{n-2}\,dx$. For $U(0,1)$ the bracket is just r and the integral contributes the factor $(1 - r)$.
Shape check: R ~ Beta(n-1, 2) means the exponents must be $(n-1)-1 = n-2$ on r and $2-1 = 1$ on $(1-r)$. Only option (a) has that pairing; option (b) has them swapped.
Normalisation test: the $\int n(n-1) r^{n-2}(1-r)$ over $(0,1)$ is $n(n-1) [1/(n-1) - 1/n] = 1$. Option (b) also integrates to 1, so use the shape argument, not normalisation, to separate them.
Options (c) and (d) are densities of the MAXIMUM and of a related order statistic, not of the range - a classic substitution trap.
solution: The $X_{i}$ are i.i.d. Uniform(0,1), so $f(x) = 1$ on $(0,1)$ and $F(x) = x$ on $(0,1)$.
The joint density of the smallest and largest order statistics is $h(u, v) = n(n-1) f(u) f(v) [F(v) - F(u)]^{n-2} = n(n-1)(v - u)^{n-2}$ for $0 < u < v < 1$.
Put $R = V - U$ and integrate out U. For a fixed r in $(0,1), U$ can range over $(0, 1 - r)$.
This is the Beta(n-1, 2) density, and it integrates to $n(n-1)[1/(n-1) - 1/n] = 1$, confirming correctness.
Hence option (a) is correct.

topic: Finite Differences: Operators, Factorial Polynomials, Separation of Symbols
subtopic: Finite Differences: Operators, Factorial Polynomials, Separation of Symbols
stem: Given $f(1)=12,f(2)=40,f(3)=90,f(4)=168,f(5)=280,f(6)=432$, the degree of the polynomial $f(x)$ is at least
shortcut: Build the difference table: first differences 28, 50, 78, 112, 152; second 22, 28, 34, 40; third 6, 6, 6 - constant. A constant third difference means degree 3.
tips: Rule: the order of the FIRST constant difference is the degree of the polynomial. Stop differencing the moment a row is constant.
You do not need the whole table - as soon as three equal entries appear in a row you can stop, since a fourth difference of zero confirms degree 3.
The word 'at least' is a hint that the data are consistent with degree 3 but any higher-degree polynomial would also fit; the minimum degree is what is asked.
Arithmetic tip: differences of 12, 40, 90, 168, 280, 432 are all even, so halving them first $(14, 25, 39, 56, 76)$ speeds up the mental subtraction.
solution: Third differences: $28-22 = 6, 34-28 = 6, 40-34 = 6$. These are constant.
Fourth differences are therefore 0, so the data are generated by a polynomial of degree exactly 3.
Hence the degree is at least 3, option (b).

topic: Finite Differences: Operators, Factorial Polynomials, Separation of Symbols
subtopic: Finite Differences: Operators, Factorial Polynomials, Separation of Symbols
stem: $f(x)=x^3$ is represented as the factorial polynomial $f(x)=Ax^{(3)}+Bx^{(2)}+Cx+D$ with interval of differencing $h=2$. The values of $A,B,C,D$ are
shortcut: With $h = 2, x^{3} = x(x-2)(x-4) = x^{3} - 6x^{2} + 8x$ and $x^{2} = x(x-2) = x^{2} - 2x$. Matching coefficients of $x^{3}$ gives $A = 1$, then $x^{2}$ gives $B = 6$ and x gives $C = 4$, with $D = 0$.
tips: Factorial notation with spacing h: $x^{n} = x(x-h)(x-2h)$...$(x-(n-1)h)$. Here $h = 2$, so the factors step down by 2 - not by 1. Using $h = 1$ gives A,B,C,$D = 1$,3,1,0 and no matching option.
D must be 0 because $x^{3}$ has no constant term and every factorial term vanishes at $x = 0$ - read that off before any algebra.
The leading coefficient always transfers unchanged: $A = 1$ because both $x^{3}$ and $x^{3}$ are monic.
Cross-check with a value: at $x = 2, x^{3} = 0$ and $x^{2} = 0$, so $f(2) = 2C = 8$, giving $C = 4$ in a single substitution.
solution: With interval of differencing $h = 2$, the factorial polynomials are $x^{3} = x(x-2)(x-4)$ and $x^{2} = x(x-2)$.
So $A x^{3} + B x^{2}$ + Cx + $D = A(x^{3} - 6x^{2} + 8x) + B(x^{2} - 2x)$ + Cx + D, which must equal $x^{3}$.
Coefficient of $x^{3}$: $A = 1$. Coefficient of $x^{2}$: -$6A + B = 0$, so $B = 6$.
Coefficient of x: $8A - 2B + C = 0$, i.e. $8 - 12 + C = 0$, so $C = 4$. Constant: $D = 0$.
Hence $(A, B, C, D) = (1, 6, 4, 0)$, option (b).

stem: The $n$th divided difference of an $n$th-degree polynomial is
shortcut: The nth divided difference of a degree-n polynomial equals its leading coefficient - a fixed number. So it is a constant.
tips: Two companion facts: the nth divided difference of a degree-n polynomial is the leading coefficient (a constant), and the $(n+1)$th and all higher divided differences are ZERO.
Do not confuse 'constant' with 'zero'. Option (c) is correct only for divided differences of order HIGHER than n - the commonest slip in this item.
Link to finite differences: for equally spaced points, the nth divided difference equals $\Delta^{n} f / (n! h^{n})$, which for a degree-n polynomial is $a_{n}$, the leading coefficient.
Divided differences are symmetric in their arguments, so the answer cannot depend on which points are used - another reason it must be a constant.
solution: Let $f(x) = a_{n} x^{n} + a_{n-1} x^{n-1}$ + ... + $a_{0}$ be a polynomial of degree n, so $a_{n}$ is not 0.
Divided differences are linear, and the kth divided difference of a polynomial of degree less than k is 0.
Hence the nth divided difference of f depends only on the leading term $a_{n} x^{n}$.
For $x^{n}$, the nth divided difference over any n+1 distinct nodes equals 1 (this is the standard result, e.g. from the Newton form of the interpolating polynomial).
Therefore the nth divided difference of f is $a_{n}, a$ fixed non-zero number independent of the nodes - i.e. a constant.
Hence option (b) is correct.

stem: RK4 solves $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=f(x),\ y(0)=0$ with step $h$. The solution at $x=h$ is given by
shortcut: When f does not involve y, RK4 has $k_{2} = k_{3} = h f(h/2)$, so $y(h) = (k_{1} + 2k2 + 2k3 + k_{4})/6 = (h/6)[f(0) + 4f(h/2) + f(h)]$ - exactly Simpson's one-third rule.
tips: The weights 1, 2, 2, 1 divided by 6 collapse to 1, 4, 1 divided by 6 when the two midpoint slopes coincide. Recognising this makes the whole question a one-liner.
Every option has the same $1/6$ prefactor, so just check whether the interior weights sum correctly: $1 + 4 + 1 = 6$, which only option (d) satisfies.
This equivalence is worth remembering conceptually: RK4 applied to a pure quadrature problem IS Simpson's rule, which is why both are fourth-order accurate.
The weights in any such formula must sum to 6 (so that a constant f is integrated exactly to h f); options (a), (b) and (c) sum to 7, 6 and 6 respectively, so use the x-symmetry check to finish.
solution: Here f depends on x only, so the y-arguments are irrelevant: $k_{1} = h f(0), k_{2} = h f(h/2), k_{3} = h f(h/2), k_{4} = h f(h)$.
Combining the two equal middle terms: $y(h) = (h/6)[f(0) + 4 f(h/2) + f(h)]$.
This is precisely Simpson's one-third rule applied on $[0, h]$.
Hence option (d) is correct.

stem: The images $f(n)$ of $n\in\{1,\ldots,99\}\setminus\{50\}$ are given. To estimate $f(50)$ from a forward difference table, the working hypothesis is
shortcut: The set {1,...,99} minus {50} has 98 points. A unique interpolating polynomial through 98 points has degree at most 97.
tips: Counting rule: k data points determine a polynomial of degree at most k - 1. Count the points first, subtract one, and you are done.
The classic slip is to count 99 points and forget that $f(50)$ is the value being ESTIMATED, not a datum - that gives 98 and lands on option (c).
'Degree not more than' is the mathematically correct phrasing; the data could accidentally lie on a lower-degree polynomial, so an exact degree cannot be asserted.
In practice a difference table for missing-value problems is truncated far earlier; the theoretical maximum degree is what this item tests.
solution: The images f(n) are given for $n = 1, 2$, ..., 99 with $n = 50$ omitted.
That is $99 - 1 = 98$ known data points.
Through 98 distinct points there passes exactly one polynomial of degree at most $98 - 1 = 97$.
The forward-difference (missing-value) technique assumes precisely this: that f is a polynomial whose degree does not exceed 97, so that the 98th difference vanishes.
Hence the working hypothesis is that the degree is not more than 97, option (d).

tips: Missing-value template: with one gap among k+1 tabulated points, set $\Delta^{k} f_{0} = 0$ and solve. The binomial coefficients with alternating signs are the whole method.
The fourth-difference operator expands with coefficients 1, -4, 6, -4, 1. Memorise the row of Pascal's triangle with alternating signs - it appears in every missing-value item.
Arithmetic care: $6f2 = 6 \times 7 = 42$ and -4f1 = -20. Combining the knowns gives 56, so $4a = 56$ and $a = 14$ in one step.
Sanity check the pattern: with $a = 14$ the first differences are 3, 2, 7, 18 and the third differences are constant at 9, confirming a genuine cubic fit.
solution: The tabulated values are $f_{0} = 2, f_{1} = 5, f_{2} = 7, f_{3} = \alpha, f_{4} = 32$ at $x = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5$ with $h = 1$.
Only four values are actually known, so the standard assumption is that f is a polynomial of degree 3; then the fourth difference vanishes.
So $56 - 4 \alpha = 0$, giving $\alpha = 14$.
Hence option (a) is correct.

Build the difference table first: $\Delta u_{10} = 30, \Delta^{2} = 5, \Delta^{3} = 2, \Delta^{4} = 0$. The series terminates automatically at the third difference.

solution: First differences: 30, 35, 42, 51. Second differences: 5, 7, 9. Third differences: 2, 2. Fourth difference: 0.

Summing gives 55.75, option (c).
