Hence the network developed by the Government of India is NICNET, option (b).

topic: Networks: LAN, WAN, Internet, Intranet
subtopic: Networks: LAN, WAN, Internet, Intranet
stem: Which one of the following communication media supports higher Internet bandwidth?
shortcut: Fibre optic supports by far the highest bandwidth of the listed media.
tips: This restates Q64 of the same paper - the examiner is testing the same ranking twice, so the medium comparison is clearly worth memorising.
Bandwidth ranking: fibre optic > coaxial > UTP > thin Ethernet in classical textbook terms, with fibre always at the top.
Fibre carries light rather than electrical current, so its bandwidth is not limited by the resistance, capacitance and interference that cap copper media.
Modern backbone links and undersea cables are all fibre for exactly this reason - a real-world anchor for the fact.
solution: The question asks which medium supports the highest internet bandwidth.
UTP cable and thin Ethernet are copper media whose bandwidth is limited by attenuation and electromagnetic interference.
Coaxial cable offers more bandwidth than twisted pair but is still an electrical medium subject to the same physical limits.
Fibre optic cable transmits information as light through a glass core, offering bandwidth orders of magnitude greater than any copper medium and negligible interference.
Hence fibre optic cable supports the highest internet bandwidth, option (c).

topic: Software, Operating Systems, Packages & Utilities
subtopic: Software, Operating Systems, Packages & Utilities
stem: A technique used by an OS for efficient management of memory space of a computer system is
shortcut: Paging divides memory into fixed-size frames and pages, allowing non-contiguous allocation - the standard OS technique for efficient management of memory SPACE.
tips: Paging's specific benefit is the elimination of EXTERNAL fragmentation: any free frame can hold any page, so memory space is used efficiently.
Swapping moves whole processes between memory and disk; it extends capacity but is a coarser mechanism than paging and is usually described as a supplement to it.
Caching (option c) speeds up ACCESS rather than managing space, and debugging (option d) is a program-development activity, not memory management.
Related terms to keep straight: paging, segmentation, virtual memory, page fault, page replacement (FIFO, LRU, optimal) and thrashing.
solution: Memory management is the operating system function that allocates and tracks main memory among competing processes.
Paging divides physical memory into fixed-size frames and each process's logical address space into pages of the same size, then maps pages to any available frames via a page table.

Because a process need not occupy contiguous physical memory, paging eliminates external fragmentation and lets the OS use every free frame - the efficient management of memory space the question describes.
Swapping transfers entire processes between main memory and backing store; caching speeds up access by holding frequently used data in fast memory; debugging is unrelated to memory management.
Hence the technique is paging, option (a).

topic: Software, Operating Systems, Packages & Utilities
subtopic: Software, Operating Systems, Packages & Utilities
stem: Which of the following are functions of an operating system? 1. Memory management 2. Device management 3. Security management
shortcut: Memory management, device management and security management are all core operating-system functions, so all three are correct.
tips: The standard list of OS functions: process management, memory management, file management, device $(I/O)$ management, security and protection, and user interface. Memorise the six.
When every listed item is drawn from that standard list, 'all of the above' is almost always the key - verify the least familiar one and move on.
Device management is exercised through DEVICE DRIVERS and I/O scheduling; security management covers authentication, access control and protection between processes.
Utilities such as antivirus supplement OS security but do not replace it - the OS itself enforces user accounts, permissions and memory protection.
solution: An operating system acts as the resource manager and interface between the user and the hardware.
Memory management: allocating and deallocating main memory, keeping track of which parts are in use, and implementing paging or segmentation and virtual memory. A core OS function.
Device management: controlling peripheral devices through device drivers, buffering, spooling and I/O scheduling. A core OS function.
Security management: user authentication, access control, file permissions and protection of one process's memory from another. A core OS function.
All three listed items are genuine operating-system functions.
Hence option (d) is correct.

topic: Memory: RAM, ROM, Cache; Units of Memory & Storage Capacity
subtopic: Memory: RAM, ROM, Cache; Units of Memory & Storage Capacity
stem: Which type of memory is suitable for mobile phones, digital cameras and iPods?
shortcut: Portable devices need memory that is non-volatile, compact, low-power and electrically rewritable - that is flash memory.
tips: Flash is electrically erasable and rewritable in blocks, non-volatile, solid state (no moving parts) and low power - exactly the requirement list for phones, cameras and music players.
PROM (option a) can be written only ONCE, so it cannot store photographs or music that change constantly.
RAM (option c) is volatile: everything would be lost when the device is switched off.
Optical disks (option d) need a mechanical drive and are far too bulky and fragile for handheld devices.
solution: Mobile phones, digital cameras and portable music players need storage that retains data with the power off, tolerates being carried about, and can be rewritten many times.
Programmable ROM can be programmed only once and cannot be updated, so it is unsuitable for user data.
RAM is volatile - its contents vanish when power is removed - so it cannot serve as the main storage of a portable device.
Optical disks require a mechanical drive with moving parts, making them unsuitable for compact handheld devices.
Flash memory is non-volatile, electrically erasable and rewritable, compact, shock-resistant and low-power, which is why it is used in SD cards, USB drives and phone storage.
Hence the answer is flash memory, option (b).

topic: Numerical Integration - Trapezoidal, Simpson's 1/3 & 3/8, Weddle's Rule
subtopic: Numerical Integration - Trapezoidal, Simpson's 1/3 & 3/8, Weddle's Rule
stem: The value estimated for $\ln2$, obtained by applying the trapezoidal rule to $\int_1^2 \frac1x\,dx$ with two equal divisions of $[1,2]$, is
tips: Trapezoidal with two strips: $T = h[(f_{0} + f_{2})/2 + f_{1}]$. Only the two END ordinates are halved.
Keep fractions: $(1/2)[(1 + 1/2)/2 + 2/3] = (1/2)(3/4 + 2/3) = (1/2)(17/12) = 17/24$. Exact fractions beat decimals when the options are fractions.
$1/x$ is convex, so the trapezoidal rule OVERESTIMATES. The true $\ln 2 = 0.6931$, and $17/24 = 0.7083$ is duly larger - a strong confirmation.
Option $(c) 19/24 = 0.7917$ is too far above $\ln 2$ to be a two-strip trapezoidal value; the overestimate for such a smooth function is small.
solution: We approximate the $\int 1/x$ from 1 to 2 using the trapezoidal rule with $n = 2$ equal divisions, so $h = (2-1)/2 = 0.5$.
Trapezoidal rule: $T = h[(f_{0} + f_{2})/2 + f_{1}]$.
Numerically $17/24 = 0.7083$, slightly above the true $\ln 2 = 0.6931$ as expected for a convex integrand. Option (b) is correct.

topic: Numerical Integration - Trapezoidal, Simpson's 1/3 & 3/8, Weddle's Rule
subtopic: Numerical Integration - Trapezoidal, Simpson's 1/3 & 3/8, Weddle's Rule
stem: Simpson's one-third rule for evaluation of $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$ requires the interval $[a,b]$ to be divided into
options: an even number of subintervals of equal width
an odd number of subintervals of equal width
any number of subintervals of equal width
shortcut: Simpson's $1/3$ rule fits a parabola over each PAIR of strips, so the number of equal-width subintervals must be even.
tips: Rule of thumb: Simpson's $1/3$ needs n divisible by 2; Simpson's $3/8$ needs n divisible by 3; the trapezoidal rule works for any n.
The word 'equal' matters too - all these Newton-Cotes formulas assume equally spaced nodes, which eliminates option (d).
The weight pattern 1, 4, 2, 4, 2, ..., 4, 1 only closes correctly when n is even; with odd n the final strip is left without a partner.
If n happens to be odd, apply the $3/8$ rule to the first three strips and the $1/3$ rule to the rest - a standard practical fix worth remembering.
solution: Simpson's one-third rule is derived by replacing f over each PAIR of adjacent subintervals by the parabola through the three corresponding points.
Each such parabola therefore consumes exactly two subintervals.
For the whole interval [a, b] to be covered by complete pairs, the number of subintervals n must be even.
The derivation also requires the nodes to be equally spaced with $h = (b-a)/n$, so the subintervals must be of equal width.
Hence [a, b] must be divided into an even number of subintervals of equal width, option (a).

topic: Numerical Integration - Trapezoidal, Simpson's 1/3 & 3/8, Weddle's Rule
subtopic: Numerical Integration - Trapezoidal, Simpson's 1/3 & 3/8, Weddle's Rule
stem: Consider the table: | x | -1 | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | f(x) | 2 | 1 | 2 | 5 | 10 | 17 | 26 | The value of $\int_{-1}^5 f(x)\,dx$, computed by Simpson's $\frac38$th rule, is
tips: Composite $3/8$ weight pattern: 1, 3, 3, 2, 3, 3, 2, ..., 3, 3, 1 - the weight 2 appears at every node where two groups of three strips join.
Check divisibility first: $n = 6$ is a multiple of 3, so the $3/8$ rule applies cleanly.
The data are exactly $f(x) = x^{2} + 1$, and Simpson's rules integrate quadratics EXACTLY, so the answer must equal the true value 48 - a decisive cross-check.
Bracket sum: $2 + 3 + 6 + 10 + 30 + 51 + 26 = 128$, and $(3/8)(128) = 48$. Keeping the weighted terms in a single column reduces slips.
solution: The tabulated points run from x = -1 to $x = 5$ with $h = 1$, giving $n = 6$ subintervals, which is a multiple of 3 so Simpson's three-eighth rule applies.
Composite three-eighth rule: $I = (3h/8)[f_{0} + 3f1 + 3f2 + 2f3 + 3f4 + 3f5 + f_{6}]$.
Check: the data satisfy $f(x) = x^{2} + 1$, whose exact integral from -1 to 5 is $[x^{3}/3 + x] = (125/3 + 5) - (-1/3 - 1) = 48$. Option (a) is correct.

topic: Numerical Solution of Differential Equations - Euler, Milne, Picard, Runge-Kutta
subtopic: Numerical Solution of Differential Equations - Euler, Milne, Picard, Runge-Kutta
stem: Consider the IVP $y'=y+2x-1$, $y(0)=1$, over $0\leq x\leq1$. The value of $y(0.2)$, obtained using Euler's method with $h=0.1$, is
tips: Euler's method: $y_{n+1} = y_{n} + h f(x_{n}, y_{n})$. Two steps of $h = 0.1$ are needed to reach $x = 0.2$ - stopping after one step gives 1 and lands on option (b).
The first slope is exactly zero here, which makes the first step trivial and is clearly deliberate on the examiner's part.
Note 2x means 2 times x, so at $x = 0.1$ the term is 0.2, not 0.1. Misreading it gives 1.010 and no matching option.
The exact solution is $y = 2e^{x} - 2x - 1$, giving $y(0.2) = 1.0428$; Euler's value 1.020 is the expected underestimate for this convex solution.
solution: Euler's method for $y' = f(x, y)$ is $y_{n+1} = y_{n} + h f(x_{n}, y_{n})$, with $f(x,y) = y + 2x - 1, y(0) = 1$ and $h = 0.1$.
Hence $y(0.2) = 1.020$, option (c). (The exact solution $y = 2e^{x} - 2x - 1$ gives 1.0428, so Euler slightly underestimates, as expected.)

topic: Numerical Solution of Differential Equations - Euler, Milne, Picard, Runge-Kutta
subtopic: Numerical Solution of Differential Equations - Euler, Milne, Picard, Runge-Kutta
stem: The third approximation of the IVP $\frac{dy}{dx}=x+y$, $y(0)=1$, obtained using Picard's method, is
tips: Picard iteration: $y_{n+1}(x) = y(0) + \int_{0}^{x} f(t, y_{n}(t))\,dt$. Each round raises the degree by one, so the THIRD approximation is a quartic.
Degree check alone decides the item: only option (a) has an $x^{4}$ term, so it is the only candidate for a third approximation.
Option (b) is y2, the second approximation - the classic 'one iteration short' trap.
Cross-check with the exact solution $y = 3e^{x} - x - 1 = 1 + x + x^{2} + x^{3}/3 + x^{4}/12$ + ...; Picard's terms agree up to $x^{3}$, as they must after three iterations.
solution: Picard's method for $dy/dx = x + y$ with $y(0) = 1$ uses $y_{n+1}(x) = 1 + \int_{0}^{x} (t + y_{n}(t))\,dt$, starting from $y_{0} = 1$.
First approximation: $y_{1} = 1 + \int_{0}^{x} (t + 1)\,dt = 1 + x + x^{2}/2$.
Integrating term by term: $y_{3} = 1 + x + x^{2} + x^{3}/3 + x^{4}/24$.
Hence option (a) is correct.

topic: Divided Differences; Newton's & Lagrange's Formulae (Unequal Intervals)
subtopic: Divided Differences; Newton's & Lagrange's Formulae (Unequal Intervals)
stem: $f(x)$ has values $f(1)=4$, $f(2)=5$, $f(7)=5$, $f(8)=4$. Then $f(x)$ attains
options: neither maximum nor minimum for any $x$
shortcut: The data are symmetric about $x = 4.5$ ($f(1) = f(8) = 4$ and $f(2) = f(7) = 5$), and the values RISE towards the centre, so the interpolating curve has a maximum at $x = 4.5$.
tips: Spot the symmetry before computing: matching values at mirror-image abscissae force the interpolating polynomial to be symmetric about the midpoint $(1+8)/2 = 4.5$.
In the shifted variable $u = x - 4.5$ the polynomial is even, so it reduces to $a + bu^{2}$. Fitting $a + 12.25b = 4$ and $a + 6.25b = 5$ gives b = -$1/6 < 0$, hence a maximum.
Direction check without algebra: moving inward from $x = 1$ to $x = 2$ the value RISES from 4 to 5, and it falls again from $x = 7$ to $x = 8$. Rise then fall means a maximum.
Option (d) places the turning point at x = -4.5, outside the data range entirely - a sign trap for candidates who mishandle the shift.
solution: The abscissae are symmetric about $x = (1 + 8)/2 = 4.5$, and the paired values are equal: $f(1) = f(8)$ and $f(2) = f(7)$.
Hence the interpolating polynomial is symmetric about $x = 4.5$, so in the variable $u = x - 4.5$ it is an even function; with four data points it takes the form $f = a + b u^{2}$.
Since $b < 0$, the parabola opens downwards and the turning point at $u = 0$ is a MAXIMUM.
Therefore f attains a maximum at $x = 4.5$, option (a).

topic: Interpolation - Newton-Gregory Forward & Backward (Equal Intervals)
subtopic: Interpolation - Newton-Gregory Forward & Backward (Equal Intervals)
stem: Let $f(x)=\log_{10}(1+x)$ with $x_0=1$, $x_1=1.1$. What is the approximate value of $f(1.04)$ by linear interpolation? [Given $\log_{10}2=0.301030$, $\log_{10}2.1=0.322219$]
tips: Linear interpolation is Newton's forward formula truncated after the first difference: $f = f_{0} + p (f_{1} - f_{0})$ with $p = (x - x_{0})/h$.
Compute the difference once: $0.322219 - 0.301030 = 0.021189$, then take 40% of it. Working with the difference rather than the raw values keeps all six decimals intact.
Sanity check: the answer must lie between 0.301030 and 0.322219, and nearer the lower end since $p = 0.4 < 0.5$. Options (b), (c) and (d) all fall outside that range.
Note that $f(x) = \log(1 + x)$, so $f(1.04) = \log10(2.04)$; the true value is 0.309630, confirming the interpolation is accurate to four decimals.
solution: We interpolate $f(x) = \log10(1 + x)$ between $x_{0} = 1$ and $x_{1} = 1.1$, so $h = 0.1$.
The tabulated values are $f(x_{0}) = \log10 2 = 0.301030$ and $f(x_{1}) = \log10 2.1 = 0.322219$.
The first difference is 0.021189, and $0.4 \times 0.021189 = 0.0084756$.

topic: Numerical Solution of Differential Equations - Euler, Milne, Picard, Runge-Kutta
subtopic: Numerical Solution of Differential Equations - Euler, Milne, Picard, Runge-Kutta
stem: What is the approximate value of $y$ at $x=1.1$ for $\frac{dy}{dx}=3x+y^2$, obtained by Runge-Kutta method of second-order formula? [Given $y=1.2$ at $x=1$]
tips: Second-order RK (Heun's method): $k_{1} = h f(x_{0}, y_{0}), k_{2} = h f(x_{0} + h, y_{0} + k_{1}), y_{1} = y_{0} + (k_{1} + k_{2})/2$. Write the three lines out before substituting.
Option (b) 1.644 is exactly y0 + k1, the plain EULER value - the trap for candidates who stop after k1.
Watch the square: $y_{0} + k_{1} = 1.644$, and $1.644^{2} = 2.7027$. Squaring the updated y, not the original, is the essential second step.
Averaging the two slopes is what makes the method second order; the final increment 0.5221 sits between $k_{1} = 0.444$ and $k_{2} = 0.600$, as it must.
solution: The problem is $dy/dx = f(x,y) = 3x + y^{2}$ with $x_{0} = 1, y_{0} = 1.2$ and $h = 0.1$.
Hence $y(1.1)$ is approximately 1.722, option (a).

topic: Finite Differences: Operators, Factorial Polynomials, Separation of Symbols
subtopic: Finite Differences: Operators, Factorial Polynomials, Separation of Symbols
stem: If $\delta$ is the central difference operator, what is $\frac12\delta^2 + \delta\sqrt{1+\frac{\delta^2}{4}}$ equal to?
shortcut: Recognise $\sqrt{1 + \delta^{2}/4} = \mu$. Then $(1/2)\delta^{2} + \delta$.$\mu = (E - 2 + E^{-1})/2 + (E - E^{-1})/2 = E - 1 = \Delta$.
tips: Memorise $\mu = \sqrt{1 + \delta^{2}/4}$ - it is the single identity that unlocks this whole family of questions.
Work in terms of $E^{1/2}$ and $E^{-1/2}$: $\delta = E^{1/2} - E^{-1/2}$ and $\mu = (E^{1/2} + E^{-1/2})/2$, so $\delta$.$\mu = (E - E^{-1})/2$ as a difference of squares.
$\delta^{2} = E - 2 + E^{-1}$. Adding half of it to $\delta$.mu makes both $E^{-1}$ terms cancel, leaving E - 1.

Sanity test on $f(x) = x$ with $h = 1$: $\delta^{2} x = 0$ and $\delta$.$\mu x = 1$, so the expression gives 1, which equals $\Delta x$. Quick numerical checks like this settle operator identities fast.
solution: Write everything in terms of the shift operator: $\delta = E^{1/2} - E^{-1/2}$ and $\mu = (E^{1/2} + E^{-1/2})/2$.
A standard identity is $\mu = \sqrt{1 + \delta^{2}/4}$, so the given expression is $(1/2)\delta^{2} + \delta$.mu.
Since $\Delta = E - 1$, the expression equals $\Delta$, option (c).

topic: Divided Differences; Newton's & Lagrange's Formulae (Unequal Intervals)
subtopic: Divided Differences; Newton's & Lagrange's Formulae (Unequal Intervals)
stem: The third divided difference of $f(x)=x^3-2x$ with arguments $2,4,9,10$ is equal to
shortcut: The third divided difference of a cubic equals its leading coefficient. For $f(x) = x^{3} - 2x$ that coefficient is 1, whatever the nodes.
tips: Rule: the nth divided difference of a degree-n polynomial is its LEADING COEFFICIENT, independent of the arguments chosen.
The awkward nodes 2, 4, 9, 10 are pure decoration - the answer would be 1 for any four distinct arguments.
The -2x term contributes nothing: divided differences of order 3 annihilate every term of degree below 3.
Contrast with the reciprocal case $f(x) = 1/x$, whose nth divided difference is $(-1)^{n}$/(product of nodes) and genuinely depends on the nodes.
solution: Divided differences are linear, and the kth divided difference of any polynomial of degree less than k is zero.
Here $f(x) = x^{3} - 2x$, so the term -2x (degree 1) contributes nothing to a third divided difference.
For $x^{3}$, the third divided difference over any four distinct nodes equals the leading coefficient, namely 1.
This follows from the Newton form of the interpolating polynomial: the coefficient of the highest-degree term is exactly the top divided difference.
Hence the third divided difference over 2, 4, 9, 10 is 1.
Option (d) is correct.

topic: Non-parametric Tests
subtopic: Non-parametric Tests
stem: The value of the Kolmogorov–Smirnov statistic to test whether $0.32,0.16,0.98,0.16,0.08$ arise from $U(0,2)$ is
shortcut: Under $U(0,2), F_{0}(x) = x/2$. Sort the data $(0.08, 0.16, 0.16, 0.32, 0.98)$ and compare the step function with F0; the largest gap occurs just after $x = 0.32$, where Fn = 0.8 and $F_{0} = 0.16$, giving $D = 0.64$.
tips: Always evaluate the gap on BOTH sides of each jump: |$i/n - F_{0}(x_{i})$| and |$(i-1)/n - F_{0}(x_{i})$|. The maximum of all these is D.
Handle the tie at 0.16 by jumping the empirical CDF straight from 0.2 to 0.6 - two observations share the point, so the step has height $2/5$.
The uniform CDF on $(0,2)$ is $x/2$, so the theoretical values 0.04, 0.08, 0.08, 0.16, 0.49 are trivial to write down; most of the work is bookkeeping, not arithmetic.
The data are heavily concentrated near 0 while $U(0,2)$ spreads to 2, so a LARGE D is expected - options (a) 0.16 and (b) 0.52 understate the mismatch.
solution: Under H0 the distribution is $U(0,2)$, so $F_{0}(x) = x/2$ for $0 \le x \le 2$.
The empirical CDF takes the values 0.2 after 0.08, 0.6 after the tied pair at 0.16, 0.8 after 0.32 and 1.0 after 0.98.
Compute the deviations at each point (both before and after the jump): at 0.08, |0.2 - 0.04| = 0.16; at 0.16, |0.6 - 0.08| = 0.52; at 0.32, |0.8 - 0.16| = 0.64; at 0.98, |1.0 - 0.49| = 0.51.
The pre-jump deviations $(0.04, 0.12, 0.44, 0.31)$ are all smaller.
The Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic is the largest of these, $D = 0.64$, option (c).

topic: Bivariate & Multivariate Data; Association & Contingency
subtopic: Bivariate & Multivariate Data; Association & Contingency
stem: Contingency table (Material vs. Leakage): | | A | B | C | D | E | Total | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | Leaked | 36 | 22 | $X_1$ | $X_2$ | 42 | 200 | | Not leaked | 90 | $Y$ | 46 | 78 | 168 | 400 | Column totals for materials C and D are equal. What are $X_1,X_2,Y$?
shortcut: Row sums give $X_{1} + X_{2} = 100$ and $Y = 18$. Equal column totals for C and D give $X_{1} + 46 = X_{2} + 78$, i.e. $X_{1} - X_{2} = 32$. Solving, $X_{1} = 66$ and $X_{2} = 34$.
tips: Extract every equation the table offers BEFORE solving: each row total is one equation and the stated condition is another. Three unknowns need three equations.
The 'not leaked' row is fully determined except for Y, so $Y = 400 - (90 + 46 + 78 + 168) = 18$ comes out immediately and independently.
Sum and difference: $X_{1} + X_{2} = 100$ and $X_{1} - X_{2} = 32$ give $X_{1} = 66$ and $X_{2} = 34$ by inspection - add and halve.
Options (a) and (b) differ only by swapping X1 and X2, so pin down which column is C: the larger leaked count goes with the SMALLER not-leaked count $(46)$ to keep the totals equal.
solution: The column total for material C is X1 + 46 and for material D is X2 + 78; these are stated to be equal.
Check: column C total = $66 + 46 = 112$ and column D total = $34 + 78 = 112$, equal as required. Option (a) is correct.

topic: Non-parametric Tests
subtopic: Non-parametric Tests
stem: In a clinical trial, $n$ persons had cream $A$ on one randomly chosen arm and cream $B$ on the other. Which test examines the difference (response is continuous)?
options: Two-sample $t$-test if normality can be assumed
Paired $t$-test if normality can be assumed
shortcut: Each person receives BOTH creams, one per arm, so the observations are naturally paired within a person. With a continuous response and normality, the paired t-test is the right procedure.
tips: Look for what shares a subject: two measurements on the SAME person are paired, and pairing must be preserved by analysing the within-person differences.
Pairing removes between-person variation, so the paired t-test is far more powerful here than the two-sample t-test, which wrongly treats the 2n measurements as independent.
The randomisation of which arm gets which cream protects against a left/right arm effect; it does not turn the design into an independent-samples one.
If normality could not be assumed, the correct non-parametric analogues would be the Wilcoxon signed-rank test or the sign test - both paired procedures, not the Mann-Whitney.
solution: Each of the n persons receives cream A on one arm and cream B on the other, so both treatments are observed on the same individual.
The two responses from one person are therefore dependent - a matched pair - and the natural analysis works with the n within-person differences $d_{i} = A_{i} - B_{i}$.
The two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test and the two-sample t-test both assume two INDEPENDENT samples, which is violated here.
A test for randomness addresses the order of a sequence and is irrelevant to comparing two treatments.
Given a continuous response and an assumption of normality for the differences, the appropriate procedure is the paired t-test on the $d_{i}$.
Hence option (c) is correct.

topic: Sampling Distributions: Sample Mean, Sample Variance, t, Chi-square, F
subtopic: Sampling Distributions: Sample Mean, Sample Variance, t, Chi-square, F
shortcut: $\operatorname{E}(X) = n/(n-2) = 10/8 = 1.25 > 1$, so statement 1 holds. Mode = $[(m-2)/m][n/(n+2)] = (3/5)(10/12) = 0.5 < 1$, so statement 2 fails.
tips: Two F formulas to memorise: mean = $n/(n-2)$ using only the DENOMINATOR d.f., and mode = $[(m-2)/m][n/(n+2)]$ using both.
The F distribution is positively skewed, so mode < median < mean. Since the mean is only 1.25, a mode below 1 is entirely expected - that intuition answers statement 2 before any arithmetic.
The mean of F(m,n) always exceeds 1 whenever $n > 2$, because $n/(n-2) > 1$. Statement 1 is therefore true for every admissible F distribution.
The mode is less than 1 for all m, n, since $[(m-2)/m] < 1$ and $[n/(n+2)] < 1 - a$ general fact worth carrying.
solution: For $X \sim F(m, n)$ with $m = 5$ and $n = 10$, the mean is $\operatorname{E}(X) = n/(n - 2)$, valid for $n > 2$.
$\operatorname{E}(X) = 10/(10 - 2) = 10/8 = 1.25$, which is greater than 1. Statement 1 is TRUE.
The mode of F(m, n) for $m > 2$ is Mode = $[(m - 2)/m]$ . $[n/(n + 2)]$.
Since $0.5 < 1$, statement 2 is FALSE.
Only statement 1 is correct, option (a).

topic: Non-parametric Tests
subtopic: Non-parametric Tests
stem: In 30 tosses of a coin, the sequence obtained is: $$\text{H T T H T H H H T H H T T H T H T H H T H T T H T H H T H T}$$ The number of runs is
shortcut: A run is a maximal block of identical symbols. Count the changeovers: the sequence switches 21 times in 30 tosses, so there are 22 runs.
tips: Runs = number of changes of symbol + 1. Counting CHANGES is faster and far less error-prone than bracketing blocks.
Mark the sequence in groups as you read: H | TT | H | T | HHH | T | HH | TT | $H \lvert T \rvert H \mid T$ | HH | T | H | TT | H | T | HH | $T \lvert H \rvert T$.

Sanity range: with 30 tosses the number of runs must lie between 2 and 30; a well-mixed fair sequence gives roughly $n/2 + 1 = 16$ or more, so 22 is plausible while 28 and 30 would be near-perfect alternation.

For the run test, the expected number of runs is $2 n_{1} n_{2}/n + 1$; here $n_{1} = 16$ heads and $n_{2} = 14$ tails give about 15.9, so 22 is on the high side, indicating more alternation than chance.
solution: A run is a maximal unbroken sequence of identical outcomes.
Reading the 30 tosses in order and grouping: H | TT | H | T | HHH | T | HH | TT | $H \lvert T \rvert H \mid T$ | HH | T | H | TT | H | T | HH | $T \lvert H \rvert T$.
Counting the groups: 1 H, 2 TT, 3 H, 4 T, 5 HHH, 6 T, 7 HH, 8 TT, 9 H, 10 T, 11 H, 12 T, 13 HH, 14 T, 15 H, 16 TT, 17 H, 18 T, 19 HH, 20 T, 21 H, 22 T.
The group lengths sum to $1+2+1+1+3+1+2+2+1+1+1+1+2+1+1+2+1+1+2+1+1+1 = 30$, confirming that every toss has been counted.
There are therefore 22 runs.
Option (b) is correct.

topic: Non-parametric Tests
subtopic: Non-parametric Tests
stem: A manufacturer claims a product's lifetime exceeds 250 hours, to be verified from 24 observed lifetimes. Which test can be used?
shortcut: One sample, a hypothesised value for the location (250 hours), and no distributional assumption - that is exactly the one-sample SIGN test.
tips: Match the test to the design: ONE sample against a stated value = sign test (or Wilcoxon signed-rank); TWO independent samples = Mann-Whitney U or median test; fit to a distribution = K-S or $\chi^{2}$.
The sign test simply counts how many of the 24 lifetimes exceed 250 and refers that count to a Binomial(24, 0.5) under H0 - no distributional assumption at all.
Mann-Whitney and the median test both need two samples, so options (b) and (c) are ruled out by the design alone.
The Kolmogorov-Smirnov test would require a fully specified distribution, not just a claim about one quantile, so option (d) is also inapplicable.
solution: The manufacturer's claim concerns the location of a single population - that the lifetime typically exceeds 250 hours - and there is only one sample, of 24 observations.

The sign test is the standard one-sample non-parametric procedure for a hypothesised median or location value: count how many observations exceed 250 and compare that count with Binomial(n, 0.5) under H0.
The Mann-Whitney U test and the median test both compare TWO independent samples, so they do not apply.
The Kolmogorov-Smirnov test compares the empirical CDF with a fully specified theoretical distribution, which is not what is claimed here.
Hence the sign test is appropriate, option (a).

topic: Order Statistics - Minimum, Maximum, Range, Median
subtopic: Order Statistics - Minimum, Maximum, Range, Median
stem: If $X_{(r)}$ is the $r$th order statistic from a sample of size $n$ from a continuous c.d.f. $F(x)$, then $F(X_{(r)})$ is the $r$th order statistic in a sample of size $n$ from the
shortcut: The probability integral transform makes $F(X) \sim U(0,1)$. Since F is increasing, it preserves order, so $F(X_{r})$ is the rth order statistic of $a U(0,1)$ sample.
tips: Probability integral transform: for continuous F, the variable $U = F(X)$ is always Uniform(0,1), whatever the parent distribution. This is the single most useful transformation in order-statistic theory.
F is non-decreasing, so it maps the rth smallest X to the rth smallest U - order is preserved and the ranks carry over unchanged.
Consequence worth memorising: $F(X_{r})$ ~ Beta($r, n - r + 1$), which gives $\operatorname{E}[F(X_{r})] = r/(n+1)$ - the basis of plotting positions in probability plots.
The result is distribution-free, which is exactly why non-parametric methods and simulation both rest on it.
solution: Let X have a continuous CDF F. The probability integral transform states that $U = F(X)$ follows the Uniform(0,1) distribution.
Indeed, for $0 < u < 1, \operatorname{P}(F(X) \le u) = \operatorname{P}(X \le F^{-1}(u)) = F(F^{-1}(u)) = u$, which is the $U(0,1)$ CDF.
Applying F to each of $X_{1}$, ..., $X_{n}$ gives a random sample $U_{1}$, ..., $U_{n}$ from $U(0,1)$.
Because F is non-decreasing, it preserves the ordering of the sample, so the rth smallest of the U values is F applied to the rth smallest X value: $U_{r} = F(X_{r})$.
Therefore $F(X_{r})$ is the rth order statistic of a sample of size n from the Uniform(0,1) distribution.
Option (b) is correct.

topic: Correlation: Distribution of r, Partial, Multiple, Intraclass, Correlation Ratio
subtopic: Correlation: Distribution of r, Partial, Multiple, Intraclass, Correlation Ratio
stem: Let $r_{ij}$ denote the correlation between $X_i,X_j$. If $r_{12}=\sin^2\theta,\ r_{13}=\cos\theta,\ r_{23}=\sin\theta$ ($-\pi\le\theta\le\pi$), the partial correlation $r_{12.3}$ is
shortcut: Substitute into r12.$3 = (r_{12} - r_{13} r_{23})/sqrt((1-r_{13}^{2})(1-r_{23}^{2}))$. The numerator is $\sin^{2} t - \sin t \cos t$ and the denominator is |$\sin t \cos t$|, so the ratio is $\tan t - 1$.
tips: The denominator simplifies first: $(1 - \cos^{2} t)(1 - \sin^{2} t) = \sin^{2} t \cos^{2} t$, whose square root is |$\sin t \cos t$| - spotting this collapses the whole expression.
Factor the numerator as $\sin t (\sin t - \cos t)$ so that the common $\sin t$ cancels against the denominator, leaving $(\sin t - \cos t)/\cos t = \tan t - 1$.
Memorise the partial correlation formula r12.$3 = (r_{12} - r_{13} r_{23})/sqrt((1 - r_{13}^{2})(1 - r_{23}^{2}))$; every item in this sub-topic is one substitution away from it.
Options (a), (b) and (d) all involve $2 \theta$, which never arises from this cancellation - a structural cue that (c) is the intended form.
solution: The partial correlation formula is r12.$3 = (r_{12} - r_{13} r_{23})/sqrt[(1 - r_{13}^{2})(1 - r_{23}^{2})]$.
Substituting $r_{12} = \sin^{2} t, r_{13} = \cos t, r_{23} = \sin t$, the numerator is $\sin^{2} t - (\cos t)(\sin t) = \sin t (\sin t - \cos t)$.
For the denominator, $1 - r_{13}^{2} = 1 - \cos^{2} t = \sin^{2} t$ and $1 - r_{23}^{2} = 1 - \sin^{2} t = \cos^{2} t$.
So the denominator is $\sqrt{\sin^{2} t \cos^{2} t}$ = |$\sin t \cos t$|.
Taking the principal branch where $\sin t \cos t > 0, r_{12}$.$3 = \sin t (\sin t - \cos t)/(\sin t \cos t) = (\sin t - \cos t)/\cos t$.
This equals $\tan t - 1$, option (c).

topic: Correlation: Distribution of r, Partial, Multiple, Intraclass, Correlation Ratio
subtopic: Correlation: Distribution of r, Partial, Multiple, Intraclass, Correlation Ratio
stem: When two judges rank two individuals only, Spearman's rank correlation coefficient can assume the values
shortcut: With only two individuals the second judge either agrees $(d = 0, \rho = 1)$ or reverses (sum $d^{2} = 2, \rho = 1 - 12/6$ = -1). No other outcome exists.
tips: Spearman's $\rho = 1 - 6$ sum($d^{2}$)/$(n(n^{2} - 1))$. With $n = 2$ the denominator is $2(3) = 6$, so $\rho = 1$ - sum($d^{2}$).
Only two rankings of two items are possible, so only two values of $\rho$ can occur - enumerate them rather than reasoning abstractly.
0 is impossible because sum($d^{2}$) would have to be 1, but with $n = 2$ the differences are either both 0 or both +-1, giving sum($d^{2}$) equal to 0 or 2.
General principle: for small n the set of attainable rank correlations is discrete, and the gaps between attainable values are large - a reason rank tests need adequate n.
solution: Spearman's rank correlation is $\rho = 1 - 6$ sum($d_{i}^{2}$)/$(n(n^{2} - 1))$, where $d_{i}$ are the differences of ranks.
There are only two possible rankings by the second judge. If the judges agree, the ranks are $(1,2)$ and $(1,2)$, so $d = (0,0)$ and sum($d^{2}$) = 0, giving $\rho = 1$.
If the judges disagree, the ranks are $(1,2)$ and $(2,1)$, so $d = (-1, +1)$ and sum($d^{2}$) = 2, giving $\rho = 1 - 2$ = -1.
No other configuration exists, so $\rho$ can only be -1 or +1; the value 0 is unattainable.
Option (b) is correct.

topic: Order Statistics - Minimum, Maximum, Range, Median
subtopic: Order Statistics - Minimum, Maximum, Range, Median
stem: $X_1,\ldots,X_5$ are five independent observations from a continuous distribution with c.d.f. $F(x)$ and p.d.f. $f(x)$. What is the p.d.f. of the sample median?
shortcut: For $n = 5$ the median is the 3rd order statistic, so the constant is 5!/$(2! 2!) = 30$ and the density is $30 F^{2} (1-F)^{2} f$.
tips: General order-statistic density: $g_{r}(x) = [n!/((r-1)!(n-r)!)] [F(x)]^{r-1} [1 - F(x)]^{n-r} f(x)$. Substitute r and n and the whole answer follows.
For the median of 5 observations, $r = 3$, so the exponents are $r - 1 = 2$ and $n - r = 2$ - symmetric, as the median should be.
The constant 5!/$(2!2!) = 120/4 = 30$ is what separates (c) from (d); option (c) has the right shape but the wrong normalising constant.
Options (a) and (b) are the densities of the MAXIMUM and the MINIMUM respectively - useful to recognise as the $r = n$ and $r = 1$ special cases.
solution: For a sample of size n from a continuous distribution, the density of the rth order statistic is $g_{r}(x) = [n!/((r-1)!(n-r)!)] [F(x)]^{r-1} [1-F(x)]^{n-r} f(x)$.
With $n = 5$ observations, the sample median is the third order statistic, so $r = 3$.
The exponents are $r - 1 = 2$ on F(x) and $n - r = 2$ on 1 - F(x).
The constant is 5!/$(2! 2!) = 120/(2 \times 2) = 30$.
Hence the density of the sample median is $30 [F(x)]^{2} [1 - F(x)]^{2} f(x)$.
Option (d) is correct.

topic: Measures of Location & Dispersion
subtopic: Measures of Location & Dispersion
stem: Consider the following statements: 1. If original scores are multiplied by a constant, mean and standard deviation are also multiplied by that constant. 2. If original scores are multiplied by a constant, the SD is multiplied by the absolute value of the constant. 3. If a constant is added to each score, the SD remains unchanged.
shortcut: Statement 1 is imprecise: multiplying by a NEGATIVE constant multiplies the mean by it but multiplies the SD by its absolute value. Statements 2 and 3 state the rules correctly.
tips: Scaling rules: mean(cX) = c mean(X) but SD(cX) = |c| SD(X). The absolute value is compulsory because a standard deviation can never be negative.
Shift rules: mean(X + k) = mean(X) + k but SD(X + k) = SD(X). Dispersion is unaffected by a change of origin.
Statements 1 and 2 make claims about the same operation, and one is a corrected version of the other - a sure sign that the imprecise one is the false statement.
Variance scales as $c^{2}$: $\operatorname{Var}(cX) = c^{2} \operatorname{Var}(X)$. Taking the square root recovers |c|, which is where the absolute value comes from.
solution: Let Y = cX for a constant c. Then mean(Y) = c mean(X) and $\operatorname{Var}(Y) = c^{2} \operatorname{Var}(X)$, so SD(Y) = |c| SD(X).

Statement 1 asserts that both the mean AND the standard deviation are multiplied by the constant. This is true for the mean but false for the SD when c is negative, since a standard deviation is non-negative. FALSE as stated.
Statement 2 asserts that the SD is multiplied by the ABSOLUTE VALUE of the constant, which is exactly correct. TRUE.
Statement 3: for $Y = X + k, \operatorname{Var}(Y) = \operatorname{Var}(X)$, so the SD is unchanged by a change of origin. TRUE.
Only statements 2 and 3 are correct.
Option (b) is correct.

topic: Bivariate & Multivariate Data; Association & Contingency
subtopic: Bivariate & Multivariate Data; Association & Contingency
stem: For attributes, the relations: 1. $(AB)>(A)$ 2. $(AB)<(A)+(B)-N$ 3. $(ABC)>(AB)+(AC)+(BC)-(A)-(B)-(C)+N$ Which are correct for **inconsistency** of data?
shortcut: Consistency requires every ultimate class frequency to be non-negative. Each of the three relations makes one such class negative - $(AB) > (A)$ makes $(A \beta) < 0, (AB) < (A)+(B)-N$ makes $(\alpha \beta) < 0$, and the third makes $(\alpha \beta \gamma) < 0$. All three signal inconsistency.
tips: Test for consistency by computing the ULTIMATE class frequencies; the data are inconsistent as soon as any of them is negative.
Two attributes give the standard bounds $\max(0, (A)+(B)-N) \le (AB) \le \min((A),(B))$. Statements 1 and 2 are simply violations of the upper and lower bound respectively.

For three attributes, inclusion-exclusion gives $(\alpha \beta \gamma) = N - (A) - (B) - (C) + (AB) + (AC) + (BC)$ - (ABC). Requiring this to be non-negative gives (ABC) <= $(AB)+(AC)+(BC)-(A)-(B)-(C)+N$; statement 3 is the violation of that bound.

When all listed relations are constructed as violations of the same non-negativity principle, expect 'all of them' - but derive at least the three-attribute one, since its sign is easy to get backwards.
solution: A set of attribute frequencies is CONSISTENT only if every ultimate class frequency is non-negative.

Statement 1: since the class AB is contained in A, we always have $(AB) \le (A)$; indeed $(A \beta) = (A) - (AB) \ge 0$. So $(AB) > (A)$ forces $(A \beta) < 0$ and the data are inconsistent. CORRECT indicator.

Statement 2: $(\alpha \beta) = N - (A) - (B) + (AB)$ must be non-negative, which gives $(AB) \ge (A) + (B) - N$. So $(AB) < (A) + (B) - N$ makes $(\alpha \beta) < 0$ and the data are inconsistent. CORRECT indicator.
Statement 3: by inclusion-exclusion, $(\alpha \beta \gamma) = N - (A) - (B) - (C) + (AB) + (AC) + (BC)$ - (ABC).

Non-negativity of ($\alpha \beta \gamma$) requires (ABC) <= $(AB) + (AC) + (BC) - (A) - (B) - (C) + N$. Hence the strict inequality in statement 3 makes $(\alpha \beta \gamma) < 0$ and signals inconsistency. CORRECT indicator.
All three relations indicate inconsistency, option (d).

topic: Correlation: Distribution of r, Partial, Multiple, Intraclass, Correlation Ratio
subtopic: Correlation: Distribution of r, Partial, Multiple, Intraclass, Correlation Ratio
stem: If $D=X-Y$ and $S_D^2=S_X^2+S_Y^2$, the correlation coefficient $r$ between $X,Y$ is
options: greater than zero but not equal to one
shortcut: In general $\operatorname{Var}(X - Y) = S_{X}^{2} + S_{Y}^{2} - 2 r S_{X} S_{Y}$. The given identity removes the cross term, so $2 r S_{X} S_{Y} = 0$ and hence $r = 0$.
tips: The variance of a difference carries a MINUS 2rS_X $S_{Y}$ term; the plain additive formula holds only when that term vanishes.
Since standard deviations are strictly positive for non-degenerate variables, $2 r S_{X} S_{Y} = 0$ forces $r = 0$ exactly - not merely 'small'.
Note this gives UNCORRELATED, not independent: the same identity would hold for dependent but uncorrelated variables.
Companion identity: $\operatorname{Var}(X + Y) = S_{X}^{2} + S_{Y}^{2} + 2 r S_{X} S_{Y}$, which likewise reduces to the additive form precisely when $r = 0$.
solution: For $D = X - Y$, the general variance formula is $S_{D}^{2} = S_{X}^{2} + S_{Y}^{2} - 2 r S_{X} S_{Y}$, where r is the correlation between X and Y.
The question states that $S_{D}^{2} = S_{X}^{2} + S_{Y}^{2}$.
Equating the two expressions gives $S_{X}^{2} + S_{Y}^{2} - 2 r S_{X} S_{Y} = S_{X}^{2} + S_{Y}^{2}$.
Hence $2 r S_{X} S_{Y} = 0$.
Since $S_{X}$ and $S_{Y}$ are positive for non-degenerate variables, $r = 0$.
Hence the correlation is exactly zero, option (c).

topic: Correlation: Distribution of r, Partial, Multiple, Intraclass, Correlation Ratio
subtopic: Correlation: Distribution of r, Partial, Multiple, Intraclass, Correlation Ratio
stem: $X$ has finite variance $\sigma^2$. If $Y=20-X$, the correlation between $X$ and $(X+Y)X$ is
shortcut: $Y = 20 - X$ makes $X + Y = 20$ identically, so $(X + Y)X = 20X$. The correlation of X with 20X is +1.
tips: Simplify the expression BEFORE computing anything: the sum X + Y collapses to the constant 20, which is the entire content of the question.
Correlation between a variable and a positive multiple of itself is exactly +1; a negative multiple would give -1.
The variance $\sigma^{2}$ is stated only to guarantee that X is non-degenerate so that the correlation is defined - it never enters the answer.
Option (a) -1 is the correlation between X and Y themselves, the natural trap if you stop at $Y = 20 - X$ without simplifying the product.
solution: Since $Y = 20 - X$, the sum $X + Y = X + (20 - X) = 20$ is a constant.
Therefore the second variable is $(X + Y)X = 20X$.
The correlation between X and 20X is $\operatorname{Cov}(X, 20X)$/(sd(X) . sd(20X)) = $20 \operatorname{Var}(X)$/(sd(X) . 20 sd(X)) = 1.
In general, corr(X, aX) equals +1 for $a > 0$, and here $a = 20 > 0$.
The finite variance $\sigma^{2} > 0$ ensures the correlation is well defined.
Hence the correlation is 1, option (d).

topic: Correlation: Distribution of r, Partial, Multiple, Intraclass, Correlation Ratio
subtopic: Correlation: Distribution of r, Partial, Multiple, Intraclass, Correlation Ratio
stem: The correlation coefficient in a bivariate set-up is $0.7$. 1. The percentage of variation in the dependent variable explained by the independent variable is 49. 2. Both regression coefficients are positive. 3. Both regression coefficients are negative.
shortcut: $r^{2} = 0.49$ gives 49% explained variation, so statement 1 holds. Since r = +$0.7 > 0$, both regression coefficients share that positive sign, so statement 2 holds and statement 3 fails.
tips: Percentage of variation explained is $r^{2} x 100$, not r x 100. Here $0.7^{2} = 0.49$, i.e. 49%.
Sign rule: $r, b_{yx}$ and $b_{xy}$ always carry the SAME sign, because $r^{2} = b_{yx} b_{xy}$ and r = sign(b) $\sqrt{b_{yx} b_{x}y}$.
Statements 2 and 3 are direct contradictions, so exactly one of them must be true - decide by the sign of r and both are settled at once.
Remember 'r^2 explains, r describes': $r^{2}$ is the coefficient of determination and r merely indicates strength and direction.
solution: The correlation coefficient is $r = 0.7$.
Statement 1: the proportion of variation in the dependent variable explained by the independent variable is the coefficient of determination $r^{2} = 0.49$, i.e. 49%. TRUE.
The two regression coefficients satisfy $b_{yx} b_{xy} = r^{2}$ and both carry the same sign as r.
Statement 2: since r = +0.7 is positive, both regression coefficients are positive. TRUE.
Statement 3: this contradicts statement 2 and is therefore FALSE.
Statements 1 and 2 are correct, option (b).

topic: Correlation: Distribution of r, Partial, Multiple, Intraclass, Correlation Ratio
subtopic: Correlation: Distribution of r, Partial, Multiple, Intraclass, Correlation Ratio
stem: In a trivariate distribution, if $r_{12}=r_{23}=r_{31}=\rho\ne1$, the value of $R_{1.23}$ is
tips: Compute R SQUARED first and take the square root only at the very end - working with R directly invites algebraic slips.
The cancellation of $(1 - \rho)$ between numerator and denominator is the whole trick; factor $1 - \rho^{2}$ as $(1-\rho)(1+\rho)$ before simplifying.
Check the limit $\rho \to 1$: $R^{2} \to 2/2 = 1$, so R -> 1 as the variables become perfectly correlated. Option (d) satisfies this; option (a) gives $1/sqrt2$ and fails.
This is the square root of the 2018 Q29 result - the same identity appears in both papers, once as $R^{2}$ and once as R.
solution: With $r_{12} = r_{13} = r_{23} = \rho$, the numerator is $\rho^{2} + \rho^{2} - 2\rho^{3} = 2\rho^{2}(1 - \rho)$.
The denominator is $1 - \rho^{2} = (1 - \rho)(1 + \rho)$.
Cancelling $(1 - \rho)$, which is non-zero since $\rho$ is not 1, gives $R^{2}_{1.23} = 2\rho^{2}/(1 + \rho)$.
Taking the positive square root: $R_{1.23} = \sqrt{2} \rho/\sqrt{1 + \rho}$.
Hence option (d) is correct.

topic: Distributions of Functions of Random Variables
subtopic: Distributions of Functions of Random Variables
stem: $X,Y$ are independent standard normal. The distribution of $U=\left(\dfrac{X-Y}{X+Y}\right)^2$ is
shortcut: X - Y and X + Y are independent $N(0,2)$ variables (their covariance is $\operatorname{Var}(X) - \operatorname{Var}(Y) = 0$). So U is the ratio of two independent $\chi^{2}_{1}/1$ quantities, i.e. $F(1,1)$.
tips: For i.i.d. normals, the sum and the difference are INDEPENDENT - a special property of the normal family that this question is built on.
$\operatorname{Cov}(X - Y, X + Y) = \operatorname{Var}(X) - \operatorname{Var}(Y) = 0$, and joint normality then upgrades zero correlation to full independence.
The common variance 2 cancels in the ratio, so no scaling constant survives - the answer is a pure F with 1 and 1 degrees of freedom.
Equivalently $(X-Y)/(X+Y)$ is a standard Cauchy, and the square of a Cauchy is $F(1,1)$. Both routes give option (d).
solution: X and Y are independent $N(0,1)$, so $X - Y \sim N(0,2)$ and $X + Y \sim N(0,2)$.
$\operatorname{Cov}(X - Y, X + Y) = \operatorname{Var}(X) - \operatorname{Var}(Y) = 1 - 1 = 0$, and since the pair is jointly normal, X - Y and X + Y are INDEPENDENT.
Set $A = (X - Y)/\sqrt{2}$ and $B = (X + Y)/\sqrt{2}$; these are independent $N(0,1)$.
Then $U = ((X-Y)/(X+Y))^{2} = A^{2}/B^{2}$, and $A^{2}$ and $B^{2}$ are independent $\chi^{2}$ variables each with 1 degree of freedom.
By definition, the ratio ($\chi$-square_1/1)/($\chi$-square_1/1) of independent $\chi$-squares follows $F(1, 1)$.
Hence $U \sim F(1,1)$, option (d).

topic: Tests of Significance & Small Sample Tests
subtopic: Tests of Significance & Small Sample Tests
stem: The df of the $F$-statistic for testing equality of variances of two normal populations (unknown means), from independent samples of sizes 20 and 37, are
shortcut: Each sample variance loses one degree of freedom for its estimated mean, so the d.f. are $20 - 1 = 19$ and $37 - 1 = 36$.
tips: Rule: the variance-ratio F test uses $(n_{1} - 1, n_{2} - 1)$ degrees of freedom when both population means are UNKNOWN and estimated from the samples.
If the means were KNOWN, no degree of freedom would be lost and the d.f. would be n1 and n2 - the reason the question specifies 'unknown means'.
Order matters only for reading the table: place the larger variance in the numerator so that $F \ge 1$, then use the corresponding d.f. first.
Option (a) subtracts 2 from each sample size, confusing this with the pooled t-test's $n_{1} + n_{2} - 2$ - keep the two adjustments apart.
solution: To test the equality of two normal variances we use the ratio of the two sample variances, $F = s_{1}^{2}/s_{2}^{2}$.
Each sample variance is computed about its own SAMPLE mean, because the population means are unknown, so one degree of freedom is lost per sample.
For the first sample of size 20, the numerator d.f. is $20 - 1 = 19$.
For the second sample of size 37, the denominator d.f. is $37 - 1 = 36$.
Hence the statistic follows $F(19, 36)$ under the null hypothesis.
Option (b) is correct.

topic: Non-parametric Tests
subtopic: Non-parametric Tests
stem: To test whether the upper 60th percentile of a continuous distribution equals 25 or less, the sign test (sample size 10) rejects $H_0$ if the number of observations larger than 25 is $\ge7$. Given $(0.6)^7\approx0.028$, the size of the test is approximately
shortcut: Under H0 the count of observations above 25 is Binomial(10, 0.6). The size is $\operatorname{P}(X \ge 7) = 0.2150 + 0.1209 + 0.0403 + 0.0060 = 0.382$.
tips: The size of a test is the rejection probability computed UNDER H0, so use $p = 0.6$ (the null quantile), not 0.5.
Sum all four upper terms: $\operatorname{P}(7), \operatorname{P}(8), \operatorname{P}(9)$ and $\operatorname{P}(10)$. Stopping at $\operatorname{P}(X = 7) = 0.215$ gives a badly understated size.
The supplied hint $(0.6)^{7} = 0.028$ feeds every term: $\operatorname{P}(7) = 120(0.028)(0.064), \operatorname{P}(8) = 45(0.0168)(0.16)$, and so on.
Since the mean of Binomial(10, 0.6) is 6, a cut-off of 7 is barely above the mean, so a LARGE size is expected - options (a), (b) and (c) are implausibly small.
solution: Under H0 the upper 60th percentile equals 25, so $\operatorname{P}(X > 25) = 0.6$ and the number of observations exceeding 25 in a sample of 10 is Binomial(10, 0.6).
The test rejects H0 when this count is at least 7, so the size is $\operatorname{P}(B \ge 7)$ with B ~ Binomial(10, 0.6).
The size of the test is approximately 0.38, option (d).

topic: Order Statistics - Minimum, Maximum, Range, Median
subtopic: Order Statistics - Minimum, Maximum, Range, Median
stem: Ten runners' finishing times (seconds) are i.i.d. $U(10,11)$, independent of each other. The expected time of the winner is
shortcut: The winner has the MINIMUM time. For U(a,b) with n observations, $\operatorname{E}[\min] = a + (b-a)/(n+1) = 10 + 1/11$.
tips: Uniform order-statistic means: $\operatorname{E}[X_{r}] = a + (b - a) r/(n+1)$. For the minimum $r = 1$ and for the maximum $r = n$ - two formulas in one.
The winner is the FASTEST, i.e. the smallest time, so $r = 1$. Reading 'winner' as the maximum gives $10 + 10/11$ and no matching option.
The n + 1 in the denominator is the standard 'plotting position' divisor - the n order statistics divide the interval into n + 1 equal expected gaps.
With 10 runners on a 1-second interval, the expected winning margin below 10 seconds is $1/11 = 0.0909 s - a$ small, plausible figure.
solution: The ten finishing times are i.i.d. Uniform(10, 11), and the winner's time is the minimum, $X_{1}$.
For a sample of size n from U(a, b), the rth order statistic has mean $\operatorname{E}[X_{r}] = a + (b - a) r/(n + 1)$.
For the minimum, $r = 1$, so $\operatorname{E}[X_{1}] = a + (b - a)/(n + 1)$.
Substituting $a = 10, b = 11$ and $n = 10$: $\operatorname{E}[X_{1}] = 10 + 1/11$.
Numerically this is 10.0909 seconds.
Hence the expected time of the winner is $10 + 1/11$, option (a).

topic: Classical & Axiomatic Probability, Consequences
subtopic: Classical & Axiomatic Probability, Consequences
stem: Consider the following statements: 1. If ordered samples of size $r$ are drawn from $n$ elements, there are $n(n-1)(n-2)\cdots(n-r+1)$ samples without replacement. 2. If $n$ distinguishable balls are randomly placed in $n$ cells, the probability that each cell is occupied is $1$.
shortcut: Statement 1 is the standard nPr count. Statement 2 is false: the probability that n distinguishable balls fill n cells is n!/$n^{n}$, which is far below 1 for $n \ge 2$.
tips: Ordered sampling counts: WITHOUT replacement $n(n-1)$...$(n-r+1)$ = nPr; WITH replacement $n^{r}$. Learn the pair together.
Total placements of n distinguishable balls in n cells is $n^{n}$; favourable ones (one per cell) number n!, so the probability is n!/$n^{n}$ - for $n = 3$ that is $6/27 = 0.22$, nowhere near 1.
Any statement asserting that a non-trivial probability equals exactly 1 deserves immediate suspicion; certainty is rare.
This is the classical occupancy problem, and n!/$n^{n}$ tends to 0 rapidly - by Stirling it behaves like $\sqrt{2 pi n} e^{-n}$.
solution: Statement 1: to draw an ordered sample of size r from n elements without replacement, the first element can be chosen in n ways, the second in n-1 ways, and so on down to $n - r + 1$ ways for the rth.
The total is $n(n-1)(n-2)$...$(n-r+1)$ = nPr, exactly as stated. TRUE.
Statement 2: placing n distinguishable balls into n cells at random gives $n^{n}$ equally likely arrangements.
The arrangements in which every cell is occupied are exactly the ones with one ball per cell, and there are n! of them.
Hence the probability is n!/$n^{n}$, which equals 1 only for $n = 1$; for $n = 3$ it is $6/27 = 0.222$. The claim that it is 1 is FALSE.
Only statement 1 is correct, option (a).

topic: Conditional Probability, Law of Total Probability, Bayes' Theorem
subtopic: Conditional Probability, Law of Total Probability, Bayes' Theorem
stem: A die is loaded so each odd number is twice as likely as each even number. $A$: number $>3$. $B$: number is a perfect square. 1. $P(B)=1/3$. 2. $P(B\mid A)=1/2$.
shortcut: Odd faces have probability $2/9$ each and even faces $1/9$ each. Then $\operatorname{P}(B) = \operatorname{P}(1) + \operatorname{P}(4) = 2/9 + 1/9 = 1/3$ (statement 1 true), while $\operatorname{P}(B\mid A) = \operatorname{P}(4)/\operatorname{P}({4,5,6}) = (1/9)/(4/9) = 1/4$, not $1/2$.
tips: Set up the weights first: 3 odd faces at 2p and 3 even faces at p give $9p = 1$, so $p = 1/9$. Everything else is a two-term sum.
The perfect squares in 1 to 6 are 1 and 4 only - 9 is out of range. Miscounting this set is the commonest error in the item.
For the conditional, intersect BEFORE dividing: A = {4,5,6} and B = {1,4}, so A n B = {4} with probability $1/9$.

Sanity check: $\operatorname{P}(B) = 1/3$ while $\operatorname{P}(B\mid A) = 1/4$, so knowing the number exceeds 3 makes a perfect square LESS likely - reasonable, since the square 1 is excluded by A.
solution: Let each even face have probability p; then each odd face has probability 2p. Since there are three of each, $3(2p) + 3p = 9p = 1$, so $p = 1/9$.
Thus $\operatorname{P}(1) = \operatorname{P}(3) = \operatorname{P}(5) = 2/9$ and $\operatorname{P}(2) = \operatorname{P}(4) = \operatorname{P}(6) = 1/9$.
Event A (number greater than 3) = {4, 5, 6}, so $\operatorname{P}(A) = 1/9 + 2/9 + 1/9 = 4/9$.
Event B (perfect square) = {1, 4}, so $\operatorname{P}(B) = 2/9 + 1/9 = 3/9 = 1/3$. Statement 1 is TRUE.
A intersect B = {4}, with probability $1/9$, so $\operatorname{P}(B\mid A) = (1/9)/(4/9) = 1/4$.
Statement 2 claims $1/2$ and is therefore FALSE. Only statement 1 holds, option (a).

topic: Random Variables & Distribution Functions
subtopic: Random Variables & Distribution Functions
stem: If $p(x)=kp^x$, $0<p<1$, $x=0,2,4,6,\ldots$, the value of $k$ for which $p(x)$ is a p.m.f. is
shortcut: The support is the EVEN integers, so the sum is $k(1 + p^{2} + p^{4} + ...) = k/(1 - p^{2}) = 1$, giving $k = 1 - p^{2}$.
tips: Read the support carefully: $x = 0, 2, 4$, ... means the ratio between consecutive terms is $p^{2}$, not p. That single observation is the whole question.
Geometric series: sum of $r^{j}$ for $j \ge 0$ is $1/(1 - r)$. Here $r = p^{2}$, so the normaliser is $1 - p^{2}$.
Option (a) 1 - p is the answer to the SAME question with support 0, 1, 2, 3, ... - the trap for candidates who skim the support.
Check with $p = 1/2$: $k = 3/4$, and the probabilities $3/4, 3/16, 3/64$, ... sum to $(3/4)/(1 - 1/4) = 1$.
solution: The probability mass function is $p(x) = k p^{x}$ for $x = 0, 2, 4, 6$, ..., i.e. only the even non-negative integers.
Writing $x = 2j$ for $j = 0, 1, 2$, ..., the masses are $k p^{2j} = k (p^{2})^{j}$.
For p(x) to be a valid pmf, the total must be 1: $k \sum (p^{2})^{j} = 1$.
Since $0 < p < 1$ we have $0 < p^{2} < 1$, so the geometric series sums to $1/(1 - p^{2})$.
Option (c) is correct.

topic: Distributions of Functions of Random Variables
subtopic: Distributions of Functions of Random Variables
stem: $X,Y$ are independent normal with means $1,2$ and SDs $3,4$. $Z=X-Y$. 1. Median and SD of $Z$ are $-1$ and $5$ respectively. 2. $P(Z+1<0)=0.5$.
shortcut: $Z = X - Y \sim N(1 - 2, 9 + 16) = N(-1, 25)$, so its median equals its mean -1 and its SD is 5 - statement 1 holds. And $\operatorname{P}(Z + 1 < 0) = \operatorname{P}(Z < -1) = \operatorname{P}\!\left(\text{Z < median}\right) = 0.5$ - statement 2 holds.
tips: Convert SDs to variances before adding: 3 and 4 give 9 and 16, whose sum is 25 and whose square root is 5. Adding the SDs directly would give 7 - the classic error.
Variances ADD for a difference of independent variables; the minus sign disappears on squaring.
The normal distribution is symmetric, so mean = median = mode. Statement 2 is then just 'the probability of being below the median is $1/2'$.
Note how statements 1 and 2 reinforce each other: once the median is identified as -1, statement 2 follows without any table look-up.
solution: $X \sim N(1, 3^{2}) = N(1, 9)$ and $Y \sim N(2, 4^{2}) = N(2, 16)$, independent.
$Z = X - Y$ is normal with mean 1 - 2 = -1 and variance $9 + 16 = 25$, so SD(Z) = 5.
Because the normal distribution is symmetric about its mean, the median of Z equals its mean, -1. Statement 1 is TRUE.
$\operatorname{P}(Z + 1 < 0) = \operatorname{P}(Z < -1)$.
Since -1 is the median of Z, this probability is exactly 0.5. Statement 2 is TRUE.
Both statements are correct, option (c).

topic: Standard Discrete Distributions
subtopic: Standard Discrete Distributions
stem: Distributions possessing the lack-of-memory property are
shortcut: The lack-of-memory (memoryless) property characterises exactly two distributions: the GEOMETRIC in the discrete case and the EXPONENTIAL in the continuous case.
tips: Memorise the pairing: geometric (discrete) and exponential (continuous) are the ONLY memoryless distributions, and each is uniquely characterised by that property.
Statement of the property: $\operatorname{P}(X > s + t \mid X > s) = \operatorname{P}(X > t)$. Waiting time already spent gives no information about remaining waiting time.
The exponential is a special $\Gamma$ (shape 1), but a general $\Gamma$ is NOT memoryless - option (a) is eliminated by that distinction.
The Cauchy has no mean at all and is defined on the whole real line, so it cannot describe a waiting time and is not memoryless.
solution: A distribution is memoryless if $\operatorname{P}(X > s + t \mid X > s) = \operatorname{P}(X > t)$ for all $s, t > 0$ - the past duration gives no information about the future.

For the exponential with rate $\lambda, \operatorname{P}(X > t) = e^{-\lambda t}$, so $\operatorname{P}(X > s+t)/\operatorname{P}(X > s) = e^{-\lambda t} = \operatorname{P}(X > t)$. Memoryless, and it is the ONLY continuous distribution with this property.
For the geometric with success probability $p, \operatorname{P}(X > k) = (1-p)^{k}$, so the same cancellation occurs. It is the only discrete distribution with the property.
The Beta distribution has bounded support and the general $\Gamma$ has an increasing or decreasing hazard rate, so neither is memoryless.
The Cauchy is symmetric on the whole real line and is not a waiting-time distribution at all.
Hence the memoryless distributions are the geometric and the exponential, option (c).

topic: Random Vectors: Joint, Marginal & Conditional Distributions
subtopic: Random Vectors: Joint, Marginal & Conditional Distributions
stem: $X,Y$ have joint p.d.f. $f(x,y)=6(1-x-y)$ for $x>0,y>0,x+y<1$ (else $0$). What is $P(X\ge0.4)$?
shortcut: Integrate out y to get the marginal $f_{X}(x) = 3(1-x)^{2}$ on $(0,1)$. Then $\operatorname{P}(X \ge 0.4)$ = the integral from 0.4 to $1 = (0.6)^{3} = 0.216$, i.e. about 0.21.
tips: Get the marginal first: for a fixed x the y-range is $(0, 1-x)$, and the inner $\int 6(1-x-y)\,dy$ is $3(1-x)^{2} - a$ clean, memorable result.
Recognise $f_{X}(x) = 3(1-x)^{2}$ as the Beta(1,3) density, so $\operatorname{P}(X > c) = (1 - c)^{3}$ directly. No second integral is needed.
$(0.6)^{3} = 0.216$ rounds to 0.21 at two decimals; option (b) 0.25 would correspond to $(0.63)^{3}$, so keep three decimals before rounding.

Sanity check: X is concentrated near 0 (its mean is $1/4$), so $\operatorname{P}(X \ge 0.4)$ should be well under a half - which rules out (c) and (d) as too large only marginally, so do the computation.
solution: The joint density is $f(x,y) = 6(1 - x - y)$ on the triangle $x > 0, y > 0, x + y < 1$.
For fixed x in $(0,1), y$ ranges over $(0, 1-x)$, so $f_{X}(x)$ = the $\int_{0}^{1-x} 6(1 - x - y)\,dy$.
Substituting $u = 1 - x - y$, the integral is 6 times the $\int u\,du$ from 0 to $1-x = 6(1-x)^{2}/2 = 3(1-x)^{2}$.
Thus X has the Beta(1,3) density $3(1-x)^{2}$ on $(0,1)$.
Rounding, the probability is about 0.21, option (a).

topic: Mathematical Expectation & Conditional Expectation
subtopic: Mathematical Expectation & Conditional Expectation
stem: The mean of $f(x)=12x^2(1-x),\ 0\le x\le1$ (else $0$), is
shortcut: $12x^{2}(1-x)$ is the Beta(3,2) density, whose mean is $a/(a+b) = 3/5 = 0.6$.
tips: Recognise the Beta kernel $x^{a-1}(1-x)^{b-1}$: here $a - 1 = 2$ and $b - 1 = 1$, so $a = 3$ and $b = 2$.
Beta mean = $a/(a+b)$ and variance = ab/$[(a+b)^{2}(a+b+1)]$. Recognition beats integration every time.
Verify the constant: $1/B(3,2) = \Gamma(5)/(\Gamma(3)\Gamma(2)) = 24/(2 \times 1) = 12$, matching the printed density - a good check that a and b are right.
Direct integration also works: the $\int 12x^{3}(1-x)\,dx$ over $(0,1) = 12(1/4 - 1/5) = 12/20 = 0.6$.
solution: The density is $f(x) = 12 x^{2} (1 - x)$ on $[0,1]$.
Comparing with the Beta density $x^{a-1}(1-x)^{b-1}/B(a,b)$, we read $a - 1 = 2$ and $b - 1 = 1$, so $a = 3$ and $b = 2$.
The normalising constant is $1/B(3,2) = \Gamma(5)/(\Gamma(3) \Gamma(2)) = 24/(2 \times 1) = 12$, confirming the identification.
For a Beta(a,b) variable the mean is $a/(a + b)$.
Hence the mean is $3/(3 + 2) = 3/5 = 0.6$.
Option (b) is correct.

topic: Characteristic Function, MGF & PGF; Inversion, Uniqueness, Continuity
subtopic: Characteristic Function, MGF & PGF; Inversion, Uniqueness, Continuity
stem: $Y$ has p.d.f. $f(y)=e^y$ if $y<0$ (else $0$). The MGF $M_Y(t)$ of $Y$ is
shortcut: M(t) = the $\int e^{ty} e^{y}\,dy$ = the $\int e^((t+1)y)\,dy$ from minus $\infty$ to $0 = 1/(t+1)$, converging when $t + 1 > 0$, i.e. t > -1.
tips: Y here is the NEGATIVE of an exponential (Y = -E with E ~ Exp(1)), so its MGF is the exponential MGF with t replaced by -t: $1/(1 + t)$.
Convergence direction flips with the sign of the support: for Exp(1) the MGF exists for $t < 1$, so for -Exp(1) it exists for t > -1.
Always state the region of convergence - it is what distinguishes option (a) from option (c), since the formulas are mirror images.
Options (b) and (d) use |t| and are not differentiable at $t = 0$, so they cannot be MGFs (an MGF must be smooth at 0 to generate moments).
solution: The density is $f(y) = e^{y}$ for $y < 0$ and 0 otherwise. Check: the $\int e^{y}$ from minus $\infty$ to 0 is 1, so f is a valid density.
$M_{Y}(t) = \operatorname{E}(e^{tY})$ = the integral from minus $\infty$ to 0 of $e^{ty} e^{y} dy$ = the $\int e^((t+1)y)\,dy$.
The antiderivative is $e^((t+1)y)/(t+1)$, evaluated from minus $\infty$ to 0.
For the lower limit to vanish we need $t + 1 > 0$, i.e. t > -1; then the value is $1/(t+1) - 0 = 1/(1 + t)$.
Option (c) is correct.

topic: Tchebycheff's & Kolmogorov's Inequalities
subtopic: Tchebycheff's & Kolmogorov's Inequalities
stem: $X$ is a non-negative random variable with finite, nonzero mean $\mu$. For every $t>0$:
shortcut: Markov's inequality: for $X \ge 0, \operatorname{P}(X \ge a) \le \operatorname{E}(X)/a$. Putting $a = t \mu$ gives $\operatorname{P}(X \ge t \mu) \le \mu/(t \mu) = 1/t$.
tips: Markov's inequality needs only non-negativity and a finite mean - exactly the assumptions stated, which is the signal to use it rather than Chebyshev.
The mu cancels completely, leaving the clean bound $1/t$. Any option retaining mu (options (a) and (c)) is therefore structurally wrong.
Direction check: an upper tail probability must be BOUNDED ABOVE, so the inequality sign must be <=. That eliminates options (a) and (d).
Chebyshev's inequality is Markov applied to $(X - \mu)^{2}$; knowing that link lets you derive one from the other under exam pressure.
solution: Markov's inequality states that for a non-negative random variable X with finite mean, and any $a > 0, \operatorname{P}(X \ge a) \le \operatorname{E}(X)/a$.
Here $\operatorname{E}(X) = \mu$, which is finite and non-zero, and $X \ge 0$ as required.
Take $a = t \mu$, which is positive for every $t > 0$.
Then $\operatorname{P}(X \ge t \mu) \le \mu/(t \mu) = 1/t$.
The bound is free of mu, as it must be, since scaling X does not change the ratio $X/\mu$.
Hence $\operatorname{P}(X \ge t \mu) \le 1/t$, option (b).

topic: Conditional Probability, Law of Total Probability, Bayes' Theorem
subtopic: Conditional Probability, Law of Total Probability, Bayes' Theorem
stem: Events $A,B$ with $P(A)=1/4,\ P(B\mid A)=1/2,\ P(A\mid B)=1/4$. Let $X=1$ if $A$ occurs (else 0), $Y=1$ if $B$ occurs (else 0). 1. $P(X^2+Y^2=1)=1/4$. 2. $P(XY=X^2Y^2)=1$.
shortcut: $\operatorname{P}(A \cap B) = \operatorname{P}(A)\operatorname{P}(B\mid A) = 1/8$ and $\operatorname{P}(B) = \operatorname{P}(A \cap B)/\operatorname{P}(A\mid B) = 1/2$. Statement 1 asks for $\operatorname{P}\!\left(\text{exactly one of A, B}\right) = 1/4 + 1/2 - 2(1/8) = 1/2$, not $1/4$ - false. Statement 2 is an identity for indicators - true.
tips: Indicators satisfy $X^{2} = X$ and $Y^{2} = Y$, so $X^{2} + Y^{2} = 1$ means exactly one of the two events occurs, and XY = $X^{2} Y^{2}$ holds identically.
Statement 2 needs no numbers at all - recognise it as an algebraic identity for $0/1$ variables and it is true with probability 1 whatever the events.

$\operatorname{P}\!\left(\text{exactly one}\right) = \operatorname{P}(A) + \operatorname{P}(B) - 2\operatorname{P}(A \cap B)$. The factor 2 is essential: it removes the intersection from BOTH marginal probabilities.

Recover P(B) from Bayes in reverse: $\operatorname{P}(B) = \operatorname{P}(A \cap B)/\operatorname{P}(A\mid B) = (1/8)/(1/4) = 1/2$. Chaining the two conditional probabilities is the only computational step in the item.
solution: From $\operatorname{P}(A) = 1/4$ and $\operatorname{P}(B\mid A) = 1/2$ we get $\operatorname{P}(A \cap B) = \operatorname{P}(A) \operatorname{P}(B\mid A) = 1/8$.
From $\operatorname{P}(A\mid B) = \operatorname{P}(A \cap B)/\operatorname{P}(B) = 1/4$ we get $\operatorname{P}(B) = (1/8)/(1/4) = 1/2$.
X and Y are indicator variables, so $X^{2} = X$ and $Y^{2} = Y$.

Statement 1: $X^{2} + Y^{2} = X + Y = 1$ means exactly one of A, B occurs. $\operatorname{P}\!\left(\text{exactly one}\right) = \operatorname{P}(A) + \operatorname{P}(B) - 2\operatorname{P}(A \cap B) = 1/4 + 1/2 - 2(1/8) = 3/4 - 1/4 = 1/2$. The claimed value $1/4$ is wrong, so statement 1 is FALSE.
Statement 2: since $X^{2} = X$ and $Y^{2} = Y$ identically, XY = $X^{2} Y^{2}$ always holds, so its probability is 1. TRUE.
Only statement 2 is correct, option (b).

topic: Bivariate Normal Distribution
subtopic: Bivariate Normal Distribution
stem: A bivariate normal random vector $(X,Y)$ with $V(X)=2,\ V(Y)=3,\ \text{Cov}(X,Y)=\alpha$ does **not** possess a density function. Then
shortcut: A bivariate normal has no density exactly when its covariance matrix is singular, i.e. |$\rho$| = 1, i.e. $Cov^{2} = \operatorname{V}(X)\operatorname{V}(Y) = 6$. So $\alpha$ = +-$\sqrt{6}$.
tips: Singular covariance matrix means the determinant $\operatorname{V}(X)\operatorname{V}(Y) - Cov^{2} = 0$, which is the same as $\rho^{2} = 1$. Compute the determinant, do not reason about $\rho$ separately.
A singular bivariate normal is concentrated on a LINE in the plane, which has zero area, so no two-dimensional density can exist.
The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality guarantees |$Cov$| <= $sqrt(\operatorname{V}(X)\operatorname{V}(Y)) = sqrt6$, so |$\alpha$| > 6 in option (d) is impossible for any distribution at all.
Option $(c) \mid \alpha$| < sqrt6 is precisely the case where the density DOES exist - the exact opposite of what is asked.
solution: The bivariate normal density exists if and only if its covariance matrix is positive definite, i.e. non-singular.
The covariance matrix here is $[[2, \alpha], [\alpha, 3]]$, with determinant $2(3) - \alpha^{2} = 6 - \alpha^{2}$.
The density fails to exist exactly when this determinant is zero, that is $\alpha^{2} = 6$.
Hence $\alpha$ = +$\sqrt{6}$ or -$\sqrt{6}$, which corresponds to correlation $\rho$ = +-1.
In that case the distribution is degenerate, concentrated on a straight line in the plane, so no two-dimensional density function exists.
Option (b) is correct.

topic: Modes of Convergence of Sequences of Random Variables
subtopic: Modes of Convergence of Sequences of Random Variables
stem: $U\sim U(0,1)$. The sequence $X_n=\sqrt n$ if $0<U<1/n^2$ (else $0$), $n\ge1$, converges
options: both with probability one and in mean square
with probability one but not in mean square
in mean square but not with probability one
neither with probability one nor in mean square
shortcut: $\operatorname{P}\!\left(X_{n}\ \text{is not 0}\right) = 1/n^{2}$, and the series of these converges, so Borel-Cantelli gives $X_{n} \to 0$ with probability one. Also $\operatorname{E}(X_{n}^{2}) = n(1/n^{2}) = 1/n \to 0$, so convergence in mean square holds too.
tips: Two separate computations, one for each mode: $\operatorname{P}\!\left(X_{n}\ \text{not 0}\right)$ for almost-sure convergence, $\operatorname{E}(X_{n}^{2})$ for mean-square convergence. Do them independently.

Borel-Cantelli I: if the sum of $\operatorname{P}(A_{n})$ converges then $\operatorname{P}\!\left(A_{n}\ \text{infinitely often}\right) = 0$. Here sum $1/n^{2}$ converges, so eventually $X_{n}$ is 0 forever.
$\operatorname{E}(X_{n}^{2}) = (sqrt n)^{2} x \operatorname{P}(U < 1/n^{2}) = n x 1/n^{2} = 1/n$. The value taken grows but its probability shrinks faster, so the second moment still dies.

Contrast with the classic counterexample $X_{n} = n$ on $(0, 1/n)$: there $\operatorname{P}\!\left(X_{n}\ \text{not 0}\right) = 1/n$ whose sum DIVERGES and $\operatorname{E}(X_{n}^{2}) = n$, so neither mode holds. Changing the exponents changes the answer completely.
solution: Let $A_{n}$ be the event {$0 < U < 1/n^{2}$}, on which $X_{n} = \sqrt{n}$; elsewhere $X_{n} = 0$. Then $\operatorname{P}(A_{n}) = 1/n^{2}$.
The series sum of $\operatorname{P}(A_{n})$ = sum of $1/n^{2}$ converges (it equals pi^2/6).

By the first Borel-Cantelli lemma, $\operatorname{P}\!\left(A_{n}\ \text{occurs infinitely often}\right) = 0$, so with probability one only finitely many $A_{n}$ occur and $X_{n} = 0$ for all large n.
Hence $X_{n}$ converges to 0 with probability one.
For mean-square convergence, $\operatorname{E}(X_{n}^{2}) = n \operatorname{P}(A_{n}) + 0 = n (1/n^{2}) = 1/n$, which tends to 0 as n grows.
So $X_{n}$ also converges to 0 in mean square. Both modes hold, option (a).

topic: Random Variables & Distribution Functions
subtopic: Random Variables & Distribution Functions
stem: The function $$F(x)=\begin{cases}0, & x<0\\[2pt] x/2, & 0\le x<1\\[2pt] (1-\alpha)x+2\alpha-1, & 1\le x<2\\[2pt] 1, & x\ge2\end{cases}$$ is a distribution function if and only if
shortcut: At $x = 1$ the first branch reaches $1/2$ while the second branch starts at $\alpha$, so no downward jump requires $\alpha \ge 1/2$; the middle slope $1 - \alpha$ must be non-negative, so $\alpha \le 1$. Hence $1/2 \le \alpha \le 1$.
tips: A distribution function must be non-decreasing, right-continuous, and run from 0 to 1. Check each junction point and each branch slope separately.
Evaluate the middle branch at both ends: at $x = 1$ it equals $\alpha$, and at $x = 2$ it equals $2 - 2\alpha + 2\alpha - 1 = 1$ automatically - so the right end never constrains $\alpha$.
An UPWARD jump is permitted in a general distribution function (it just means positive mass at that point); only a downward move is forbidden. That is why $\alpha = 1$ is admissible.
The slope condition $1 - \alpha \ge 0$ is easy to overlook; without it, $\alpha > 1$ would make F decrease on [1,2).
solution: F must be non-decreasing on the whole line, right-continuous, with F(-$\infty$) = 0 and F(+$\infty$) = 1.
On [0,1) the branch $x/2$ rises from 0 to a left-limit of $1/2$ at $x = 1$.
At $x = 1$ the middle branch takes the value $(1-\alpha)(1) + 2\alpha - 1 = \alpha$. To avoid a decrease we need $\alpha \ge 1/2$ (an upward jump is permissible).
On [1,2) the middle branch has slope $1 - \alpha$, which must be non-negative, giving $\alpha \le 1$.
At $x = 2$ the middle branch gives $(1-\alpha)(2) + 2\alpha - 1 = 2 - 2\alpha + 2\alpha - 1 = 1$, matching the final branch, so continuity holds there for every $\alpha$.
Combining, F is a distribution function if and only if $1/2 \le \alpha \le 1$, option (b).

topic: Standard Continuous Distributions
subtopic: Standard Continuous Distributions
stem: The maximum possible probability an exponential distribution (any parameter) can give to the interval $[3,6]$ is
shortcut: $\operatorname{P}(3 \le X \le 6) = e^{-3L} - e^{-6L}$. Put $u = e^{-3L}$ in $(0,1)$, so the probability is $u - u^{2}$, maximised at $u = 1/2$ with value $1/4$.
tips: Substituting $u = e^{-3 \lambda}$ turns a transcendental maximisation into the elementary quadratic $u - u^{2}$ - the key move in this item.
Note that $6 = 2 \times 3$, so $e^{-6 \lambda} = u^{2}$ exactly. The doubling of the endpoints is what makes the substitution work.

$u - u^{2}$ has its maximum at $u = 1/2$, i.e. $e^{-3 \lambda} = 1/2$ and $\lambda = (\ln 2)/3 = 0.231$. The optimal mean is therefore about 4.33, comfortably inside $[3,6] - a$ good plausibility check.
The maximum value $1/4$ is a bound over ALL exponential distributions, so no single choice of parameter can do better - the reason option $(a) 1/2$ is unattainable.
solution: For an exponential distribution with rate $\lambda, \operatorname{P}(3 \le X \le 6) = e^{-3 \lambda} - e^{-6 \lambda}$.
Let $u = e^{-3 \lambda}$, which ranges over $(0, 1)$ as $\lambda$ ranges over $(0, \infty)$. Then $e^{-6 \lambda} = u^{2}$.
So the probability is $g(u) = u - u^{2}$.
Differentiating, $g'(u) = 1 - 2u = 0$ at $u = 1/2$, and $g''(u)$ = -$2 < 0$, so this is a maximum.
The maximum value is $g(1/2) = 1/2 - 1/4 = 1/4$, attained when $e^{-3 \lambda} = 1/2$, i.e. $\lambda = (\ln 2)/3$.
Hence the maximum possible probability is $1/4$, option (c).

topic: Characteristic Function, MGF & PGF; Inversion, Uniqueness, Continuity
subtopic: Characteristic Function, MGF & PGF; Inversion, Uniqueness, Continuity
stem: The p.g.f. of a Poisson distribution has value $e^{-1}$ at $2/3$. The mean of the distribution is
shortcut: Poisson PGF is $\operatorname{P}(s) = e^(\lambda(s-1))$. At $s = 2/3$ this is $e^{-\lambda/3} = e^{-1}$, so $\lambda/3 = 1$ and $\lambda = 3$. The Poisson mean is $\lambda = 3$.
tips: Poisson PGF: $\operatorname{P}(s) = e^(\lambda(s - 1))$; the MGF is $e^(\lambda(e^{t} - 1))$. Keep the two apart - substituting into the wrong one is the main trap.
$s - 1 = 2/3 - 1$ = -$1/3$, so the exponent is -$\lambda/3$. Equating exponents is faster than taking logarithms.
For the Poisson, mean = variance = $\lambda$, so once $\lambda = 3$ is found the answer is immediate.
Check: $\operatorname{P}(1) = e^{0} = 1$ for every $\lambda$, as any PGF must satisfy - a quick validity test of the formula you are using.
solution: The probability generating function of a Poisson variable with parameter $\lambda$ is $\operatorname{P}(s) = \operatorname{E}(s^{X}) = e^(\lambda(s - 1))$.
We are told $\operatorname{P}(2/3) = e^{-1}$.
Substituting $s = 2/3$: $\operatorname{P}(2/3) = e^(\lambda(2/3 - 1)) = e^{-\lambda/3}$.
Setting $e^{-\lambda/3} = e^{-1}$ gives $\lambda/3 = 1$, so $\lambda = 3$.
For the Poisson distribution the mean equals $\lambda$.
Hence the mean is 3, option (d).

topic: Random Variables & Distribution Functions
subtopic: Random Variables & Distribution Functions
stem: The function $$F(x)=\begin{cases}0, & x<0\\[2pt] x/3, & 0\le x<2\\[2pt] (1-\alpha)x+3\alpha-2, & 2\le x<3\\[2pt] 1, & x\ge3\end{cases}$$ is the distribution function of a continuous random variable
shortcut: For a CONTINUOUS variable F must have no jumps. At $x = 2$ the first branch gives $2/3$ and the second gives $\alpha$, so continuity forces $\alpha = 2/3$ exactly.
tips: 'Continuous random variable' is a strictly stronger requirement than 'distribution function': every junction must match exactly, with no jump allowed anywhere.
Evaluate both branches AT the junction: $x/3$ at $x = 2$ is $2/3$, and $(1-\alpha)x + 3\alpha - 2$ at $x = 2$ is $2 - 2\alpha + 3\alpha - 2 = \alpha$. Equate them.
The junction at $x = 3$ imposes nothing: $(1-\alpha)(3) + 3\alpha - 2 = 1$ identically, so only the $x = 2$ junction matters.
Contrast with Q33 of the same paper, where an upward jump was allowed and the answer was an interval. The word 'continuous' is what collapses the interval to a single point here.
solution: For F to be the distribution function of a CONTINUOUS random variable, F must be continuous everywhere - no jumps are permitted.
As x approaches 2 from below, the branch $x/3$ tends to $2/3$.
At $x = 2$ the middle branch gives $(1 - \alpha)(2) + 3\alpha - 2 = 2 - 2\alpha + 3\alpha - 2 = \alpha$.
Continuity at $x = 2$ therefore requires $\alpha = 2/3$.
At $x = 3$ the middle branch gives $(1-\alpha)(3) + 3\alpha - 2 = 3 - 3\alpha + 3\alpha - 2 = 1$, matching the final branch for every $\alpha$, so this junction imposes no extra condition.
With $\alpha = 2/3$ the middle slope is $1 - 2/3 = 1/3 > 0$, so F is non-decreasing. Hence F is a continuous distribution function if and only if $\alpha = 2/3$, option (d).

topic: Random Vectors: Joint, Marginal & Conditional Distributions
subtopic: Random Vectors: Joint, Marginal & Conditional Distributions
stem: The function $$F(x,y)=\begin{cases}\alpha, & x,y>0;\ x+y<1\\ 1, & x,y>0;\ x+y\ge1\\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$ is the c.d.f. of a random vector $(X,Y)$
shortcut: The rectangle (0.2, 0.8] x (0.2, 0.8] has F-measure $1 - 1 - 1 + \alpha = \alpha - 1$, which is negative for every $\alpha < 1$; and $\alpha = 1$ destroys right-continuity along the axes. So no value of $\alpha$ works.
tips: A bivariate CDF must satisfy the RECTANGLE inequality $F(b,d) - F(b,c) - F(a,d) + F(a,c) \ge 0$ for all $a < b, c < d$. Marginal monotonicity alone is not enough - this is the test the examiner is probing.
Choose the rectangle so that three corners lie in the region $x + y \ge 1$ and one corner in $x + y < 1$; then the expression collapses to $\alpha - 1$.
Even $\alpha = 1$ fails: F would be 1 for all $x, y > 0$ but 0 on the axes, so $\lim$ as x decreases to 0 of $F(x,y) = 1$ while $F(0,y) = 0$ - right-continuity is violated.
