stem: What is $\Delta E^2[(3x-3)^{(-2)}]$ at $x=1$ equal to? (interval of differencing $=1$)
tips: Negative factorial with a linear argument and coefficient a: $u^{-n} = 1/[(u+a)(u+2a)...(u+na)]$. Here $a = 3$, so $(3x-3)^{-2} = 1/[(3x)(3x+3)]$.
The difference rule $\Delta u^{n} = n a u^{n-1}$ holds for negative n too, with n = -2 giving the factor $(-2)(3)$ = -6.
E and $\Delta$ commute, so apply the difference rule first and the double shift afterwards - far cleaner than expanding four separate fractions.
Sign check: a negative factorial power decreases in magnitude as x grows, so its forward difference must be NEGATIVE - options (b) and (d) are eliminated at once.
solution: With interval 1 and a linear argument of coefficient $a = 3$, the generalised factorial rule is $\Delta u^{n} = n a u^{n-1}$, valid for negative n as well.
Since E and $\Delta$ commute, apply $E^{2}$, which replaces x by x + 2: $E^{2}[-6(3x-3)^{-3}]$ = -$6(3x+3)^{-3}$.
By definition of the negative factorial, $(3x+3)^{-3} = 1/[(3x+3+3)(3x+3+6)(3x+3+9)] = 1/[(3x+6)(3x+9)(3x+12)]$.
At $x = 1$ the three factors are 9, 12 and 15, so the value is -$6/(9 \times 12 \times 15)$ = -$6/1620$ = -$1/270$, option (c).

topic: Memory: RAM, ROM, Cache; Units of Memory & Storage Capacity
subtopic: Memory: RAM, ROM, Cache; Units of Memory & Storage Capacity
stem: On which type of ROM can data be written only once?
shortcut: PROM - Programmable ROM - is blank when manufactured and can be programmed exactly ONCE by blowing internal fuses.
tips: ROM family by erasability: ROM (fixed at manufacture), PROM (write once), EPROM (erasable by ultraviolet light), EEPROM/flash (electrically erasable, many times).
The 'E' prefixes signal ERASABLE, so any option beginning with E can be rewritten and cannot be the write-once answer.
PROM is programmed by permanently blowing fuse links, which is why the process is irreversible - a one-line justification worth quoting.
'EROM' in option (d) is not a standard device name; the genuine family members are ROM, PROM, EPROM, EEPROM and flash.
solution: Plain ROM has its contents fixed during manufacture and cannot be written by the user at all.

PROM (Programmable Read-Only Memory) is supplied blank and can be programmed once by the user, typically by blowing internal fuse links. Because the fuses are destroyed permanently, the process cannot be reversed or repeated.
EPROM (Erasable PROM) can be erased by exposure to ultraviolet light and reprogrammed many times.
EEPROM (Electrically Erasable PROM) can be erased and rewritten electrically, byte by byte, without removal from the circuit.
'EROM' is not a standard device designation.
Hence data can be written only once on PROM, option (a).

topic: Software, Operating Systems, Packages & Utilities
subtopic: Software, Operating Systems, Packages & Utilities
stem: What is the correct sequence of a cycle of a process in execution?
shortcut: A process is admitted from the waiting/new queue, becomes Ready, is dispatched to Executing, and finally Terminates - the only option that ends in a terminal state.
tips: Process state model: New -> Ready -> Running -> Terminated, with excursions to Blocked/Waiting and back to Ready whenever I/O is needed.
A complete life cycle must END in Terminated; options ending in 'Blocked' describe an intermediate excursion rather than a completed cycle.
A process never goes directly from Ready to Waiting - it must be dispatched to Running first and then block on a request. That rules out options (a) and (b).
Only the scheduler moves a process from Ready to Running (dispatch), and only an I/O request moves it from Running to Blocked - keep the transition triggers in mind.
solution: The standard process state diagram is: a new process is admitted to the READY queue, the scheduler dispatches it to the RUNNING (executing) state, and on completion it moves to TERMINATED.
While running, a process may issue an I/O request and move to the BLOCKED/WAITING state, returning to READY when the I/O completes.
Option (a) places Blocked after Terminated, which is impossible since termination is a final state.
Options (b) and (c) end at Blocked, which is an intermediate state rather than the end of a life cycle; option (b) additionally moves from Ready to Waiting directly, a transition that does not exist.
Option (d), Waiting -> Ready -> Executing -> Terminated, follows the admission, dispatch and completion path and ends in the terminal state.
Hence option (d) is correct.

topic: Computer Organisation: CPU, ALU, Control & Memory Units, I/O Units
subtopic: Computer Organisation: CPU, ALU, Control & Memory Units, I/O Units
stem: By using which units is data processing performed by a computer system? 1. Monitor, 2. Memory unit, 3. CPU
shortcut: Processing is done by the CPU using data held in the memory unit. The monitor is an OUTPUT device and takes no part in processing.
tips: Functional units: input, memory, ALU, control, output. Processing is the ALU and control unit (i.e. the CPU) acting on data in memory.
The monitor merely DISPLAYS results after processing, so it belongs to the output stage - any option containing item 1 is out.
Data must be loaded into main memory before the CPU can operate on it, which is why the memory unit is genuinely part of processing rather than mere storage.
Input-process-output is the standard model: keyboard/mouse in, CPU plus memory processing, monitor/printer out.
solution: A computer system is organised into input units, a memory unit, a central processing unit (comprising the ALU and control unit) and output units.
Item 3, the CPU: performs all arithmetic and logical operations and controls the sequence of execution - the processing element itself.
Item 2, the memory unit: holds the program and the data being operated on; the CPU cannot process data that is not in memory, so it is an essential part of the processing stage.
Item 1, the monitor: is an output device that displays results once processing is complete, and plays no part in the processing itself.
Hence data processing is performed by the memory unit and the CPU.
Option (b) is correct.

topic: Computer Organisation: CPU, ALU, Control & Memory Units, I/O Units
subtopic: Computer Organisation: CPU, ALU, Control & Memory Units, I/O Units
stem: Consider statements on machine cycle: 1. It consists of four phases — fetching, decoding, executing, storing. 2. It is a cycle in which machine language instructions are executed. 3. A program of 6 machine language instructions runs in 6 separate machine cycles.
shortcut: The machine cycle has the four phases fetch, decode, execute and store; it is the cycle in which machine instructions are executed; and each instruction consumes its own cycle, so six instructions take six cycles. All three statements hold.
tips: Four phases to memorise: FETCH the instruction, DECODE it, EXECUTE it, STORE the result. Some texts merge the last two, but four is the standard exam answer.
One instruction per machine cycle is the defining relationship - hence a program of n instructions requires n machine cycles in a simple non-pipelined processor.
Distinguish the machine cycle from the CLOCK cycle: one machine cycle spans several clock cycles, which is why clock speed alone does not determine instruction throughput.
When all three statements restate parts of the same standard definition, 'all of them' is the natural key.
solution: Statement 1: the machine cycle is conventionally described as having four phases - fetching the instruction from memory, decoding it in the control unit, executing it in the ALU, and storing the result. TRUE.
Statement 2: the machine cycle is precisely the repeating sequence by which the processor carries out machine-language instructions one after another. TRUE.
Statement 3: in a simple non-pipelined processor each instruction occupies one complete machine cycle, so a program of 6 machine-language instructions requires 6 machine cycles. TRUE.
Note that one machine cycle spans several clock cycles; the two must not be confused.
All three statements are correct.
Hence option (d) is correct.

topic: Networks: LAN, WAN, Internet, Intranet
subtopic: Networks: LAN, WAN, Internet, Intranet
stem: Which one of the following provides application-independent security and privacy over the internet?
shortcut: IPsec operates at the NETWORK layer, so it protects all traffic transparently regardless of the application; SSL sits above the transport layer and each application must be written to use it.
tips: Layer determines transparency: IPsec at layer 3 secures every packet automatically, while SSL/TLS at the transport-session boundary must be invoked by the application (HTTPS, FTPS and so on).
'Application-independent' is the key phrase - it points to the layer BELOW the applications, which is where IPsec lives.
IPsec provides authentication (AH) and confidentiality (ESP) and is the basis of most VPNs, which is why it can protect legacy applications unchanged.
Plain IP and TCP (options c and d) provide no security at all - they are the protocols IPsec was designed to protect.
solution: The question asks for a mechanism that secures internet communication without the applications needing to be aware of it.

IPsec operates at the network (IP) layer, encrypting and authenticating IP packets themselves. Because it sits below the transport and application layers, every application's traffic is protected transparently, with no modification to the applications.

SSL (and its successor TLS) operates above the transport layer; an application must be explicitly written to open an SSL connection, which is why HTTPS, FTPS and SMTPS exist as separate application-level variants.
IP and TCP provide addressing, routing and reliable delivery but offer no security services of their own.
Hence the application-independent mechanism is the IP security protocol, option (a).

topic: Memory: RAM, ROM, Cache; Units of Memory & Storage Capacity
subtopic: Memory: RAM, ROM, Cache; Units of Memory & Storage Capacity
stem: Which of the following is/are non-volatile? 1. DRAM, 2. SRAM, 3. EPROM
shortcut: DRAM and SRAM are both volatile forms of RAM; only EPROM, a member of the ROM family, retains its contents without power.
tips: Volatility rule of thumb: anything called RAM is volatile; anything in the ROM family (ROM, PROM, EPROM, EEPROM, flash) is non-volatile.
DRAM additionally needs periodic REFRESH even while powered, and SRAM holds its value only while power is applied - both lose everything at power-off.
EPROM stores charge on floating gates that persists for years without power, which is exactly what non-volatility means.
Practical anchor: main memory (RAM) is wiped on reboot, whereas the BIOS held in EPROM/flash survives - the everyday demonstration of the distinction.
solution: Volatile memory loses its contents when the power supply is removed; non-volatile memory retains them.
Item 1, DRAM (Dynamic RAM): stores each bit as charge on a capacitor, requiring periodic refresh even while powered, and loses everything when power is removed. VOLATILE.
Item 2, SRAM (Static RAM): stores each bit in a flip-flop; no refresh is needed but power is, so the contents vanish at power-off. VOLATILE.
Item 3, EPROM (Erasable Programmable ROM): stores bits as trapped charge on floating gates, which persists for years without power and is removed only by ultraviolet exposure. NON-VOLATILE.
Hence only item 3 is non-volatile.
Option (b) is correct.

topic: Networks: LAN, WAN, Internet, Intranet
subtopic: Networks: LAN, WAN, Internet, Intranet
stem: Consider network topologies: 1. Bus, 2. Star, 3. Ring, 4. Mesh. In which does the failure of one computer not affect the others?
shortcut: In bus, star and mesh topologies a failed node simply drops off the network. In a RING the signal must pass through every node, so one failure breaks the loop for everyone.
tips: The discriminator is whether traffic must PASS THROUGH the failed node. Only the ring routes every message through each station in turn.
In a bus, nodes tap a shared cable passively; in a star, each node has its own link to the hub; in a mesh, redundant paths bypass any failure. None depends on a particular node.
Note the caveat for the star: a HUB failure disables the network, but the question asks about the failure of a computer, not of the hub.
Ring networks mitigate this with dual counter-rotating rings (as in FDDI) precisely because the single-ring weakness is so severe.
solution: The question is whether the failure of one computer disrupts the rest of the network.

Item 1, bus: all nodes tap a single shared backbone passively, so a failed node simply stops transmitting and the others continue. UNAFFECTED. (A break in the backbone cable itself is a different matter.)
Item 2, star: each node has its own dedicated link to the central hub, so a failed node affects only its own link. UNAFFECTED by another computer's failure.
Item 3, ring: data circulate from node to node around the loop, and every station must forward the signal. A single failed node breaks the ring and halts communication for all. AFFECTED.
Item 4, mesh: multiple redundant paths connect the nodes, so traffic is rerouted around any failure. UNAFFECTED.
Hence the failure of one computer does not affect the others in topologies 1, 2 and 4, option (a).

topic: Software, Operating Systems, Packages & Utilities
subtopic: Software, Operating Systems, Packages & Utilities
stem: Consider: 1. Shared region, 2. Cache memory, 3. Message passing, 4. Shared memory. Which are related to interprocess communication?
shortcut: The two standard models of interprocess communication are SHARED MEMORY and MESSAGE PASSING - items 3 and 4.
tips: Memorise the pair: IPC = shared memory model + message passing model. Everything else in an options list is a distractor.
Cache memory is a hardware performance device managed by the processor, entirely invisible to processes - it is never an IPC mechanism.

Shared memory is fast (processes read and write a common region directly) but needs explicit synchronisation such as semaphores; message passing is slower but needs no shared address space and works across machines.
'Shared region' in item 1 is loose phrasing for the same idea as shared memory, but the option set pairs the two canonical mechanisms 3 and 4.
solution: Interprocess communication (IPC) is the set of mechanisms by which cooperating processes exchange data and synchronise their actions.

Item 4, shared memory: the operating system maps a common region of memory into the address spaces of two or more processes, which then read and write it directly (with semaphores or mutexes for synchronisation). A standard IPC model.

Item 3, message passing: processes exchange data through send and receive primitives supplied by the kernel, requiring no shared address space and extending naturally across a network. The other standard IPC model.
Item 2, cache memory: a hardware buffer between the CPU and main memory, managed transparently by the processor and unrelated to communication between processes.
Hence the mechanisms related to interprocess communication are message passing and shared memory, option (d).

topic: Software, Operating Systems, Packages & Utilities
subtopic: Software, Operating Systems, Packages & Utilities
stem: Which of the following are goals of an operating system? 1. Efficient use of CPU, 2. Efficient use of memory, 3. Efficient use of I/O devices
shortcut: The operating system is the resource manager for the whole machine, so efficient use of the CPU, of memory and of I/O devices are all among its goals.
tips: The OS is defined as a RESOURCE MANAGER; the three principal resources are the processor, memory and I/O devices, so all three appear in its goals.
Concrete mechanisms: CPU scheduling for the processor, paging and virtual memory for memory, buffering and spooling for I/O.
The complementary goal is CONVENIENCE - providing an easy interface for the user - which sits alongside efficiency in every textbook list.
When all listed items are standard entries from the same textbook list, 'all of them' is almost always the key.
solution: An operating system acts as the manager of all the computer's resources and as the interface between the user and the hardware.
Goal 1, efficient use of the CPU: achieved through multiprogramming and CPU scheduling, keeping the processor busy while other jobs wait for I/O. A genuine goal.
Goal 2, efficient use of memory: achieved through allocation strategies, paging, segmentation and virtual memory, so that as many processes as possible are resident. A genuine goal.
Goal 3, efficient use of I/O devices: achieved through buffering, caching, spooling and device scheduling, so that slow peripherals do not stall the system. A genuine goal.
All three are standard goals, alongside the complementary aim of user convenience.
Hence option (d) is correct.

topic: Data, Information, Database & DBMS; Frontend/Backend
subtopic: Data, Information, Database & DBMS; Frontend/Backend
stem: Which properties of the transaction mechanism in a database system are correct? 1. Atomicity, 2. Durability, 3. Isolation, 4. Security
shortcut: Transactions obey the ACID properties: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation and Durability. Security is not one of them, so items 1, 2 and 3 are correct.
tips: ACID is the mnemonic: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability. Any item outside those four is a distractor.
Consistency is the member NOT listed among the four items here, and Security is the intruder - identify the intruder and the answer follows.

Meanings: Atomicity = all or nothing; Consistency = the database moves from one valid state to another; Isolation = concurrent transactions do not interfere; Durability = committed changes survive failures.
Security is a broader access-control concern handled by authentication and authorisation, not by the transaction manager.
solution: A database transaction is required to satisfy the four ACID properties.
Item 1, Atomicity: a transaction is indivisible - either all of its operations take effect or none do, with rollback on failure. CORRECT.
Item 2, Durability: once a transaction commits, its effects survive subsequent system crashes, being recoverable from the $\log$. CORRECT.
Item 3, Isolation: concurrently executing transactions do not interfere with one another; each sees a state as if it ran alone. CORRECT.

Item 4, Security: protecting data against unauthorised access is achieved by authentication and authorisation mechanisms, not by the transaction manager, and is not one of the ACID properties. INCORRECT.
Hence items 1, 2 and 3 are the transaction properties, option (a).

topic: Conditional Probability, Law of Total Probability, Bayes' Theorem
subtopic: Conditional Probability, Law of Total Probability, Bayes' Theorem
stem: The members of a firm rent cars from three rental agencies: 60% from Agency-1, 30% from Agency-2 and 10% from Agency-3. If 9% of cars from Agency-1 need an oil change, 20% of cars from Agency-2 need an oil change and 6% of cars from Agency-3 need an oil change, then what is the probability that a rental car delivered to the firm will need an oil change?
tips: Lay the three branches out as (share x rate) products before adding: 0.054, 0.060, 0.006. The sum is the overall rate.
Work in per-cent-of-a-per-cent to avoid decimal slips: $54 + 60 + 6 = 120$ ten-thousandths, i.e. $0.0120 \times 10 = 0.12$.
Sanity bound: the answer must lie between the smallest rate $(6\%)$ and the largest $(20\%)$. Only 0.12 does - options (a) and (b) are individual branch products.
Option (b) 0.054 is the Agency-1 branch alone and option (a) 0.006 the Agency-3 branch - both punish stopping before the addition.
solution: Let A1, A2, A3 be the events that a car comes from Agency-1, 2 and 3, with $\operatorname{P}(A_{1}) = 0.6, \operatorname{P}(A_{2}) = 0.3, \operatorname{P}(A_{3}) = 0.1$.
Let C be the event that the car needs an oil change, with $\operatorname{P}(C\mid A_{1}) = 0.09, \operatorname{P}(C\mid A_{2}) = 0.20, \operatorname{P}(C\mid A_{3}) = 0.06$.

By the law of total probability, $\operatorname{P}(C) = \operatorname{P}(A_{1})\operatorname{P}(C\mid A_{1}) + \operatorname{P}(A_{2})\operatorname{P}(C\mid A_{2}) + \operatorname{P}(A_{3})\operatorname{P}(C\mid A_{3})$.
Hence the probability is 0.12, option (d).

topic: Mathematical Expectation & Conditional Expectation
subtopic: Mathematical Expectation & Conditional Expectation
stem: If $X \sim N(0,1)$ and $Y \mid X=x \sim U(x-1,\,x+1)$, then what is the value of $E\left(E^2(Y \mid X)\right)$?
shortcut: Y given $X = x$ is uniform on $(x-1, x+1)$, whose mean is the midpoint x. So $\operatorname{E}(Y\mid X) = X$ and $\operatorname{E}[E^{2}(Y\mid X)] = \operatorname{E}(X^{2}) = 1$.
tips: The mean of U(a,b) is the midpoint $(a+b)/2$; here $((x-1) + (x+1))/2 = x$ exactly, so the conditional mean is X itself.
Read the notation carefully: $E^{2}(Y\mid X)$ means the SQUARE of the conditional mean, not the second conditional moment.
For $X \sim N(0,1), \operatorname{E}(X^{2}) = \operatorname{Var}(X) + [\operatorname{E}(X)]^{2} = 1 + 0 = 1$ - the whole answer once the conditional mean is identified.
The half-width 1 of the uniform affects the conditional VARIANCE $(1/3)$ but not the conditional mean, so it never enters this calculation.
solution: Given $X = x$, the variable Y is uniform on the interval $(x - 1, x + 1)$.
The mean of a uniform distribution is the midpoint of its range, so $\operatorname{E}(Y \mid X = x) = ((x-1) + (x+1))/2 = x$.
Hence $\operatorname{E}(Y \mid X) = X$ as a random variable.
Therefore $E^{2}(Y\mid X) = X^{2}$, and $\operatorname{E}[E^{2}(Y\mid X)] = \operatorname{E}(X^{2})$.
For $X \sim N(0,1), \operatorname{E}(X^{2}) = \operatorname{Var}(X) + [\operatorname{E}(X)]^{2} = 1 + 0 = 1$.
Hence the value is 1, option (a).

topic: Standard Continuous Distributions
subtopic: Standard Continuous Distributions
stem: If $X \sim \exp(\theta)$, then consider the following statements: 1. Variance > Mean if $0 < \theta < 1$ 2. Minimum order statistic is chi-square distribution 3. Lack of memory property exists only if $\theta > 1$ Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
shortcut: Only statement 1 holds: $Var$/Mean = $1/\theta$, so the variance exceeds the mean exactly when $\theta < 1$. The minimum of exponentials is exponential, not $\chi^{2}$, and memorylessness holds for every $\theta$.
tips: Exponential($\theta$) with $\theta$ as RATE: mean $1/\theta$, variance $1/\theta^{2}$, so the ratio is $1/\theta$ and the comparison reduces to $\theta$ versus 1.
Minimum of n i.i.d. Exp($\theta$) is Exp($n \theta$) - the exponential family is closed under minima, which is the standard result statement 2 misquotes.
Memorylessness is a property of the exponential FAMILY, holding for every rate parameter; no condition on $\theta$ is needed, so statement 3 is false.
The $\chi^{2}$ link that does exist is Exp($1/2$) = $\chi^{2}_{2} - a$ special case, not a statement about minima.
solution: For X ~ Exponential with rate $\theta$, the mean is $1/\theta$ and the variance is $1/\theta^{2}$.
Statement 1: $Var$/Mean = $(1/\theta^{2})/(1/\theta) = 1/\theta$, which exceeds 1 exactly when $\theta < 1$. So the variance exceeds the mean for $0 < \theta < 1$. TRUE.

Statement 2: for a sample of n i.i.d. Exponential($\theta$) variables, $\operatorname{P}\!\left(\text{min > x}\right) = e^{-n \theta x}$, so the minimum is Exponential($n \theta$), not $\chi^{2}$. FALSE.

Statement 3: the lack-of-memory property $\operatorname{P}(X > s+t \mid X > s) = \operatorname{P}(X > t)$ follows from $e^(-\theta(s+t))/e^{-\theta s} = e^{-\theta t}$, which holds for every $\theta > 0$. No restriction to $\theta > 1$ exists. FALSE.
Only statement 1 is correct.
Hence option (a) is correct.

topic: Standard Discrete Distributions
subtopic: Standard Discrete Distributions
stem: A random variable $X$ has probability mass function given by $$P(X=x) = \frac{1}{5^{10}}\binom{10}{x}2^x 3^{10-x}, \quad x=0,1,2,\ldots,10$$ The mean and variance of $X$ are respectively:
shortcut: Rewrite the pmf as $\binom{10}{x}(2/5)^{x} (3/5)^{10-x}$: a Binomial(10, 0.4). Mean = 4 and variance = $10(0.4)(0.6) = 2.4$.
tips: Divide the $5^{10}$ into the two factors: $2^{x}/5^{x} = (2/5)^{x}$ and $3^{10-x}/5^{10-x} = (3/5)^{10-x}$. The binomial form then appears immediately.
Read off $n = 10$ and $p = 2/5 = 0.4$, giving $q = 0.6$. Everything else is two multiplications.
For a binomial the variance npq is always LESS than the mean np, since $q < 1$ - that ordering alone eliminates options (a) and (b).
Mean 4 and variance 2.4 in that order; option (b) 2.4, 4 reverses them, the classic careless-reading trap.
solution: The pmf is $\operatorname{P}(X = x) = \binom{10}{x} 2^{x} 3^{10-x}/5^{10}$ for $x = 0, 1$, ..., 10.
Split the denominator: $5^{10} = 5^{x}$ . $5^{10-x}$, so $\operatorname{P}(X = x) = \binom{10}{x}(2/5)^{x} (3/5)^{10-x}$.
This is exactly the Binomial distribution with $n = 10$ and $p = 2/5 = 0.4$, so $q = 0.6$.
Hence the mean and variance are 4 and 2.4, option (c).

topic: Distributions of Functions of Random Variables
subtopic: Distributions of Functions of Random Variables
stem: If $X \sim \text{log-normal}(\mu,\sigma^2)$ and $Y=\sigma X^{\mu}$; $\sigma>0$, $-\infty<\mu<\infty$, then what is the value of $$\mathrm{Var}\left(\left(\log\frac{Y}{\sigma}-\mu^2\right)^2\right)?$$
shortcut: $\log(Y/\sigma) = \mu \log X = \mu W$ with $W \sim N(\mu, \sigma^{2})$, so the bracket is $\mu(W - \mu) = \mu \sigma Z$. Its square is $\mu^{2} \sigma^{2} Z^{2}$ and $\operatorname{Var}(Z^{2}) = 2$, giving $2 \mu^{4} \sigma^{4}$.
tips: Peel the transformation one layer at a time: $Y = \sigma X^{\mu}$ gives $Y/\sigma = X^{\mu}$, so $\log(Y/\sigma) = \mu \log X$ - the $\sigma$ cancels by design.
X lognormal means $W = \log X \sim N(\mu, \sigma^{2})$, so $\mu W - \mu^{2} = \mu(W - \mu), a$ centred normal with SD $\mu \sigma$.
The square of a centred normal is $(\mu \sigma)^{2}$ times $a \chi^{2}_{1}$, and $Var$($\chi^{2}_{1}$) = 2 - the source of the factor 2.
The distractors encode wrong $\chi^{2}$ variances: 3 (option c) and 15 or 105 (options b, a) come from higher moments of the normal, so pinning $\operatorname{Var}(Z^{2}) = 2$ is decisive.
solution: X is lognormal($\mu, \sigma^{2}$), so $W = \log X$ follows $N(\mu, \sigma^{2})$.
$Y = \sigma X^{\mu}$ gives $Y/\sigma = X^{\mu}$, hence $\log(Y/\sigma) = \mu \log X = \mu W$.
Therefore $\log(Y/\sigma) - \mu^{2} = \mu W - \mu^{2} = \mu(W - \mu)$.
Write $W - \mu = \sigma Z$ with $Z \sim N(0,1)$. Then the bracket is $\mu \sigma Z$ and its square is $\mu^{2} \sigma^{2} Z^{2}$.
Since $Z^{2} \sim \chi^{2}$ with 1 degree of freedom, $\operatorname{Var}(Z^{2}) = 2$.
Hence $\operatorname{Var}(\mu^{2} \sigma^{2} Z^{2}) = \mu^{4} \sigma^{4} \operatorname{Var}(Z^{2}) = 2 \mu^{4} \sigma^{4}$, option (d).

topic: Random Variables & Distribution Functions
subtopic: Random Variables & Distribution Functions
stem: The pdf of a random variable $X$ is given by $$f(x) = \begin{cases}0.2, & 0 \le x \le 5\\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$ Consider the following probabilities: 1. $P(2 \le X \le 3) = 0.2$ 2. $P(X>3.5)=0.3$ 3. $P(|x|\ge 2)=0.6$ 4. $P(X<4)=0.8$ How many of the probabilities given above are correct?
shortcut: The density is Uniform(0,5), so every probability is (interval length)/5. All four values - 0.2, 0.3, 0.6 and 0.8 - check out.
tips: A constant density 0.2 over a range of length 5 is $U(0,5)$; probabilities are then just lengths divided by 5, with no integration at all.
Statement 3 has the trap: |X| >= 2 looks two-sided, but X is confined to $[0,5]$, so it reduces to $X \ge 2$ and gives $3/5 = 0.6$.
When every statement in a set is a straightforward computation from the same simple density, expect 'all four' - but verify the one with the absolute value.
solution: The density is $f(x) = 0.2$ on $[0,5]$, which is the Uniform(0,5) distribution; probabilities equal interval length divided by 5.
Statement 1: $\operatorname{P}(2 \le X \le 3) = (3 - 2)/5 = 0.2$. CORRECT.
Statement 2: $\operatorname{P}(X > 3.5) = (5 - 3.5)/5 = 1.5/5 = 0.3$. CORRECT.
Statement 3: since X takes only non-negative values, |X| >= 2 is the same as $X \ge 2$, giving $(5 - 2)/5 = 0.6$. CORRECT.
Statement 4: $\operatorname{P}(X < 4) = (4 - 0)/5 = 0.8$. CORRECT.
All four probabilities are correct, option (d).

topic: Standard Continuous Distributions
subtopic: Standard Continuous Distributions
stem: If $\varphi(\cdot)$ is pdf of $N(0,1)$ distribution and $A$ represents a circle of unit area with centre at origin, then what is the value of $\displaystyle\iint_A \varphi(x)\varphi(y)\,dx\,dy$?
shortcut: Unit area means pi $r^{2} = 1$, so $r^{2} = 1/pi$. The integral is $\operatorname{P}(X^{2} + Y^{2} \le r^{2})$ with $X^{2}+Y^{2} \sim \chi^{2}_{2}$ = Exp($1/2$), giving $1 - e^{-r^{2}/2} = 1 - e^(-1/(2 pi))$.
tips: 'Unit AREA' not unit radius - solve pi $r^{2} = 1$ first to get $r^{2} = 1/pi$. Reading it as $r = 1$ leads straight to option (c).
For independent standard normals, $X^{2} + Y^{2} \sim \chi^{2}$ with 2 d.f., which is Exponential with rate $1/2 - a$ fact worth memorising.
Hence $\operatorname{P}(X^{2}+Y^{2} \le c) = 1 - e^{-c/2}$ for any $c > 0$; substituting $c = 1/pi$ gives the answer in one step.
The bivariate standard normal density is circularly symmetric, which is precisely why a circular region turns a double integral into a one-dimensional $\chi^{2}$ probability.
solution: The integrand $\phi(x)\phi(y)$ is the joint density of two independent standard normal variables, so the integral is P((X,Y) lies in A).
A is a circle centred at the origin with unit AREA, so pi $r^{2} = 1$ and $r^{2} = 1/pi$.
The event is therefore $X^{2} + Y^{2} \le r^{2} = 1/pi$.
For independent standard normals, $X^{2} + Y^{2}$ follows $a \chi^{2}$ distribution with 2 degrees of freedom, which is exponential with rate $1/2$.
Hence $\operatorname{P}(X^{2} + Y^{2} \le c) = 1 - e^{-c/2}$, and with $c = 1/pi$ this is $1 - e^(-1/(2 pi))$.
Option (b) is correct.

topic: Random Vectors: Joint, Marginal & Conditional Distributions
subtopic: Random Vectors: Joint, Marginal & Conditional Distributions
sharedStem: *Questions 8–10 are based on the following: let the joint pdf of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ be* $$f(x,y) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi y}}\,e^{-\frac{1}{2y}(x-12y)^2}, \quad -\infty<x<\infty,\ 0<y<1$$
stem: What is the value of $E(X)$?
shortcut: The density says $X \mid Y = y \sim N(12y, y)$, and integrating out x leaves $f_{Y}(y) = 1$ on $(0,1)$, so $Y \sim U(0,1)$. Then $\operatorname{E}(X) = \operatorname{E}(12Y) = 12(1/2) = 6$.
tips: Recognise the normal kernel in x: $(1/\sqrt{2 pi y}) \exp(-(x - 12y)^{2}/(2y))$ is exactly the $N(12y, y)$ density, so the conditional law is read off directly.
Because that kernel integrates to 1 for each y, the marginal of Y is the constant 1 on $(0,1)$ - i.e. Y is Uniform(0,1). This identification drives all three parts.
Tower property: $\operatorname{E}(X) = \operatorname{E}[\operatorname{E}(X\mid Y)] = \operatorname{E}(12Y)$. Never attempt the double integral directly.
$\operatorname{E}(Y) = 1/2, \operatorname{E}(Y^{2}) = 1/3$ and $\operatorname{Var}(Y) = 1/12$ for $U(0,1)$ - keep all three ready, since the next two parts need them.
solution: Write the joint density as $f(x,y) = [1/\sqrt{2 pi y}] \exp(-(x - 12y)^{2}/(2y))$ for -$\infty < x < \infty$ and $0 < y < 1$.
For fixed y this is exactly the $N(12y, y)$ density in x, so $X \mid Y = y \sim N(12y, y)$.
Integrating that normal density over x gives 1 for every y, so the marginal density of Y is 1 on $(0,1)$, i.e. Y ~ Uniform(0,1).
By the tower property, $\operatorname{E}(X) = \operatorname{E}[\operatorname{E}(X \mid Y)] = \operatorname{E}(12Y)$.
Since $\operatorname{E}(Y) = 1/2$ for $U(0,1), \operatorname{E}(X) = 12(1/2) = 6$.
Hence option (d) is correct.

sharedStem: *Questions 8–10 are based on the following: let the joint pdf of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ be* $$f(x,y) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi y}}\,e^{-\frac{1}{2y}(x-12y)^2}, \quad -\infty<x<\infty,\ 0<y<1$$
stem: What is the value of $\mathrm{Var}(X)$?
shortcut: $\operatorname{Var}(X) = \operatorname{E}[\operatorname{Var}(X\mid Y)] + \operatorname{Var}[\operatorname{E}(X\mid Y)] = \operatorname{E}(Y) + \operatorname{Var}(12Y) = 1/2 + 144(1/12) = 0.5 + 12 = 12.5$.
tips: Law of total variance: $\operatorname{Var}(X) = \operatorname{E}[\operatorname{Var}(X\mid Y)] + \operatorname{Var}[\operatorname{E}(X\mid Y)]$. Both pieces are needed - dropping either gives 12 or 0.5, and option (c) 12 is planted for exactly that slip.
From $X\mid Y \sim N(12Y, Y)$: the conditional variance is Y itself, whose expectation is $1/2$; the conditional mean is 12Y, whose variance is $144 \operatorname{Var}(Y)$.
$\operatorname{Var}(Y) = 1/12$ for $U(0,1)$, so $144(1/12) = 12$ - the clean cancellation confirms the set-up.
The two contributions are of very different sizes here (0.5 versus 12), which is a useful reminder that the between-group term usually dominates.
solution: From the joint density, $X \mid Y = y \sim N(12y, y)$ and Y ~ Uniform(0,1).
The law of total variance gives $\operatorname{Var}(X) = \operatorname{E}[\operatorname{Var}(X \mid Y)] + \operatorname{Var}[\operatorname{E}(X \mid Y)]$.
The conditional variance is $\operatorname{Var}(X \mid Y) = Y$, so $\operatorname{E}[\operatorname{Var}(X\mid Y)] = \operatorname{E}(Y) = 1/2$.
The conditional mean is $\operatorname{E}(X\mid Y) = 12Y$, so $\operatorname{Var}[\operatorname{E}(X\mid Y)] = 144 \operatorname{Var}(Y) = 144(1/12) = 12$.
Adding: $\operatorname{Var}(X) = 0.5 + 12 = 12.5$.
Hence option (d) is correct.

sharedStem: *Questions 8–10 are based on the following: let the joint pdf of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ be* $$f(x,y) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi y}}\,e^{-\frac{1}{2y}(x-12y)^2}, \quad -\infty<x<\infty,\ 0<y<1$$
stem: What is the value of $\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)$?
shortcut: $\operatorname{E}(XY) = \operatorname{E}[Y \operatorname{E}(X\mid Y)] = \operatorname{E}(12Y^{2}) = 12(1/3) = 4$, and $\operatorname{E}(X)\operatorname{E}(Y) = 6(1/2) = 3$, so $Cov = 4 - 3 = 1$.
tips: Condition first: $\operatorname{E}(XY) = \operatorname{E}[\operatorname{E}(XY\mid Y)] = \operatorname{E}[Y \operatorname{E}(X\mid Y)]$, because Y is fixed inside the inner expectation.
For $U(0,1), \operatorname{E}(Y^{2}) = 1/3$ - not $1/4$. Confusing $\operatorname{E}(Y^{2})$ with $[\operatorname{E}(Y)]^{2}$ gives 3 and a covariance of 0.
Reuse $\operatorname{E}(X) = 6$ from the first part rather than recomputing; shared-stem items are built to chain.
Consistency check: $Cov = 12 \operatorname{Var}(Y) = 12/12 = 1$, since $X = 12Y$ plus conditional noise that is uncorrelated with Y - a neat one-line confirmation.
solution: From the joint density, $X \mid Y = y \sim N(12y, y)$ and Y ~ Uniform(0,1), with $\operatorname{E}(X) = 6$ from the earlier part.
$\operatorname{E}(XY) = \operatorname{E}[\operatorname{E}(XY \mid Y)] = \operatorname{E}[Y \operatorname{E}(X \mid Y)] = \operatorname{E}[Y (12Y)] = 12 \operatorname{E}(Y^{2})$.
For $U(0,1), \operatorname{E}(Y^{2}) = 1/3$, so $\operatorname{E}(XY) = 12(1/3) = 4$.
$\operatorname{E}(X)\operatorname{E}(Y) = 6 x (1/2) = 3$.
$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y) = \operatorname{E}(XY) - \operatorname{E}(X)\operatorname{E}(Y) = 4 - 3 = 1$.
Equivalently $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y) = \operatorname{Cov}(12Y, Y) = 12 \operatorname{Var}(Y) = 12/12 = 1$. Option (a) is correct.

stem: If random variable $X$ follows Binomial distribution with $n=10$ and $p=\dfrac{1}{4}$, then what is the value of third cumulant of $Y=10-X$?
tips: Reflection rule: $X \sim B(n,p)$ implies $n - X \sim B(n, 1-p)$. Apply it FIRST and then use the standard cumulant formula.
Third cumulant of the binomial: k3 = npq(q - p). It changes sign with the skewness, so $p > 1/2$ gives a negative value.
Here $p = 3/4$ exceeds $q = 1/4$, so q - p = -$1/2$ and the answer must be NEGATIVE - only option (a) qualifies.
Alternative route: cumulants of a reflected variable satisfy $k_{3}(c - X)$ = -k3(X). Since $k_{3}(X) = 10(1/4)(3/4)(1/2) = 15/16$, the reflection gives -$15/16$.
solution: X ~ Binomial($10, 1/4$), and $Y = 10 - X$ counts the failures, so Y ~ Binomial($10, 3/4$).
For Y the parameters are $n = 10, p = 3/4$ and $q = 1/4$.
The third cumulant of a binomial variable is $k_{3} = n p q (q - p)$.

stem: If $X, Y$ and $Z$ are iid Exponential(1) variates, then the distribution of $\dfrac{X+Y+Z}{3}$ is:
shortcut: The sum of three i.i.d. Exp(1) variables is $\Gamma$(shape 3, rate 1); dividing by 3 multiplies the rate by 3, giving $\Gamma(n = 3, \lambda = 3)$.
tips: Additive property: the sum of n i.i.d. Exp($\lambda$) variables is $\Gamma$(shape n, rate $\lambda$). Here the sum is $\Gamma(3, 1)$.
Scaling rule: if $W \sim \Gamma$(shape a, rate b) then $W/c \sim \Gamma$(shape a, rate bc). Dividing by 3 raises the rate from 1 to 3, leaving the shape unchanged.
The SHAPE never changes under scaling, so any answer with shape other than 3 - options (a) and (b), which are exponential, i.e. shape 1 - is wrong.
Check the mean: E of the average of three Exp(1) variables is 1, and $\Gamma$(3, rate 3) has mean $3/3 = 1$. Confirmed.
solution: X, Y, Z are i.i.d. Exponential(1), which is $\Gamma$ with shape 1 and rate 1.
By the additive property of the $\Gamma$ family with a common rate, $X + Y + Z \sim \Gamma$(shape 3, rate 1).
Let $W = X + Y + Z$ and consider $W/3$.
If $W \sim \Gamma$(shape a, rate b), then $W/c \sim \Gamma$(shape a, rate bc); with $c = 3$ and $b = 1$ the rate becomes 3.
Hence $(X+Y+Z)/3 \sim \Gamma$ with $n = 3$ and $\lambda = 3$, whose mean is $3/3 = 1$, agreeing with the mean of an average of Exp(1) variables.
Option (d) is correct.

stem: If random variable $X$ assumes non-negative integral values and $P(s)=E(s^X)$, then what is the value of $\displaystyle\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} s^{2n}P(X\le n)$?
shortcut: Swap the order of summation: $\sum s^{2n}$ sum over $k \le n$ of $p_{k} = \sum p_{k} \sum s^{2n}$ = sum of $p_{k} s^{2k}/(1-s^{2}) = \operatorname{P}(s^{2})/(1-s^{2})$.
tips: Interchange the summations - the double sum over the region $k \le n$ is the standard manoeuvre for turning a CDF generating function into a pmf one.
The inner geometric sum over $n \ge k$ gives $s^{2k}/(1 - s^{2})$, which supplies both the argument $s^{2}$ and the denominator.
The surviving sum of $p_{k} (s^{2})^{k}$ is by definition $\operatorname{P}(s^{2})$, since P(t) = sum $p_{k} t^{k}$. Substituting the argument correctly is what separates the options.

Sanity check at $s = 0$: the left side is $\operatorname{P}(X \le 0) = p_{0}$, and $\operatorname{P}(0)/(1-0) = p_{0}$. Only options with argument $s^{2}$ or s pass, and the general identity settles it.
solution: Write $\operatorname{P}(X \le n)$ = sum over $k = 0$ to n of $p_{k}$, where $p_{k} = \operatorname{P}(X = k)$.
Then the required sum is $S = \sum s^{2n}$ sum over $k = 0$ to n of $p_{k}$.
Interchange the order of summation over the region $0 \le k \le n$: $S = \sum p_{k} \sum s^{2n}$.
The inner geometric series is $s^{2k} + s^{2k+2}$ + ... = $s^{2k}/(1 - s^{2})$ for |s| < 1.
So $S = [1/(1 - s^{2})] \sum p_{k} (s^{2})^{k} = \operatorname{P}(s^{2})/(1 - s^{2})$, since $\operatorname{P}(t) = \operatorname{E}(t^{X})$ = sum $p_{k} t^{k}$.
Hence option (c) is correct.

stem: If a random variable assumes non-negative integral values and $E(X)=\mu$, $\mathrm{Var}(X)=\sigma^2$, then what is the value of $2\displaystyle\sum_{x=0}^{\infty}xP(X>x)$?
shortcut: Interchanging sums, $\sum x \operatorname{P}(X > x) = \sum p_{k} [k(k-1)/2] = [\operatorname{E}(X^{2}) - \operatorname{E}(X)]/2$. Doubling gives $\operatorname{E}(X^{2}) - \operatorname{E}(X) = \sigma^{2} + \mu^{2} - \mu$.
tips: Swap the summations: $\sum x \sum p_{k} = \sum p_{k}$ sum over $x = 0$ to k-1 of x, and the inner sum is $k(k-1)/2$.
The factor 2 outside is placed exactly to cancel the $1/2$ from the triangular number - a strong hint that the identity is being tested.
Finish with $\operatorname{E}(X^{2}) = \sigma^{2} + \mu^{2}$, so the answer is $\sigma^{2} + \mu^{2} - \mu$. Options (c) and (d) retain a stray $1/2$.
Companion identity worth knowing: $\sum \operatorname{P}(X > x) = \operatorname{E}(X)$ for non-negative integer variables - the first-moment version of the same trick.
solution: Write $S = \sum x \operatorname{P}(X > x) = \sum x \sum p_{k}$, where $p_{k} = \operatorname{P}(X = k)$.
Interchange the order of summation over the region $0 \le x < k$: $S = \sum p_{k}$ sum over $x = 0$ to k-1 of x.
The inner sum is the triangular number $k(k-1)/2$.
So $S = \sum p_{k} k(k-1)/2 = [\operatorname{E}(X^{2}) - \operatorname{E}(X)]/2$.
Therefore $2S = \operatorname{E}(X^{2}) - \operatorname{E}(X)$.
Since $\operatorname{E}(X^{2}) = \sigma^{2} + \mu^{2}$ and $\operatorname{E}(X) = \mu$, the value is $\sigma^{2} + \mu^{2} - \mu$, option (b).

sharedStem: *Questions 15–17 are based on the following joint pmf of $X$ and $Y$ ($0<\theta<1$):* | $X\backslash Y$ | −2 | −1 | 0 | 1 | 2 | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | **−1** | $\theta$ | $2\theta$ | $3\theta$ | $\theta$ | $\theta$ | | **0** | $2\theta$ | $3\theta$ | $\theta$ | $0$ | $0$ | | **1** | $\theta$ | $\theta$ | $\theta$ | $\theta$ | $2\theta$ |
stem: What is the moment generating function of $X \mid Y=2$?
shortcut: The $Y = 2$ column has masses $\theta, 0, 2\theta$ for X = -1, 0, 1, so the conditional probabilities are $1/3, 0, 2/3$. The MGF is $(e^{-t} + 2e^{t})/3$.
tips: For a conditional distribution, take only the relevant COLUMN and renormalise by its total - the value of $\theta$ never matters.
Column $Y = 2$ totals $\theta + 0 + 2\theta = 3\theta$, so the weights are $1/3$ and $2/3$ on X = -1 and X = +1.
MGF = $\sum e^{tx} \operatorname{P}(X = x \mid Y = 2) = (1/3)e^{-t} + (2/3)e^{t}$. Options (b) and (c) attach the weights to the wrong values.
Validity check: every MGF must equal 1 at $t = 0$. Here $(1 + 2)/3 = 1$, as required; option (b) gives $3/3 = 1$ too, so use the weights, not this test, to choose.
solution: Summing the whole table: row X = -1 gives $8\theta$, row $X = 0$ gives $6\theta$ and row $X = 1$ gives $6\theta, a$ total of $20\theta = 1$, so $\theta = 1/20$.
The column $Y = 2$ has entries $\theta$ at X = -1, 0 at $X = 0$ and $2\theta$ at $X = 1$, totalling $3\theta$.
Conditional probabilities: $\operatorname{P}(X = -1 \mid Y = 2) = \theta/3\theta = 1/3, \operatorname{P}(X = 0 \mid Y = 2) = 0, \operatorname{P}(X = 1 \mid Y = 2) = 2\theta/3\theta = 2/3$.
The moment generating function is $M(t) = \operatorname{E}(e^{tX} \mid Y = 2) = (1/3)e^{-t} + 0 + (2/3)e^{t} = (e^{-t} + 2e^{t})/3$.
Check $M(0) = (1 + 2)/3 = 1$. Option (a) is correct.

sharedStem: *Questions 15–17 are based on the following joint pmf of $X$ and $Y$ ($0<\theta<1$):* | $X\backslash Y$ | −2 | −1 | 0 | 1 | 2 | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | **−1** | $\theta$ | $2\theta$ | $3\theta$ | $\theta$ | $\theta$ | | **0** | $2\theta$ | $3\theta$ | $\theta$ | $0$ | $0$ | | **1** | $\theta$ | $\theta$ | $\theta$ | $\theta$ | $2\theta$ |
stem: What is the value of $\mathrm{Var}(X \mid Y=2)$?
shortcut: With conditional probabilities $1/3$ on -1 and $2/3$ on +1: $\operatorname{E}(X\mid Y=2) = 1/3$ and $\operatorname{E}(X^{2}\mid Y=2) = 1$, so the variance is $1 - 1/9 = 8/9$.
tips: Since X takes only the values -1 and +1 here, $X^{2} = 1$ with certainty, so $\operatorname{E}(X^{2} \mid Y = 2) = 1$ without any computation.
$\operatorname{E}(X\mid Y=2)$ = -$1(1/3) + 1(2/3) = 1/3$ - the same conditional distribution as the previous part, so reuse it.
Variance = $1 - (1/3)^{2} = 8/9$. Option $(a) 1/3$ is the conditional MEAN, the classic mis-selection.
A two-point variable on {-1, 1} with probability p on +1 has variance $4p(1-p) = 4(2/3)(1/3) = 8/9 - a$ fast cross-check.
solution: From the previous part, conditionally on $Y = 2$ the variable X takes the value -1 with probability $1/3$ and +1 with probability $2/3$.
Since X takes only the values -1 and +1 in this conditional distribution, $X^{2} = 1$ always, so $\operatorname{E}(X^{2} \mid Y = 2) = 1$.
$\operatorname{Var}(X \mid Y = 2) = \operatorname{E}(X^{2} \mid Y = 2) - [\operatorname{E}(X \mid Y = 2)]^{2} = 1 - 1/9 = 8/9$.
Equivalently, for a two-point variable on {-1, 1} with $\operatorname{P}(+1) = p$, the variance is $4p(1-p) = 4(2/3)(1/3) = 8/9$. Option (c) is correct.

sharedStem: *Questions 15–17 are based on the following joint pmf of $X$ and $Y$ ($0<\theta<1$):* | $X\backslash Y$ | −2 | −1 | 0 | 1 | 2 | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | **−1** | $\theta$ | $2\theta$ | $3\theta$ | $\theta$ | $\theta$ | | **0** | $2\theta$ | $3\theta$ | $\theta$ | $0$ | $0$ | | **1** | $\theta$ | $\theta$ | $\theta$ | $\theta$ | $2\theta$ |
stem: What is the value of $E(XY \mid Y=2)$?
shortcut: Given $Y = 2$, the factor Y is the constant 2, so $\operatorname{E}(XY \mid Y = 2) = 2 \operatorname{E}(X \mid Y = 2) = 2(1/3) = 2/3$.
tips: Conditioning on $Y = 2$ makes Y a CONSTANT inside the expectation, so it can be pulled straight out - no joint computation is needed.
Reuse $\operatorname{E}(X \mid Y = 2) = 1/3$ from the previous part; these three items are deliberately chained.
Option $(b) 1/3$ is $\operatorname{E}(X\mid Y=2)$ itself, the trap for candidates who forget to multiply by 2.
General rule: $\operatorname{E}(g(Y) h(X) \mid Y = y) = g(y) \operatorname{E}(h(X) \mid Y = y)$ - worth stating as a formula, since it appears constantly.
solution: We condition on the event $Y = 2$, so within this conditional distribution Y takes the constant value 2.
Hence $\operatorname{E}(XY \mid Y = 2) = \operatorname{E}(2X \mid Y = 2) = 2 \operatorname{E}(X \mid Y = 2)$.
From the earlier parts, the conditional distribution of X given $Y = 2$ puts mass $1/3$ on -1 and $2/3$ on +1.
Therefore $\operatorname{E}(XY \mid Y = 2) = 2(1/3) = 2/3$.
Option (c) is correct.

sharedStem: *Questions 18–20 are based on the following: let the joint pdf of $X$ and $Y$ be* $$f(x,y) = \begin{cases}\dfrac{\lambda x^{12}}{(1+xy)^{20}}, & x>0,\ y>1\\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$
stem: What is the value of $\lambda$? (where $B(m,n) = \displaystyle\int_0^1 x^{m-1}(1-x)^{n-1}\,dx$)
shortcut: Integrating x first (substituting u = xy) gives $B(13,7)/y^{13}$; integrating that over $y > 1$ gives $B(13,7)/12$. So $\lambda = 12/B(13,7) = 19/B(12,7)$, since $B(13,7) = (12/19)B(12,7)$.
tips: Beta second-kind integral: the $\int_{0}^{\infty} u^{m-1}/(1+u)^{m+n}\,du = B(m,n)$. With numerator power 12 and denominator power $20, m = 13$ and $n = 7$.
The substitution u = xy turns $(1 + xy)$ into $(1 + u)$ and produces the factor $y^{-13}$, which then integrates cleanly over $(1, \infty)$ to $1/12$.
Convert $B(13,7)$ to $B(12,7)$ using $B(m,n) = \Gamma(m)\Gamma(n)/\Gamma(m+n)$: the ratio $B(13,7)/B(12,7) = 12/19$, so $\lambda = 12 \times 19/12$ divided by $B(12,7) = 19/B(12,7)$.
The options are all expressed in $B(12,7)$, which is the signal that $a \Gamma$-ratio conversion is expected - do it at the very end.
solution: Require the double $\int \lambda x^{12}/(1+xy)^{20}$ over $x > 0, y > 1$ to equal 1.
Inner integral over x: substitute u = xy, so $x = u/y$ and $dx = du/y$, giving the $\int (u/y)^{12}/(1+u)^{20}\,du/y = (1/y^{13})$ times the $\int u^{12}/(1+u)^{20}\,du$.
That standard integral is B(m,n) with $m - 1 = 12$ and $m + n = 20$, i.e. $B(13,7)$. So the inner integral equals $B(13,7)/y^{13}$.
Outer integral over y from 1 to $\infty$: the $\int y^{-13}\,dy = [y^{-12}/(-12)]$ from 1 to $\infty = 1/12$.
Hence $\lambda B(13,7)/12 = 1$, giving $\lambda = 12/B(13,7)$.

sharedStem: *Questions 18–20 are based on the following: let the joint pdf of $X$ and $Y$ be* $$f(x,y) = \begin{cases}\dfrac{\lambda x^{12}}{(1+xy)^{20}}, & x>0,\ y>1\\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$
stem: What is the marginal distribution of $X$?
shortcut: Integrating out y gives $f_{X}(x) = \lambda x^{11}/[19(1+x)^{19}] = x^{11}/[B(12,7)(1+x)^{19}]$, the Beta second-kind density with $m = 12$ and $n = 7$.
tips: Beta type-II (second kind) density: $f(x) = x^{m-1}/[B(m,n)(1+x)^{m+n}]$ on $x > 0$. Match the two exponents to read off m and n.
Here the numerator power is 11 so $m = 12$, and the denominator power is 19 so $m + n = 19$, giving $n = 7$.
Support decides the type: X ranges over $(0, \infty)$, which is Beta type-II; Beta type-I lives on $(0,1)$. That eliminates options (c) and (d) at once.
The substitution $t = 1 + xy$ with y from 1 to $\infty$ makes t run from 1 + x to $\infty$, which is what produces the $(1+x)^{-19}$ factor.
solution: The marginal of X is $f_{X}(x)$ = the $\int \lambda x^{12}/(1 + xy)^{20}\,dy$.
Substitute $t = 1 + xy$, so $dt = x dy$ and $y = 1$ corresponds to $t = 1 + x$, with t running to $\infty$.
$f_{X}(x) = \lambda x^{12}$ times the $\int_{1+x}^{\infty} t^{-20}\,dt/x = \lambda x^{11} [t^{-19}/19]$ evaluated at $t = 1 + x = \lambda x^{11}/[19(1+x)^{19}]$.
The Beta distribution of the second kind with parameters (m, n) has density $x^{m-1}/[B(m,n)(1+x)^{m+n}]$; matching gives $m - 1 = 11$ and $m + n = 19$, so $m = 12$ and $n = 7$.
Hence X follows a Beta Type-II distribution with parameters $(12, 7)$, option (a).

sharedStem: *Questions 18–20 are based on the following: let the joint pdf of $X$ and $Y$ be* $$f(x,y) = \begin{cases}\dfrac{\lambda x^{12}}{(1+xy)^{20}}, & x>0,\ y>1\\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$
stem: Marginal distribution of $Y$ has pdf:
shortcut: The x-integral computed earlier gives $B(13,7)/y^{13}$, so $f_{Y}(y) = \lambda B(13,7)/y^{13} = 12/y^{13}$ on $y > 1$.
tips: Reuse the inner integral from the normalisation step: it already equals $B(13,7)/y^{13}$, so only the constant $\lambda$ needs attaching.
$\lambda B(13,7) = 12$ exactly, because $\lambda$ was chosen to make the whole double integral 1 and the $y-\int y^{-13}$ is $1/12$.
Validity check: the $\int 12 y^{-13}$ over $(1, \infty)$ is $12/12 = 1$. Options (a), (b) and (c) integrate to 1 as well, so use the derivation rather than this test.
This is a Pareto density with shape 12 on $(1, \infty)$ - recognising the family makes the exponent pairing $(12, 13)$ easy to remember.
solution: The marginal of Y is $f_{Y}(y)$ = the $\int \lambda x^{12}/(1 + xy)^{20}\,dx$.
As computed in the normalisation step, substituting u = xy gives this integral as $\lambda B(13,7)/y^{13}$ for $y > 1$.
From the normalisation, $\lambda B(13,7)/12 = 1$, so $\lambda B(13,7) = 12$.
Hence $f_{Y}(y) = 12/y^{13}$ for $y > 1$, and 0 otherwise.
Check: the $\int 12 y^{-13}\,dy$ from 1 to $\infty = 12 [y^{-12}/(-12)]$ from 1 to $\infty = 1, a$ valid density.
Option (d) is correct.

topic: Collection, Compilation & Presentation of Data; Frequency Distributions
subtopic: Collection, Compilation & Presentation of Data; Frequency Distributions
stem: Which of the following are examples of data condensing? 1. Data array 2. Frequency distribution 3. Histogram 4. Ogives Select the correct answer using the code given below:
shortcut: Condensation means reducing bulk. A frequency distribution, a histogram and an ogive all summarise the data into classes; a data array merely re-orders the same n observations without reducing them.
tips: Test each device by asking whether the number of items reported FALLS. A data array still lists every observation, so nothing is condensed.
A frequency distribution replaces n raw values by a handful of class frequencies - the primary act of condensation.
Histograms and ogives are drawn FROM the frequency distribution, so they inherit its condensed class structure and present it visually.
Keep the vocabulary apart: arraying = ordering, classification and tabulation = condensing, diagrams and graphs = presenting condensed data.
solution: Condensation of data means reducing a mass of raw observations to a compact summary that is easier to comprehend.
Item 1, data array: the raw observations are simply arranged in ascending or descending order. All n values are still listed, so the bulk is unchanged - this is organisation, not condensation.
Item 2, frequency distribution: the observations are grouped into classes and only the class frequencies are reported, which genuinely reduces the volume of data. CONDENSING.
Item 3, histogram: a graphical display of the grouped frequency distribution, presenting the condensed class information. CONDENSING.
Item 4, ogive: the cumulative frequency curve, again built from the grouped distribution. CONDENSING.
Hence items 2, 3 and 4 are examples of data condensing, option (c).

stem: For the variable $X$, following observations are taken: $X=2,5,0,6,3,8,1,3,0,2$. What is $\mathrm{Var}(2X+2)$?
shortcut: Mean = $30/10 = 3$ and sum of squares = 152, so $\operatorname{Var}(X) = 15.2 - 9 = 6.2$. Then $\operatorname{Var}(2X+2) = 4(6.2) = 24.8$.
tips: $\operatorname{Var}(aX + b) = a^{2} \operatorname{Var}(X)$ - the constant b vanishes and the multiplier is SQUARED. Adding 2 changes nothing.
Use the computing formula $Var$ = (sum $x^{2}$)/$n - \bar{x}$^2 rather than deviations: $152/10 - 3^{2} = 6.2$ in one line.
Check the two totals separately: sum $x = 30$ and sum $x^{2} = 4+25+0+36+9+64+1+9+0+4 = 152$. Recomputing these is where marks are lost.
This is the population (divisor n) variance; with divisor n - 1 the answer would be 6.889 and 27.6, so note which convention the options match - here it is n.
solution: The ten observations are 2, 5, 0, 6, 3, 8, 1, 3, 0, 2.
Sum = 30, so the mean is $\bar{x} = 30/10 = 3$.
For a linear transformation, $\operatorname{Var}(2X + 2) = 2^{2} \operatorname{Var}(X) = 4(6.2) = 24.8$, option (a).

topic: Skewness & Kurtosis (Moments)
subtopic: Skewness & Kurtosis (Moments)
stem: What is the 3rd central moment of Binomial distribution with parameters $n=10$ and $p=1/2$?
shortcut: The third central moment of B(n,p) is npq(q - p). With $p = q = 1/2$ the factor $(q - p)$ is 0, so the moment is 0.
tips: Formula: $\mu_{3}$ = npq(q - p). Its sign is the sign of the skewness, and it vanishes exactly when $p = 1/2$.
A binomial with $p = 1/2$ is SYMMETRIC about $n/2$, and every odd central moment of a symmetric distribution is zero - no formula is needed.
Do not confuse $\mu_{3}$ (third central moment) with the coefficient of skewness $\mu_{3}/\sigma^{3}$; both are 0 here, but they are different quantities.
For comparison, $\mu_{2}$ = npq = 2.5 here, which is planted as option (c) to catch a mis-read of the moment order.
solution: For the binomial distribution the third central moment is $\mu_{3} = n p q (q - p)$.
Therefore $q - p = 1/2 - 1/2 = 0$.
This is consistent with the fact that $B(n, 1/2)$ is symmetric about $n/2$, so all its odd central moments vanish.
Option (d) is correct.

topic: Bivariate & Multivariate Data; Association & Contingency
subtopic: Bivariate & Multivariate Data; Association & Contingency
stem: Consider the contingency table presenting the number of skilled and unskilled labour against their gender. What is the value of $\chi^2$ for testing the association between gender and the nature of work? | | Skilled | Unskilled | |---|---|---| | Male | 30 | 30 | | Female | 20 | 20 |
shortcut: Row totals 60 and 40, column totals 50 and $50, N = 100$, so every expected frequency equals the observed one $(30, 30, 20, 20)$. Hence $\chi^{2} = 0$.
tips: Compute one expected value first: $60 \times 50/100 = 30$, which already equals the observed 30 - a strong hint that the whole table is exactly independent.
Independence test by cross products: ad - bc = $30(20) - 30(20) = 0$, so the attributes are exactly independent and $\chi^{2}$ must be 0.
In this table each row splits 50:50 between skilled and unskilled, so gender carries NO information about the nature of work.
$\chi^{2}$ is non-negative and equals 0 only under exact independence - recognising that here saves all four cell computations.
solution: The observed table is Male: 30 skilled, 30 unskilled; Female: 20 skilled, 20 unskilled.
Row totals are 60 and 40; column totals are 50 and 50; the grand total is $N = 100$.
Expected frequencies under independence: Male-Skilled = $60 \times 50/100 = 30$, Male-Unskilled = 30, Female-Skilled = $40 \times 50/100 = 20$, Female-Unskilled = 20.
Every expected frequency equals the corresponding observed frequency, so each term $(O - E)^{2}/E$ is zero.
Equivalently, ad - bc = $30(20) - 30(20) = 0$, the condition for exact independence.
Hence $\chi^{2} = 0$, option (d).

topic: Correlation: Distribution of r, Partial, Multiple, Intraclass, Correlation Ratio
subtopic: Correlation: Distribution of r, Partial, Multiple, Intraclass, Correlation Ratio
stem: If $\mathrm{Var}(X)=4$, $\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)=32$ and correlation coefficient $r(X,Y)=0.8$ for some bivariate data, then what is $V(Y)$ equal to?
shortcut: $r = Cov/(sd_{X} sd_{Y})$ gives $0.8 = 32/(2 sd_{Y})$, so sd_Y = 20 and $\operatorname{V}(Y) = 400$.
tips: Take the square root of $\operatorname{Var}(X) = 4$ to get sd_X = 2 BEFORE substituting - using 4 directly is the standard error here.
Rearranged form: sd_Y = $Cov/(r sd_{X}) = 32/(0.8 \times 2) = 20$. One division and one multiplication.
Remember to SQUARE the standard deviation at the end: the question asks for the variance, so 20 becomes 400.
Consistency check: $Cov = r$ sd_X sd_Y = $0.8 \times 2 \times 20 = 32$, matching the datum exactly.
solution: The correlation coefficient is $r = \operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)/(sd(X) sd(Y))$.
Given $\operatorname{Var}(X) = 4$, the standard deviation is sd(X) = 2.
Substituting the known values: $0.8 = 32/(2 sd(Y))$.
Therefore $\operatorname{V}(Y) = 20^{2} = 400$.
Check: r sd(X) sd(Y) = $0.8(2)(20) = 32 = \operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)$. Option (a) is correct.

topic: Bivariate Normal Distribution
subtopic: Bivariate Normal Distribution
sharedStem: *Questions 26–30 are based on the following: the pdf of bivariate normal distribution is given by* $$f(x,y) = \lambda e^{-(2x^2+3xy+4y^2-7x-11y)}, \quad -\infty<x<\infty,\ -\infty<y<\infty$$ *where $\lambda$ is a constant.*
stem: What is the value of $E(X)+E(Y)+3$?
shortcut: The means are where the quadratic form is stationary: $4x + 3y = 7$ and $3x + 8y = 11$ give $x = y = 1$. So $\operatorname{E}(X) + \operatorname{E}(Y) + 3 = 5$.
tips: The mean vector of a normal density is the MINIMISER of the exponent's quadratic form - set both partial derivatives to zero and solve the 2x2 system.
Partial derivatives: $d/dx$ of $(2x^{2} + 3xy - 7x)$ is $4x + 3y - 7$; $d/dy$ of $(3xy + 4y^{2} - 11y)$ is $3x + 8y - 11$. Watch the factor 2 on the squared terms.
Elimination: $8(4x + 3y) - 3(3x + 8y) = 32x - 9x = 23x$, and $8(7) - 3(11) = 23$, so $x = 1$ immediately - the determinant 23 reappears throughout this set.
The offset '+3' in the question is pure decoration; find the two means and add.
solution: Write the exponent as -Q(x,y) with $Q = 2x^{2} + 3$xy + $4y^{2} - 7x - 11y$.
For a bivariate normal density the mean vector is the point at which the quadratic form Q attains its minimum, i.e. where both partial derivatives vanish.
Multiply the first by 8 and the second by 3: $32x + 24y = 56$ and $9x + 24y = 33$. Subtracting gives $23x = 23$, so $x = 1$.
Substituting back, $4(1) + 3y = 7$ gives $y = 1$. Hence $\operatorname{E}(X) = 1$ and $\operatorname{E}(Y) = 1$.
Therefore $\operatorname{E}(X) + \operatorname{E}(Y) + 3 = 1 + 1 + 3 = 5$, option (d).

topic: Bivariate Normal Distribution
subtopic: Bivariate Normal Distribution
sharedStem: *Questions 26–30 are based on the following: the pdf of bivariate normal distribution is given by* $$f(x,y) = \lambda e^{-(2x^2+3xy+4y^2-7x-11y)}, \quad -\infty<x<\infty,\ -\infty<y<\infty$$ *where $\lambda$ is a constant.*
stem: What is the value of $23(\mathrm{Var}(X)+\mathrm{Var}(Y))$?
shortcut: The precision matrix is $A = [[4,3],[3,8]]$ with determinant 23, so the covariance matrix is $(1/23)[[8,-3],[-3,4]]$. Then $23(Var X + Var Y) = 8 + 4 = 12$.
tips: Reading the precision matrix: $\exp(-Q)$ with $Q = a x^{2} + b$ xy + $c y^{2}$ means $Q = (1/2)z'$Az, so $A_{11} = 2a, A_{22} = 2c$ and $A_{12} = b$. Here $A = [[4,3],[3,8]]$.
Covariance = inverse of the precision matrix: for a 2x2 matrix, swap the diagonal, negate the off-diagonal and divide by the determinant $4(8) - 9 = 23$.
$\operatorname{Var}(X) = 8/23$ and $\operatorname{Var}(Y) = 4/23$ - note the SWAP: the larger variance goes with the smaller coefficient in the quadratic form.
The factor 23 in the question is exactly the determinant, placed there to clear the denominators - a strong hint that this route is intended.
solution: The exponent is -Q with $Q = 2x^{2} + 3$xy + $4y^{2} - 7x - 11y$; the quadratic part is $2x^{2} + 3$xy + $4y^{2}$.
Writing the quadratic part as $(1/2) z' A z$ with $z = (x - \mu1, y - \mu2)'$, we read $A_{11} = 2(2) = 4, A_{22} = 2(4) = 8$ and $A_{12} = A_{21} = 3$.
So the precision matrix is $A = [[4, 3], [3, 8]]$, with determinant $4(8) - 3(3) = 32 - 9 = 23$.
The covariance matrix is the inverse: $\Sigma = (1/23)[[8, -3], [-3, 4]]$.
Hence $\operatorname{Var}(X) = 8/23$ and $\operatorname{Var}(Y) = 4/23$.
Therefore $23(\operatorname{Var}(X) + \operatorname{Var}(Y)) = 8 + 4 = 12$, option (c).

topic: Bivariate Normal Distribution
subtopic: Bivariate Normal Distribution
sharedStem: *Questions 26–30 are based on the following: the pdf of bivariate normal distribution is given by* $$f(x,y) = \lambda e^{-(2x^2+3xy+4y^2-7x-11y)}, \quad -\infty<x<\infty,\ -\infty<y<\infty$$ *where $\lambda$ is a constant.*
stem: If $r$ is the correlation coefficient between $X$ and $Y$, then what is the value of $\sqrt{2}\,r$?
tips: The 23s cancel in the correlation, leaving r = -$3/\sqrt{8 \times 4}$ = -$3/\sqrt{32}$ - so the determinant never needs to be carried through.
Sign rule: the correlation takes the OPPOSITE sign to the off-diagonal entry of the precision matrix. Here that entry is +3, so r is negative - all four options duly are.
$\sqrt{32} = 4 \sqrt{2}$, so multiplying by $\sqrt{2}$ clears the surd exactly and gives the clean -$3/4$. The question's $\sqrt{2}$ factor is the hint that this will happen.
Validity check: |r| = $3/(4 sqrt2) = 0.53 < 1$, so the covariance matrix is positive definite and the density exists.
solution: From the previous part, the covariance matrix is $\Sigma = (1/23)[[8, -3], [-3, 4]]$.
So $\operatorname{Var}(X) = 8/23, \operatorname{Var}(Y) = 4/23$ and $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)$ = -$3/23$.
The correlation is $r = Cov/sqrt(\operatorname{Var}(X) \operatorname{Var}(Y)) = (-3/23)/sqrt((8/23)(4/23)) = (-3/23)/(\sqrt{32}/23)$.
The factors of 23 cancel, giving r = -$3/\sqrt{32}$ = -$3/(4 \sqrt{2})$.
Multiplying by $\sqrt{2}$: $\sqrt{2} r$ = -$3 \sqrt{2}/(4 \sqrt{2})$ = -$3/4$.
Option (a) is correct.

topic: Bivariate Normal Distribution
subtopic: Bivariate Normal Distribution
sharedStem: *Questions 26–30 are based on the following: the pdf of bivariate normal distribution is given by* $$f(x,y) = \lambda e^{-(2x^2+3xy+4y^2-7x-11y)}, \quad -\infty<x<\infty,\ -\infty<y<\infty$$ *where $\lambda$ is a constant.*
stem: What is the distribution of $Y \mid X=x$ equal to?
shortcut: Collect the y-terms of the exponent: $4y^{2} + (3x - 11)y$. Completing the square gives a normal with mean $(11 - 3x)/8$ and variance $1/(2 \times 4) = 1/8$.
tips: For a conditional distribution, treat x as FIXED and complete the square in y only - the x-only terms are absorbed into the normalising constant.
Coefficient reading: $\exp(-c y^{2} + ...)$ corresponds to variance $1/(2c)$. Here $c = 4$, so the conditional variance is $1/8$ regardless of x.
The conditional mean is -(coefficient of y)/$(2c)$ = -$(3x - 11)/8 = (11 - 3x)/8$. Getting the sign right is the crux.
Cross-check at $x = 1$ (the mean of X): the conditional mean is $(11-3)/8 = 1 = \operatorname{E}(Y)$, exactly as the regression line must pass through the means.
solution: The joint density is proportional to $\exp(-(2x^{2} + 3xy + 4y^{2} - 7x - 11y))$.
For fixed x, keep only the terms involving y: -$(4y^{2} + 3xy - 11y)$ = -$(4y^{2} + (3x - 11)y)$.
Complete the square: $4y^{2} + (3x-11)y = 4[y + (3x-11)/8]^{2}$ - constant, where the constant depends only on x.
So the conditional density of Y given $X = x$ is proportional to $\exp(-4[y - (11 - 3x)/8]^{2})$.
Comparing with $\exp(-(y - m)^{2}/(2 \sigma^{2}))$ gives $2 \sigma^{2} = 1/4$, i.e. $\sigma^{2} = 1/8$, and $m = (11 - 3x)/8$.
Hence $Y \mid X = x \sim N((11 - 3x)/8, 1/8)$. At $x = 1$ the mean is $1 = \operatorname{E}(Y)$, as required. Option (a) is correct.

topic: Bivariate Normal Distribution
subtopic: Bivariate Normal Distribution
sharedStem: *Questions 26–30 are based on the following: the pdf of bivariate normal distribution is given by* $$f(x,y) = \lambda e^{-(2x^2+3xy+4y^2-7x-11y)}, \quad -\infty<x<\infty,\ -\infty<y<\infty$$ *where $\lambda$ is a constant.*
stem: If $E(X)=\mu_1$ and $E(Y)=\mu_2$, then what is the value of $2\pi f(\mu_1,\mu_2)$?
shortcut: At the mean vector the bivariate normal density attains its maximum $1/(2 pi \sqrt{\det \Sigma})$. Here $\det \Sigma = 1/23$, so 2 pi $f(\mu1, \mu2) = \sqrt{23}$.
tips: Peak value of a bivariate normal: $f(\mu) = 1/(2 pi \sqrt{\det \Sigma}) = \sqrt{\det A}/(2 pi)$, where A is the precision matrix. Multiplying by 2 pi leaves sqrt($\det A$).
$\det A = 23$ was already computed for the variances, so this part is a one-line reuse - the 2 pi in the question exists precisely to cancel.
Equivalently $f(\mu) = 1/(2 pi \sigma1 \sigma2 \sqrt{1 - r^2})$; substituting $\sigma1^{2} = 8/23, \sigma2^{2} = 4/23$ and $r^{2} = 9/32$ gives the same $\sqrt{23}/(2 pi)$.
The exponential factor is $\exp(0) = 1$ at the mean, which is why only the normalising constant survives.
solution: For a bivariate normal density, the maximum occurs at the mean vector and equals the normalising constant $1/(2 pi \sqrt{\det \Sigma})$.
From the earlier parts, the precision matrix is $A = [[4,3],[3,8]]$ with $\det A = 23$, so $\Sigma = A^{-1}$ has $\det \Sigma = 1/23$.
Hence $f(\mu1, \mu2) = 1/(2 pi \sqrt{1/23}) = \sqrt{23}/(2 pi)$.
Multiplying by 2 pi: 2 pi $f(\mu1, \mu2) = \sqrt{23}$.
Equivalently, using $f(\mu) = 1/(2 pi \sigma1 \sigma2 \sqrt{1-r^2})$ with $\sigma1 \sigma2 = \sqrt{32}/23$ and $1 - r^{2} = 23/32$ gives the same value.
Option (a) is correct.

topic: Bivariate Normal Distribution
subtopic: Bivariate Normal Distribution
stem: If $(X,Y)\sim BVN(0,0,1,1;\rho)$, then what is the value of $\dfrac{E\left((Y-\rho X)^4 \mid X\right)}{(1-\rho^2)^2}$?
shortcut: Given X, the residual $Y - \rho X$ is $N(0, 1 - \rho^{2})$. The fourth moment of a centred normal is $3 \sigma^{4} = 3(1-\rho^{2})^{2}$, so the ratio is 3.
tips: Conditional law for a standard bivariate normal: $Y \mid X = x \sim N(\rho x, 1 - \rho^{2})$. Subtracting $\rho X$ centres it at zero.
Fourth central moment of $N(0, \sigma^{2})$ is $3 \sigma^{4}$ - memorise the sequence $1, 0, \sigma^{2}, 0, 3 \sigma^{4}$ for the first four moments.
The denominator $(1 - \rho^{2})^{2}$ is placed exactly to cancel $\sigma^{4}$, leaving the pure constant 3 - free of both x and $\rho$.
Note the answer does not depend on X at all, so the conditional expectation is a constant and equals the unconditional one - a useful structural observation.
solution: For (X,Y) ~ BVN(0,0,1,1,$\rho$), the conditional distribution is $Y \mid X = x \sim N(\rho x, 1 - \rho^{2})$.
Hence the residual $Y - \rho X$, conditionally on X, is normal with mean 0 and variance $\sigma^{2} = 1 - \rho^{2}$.
For a centred normal variable with variance $\sigma^{2}$, the fourth moment is $\operatorname{E}(W^{4}) = 3 \sigma^{4}$.
So $\operatorname{E}[(Y - \rho X)^{4} \mid X] = 3(1 - \rho^{2})^{2}$.
Dividing by $(1 - \rho^{2})^{2}$ gives 3, independently of x and of $\rho$.
Option (b) is correct.

topic: Correlation: Distribution of r, Partial, Multiple, Intraclass, Correlation Ratio
subtopic: Correlation: Distribution of r, Partial, Multiple, Intraclass, Correlation Ratio
stem: For $h$ families containing equal number $k$ of members in each family, the range of intra-class correlation coefficient $\rho$ is:
shortcut: The intra-class correlation lies between -$1/(k-1)$ and +1, the lower bound arising because the k members' deviations within a family must sum to zero.
tips: Range to memorise: -$1/(k-1) \le \rho \le 1$, where k is the family (group) size. The lower bound is NOT -1 - that is the key discriminator.
Reason for the asymmetry: within a group the deviations from the group mean sum to zero, so the members cannot all be strongly negatively correlated with one another.
As k grows the lower bound tends to 0, so large groups permit almost no negative intra-class correlation - a useful sanity anchor.
For $k = 2$ the bound is -1, which is why the pairwise case looks like an ordinary correlation and can mislead you into choosing option (b).
solution: The intra-class correlation coefficient measures the similarity of members within the same group, here families of k members each.
It can be written as $\rho$ = (MS_between - MS_within)/(MS_between + $(k-1)$ MS_within) in the analysis-of-variance formulation.
Its maximum is +1, attained when all members of a family are identical so that the within-family variation vanishes.

Its minimum is not -1: because the k deviations from the family mean must sum to zero, the members cannot be arbitrarily negatively correlated. Setting the between-family mean square to zero gives the smallest value -$1/(k-1)$.
Hence the range is -$1/(k - 1)$ to 1.
Option (d) is correct.

topic: Standard Errors & Large Sample Tests
subtopic: Standard Errors & Large Sample Tests
stem: If the correlation coefficient between heights of fathers and sons from a random sample of 900 is calculated as 0.67, what is the standard error?
tips: Standard error of a sample correlation: $\operatorname{SE}(r) = (1 - r^{2})/\sqrt{n}$. The numerator is 1 - r SQUARED, not 1 - r.
$\sqrt{900} = 30$ makes the arithmetic clean: $0.5511/30 = 0.01837$.
The SE shrinks like $1/\sqrt{n}$, so with $n = 900$ it must be small - roughly 0.02 - which identifies option (a) at a glance.
For inference on a non-zero $\rho$, prefer Fisher's z transformation with variance $1/(n-3)$; this simple SE formula is used chiefly for a quick significance check.
solution: The standard error of the sample correlation coefficient is $\operatorname{SE}(r) = (1 - r^{2})/\sqrt{n}$.
The sample size is $n = 900$, so $\sqrt{n} = 30$.
Rounded, this is 0.018.
Option (a) is correct.

topic: Standard Errors & Large Sample Tests
subtopic: Standard Errors & Large Sample Tests
stem: The mean height obtained from a random sample of size 100 is 64 inches. The standard deviation of the height distribution is known to be 3 inches. What is the 95% confidence interval for mean height of the population? (Assume $Z_{0.025}=2$)
shortcut: $SE = 3/\sqrt{100} = 0.3$, so the margin is $2(0.3) = 0.6$ and the interval is 64 +- $0.6 = (63.4, 64.6)$.
tips: $SE = \sigma/\sqrt{n} = 3/10 = 0.3$. The population SD is given, so the normal multiplier applies rather than t.
The question supplies $Z = 2$ rather than 1.96 to keep the arithmetic exact - use the value given, not the one you remember.
The interval must be SYMMETRIC about the sample mean 64: check that $(63.4 + 64.6)/2 = 64$. Option (b) fails this test at once.
Interval width $2 \times 2 \times 0.3 = 1.2$ inches; options (c) and (d) are three and five times too wide, corresponding to forgetting the sqrt(n).
solution: The sample mean is $\bar{x} = 64$ inches, the population standard deviation is $\sigma = 3$ inches and the sample size is $n = 100$.
The standard error of the mean is $\sigma/\sqrt{n} = 3/10 = 0.3$.
For a 95% confidence interval with $\sigma$ known, the multiplier supplied is $Z(0.025) = 2$.
Margin of error = $2 \times 0.3 = 0.6$.
The interval is 64 +- 0.6, i.e. from 63.4 to 64.6.
Option (a) is correct.

topic: Standard Errors & Large Sample Tests
subtopic: Standard Errors & Large Sample Tests
stem: In an art school, 380 children out of 800 were found to be singers. If $E$ is the standard error of proportion of singers, then what is $1280000E^2$ equal to?
tips: SE of a proportion: $E = \sqrt{pq/n}$, so $E^{2}$ = pq/n - the question asks for $E^{2}$, which spares you the square root entirely.
pq = $0.475 \times 0.525 = 0.249375$. Note that pq is always close to 0.25 when p is near $1/2, a$ useful check.
1,280,$000/800 = 1600$, so the answer is $1600 \times 0.249375 = 399$ - factor the constant before multiplying.
The tidy result 399 confirms the arithmetic; a value near 400 is exactly what 1600 x 0.25 would give.
solution: The sample proportion of singers is $p = 380/800 = 0.475$, so $q = 1 - p = 0.525$, with $n = 800$.
The standard error of a proportion is $E = \sqrt{pq/n}$, hence $E^{2}$ = pq/n.
Option (b) is correct.

topic: Sampling Distributions: Sample Mean, Sample Variance, t, Chi-square, F
subtopic: Sampling Distributions: Sample Mean, Sample Variance, t, Chi-square, F
stem: If a sample of size $n$ is taken from $N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ and let $\bar x$ and $s^2$ be sample mean and sample variance respectively, then distribution of $\dfrac{(n-1)s^2}{\sigma^2}$ is:
shortcut: In normal sampling, $(n-1)s^{2}/\sigma^{2}$ follows $a \chi^{2}$ distribution with n - 1 degrees of freedom.
tips: One degree of freedom is lost because the sample mean is estimated from the data - hence n - 1, not n.
The statistic is non-negative and skewed, so it cannot be a t distribution; t variables range over the whole line. That kills options (c) and (d) immediately.
Companion facts: $\bar{x}$ and $s^{2}$ are INDEPENDENT in normal sampling, and their combination gives the t statistic $(\bar{x} - \mu)/(s/sqrt n) \sim t$ with n-1 d.f.
This result underpins both the confidence interval for $\sigma^{2}$ and the $\chi^{2}$ test of a specified variance.
solution: Let $x_{1}$, ..., $x_{n}$ be a random sample from $N(\mu, \sigma^{2})$, with sample mean $\bar{x}$ and sample variance $s^{2}$ = sum $(x_{i} - \bar{x})^{2}/(n-1)$.
Then sum $(x_{i} - \bar{x})^{2} = (n-1)s^{2}$, and dividing by $\sigma^{2}$ standardises the sum of squared deviations.
Because the deviations are taken about the ESTIMATED mean $\bar{x}$ rather than the true mean mu, one linear constraint is imposed and one degree of freedom is lost.
The classical result is that $(n-1)s^{2}/\sigma^{2}$ follows $a \chi^{2}$ distribution with n - 1 degrees of freedom, independently of $\bar{x}$.
The statistic is non-negative and skewed, consistent with $a \chi^{2}$ rather than a t distribution.
Option (a) is correct.

topic: Curve Fitting & Orthogonal Polynomials
subtopic: Curve Fitting & Orthogonal Polynomials
stem: For a bivariate data, using the principles of least-squares, the following models were constructed: $E_1$: $Y=3X+5$ with $\sum(Y_i-3X_i-5)^2=15.48$ $E_2$: $Y=-X^2+8X+2$ with $\sum(Y_i+X_i^2-8X_i-2)^2=13.36$ What is the estimated value of $Y$ for $X=6$?
shortcut: Choose the model with the smaller residual sum of squares: E2 has 13.36 against $E_{1}'s 15.48$. Then Y = -$36 + 48 + 2 = 14$ at $X = 6$.
tips: Least squares selects the model with the SMALLER sum of squared residuals - that single comparison decides which equation to substitute into.
Compute both predictions to see the trap: E1 gives $3(6) + 5 = 23$ and E2 gives 14. Both appear as options, so the model choice is the whole question.
Substitute carefully into the quadratic: -$(6^{2}) + 8(6) + 2$ = -$36 + 48 + 2 = 14$. The leading minus sign applies to the square.
The quadratic's advantage here is modest (13.36 against 15.48), a reminder that a better fit is not automatically a better model - but the question asks only for the least-squares choice.
solution: Two least-squares models are offered, with their residual sums of squares stated.
Model E1: $Y = 3X + 5$ with sum of squared residuals 15.48.
Model E2: Y = -$X^{2} + 8X + 2$ with sum of squared residuals 13.36.
The principle of least squares prefers the model with the smaller residual sum of squares, so E2 is selected since $13.36 < 15.48$.
Substituting $X = 6$ into E2: Y = -$(36) + 8(6) + 2$ = -$36 + 48 + 2 = 14$, option (b). (Model E1 would have given 23, which is offered as option (d).)

topic: Sampling Distributions: Sample Mean, Sample Variance, t, Chi-square, F
subtopic: Sampling Distributions: Sample Mean, Sample Variance, t, Chi-square, F
stem: Let $x_1,x_2,x_3,\ldots,x_n$ be a random sample from a Normal population with mean $\mu_0$ and variance $\sigma^2$. If $\bar X$ is the sample mean, then the distribution of $\dfrac{\bar X-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}}$ is:
shortcut: The population standard deviation $\sigma$ is used, not the sample s, so the standardised sample mean is exactly standard normal.
tips: $\sigma$ in the denominator gives $N(0,1)$; s in the denominator gives t with n - 1 degrees of freedom. Check which symbol appears before choosing.
For a NORMAL parent the result is exact for every n, not merely asymptotic - no appeal to the CLT is needed.
$\bar{x} \sim N(\mu, \sigma^{2}/n)$, so subtracting mu and dividing by $\sigma/\sqrt{n}$ standardises it exactly.
The t distribution arises only because s is itself random; replacing $\sigma$ by s adds variability and fattens the tails.
solution: The sample comes from a normal population with mean $\mu0$ and variance $\sigma^{2}$, so the sample mean is exactly normal: $\bar{X} \sim N(\mu0, \sigma^{2}/n)$.
Subtracting the mean gives $\bar{X} - \mu0 \sim N(0, \sigma^{2}/n)$.
Dividing by the standard deviation of $\bar{X}$, namely $\sigma/\sqrt{n}$, standardises it.
Since $\sigma$ is the KNOWN population standard deviation and not a sample estimate, no additional randomness is introduced.
Hence $(\bar{X} - \mu0)/(\sigma/\sqrt{n}) \sim N(0,1)$ exactly, for every sample size n.
Option (a) is correct.

topic: Bivariate Normal Distribution
subtopic: Bivariate Normal Distribution
sharedStem: *Questions 39–40 are based on: $(X,Y)\sim BVN(0,0,1,1;\rho)$*
stem: What is the value of $\mathrm{Cov}(Y-\rho X, X)$?
shortcut: $\operatorname{Cov}\!\left(\text{Y - rho X, X}\right) = \operatorname{Cov}(Y,X) - \rho \operatorname{Var}(X) = \rho - \rho(1) = 0$.
tips: Use bilinearity of covariance: $\operatorname{Cov}\!\left(\text{Y - rho X, X}\right) = \operatorname{Cov}(Y,X) - \rho \operatorname{Cov}(X,X)$. No integration is needed.
For the standard bivariate normal, $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y) = \rho$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X) = 1$, so the two terms cancel exactly.
Interpretation: $Y - \rho X$ is the RESIDUAL from the regression of Y on X, and a least-squares residual is always uncorrelated with the predictor.
Under joint normality this zero covariance upgrades to full independence - which is exactly what the next part exploits.
solution: For (X,Y) ~ BVN(0,0,1,1,$\rho$) we have $\operatorname{Var}(X) = \operatorname{Var}(Y) = 1$ and $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y) = \rho$.
By the bilinearity of covariance, $\operatorname{Cov}\!\left(\text{Y - rho X, X}\right) = \operatorname{Cov}(Y, X) - \rho \operatorname{Cov}(X, X)$.
$\operatorname{Cov}(X,X) = \operatorname{Var}(X) = 1$.
So the expression is $\rho - \rho(1) = 0$.
This reflects the general fact that the residual $Y - \rho X$ from the regression of Y on X is uncorrelated with X, and under joint normality it is in fact independent of X.
Option (a) is correct.
