subtopic: Programming Basics: Algorithm, Flowchart, Control Structures, Arrays, Functions
stem: Consider the following statements in respect of debugger: I. Debugger is a program used to detect errors and bugs in a program. II. In order to debug the program, a debugger helps us perform step-by-step execution of a program. III. In order to debug the program, a debugger helps us perform stopping the execution of the program until the errors are corrected. Which of the statements given above are correct?
shortcut: Detecting bugs, single-stepping through code and halting execution at breakpoints are all standard debugger facilities, so all three statements hold.
tips: Core debugger facilities to remember: breakpoints, single-stepping, watching variables, examining the call stack, and modifying values at run time.
Statement II describes SINGLE-STEPPING and statement III describes BREAKPOINTS - two distinct, genuine features, not duplicates.
A debugger locates run-time and LOGICAL errors, the ones a compiler cannot report - which is exactly why it is a separate tool.
When every statement in a set names a textbook feature of the same tool, 'all of them' is the natural key.
solution: A debugger is a software tool that assists the programmer in locating and correcting faults in a program.
Statement I: it is used to detect errors and bugs - particularly run-time and logical errors that the compiler cannot report. TRUE.
Statement II: single-stepping lets the programmer execute one statement at a time and observe the effect on variables and control flow. TRUE.
Statement III: breakpoints let the programmer halt execution at chosen points, inspect the program state and resume once the problem is understood or corrected. TRUE.
All three describe standard debugger facilities.
Hence option (d) is correct.

topic: Software, Operating Systems, Packages & Utilities
subtopic: Software, Operating Systems, Packages & Utilities
stem: Consider the following statements in respect of Operating System: I. It is the principal component of system software. II. It is responsible for overall management of the computer resources. III. It provides an interface between the computer and user and helps in implementing the application programs. Which of the statements given above are correct?
shortcut: The operating system is the principal system software, the manager of all machine resources, and the interface between user and hardware - all three statements are standard definitions.
tips: Three standard descriptions of an OS: principal system software, resource manager, and user-hardware interface. Each statement matches one.
Resource management covers the processor, memory, files and I/O devices - the four resources every textbook lists.
The OS also provides the environment in which application programs are loaded and run, which is the second half of statement III.
When all three statements paraphrase the same textbook definition from different angles, 'all of them' is almost always the key.
solution: Statement I: system software comprises the operating system, device drivers, language translators and utilities, and the operating system is its principal component - without it no other software can run. TRUE.
Statement II: the operating system allocates and manages the processor, main memory, files and I/O devices among competing processes. TRUE.

Statement III: it provides the interface - command line or graphical - through which the user directs the machine, and it loads and runs application programs, providing them with system services. TRUE.
All three are standard descriptions of an operating system.
Hence option (d) is correct.

topic: Computer Security: Virus, Antivirus, Firewall, Spyware, Malware
subtopic: Computer Security: Virus, Antivirus, Firewall, Spyware, Malware
stem: Consider the following tasks: I. Search and replace II. Encryption III. Virus scanner IV. Backup V. Data recovery How many of the above are tasks of Utility Programs?
shortcut: Encryption, virus scanning, backup and data recovery are all system-maintenance tasks performed by utility programs. 'Search and replace' is a text-editing feature of application software, so four of the five qualify.
tips: Utility programs MAINTAIN and PROTECT the system: antivirus, backup, data recovery, encryption, compression, disk defragmentation, file management.
Search and replace is an editing operation inside a word processor or editor - application software performing work for the user, not housekeeping for the system.
Ask of each item: 'does this look after the computer, or does it do the user's work?'. That test sorts the five instantly.
Note the distinction from system software proper (the OS and translators); utilities are a maintenance sub-category sitting alongside them.
solution: Utility programs are system software that maintain, analyse, configure and protect the computer system.
Item II, encryption: protecting stored or transmitted data is a standard security utility. UTILITY.
Item III, virus scanner: antivirus software is the archetypal utility program. UTILITY.
Item IV, backup: copying data for safekeeping is a standard maintenance utility. UTILITY. Item V, data recovery: restoring lost or damaged files is likewise a maintenance utility. UTILITY.

Item I, search and replace: this is an editing operation provided by a word processor or text editor, i.e. application software doing the user's work rather than maintaining the system. NOT a utility task.
Four of the five are tasks of utility programs, option (c).

topic: Computer Security: Virus, Antivirus, Firewall, Spyware, Malware
subtopic: Computer Security: Virus, Antivirus, Firewall, Spyware, Malware
stem: Which of the following security services prevents either sender or receiver from denying a transmitted message?
shortcut: Preventing a party from later denying that a message was sent or received is precisely the definition of non-repudiation.
tips: The five classical security services: confidentiality (secrecy), integrity (no alteration), authentication (identity), non-repudiation (no denial), availability (access).
The word 'denying' in the stem maps directly onto 'repudiation' - the vocabulary itself gives the answer.
Digital signatures provide non-repudiation because only the holder of the private key could have produced the signature.
Authentication proves who you ARE at the time; non-repudiation proves who acted LATER, in a way that stands up to subsequent denial - a subtle but examinable distinction.
solution: Non-repudiation is the security service that prevents either party from later denying an action they performed.
Non-repudiation of origin prevents the sender from denying having sent the message; non-repudiation of delivery prevents the receiver from denying having received it.
It is typically implemented with digital signatures, since only the holder of the private key could have generated the signature.

Authentication verifies identity at the time of access, confidentiality prevents unauthorised disclosure, and integrity ensures the message has not been altered - none of these addresses subsequent denial.
Hence the required service is non-repudiation, option (c).

topic: Networks: LAN, WAN, Internet, Intranet
subtopic: Networks: LAN, WAN, Internet, Intranet
stem: At which layer of TCP/IP do ICMP and ARP function?
shortcut: ICMP and ARP are both support protocols for IP, so in the TCP/IP model they are placed at the network (internet) layer.
tips: ICMP carries error and control messages for IP itself (ping, destination unreachable, time exceeded), so it sits alongside IP at the network layer.
ARP resolves IP addresses to MAC addresses; it straddles the network-data link boundary but is conventionally grouped with the network layer in the TCP/IP model.
Neither carries user data end to end, so they cannot be transport or application protocols - options (b) and (c) are out of category.
Companion facts: ICMP messages are encapsulated inside IP datagrams, and ARP requests are broadcast on the local link only.
solution: The TCP/IP model has four layers: application, transport, network (internet) and network access.

ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) carries error reports and diagnostic messages about IP delivery, such as 'destination unreachable' and the echo request and reply used by ping. Its messages are encapsulated in IP datagrams, so it belongs with IP at the network layer.

ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) maps an IP address to the corresponding MAC address so that a datagram can be delivered on the local link. It supports IP addressing and is conventionally placed at the network layer of the TCP/IP model.
Neither protocol provides end-to-end data transfer (transport layer) nor user services (application layer).
Hence both function at the network layer, option (a).

topic: Number Systems & Binary Arithmetic
subtopic: Number Systems & Binary Arithmetic
stem: What is the representation of $-59$ in the 2's complement system?
tips: Two's complement = one's complement PLUS ONE. Stopping at the inversion gives 11000100, which is planted as option (b).
$59 = 32 + 16 + 8 + 2 + 1 = 00111011$ - build from powers of two rather than by repeated division.
The sign bit must be 1 for a negative number, which eliminates any option beginning with 0.
Verify by addition: $00111011 + 11000101 = 1 00000000$, and discarding the carry leaves zero - the definitive check.
solution: Write the magnitude in 8-bit binary: $59 = 32 + 16 + 8 + 2 + 1$, so $59 = 00111011$.
Take the one's complement by inverting every bit: 11000100.
The leading bit is 1, correctly marking a negative value.
Check: $00111011 + 11000101 = 100000000$; discarding the carry out of the 8-bit word leaves 00000000, confirming the two are additive inverses.
Hence -59 is 11000101, option (a).

topic: Languages, Compiler, Assembler, Interpreter; Low & High Level
subtopic: Languages, Compiler, Assembler, Interpreter; Low & High Level
stem: Consider the following statements: I. Both compiler and interpreter can translate the program written in high-level language into machine-level instructions. II. The interpreter translates the whole program into machine language program before executing any of the instructions. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
shortcut: Statement I is true - both translators convert high-level source to machine instructions. Statement II describes the COMPILER, not the interpreter, so it is false.
tips: One-line contrast: compiler translates the WHOLE program before any execution; interpreter translates and executes ONE statement at a time.
Statement II simply swaps the two definitions - the classic falsification device in this topic.
Both are translators, which is why statement I is safe; the difference lies in WHEN translation happens, not in what is produced.
Consequences: a compiler produces a separate object/executable file and reports all errors up front, whereas an interpreter produces no object file and stops at the first error encountered.
solution: Statement I: both compilers and interpreters are language translators that convert a program written in a high-level language into machine-level instructions the processor can execute. TRUE.
Statement II: it is the COMPILER that reads and translates the entire program before any execution takes place, producing an object program.
An interpreter takes the source one statement at a time, translates that statement and immediately executes it before moving on, so it never translates the whole program in advance.
The statement therefore attributes the compiler's behaviour to the interpreter. FALSE.
Only statement I is correct.
Hence option (a) is correct.

topic: Hardware: Input, Output & Peripheral Devices
subtopic: Hardware: Input, Output & Peripheral Devices
stem: Consider the following statements in respect of Webcam: I. It is an input device. II. The quality of the video taken through the Webcam largely depends on frame rate and resolution. III. For a video to be smooth and clear, the frame rate is maximum and resolution is minimum. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
shortcut: A webcam is an input device and its quality does depend on frame rate and resolution, so I and II hold. Statement III is wrong: BOTH frame rate and resolution should be high for smooth, clear video.
tips: Separate the two quality dimensions: FRAME RATE governs smoothness of motion, RESOLUTION governs sharpness of detail. Good video needs both to be high.
Statement III asks for minimum resolution, which would give smooth but BLURRED video - internally contradictory with the word 'clear'.
A webcam captures images and sends them into the computer, so it is unambiguously an input device.
The trade-off in practice is bandwidth: raising both frame rate and resolution increases the data rate, which is why compression is used - but neither is deliberately minimised.
solution: Statement I: a webcam captures live images and video and transmits them into the computer, so it is an input device. TRUE.
Statement II: video quality is governed principally by the frame rate (frames per second, controlling smoothness of motion) and the resolution (pixels per frame, controlling detail). TRUE.
Statement III: smooth motion requires a HIGH frame rate, and clear, detailed images require a HIGH resolution.
Minimising the resolution would make the picture blurred, contradicting the requirement that the video be 'clear'. FALSE.
Only statements I and II are correct.
Hence option (b) is correct.

topic: Computer Organisation: CPU, ALU, Control & Memory Units, I/O Units
subtopic: Computer Organisation: CPU, ALU, Control & Memory Units, I/O Units
stem: Which of the following are main operations of CPU? I. Fetching instructions from the memory II. Decoding the instructions III. Executing the instructions IV. Storing the results back in the memory Select the correct answer using the code given below:
shortcut: Fetch, decode, execute and store are the four phases of the machine cycle, so all four listed operations are CPU operations.
tips: The machine cycle is fetch - decode - execute - store; memorising these four words answers a family of questions.
The control unit handles fetching and decoding while the ALU performs execution, but both are parts of the CPU, so all four remain CPU operations.
Storing the result back to memory is genuinely part of the cycle (the write-back phase), so item IV must be included.
This repeats $2022 Q_{74}'s$ content in list form - the machine cycle is clearly a recurring theme.
solution: The CPU repeatedly executes the machine cycle, which consists of four phases.
Item I, fetch: the control unit uses the program counter to read the next instruction from memory into the instruction register.
Item II, decode: the control unit interprets the instruction and determines the operation and operands required.
Item III, execute: the arithmetic and logic unit performs the required arithmetic, logical or data-movement operation.
Item IV, store: the result is written back to a register or to memory, completing the cycle.
All four are main operations of the CPU, option (d).

topic: Networks: LAN, WAN, Internet, Intranet
subtopic: Networks: LAN, WAN, Internet, Intranet
stem: In an e-mail service, the protocols used are SMTP, POP3 and IMAP. What are the port numbers in sequence?
shortcut: SMTP uses port 25, POP3 uses 110 and IMAP uses 143 - in the order asked, 25, 110, 143.
tips: Memorise the email trio in ascending order: 25 (SMTP), 110 (POP3), 143 (IMAP). They happen to run low to high in the same order the question lists them.
Other well-known ports: HTTP 80, HTTPS 443, FTP 21 (control) and 20 (data), Telnet 23, DNS 53, SSH 22.
Secure variants: SMTPS $465/587$, POP3S 995, IMAPS 993 - useful if a question asks about encrypted mail.
Read the requested SEQUENCE carefully; options (a), (b) and (c) contain the same three numbers in different orders, so the ordering is the entire question.
solution: SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) transfers outgoing mail and uses well-known port 25.
POP3 (Post Office Protocol version 3) retrieves mail from a server, downloading and typically deleting it, and uses port 110.
IMAP (Internet Message Access Protocol) also retrieves mail but leaves it on the server for synchronisation across devices, and uses port 143.
The question asks for the ports in the sequence SMTP, POP3, IMAP.
That sequence is 25, 110, 143.
Option (d) is correct.

topic: Computer Organisation: CPU, ALU, Control & Memory Units, I/O Units
subtopic: Computer Organisation: CPU, ALU, Control & Memory Units, I/O Units
stem: What are the functions of BIOS in computer system? I. It performs power-on self-test. II. It boots the computer system. III. It provides hardware-independent access to the physical devices. Select the correct answer using the code given below:
shortcut: The BIOS runs the power-on self-test, bootstraps the operating system, and supplies a standard low-level interface to the hardware - all three functions are genuine.
tips: BIOS duties in order of execution: POST (test the hardware), then bootstrap (find and load the OS), then provide run-time hardware services.
Statement III captures the abstraction role: BIOS routines let software access disks, keyboard and display without knowing the specific hardware details.
BIOS resides in ROM or flash so that it is available before any disk has been read - a key reason it can bootstrap the machine.
Modern machines use UEFI, the successor to BIOS, performing the same three functions with a richer interface.
solution: BIOS (Basic Input Output System) is firmware held in ROM or flash memory on the motherboard, available as soon as power is applied.
Statement I: on power-up the BIOS runs the Power-On Self-Test, checking the processor, memory and essential peripherals before anything else happens. TRUE.
Statement II: it then locates the boot device, loads the bootstrap loader and hands control to the operating system. TRUE.

Statement III: the BIOS provides a standard set of low-level service routines through which software can access disks, the keyboard and the display without needing to know the specific hardware details - a hardware-independent access layer. TRUE.
All three are genuine BIOS functions.
Hence option (d) is correct.

topic: Networks: LAN, WAN, Internet, Intranet
subtopic: Networks: LAN, WAN, Internet, Intranet
stem: Sending messages using IPSEC protocol on the internet between two IPSEC compliant router servers is also termed as:
shortcut: Encapsulating IPSec-protected packets inside ordinary IP packets between two gateway routers is called TUNNELLING - the basis of a VPN.
tips: IPSec has two modes: TRANSPORT mode (host to host, only the payload protected) and TUNNEL mode (gateway to gateway, the whole original packet encapsulated). Router-to-router means tunnel mode.
The tunnel is what creates a Virtual Private Network across the public internet - a useful real-world anchor.
A leased line is a physical dedicated circuit, not a software encapsulation, so option (b) is a different category entirely.
Packet filtering is a firewall function and message switching is a store-and-forward transmission technique - neither describes IPSec encapsulation.
solution: IPSec can operate in transport mode, protecting only the payload between two hosts, or in tunnel mode, in which the entire original IP packet is encrypted and encapsulated inside a new IP packet.
When two IPSec-compliant routers exchange traffic across the public internet, they use tunnel mode: each router encapsulates the packets of its internal network and the peer router decapsulates them.
This encapsulation of one protocol's packets inside another's is called TUNNELLING, and it is the mechanism underlying a Virtual Private Network.
A leased line is a physical dedicated circuit rented from a carrier, not an encapsulation technique.
Packet filtering is a firewall function, and message switching is a store-and-forward transmission method.
Hence the term is tunnelling, option (a).

topic: Software, Operating Systems, Packages & Utilities
subtopic: Software, Operating Systems, Packages & Utilities
stem: Which one of the following methods is used for interprocess communication in distributed systems?
shortcut: Distributed systems have no shared physical memory, so processes must communicate by MESSAGE PASSING.
tips: The two IPC models are shared memory and message passing; in a DISTRIBUTED system the machines have separate memories, so only message passing is available.
Every option except (b) presupposes some shared memory or cache, which by definition does not exist across independent machines.
Message passing is realised in practice by sockets, remote procedure calls (RPC) and message queues - worth naming as examples.
The trade-off: message passing is slower than shared memory but requires no common address space and scales across a network.
solution: A distributed system consists of autonomous computers, each with its own local memory, connected only by a communication network.
Because there is no physical memory common to the machines, shared-memory mechanisms - shared regions, shared caches - cannot be used across nodes.
The remaining interprocess communication model is message passing, in which processes exchange data using send and receive primitives supplied by the operating system.
In practice this is implemented through sockets, remote procedure calls or message queues.
Options (a), (c) and (d) all presuppose memory shared between the communicating processes, which distributed systems lack.
Hence the method is message passing, option (b).

topic: Number Systems & Binary Arithmetic
subtopic: Number Systems & Binary Arithmetic
stem: Consider the following statements: I. The hexadecimal equivalent of $(1101010101)_2$ is 355. II. The complement of $(47)_{10}$ is $(53)_{10}$. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
shortcut: Grouping 1101010101 in fours from the right gives $0011 0101 0101 = 355$ in hex, so statement I holds. And the radix $(10's)$ complement of 47 is $100 - 47 = 53$, so statement II holds too.
tips: Binary to hex: pad on the LEFT to a multiple of four bits, then translate each nibble. Here 1101010101 becomes $0011\mid 0101\mid 0101 = 3, 5, 5$.
For a two-digit decimal number the $r's (10's)$ complement is 100 - n, so $100 - 47 = 53$; the $(r-1)'s (9's)$ complement would be $99 - 47 = 52$.
When 'complement' is stated without qualification for base r it conventionally means the $r's$ complement - which is what makes statement II true as printed.
solution: Statement I: group the binary digits in fours from the right, padding on the left: 1101010101 becomes $0011 \lvert 0101 \rvert 0101$.
Translating each group: $0011 = 3, 0101 = 5, 0101 = 5$, so the hexadecimal equivalent is 355.
Statement II: for a decimal number of n digits, the radix $(10's)$ complement is $10^{n}$ minus the number. With $n = 2$ and the number 47, this is $100 - 47 = 53$.
(The diminished-radix or $9's$ complement would be $99 - 47 = 52$; 'the complement' without qualification conventionally denotes the radix complement.) TRUE.
Both statements are correct, option (c).

topic: Networks: LAN, WAN, Internet, Intranet
subtopic: Networks: LAN, WAN, Internet, Intranet
stem: Which of the following are network layer protocols? I. HTTP II. FTP III. NMP IV. SMTP Select the correct answer using the code given below:
issue: SOURCE NOTE: HTTP, FTP and SMTP are strictly APPLICATION-layer protocols of the TCP/IP model, not network-layer protocols (the network layer carries IP, ICMP and ARP). 'NMP' is not a standard TCP/IP protocol name - the recognised network-management protocol is SNMP, itself an application-layer protocol. Under the literal reading of the stem none of the four items is a network-layer protocol; option (b) is selected because it names the three genuine, universally recognised protocols in the list, and the discrepancy is flagged rather than the stem altered.
shortcut: HTTP, FTP and SMTP are the three genuine, standard protocols listed; 'NMP' is not a recognised TCP/IP protocol name (the network-management protocol is SNMP).
tips: Correct layer map: application - HTTP, FTP, SMTP, DNS, SNMP, Telnet; transport - TCP, UDP; network - IP, ICMP, ARP, RARP.
If a question about the 'network layer' lists only application-layer names, work by elimination on which items are genuine protocols at all.
SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) is the real protocol; 'NMP' with the S omitted is not a standard designation.
Keep the true network-layer list short and firm - IP, ICMP, ARP - so that mislabelled options are easy to spot.
solution: In the TCP/IP reference model the network (internet) layer carries IP, ICMP, ARP and RARP.
Item I, HTTP: transfers web pages between browser and server - an APPLICATION-layer protocol.
Item II, FTP: transfers files on behalf of users - an APPLICATION-layer protocol.
Item IV, SMTP: transfers outgoing email - an APPLICATION-layer protocol.
Item III, 'NMP': not a standard TCP/IP protocol name; the recognised network-management protocol is SNMP, which is itself an application-layer protocol.

None of the four is genuinely a network-layer protocol, so the item is flagged; among the printed options only (b) names the three universally recognised protocols HTTP, FTP and SMTP, and it is selected on that basis.

topic: Networks: LAN, WAN, Internet, Intranet
subtopic: Networks: LAN, WAN, Internet, Intranet
stem: Which of the following are network connecting devices? I. Repeater II. Bridge III. Hub IV. Bluetooth Select the correct answer using the code given below:
shortcut: Repeater, bridge and hub are all network connecting devices. Bluetooth is a short-range wireless communication STANDARD, not a device.
tips: Connecting devices by layer: repeater and hub at layer 1 (physical), bridge and switch at layer 2 (data link), router at layer 3 (network), gateway above that.
Bluetooth is a technology/standard (IEEE 802.15) like Wi-Fi, not a piece of connecting hardware - a category difference, not a technical detail.
A repeater regenerates a weakened signal; a hub repeats it to all ports; a bridge forwards frames selectively between segments using MAC addresses.
Sorting the list by category before comparing details identifies the odd one out immediately.
solution: Network connecting devices are hardware components used to link segments or nodes of a network.
Item I, repeater: regenerates and retransmits a weakened signal to extend the reach of a segment - a physical-layer connecting device.
Item II, bridge: connects two network segments and forwards frames selectively using MAC addresses - a data-link-layer connecting device.
Item III, hub: a multiport repeater that connects several nodes into one segment - a physical-layer connecting device.
Item IV, Bluetooth: a short-range wireless communication STANDARD (IEEE 802.15), not a connecting device in its own right.
Hence items I, II and III are the connecting devices, option (a).

topic: Data, Information, Database & DBMS; Frontend/Backend
subtopic: Data, Information, Database & DBMS; Frontend/Backend
stem: Consider the following statements regarding Database Management System (DBMS): I. It helps the user in maintaining data integrity while performing the various operations on the database values. II. It helps the user in maintaining consistency in the information stored in the database. III. It allows the user to maintain the security of the confidential information by password-protecting the database. Which of the statements given above are correct?
shortcut: Data integrity, consistency and security are three of the standard advantages of a DBMS over file-based storage, so all three statements hold.
tips: Standard DBMS advantages: controlled redundancy, data consistency, integrity constraints, security, concurrent access, backup and recovery, data independence.
Integrity is enforced through constraints (primary keys, foreign keys, check conditions) that the DBMS validates on every operation.
Consistency follows from controlled redundancy: because a fact is stored once, it cannot disagree with itself across files.
Security is enforced through authentication, user accounts and privilege grants - password protection being the simplest form.
solution: A Database Management System sits between users and the stored data and enforces rules that a plain file system cannot.
Statement I: integrity constraints - primary keys, foreign keys, domain and check constraints - are validated by the DBMS on every insertion, update and deletion, so invalid data cannot enter. TRUE.
Statement II: by controlling redundancy so that each fact is stored once, and by propagating updates centrally, the DBMS keeps the stored information consistent. TRUE.
Statement III: the DBMS provides authentication and authorisation, allowing access to be restricted by user account and privilege, of which password protection is the basic form. TRUE.
All three are standard advantages of a DBMS.
Hence option (d) is correct.

topic: Hardware: Input, Output & Peripheral Devices
subtopic: Hardware: Input, Output & Peripheral Devices
stem: Consider the following statements: I. Light pen is an electro-optical pointing device which is generally connected to the Visual Display Unit (VDU) of the computer. II. Touchscreen is a pointing device that enables us to enter data such as text, pictures and images by directly touching the screen. III. Joystick is a pointing device which controls the movement of the cursor on the screen by pointing in a particular direction only. Which of the statements given above are correct?
shortcut: All three are standard textbook descriptions: the light pen is an electro-optical device used against the VDU, the touchscreen accepts input by direct touch, and the joystick moves the cursor in the direction it is pushed.
tips: Pointing devices to know: mouse, trackball, joystick, light pen, touchpad, touchscreen, stylus - all convert physical motion or contact into cursor movement or coordinates.
The light pen contains a photodetector that senses the screen's refresh beam, which is why it works only against a CRT-style VDU - hence 'electro-optical'.
The classic distinction for statement III: with a mouse the cursor stops when the mouse stops, whereas with a joystick the cursor keeps moving in the direction the stick is held.
Touchscreens are unusual in being both an input and an output device, since the display and the sensor share the same surface.
solution: Statement I: a light pen contains a photodetector and is held against the screen of the visual display unit, sensing the display's own light to determine its position. It is therefore an electro-optical pointing device connected to the VDU. TRUE.
Statement II: a touchscreen senses the position of a finger or stylus on the display surface, allowing text, drawings and selections to be entered by touching the screen directly. TRUE.
Statement III: a joystick moves the cursor in whichever direction the stick is pushed, and - unlike a mouse - the cursor continues to move while the stick is held in that direction. TRUE.
All three descriptions match the standard textbook accounts of these pointing devices.
Hence option (d) is correct.

topic: Programming Basics: Algorithm, Flowchart, Control Structures, Arrays, Functions
subtopic: Programming Basics: Algorithm, Flowchart, Control Structures, Arrays, Functions
stem: Which of the following are looping statements in general of a computer programming language? I. While II. Break III. For IV. Continue V. Do while Select the correct answer using the code given below:
shortcut: While, for and do-while are the three loop constructs; break and continue are jump statements that alter the flow WITHIN a loop but are not loops themselves.
tips: Three loop constructs in C-family languages: while (entry-controlled), for (entry-controlled with initialisation and update), do-while (exit-controlled, body runs at least once).
break and continue are JUMP statements, alongside goto and return - they modify loop behaviour but do not create iteration.
The distinguishing test: a looping statement can repeat a block on its own; break and continue cannot repeat anything.
do-while is the only exit-controlled loop, guaranteeing at least one execution of the body - a common follow-up question.
solution: A looping (iteration) statement repeatedly executes a block of code while a condition holds.
Item I, while: tests the condition before each iteration - an entry-controlled loop. LOOP.
Item III, for: combines initialisation, condition and update in one header and is likewise entry-controlled. LOOP.
Item V, do while: executes the body first and tests the condition afterwards, so the body runs at least once - an exit-controlled loop. LOOP.
Item II, break: a jump statement that terminates the enclosing loop or switch immediately. Item IV, continue: a jump statement that skips to the next iteration. Neither creates iteration by itself.
Hence the looping statements are I, III and V, option (d).

topic: Data, Information, Database & DBMS; Frontend/Backend
subtopic: Data, Information, Database & DBMS; Frontend/Backend
stem: In which of the following data models are the records arranged in the form of a tree?
shortcut: Records arranged as a tree, each child having exactly one parent, define the HIERARCHICAL data model.
tips: Model shapes: hierarchical = tree (one parent per child), network = graph (many parents allowed), relational = tables joined by keys.
The hierarchical model supports only one-to-many relationships; many-to-many requires the network model - the key discriminator between options (c) and (d).
IBM's IMS is the classic hierarchical DBMS and CODASYL/IDMS the classic network one; almost all modern systems are relational.
The entity(-relationship) model is a DESIGN notation used before implementation, not a storage model - which places option (a) in a different category.
solution: In the hierarchical data model, records are organised as a tree: there is a single root, and every child record has exactly one parent.
Navigation proceeds from the root downwards along parent-child links, which makes access fast for naturally tree-shaped data but rigid otherwise.
The network model generalises this to a graph in which a record may have several parents, so it is not a tree.
The relational model stores data in flat tables related by keys, with no inherent hierarchy.
The entity model (entity-relationship diagram) is a conceptual design notation rather than a storage structure.
Hence records are arranged as a tree in the hierarchical model, option (c).

topic: Numerical Solution of Differential Equations - Euler, Milne, Picard, Runge-Kutta
subtopic: Numerical Solution of Differential Equations - Euler, Milne, Picard, Runge-Kutta
stem: If $y$ satisfies the initial value problem $$\frac{dy}{dx}=1+xy;\quad y(2)=0$$ then what is the approximation of $y$ at $x=3$? (Use second approximation of Picard's method)
tips: Picard iteration starts at the GIVEN point: $y_{n+1}(x) = y(2) + \int_{2}^{x} f(t, y_{n}(t))\,dt$. Using 0 as the lower limit is the standard error.
First iterate: with $y_{0} = 0$ the integrand is just 1, so $y_{1} = x - 2 - a$ clean start.
Second iterate: the integrand becomes $1 + t(t - 2) = t^{2} - 2t + 1$, whose antiderivative is $t^{3}/3 - t^{2} + t$; evaluate between 2 and x.
The constant is -$(8/3 - 4 + 2)$ = -$2/3$; keeping it as a fraction avoids rounding drift before the final substitution.
solution: Picard's method for $dy/dx = 1 + xy$ with $y(2) = 0$ uses $y_{n+1}(x) = 0 + \int_{2}^{x} (1 + t y_{n}(t))\,dt$, starting from $y_{0} = 0$.
First approximation: $y_{1}(x) = \int_{2}^{x} 1\,dt = x - 2$.
Second approximation: the integrand is $1 + t(t - 2) = t^{2} - 2t + 1$, whose antiderivative is $t^{3}/3 - t^{2} + t$.

topic: Numerical Solution of Differential Equations - Euler, Milne, Picard, Runge-Kutta
subtopic: Numerical Solution of Differential Equations - Euler, Milne, Picard, Runge-Kutta
stem: Consider the following statements: I. Forward Euler method and backward Euler method for initial value problem have same order. II. Classical fourth order Runge-Kutta method for initial value problem has higher order than forward Euler method. III. Classical fourth order Runge-Kutta method for initial value problem has higher order than backward Euler method. Which of the statements given above are correct?
shortcut: Forward and backward Euler are both first-order methods, and RK4 is fourth order, so it exceeds both. All three statements hold.
tips: Order table: forward Euler 1, backward Euler 1, RK2 (Heun/midpoint) 2, RK4 4. Memorise it and all three statements answer themselves.
Forward and backward Euler differ in STABILITY, not in order: backward Euler is implicit and unconditionally stable, but still first order.
Order refers to the GLOBAL error exponent: O(h) for Euler, $O(h^{4})$ for RK4 - a difference of three powers of h.
Do not confuse order with stability or with cost per step; the question asks only about order.
solution: Forward Euler, $y_{n+1} = y_{n} + h f(x_{n}, y_{n})$, matches the Taylor expansion through the h term, so its local error is $O(h^{2})$ and its global error O(h) - first order.
Backward Euler, $y_{n+1} = y_{n} + h f(x_{n+1}, y_{n+1})$, is implicit but likewise matches only through the h term, so it is also first order.
Statement I: both Euler methods therefore have the same order, namely 1. TRUE. (They differ in stability, not order.)
The classical fourth-order Runge-Kutta method matches the Taylor expansion through $h^{4}$, giving a global error $O(h^{4})$ - fourth order.
Statements II and III: RK4's order 4 exceeds the order 1 of both forward and backward Euler. Both TRUE.
All three statements are correct, option (d).

topic: Numerical Integration - Trapezoidal, Simpson's 1/3 & 3/8, Weddle's Rule
subtopic: Numerical Integration - Trapezoidal, Simpson's 1/3 & 3/8, Weddle's Rule
stem: Use Simpson's one-third rule to evaluate $\displaystyle\int_1^3 x^4\,dx$ by dividing $[1,3]$ into two parts. What is the value of the error?
shortcut: With $h = 1$ and nodes 1, 2, 3, Simpson gives $(1/3)[1 + 64 + 81] = 48.667$, while the exact value is $242/5 = 48.4$. The error is 0.267, i.e. about 0.27.
tips: Simpson's $1/3$ is exact only up to CUBICS, so for $x^{4}$ there is a genuine error - that is the point of the question.
Compute both values: Simpson's bracket is $1 + 4(16) + 81 = 146$, so the estimate is $146/3 = 48.6667$; the exact integral is $(3^{5} - 1)/5 = 48.4$.
Error formula check: -$(b-a)h^{4} f''''(\xi)/180$ with $f'''' = 24$ gives $(2)(1)(24)/180 = 0.2667$ in magnitude - matching exactly, since the fourth derivative is constant.
Simpson OVERestimates here (the fourth derivative is positive), so the error 48.667 - 48.4 is positive - a useful sign check.
solution: Dividing $[1,3]$ into two parts gives $h = 1$ with nodes $x = 1, 2, 3$ and ordinates $f = 1, 16, 81$.
The exact value is the $\int x^{4}$ from 1 to $3 = [x^{5}/5]$ from 1 to $3 = (243 - 1)/5 = 48.4$.
This agrees with the error formula -$(b-a)h^{4} f''''(\xi)/180$ = -$(2)(1)(24)/180$ = -0.2667 in magnitude, since $f''''(x) = 24$ is constant for $x^{4}$.
The error is approximately 0.27, option (c).

topic: Numerical Solution of Differential Equations - Euler, Milne, Picard, Runge-Kutta
subtopic: Numerical Solution of Differential Equations - Euler, Milne, Picard, Runge-Kutta
stem: Runge-Kutta method of order four is used to find the solution of the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=f(x);\ y(0)=0$ with step size $h$. If the solution is $$y(h) = h\left[af(0)+bf\left(\frac{h}{2}\right)+cf(h)\right]$$ then what are the values of $a, b, c$ respectively?
shortcut: For f independent of y, RK4 reduces to Simpson's rule: $y(h) = (h/6)[f(0) + 4f(h/2) + f(h)] = h[(1/6)f(0) + (2/3)f(h/2) + (1/6)f(h)]$.
tips: When f does not involve y, the two midpoint stages coincide, so the weights 1, 2, 2, 1 over 6 collapse to 1, 4, 1 over 6.
Divide by 6 to read off the coefficients: $1/6, 4/6 = 2/3, 1/6$. The end weights must be EQUAL by symmetry, which only option (d) satisfies.
The weights must sum to 1 so that a constant f integrates to h f: $1/6 + 2/3 + 1/6 = 1$. Options (a), (b) and (c) sum to 1.5, 1.5 and 1 respectively - so use the symmetry test.
This is the same identity as 2018 Q44: RK4 applied to a pure quadrature problem IS Simpson's one-third rule.
solution: For $dy/dx = f(x)$ the RK4 increments are $k_{1} = h f(0), k_{2} = h f(h/2), k_{3} = h f(h/2)$ and $k_{4} = h f(h)$, since the y-arguments are irrelevant.
The two identical midpoint terms combine: $y(h) = (h/6)[f(0) + 4f(h/2) + f(h)]$.
Writing this as $h[a f(0) + b f(h/2) + c f(h)]$ gives $a = 1/6, b = 4/6 = 2/3$ and $c = 1/6$.
The weights are symmetric and sum to 1, as any such quadrature rule requires.

topic: Numerical Integration - Trapezoidal, Simpson's 1/3 & 3/8, Weddle's Rule
subtopic: Numerical Integration - Trapezoidal, Simpson's 1/3 & 3/8, Weddle's Rule
stem: $y=x^2+2x+3$ and $y_0, y_1, y_2$ are the values of $y$ for $x=a, a+h, a+2h$ respectively. What is the value of $\displaystyle\int_a^{a+2h} y\,dx$? (Use trapezoidal rule)
shortcut: Composite trapezoidal over two strips: $(h/2)[y_{0} + 2y1 + y_{2}]$ - the interior ordinate carries weight 2 and the ends weight 1.
tips: Composite trapezoidal weights are 1, 2, 2, ..., 2, 1 with prefactor $h/2$ - only the two END ordinates are halved.
The weights must total 2n for n strips so that a constant integrates correctly: here $1 + 2 + 1 = 4 = 2(2)$. Options (b), (c) and (d) fail this test.
The specific function $x^{2} + 2x + 3$ is a distractor - the trapezoidal FORMULA does not depend on it (though the rule is not exact for a quadratic).
Contrast with Simpson's $1/3$ over the same two strips, which would be $(h/3)[y_{0} + 4y1 + y_{2}]$ and WOULD be exact for this quadratic.
solution: The interval $[a, a+2h]$ is divided into two equal strips of width h, with ordinates y0, y1, y2 at $x = a, a+h, a+2h$.
The trapezoidal rule approximates the curve by a straight line on each strip.
First strip: $(h/2)(y_{0} + y_{1})$. Second strip: $(h/2)(y_{1} + y_{2})$.
The weights 1, 2, 1 sum to $4 = 2 \times 2$, as required for two strips.
Hence the value is $(h/2)(y_{0} + 2y1 + y_{2})$, option (a).

topic: Finite Differences: Operators, Factorial Polynomials, Separation of Symbols
subtopic: Finite Differences: Operators, Factorial Polynomials, Separation of Symbols
stem: What is the value of the following? $$4y_0+6\Delta y_0+4\Delta^2 y_0+\Delta^3 y_0$$
shortcut: Since $E = 1 + \Delta$, expanding $1 + E + E^{2} + E^{3}$ gives $4 + 6 \Delta + 4 \Delta^{2} + \Delta^{3}$. So the expression equals $y_{0} + y_{1} + y_{2} + y_{3}$.
tips: Recognise the coefficients 4, 6, 4, 1 - they are the sums of the binomial columns from $(1+\Delta)^{0}$ through $(1+\Delta)^{3}$, which is the signature of $y_{0} + y_{1} + y_{2} + y_{3}$.
Work backwards from the operator: $1 + E + E^{2} + E^{3}$ applied to y0 gives the four consecutive values, and substituting $E = 1 + \Delta$ reproduces the printed expression.
Verify the constant: the four expansions contribute $1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 4$, matching the leading coefficient exactly.
The alternating-sign options (a), (c) and (d) would require alternating operator signs, which the all-positive coefficients rule out.
solution: Since $E = 1 + \Delta$, we have $E^{2} = 1 + 2\Delta + \Delta^{2}$ and $E^{3} = 1 + 3\Delta + 3\Delta^{2} + \Delta^{3}$.
Adding: $1 + E + E^{2} + E^{3} = (1 + 1 + 1 + 1) + (1 + 2 + 3)\Delta + (1 + 3)\Delta^{2} + \Delta^{3} = 4 + 6 \Delta + 4 \Delta^{2} + \Delta^{3}$, which is exactly the given operator.
So the expression equals the sum of the four consecutive ordinates.
Option (b) is correct.

topic: Finite Differences: Operators, Factorial Polynomials, Separation of Symbols

stem: What is the value of $\nabla^5 y_n$?
shortcut: The bridge identity is nabla^n $y_{k} = \Delta^{n} y_{k-n}$. With $n = 5$ this gives nabla^5 $y_{n} = \Delta^{5} y_{n-5}$.
tips: Memorise nabla^n $y_{k} = \Delta^{n} y_{k-n}$: the same table entry read backwards from $y_{k}$ or forwards from $y_{k-n}$.
Operator proof: nabla = $1 - E^{-1} = (E - 1)E^{-1} = \Delta E^{-1}$, so nabla^n = $\Delta^{n} E^{-n}$, which shifts the index down by n.
Index check: a fifth backward difference at n reaches back to n - 5, so the forward form must START at n - 5. Option (c) keeps the index at n and is wrong.
Option (a) restates nabla in terms of itself with a shifted index and is simply false; the identity must convert between the two OPERATORS.
solution: The backward difference operator is nabla = $1 - E^{-1}$, where E is the shift operator.
Factorising, nabla = $(E - 1)E^{-1} = \Delta E^{-1}$.
Since $\Delta$ and E commute, nabla^n = $\Delta^{n} E^{-n}$.

Applying this to $y_{n}$: nabla^n $y_{n} = \Delta^{n} E^{-n} y_{n} = \Delta^{n} y_{n-n} = \Delta^{n} y_{n-n}$... more precisely, $E^{-n} y_{n} = y_{n-n}$ is the value at index n - n; in general nabla^n $y_{k} = \Delta^{n} y_{k-n}$.
With $n = 5$ and index n: nabla^5 $y_{n} = \Delta^{5} y_{n-5}$. Both expand to $y_{n} - 5y_{n-1} + 10y_{n-2} - 10y_{n-3} + 5y_{n-4} - y_{n-5}$.
Option (d) is correct.

topic: Numerical Integration - Trapezoidal, Simpson's 1/3 & 3/8, Weddle's Rule
subtopic: Numerical Integration - Trapezoidal, Simpson's 1/3 & 3/8, Weddle's Rule
stem: To find the approximate value of $\displaystyle\int_a^b y\,dx$, where $b=a+8h$, which of the following rules can be applied?
options: Trapezoidal rule and Simpson's three-eighths rule
Trapezoidal rule and Simpson's one-third rule
Simpson's one-third rule and Weddle rule
Simpson's three-eighths rule and Weddle rule
shortcut: $b = a + 8h$ means 8 strips. Trapezoidal needs no condition and Simpson's $1/3$ needs an even count - 8 qualifies. Simpson's $3/8$ needs a multiple of 3 and Weddle a multiple of 6, neither of which 8 is.
tips: Divisibility table: trapezoidal any n; Simpson's $1/3$ needs n even; Simpson's $3/8$ needs n divisible by 3; Weddle's needs n divisible by 6.
Read the number of strips straight from $b - a = 8h$, so $n = 8$. Everything else is a divisibility check.
8 is even but not divisible by 3 or 6, so exactly two of the four rules apply - which pins the answer without further thought.
In practice one could still apply the $3/8$ rule to a sub-range and the $1/3$ rule to the rest, but the question asks which rules apply to the whole interval.
solution: Since $b = a + 8h$, the interval [a, b] is divided into $n = 8$ subintervals of equal width h.
The trapezoidal rule places no condition on n, so it applies.
Simpson's one-third rule requires n to be even; 8 is even, so it applies.
Simpson's three-eighth rule requires n to be a multiple of 3; 8 is not, so it does not apply.
Weddle's rule requires n to be a multiple of 6; 8 is not, so it does not apply.
Hence the applicable rules are the trapezoidal rule and Simpson's one-third rule, option (b).

topic: Numerical Integration - Trapezoidal, Simpson's 1/3 & 3/8, Weddle's Rule
subtopic: Numerical Integration - Trapezoidal, Simpson's 1/3 & 3/8, Weddle's Rule
stem: The value of the integral $\displaystyle\int_1^3 f(x)\,dx$ is 5 by using trapezoidal rule and 3 by using Simpson's one-third rule dividing $[1,3]$ into minimum number of intervals. What is the value of $f(2)$?
shortcut: The minimum for the trapezoidal rule is one strip: $f(1) + f(3) = 5$. The minimum for Simpson's $1/3$ is two strips: $(1/3)[f(1) + 4f(2) + f(3)] = 3$, so $f(1) + 4f(2) + f(3) = 9$ and $4f(2) = 4$, giving $f(2) = 1$.
tips: 'Minimum number of intervals' differs by rule: 1 for the trapezoidal rule $(h = 2)$ but 2 for Simpson's $1/3$ ($h = 1$, since n must be even).
The trapezoidal equation supplies $f(1) + f(3) = 5$ with no $f(2)$ in it - substituting that into Simpson's equation isolates $f(2)$ immediately.
Simpson's bracket must equal 9 because the prefactor is $h/3 = 1/3$ and the stated value is 3.
Consistency check: with $f(1) + f(3) = 5$ and $f(2) = 1$, Simpson gives $(1/3)(5 + 4) = 3$, exactly as stated.
solution: For the trapezoidal rule the minimum number of intervals is 1, so $h = 2$ and the estimate is $(h/2)[f(1) + f(3)] = f(1) + f(3)$.
Setting this equal to 5 gives $f(1) + f(3) = 5$.
For Simpson's one-third rule the number of intervals must be even, so the minimum is 2, giving $h = 1$ with nodes 1, 2, 3.
The estimate is $(h/3)[f(1) + 4f(2) + f(3)] = (1/3)[f(1) + 4f(2) + f(3)]$, and setting this equal to 3 gives $f(1) + 4f(2) + f(3) = 9$.
Hence $f(2) = 1$, option (b).

topic: Divided Differences; Newton's & Lagrange's Formulae (Unequal Intervals)
subtopic: Divided Differences; Newton's & Lagrange's Formulae (Unequal Intervals)
stem: The third divided difference of a cubic polynomial is:
options: always constant but not necessarily zero
shortcut: The third divided difference of a cubic equals its leading coefficient, which is non-zero by definition of 'cubic' - so it is always constant but not necessarily zero.
tips: Rule: the nth divided difference of a degree-n polynomial is its leading coefficient $a_{n}$, and all HIGHER divided differences are zero.
'Cubic' means the $x^{3}$ coefficient is non-zero, so the value cannot be zero - that distinction is exactly what separates options (a) and (b).
Option (c) 'sum of arguments' is the SECOND divided difference of $x^{3} (as in 2023 Q_{42}) - a$ neighbouring fact deliberately offered as a distractor.
The value is independent of which four nodes are used, which is the sense in which it is 'constant'.
solution: Divided differences are linear, and the kth divided difference of a polynomial of degree less than k is zero.
For a cubic $f(x) = a_{3} x^{3} + a_{2} x^{2} + a_{1} x + a_{0}$, only the leading term survives a third divided difference.
For $x^{3}$ the third divided difference over any four distinct nodes equals 1, so for f it equals a3.
Since f is a cubic, a3 is non-zero by definition, so the third divided difference is a non-zero constant, the same for every choice of nodes.
It would be zero only for a polynomial of degree less than 3, and the SECOND divided difference of $x^{3}$ - not the third - is the sum of the arguments.
Hence it is always constant but not necessarily zero, option (a).

topic: Finite Differences: Operators, Factorial Polynomials, Separation of Symbols
subtopic: Finite Differences: Operators, Factorial Polynomials, Separation of Symbols
stem: If $\Delta^2(ab^x)=\alpha b^x$, the interval of differencing being 1, then what is the value of $\alpha$?
shortcut: $\Delta(a b^{x}) = a b^{x} (b - 1)$, so applying $\Delta$ twice gives $a b^{x} (b-1)^{2}$. Hence $\alpha = a(b-1)^{2}$.
tips: For an exponential, each $\Delta$ multiplies by the constant $(b - 1)$: $\Delta b^{x} = b^{x+1} - b^{x} = b^{x}(b-1)$.
The multiplicative constant a passes straight through the operator, so it must appear in $\alpha$ - eliminating option (c).
Two differences give the SQUARE of $(b-1)$; one difference would give option (d), the 'one step short' trap.
Check with $a = 1, b = 2$: $\Delta^{2} 2^{x} = 2^{x}$, and $a(b-1)^{2} = 1$. Correct.
solution: With interval of differencing $1, \Delta(a b^{x}) = a b^{x+1} - a b^{x} = a b^{x} (b - 1)$.
Applying $\Delta a$ second time multiplies by the same constant factor $(b - 1)$.
Comparing with the given form $\alpha b^{x}$, we read $\alpha = a(b - 1)^{2}$.
Check with $a = 1$ and $b = 2$: $\Delta^{2} 2^{x} = 2^{x}$ and $a(b-1)^{2} = 1$, consistent.
Option (a) is correct.

topic: Finite Differences: Operators, Factorial Polynomials, Separation of Symbols
subtopic: Finite Differences: Operators, Factorial Polynomials, Separation of Symbols
stem: If $\left(\dfrac{\Delta^2}{E}\right)x^3=\alpha x+\beta$, the interval of differencing being 1, then what are the values of $\alpha$ and $\beta$ respectively?
shortcut: $\Delta^{2} x^{3} = 6x + 6$, and dividing by E shifts x to x - 1, giving $6(x-1) + 6 = 6x$. So $\alpha = 6$ and $\beta = 0$.
tips: $1/E$ is the BACKWARD shift $E^{-1}$, replacing x by x - 1 - not an algebraic division. Misreading it is the main trap.
Compute in two stages: $\Delta x^{3} = 3x^{2} + 3x + 1$, then $\Delta^{2} x^{3} = 6x + 6$.
The shift cancels the constant exactly: $6(x-1) + 6 = 6x - 6 + 6 = 6x$, so $\beta = 0$. Skipping the shift would give $\alpha = 6, \beta = 6$ - option (a).
This repeats 2021 Q67, where the same expression was asked for directly - the operator identity is clearly a favourite.
solution: The operator $1/E$ is the backward shift $E^{-1}$, which replaces x by x - 1.
Comparing with $\alpha x + \beta$ gives $\alpha = 6$ and $\beta = 0$.
Option (b) is correct.

topic: Finite Differences: Operators, Factorial Polynomials, Separation of Symbols
subtopic: Finite Differences: Operators, Factorial Polynomials, Separation of Symbols
stem: If $\delta=\alpha\nabla E^n$, the interval of differencing being 1, then what are the values of $\alpha$ and $n$ respectively?
shortcut: nabla $E^{n} = E^{n} - E^{n-1}$, and $\delta = E^{1/2} - E^{-1/2}$. Matching the exponents gives $n = 1/2$ and $\alpha = 1$.
tips: Write both sides in powers of E: the right side is $\alpha(E^{n} - E^{n-1})$ and the left is $E^{1/2} - E^{-1/2}$.
Match the leading exponent first: $n = 1/2$, and then n - 1 = -$1/2$ automatically - a built-in consistency check.
With the exponents matched, the coefficients give $\alpha = 1$; no scaling is needed.
Companion identity: $\delta = \Delta E^{-1/2}$ as well, since $\Delta = E - 1$ gives $E^{-1/2}(E-1) = E^{1/2} - E^{-1/2}$.
solution: The central difference operator is $\delta = E^{1/2} - E^{-1/2}$, and the backward difference is nabla = $1 - E^{-1}$.
Therefore nabla $E^{n} = (1 - E^{-1})E^{n} = E^{n} - E^{n-1}$.
Setting $\alpha(E^{n} - E^{n-1}) = E^{1/2} - E^{-1/2}$ and comparing the leading terms gives $\alpha = 1$ and $n = 1/2$.
The second terms then match automatically: $n - 1 = 1/2 - 1$ = -$1/2$.
So $\delta$ = nabla $E^{1/2}$, i.e. $\alpha = 1$ and $n = 1/2$.
Option (b) is correct.

topic: Interpolation - Newton-Gregory Forward & Backward (Equal Intervals)

stem: Which one of the following is the best possible choice for the step size $h$ to tabulate $f(x)=\sin x$ on $[0,\pi/4]$ that results in truncation error for the linear interpolation at most $10^{-5}$?
shortcut: Linear interpolation error <= $h^{2} M/8$ with $M = \max\mid f''$| = $\sin(pi/4) = 0.7071$. Requiring $h^{2}(0.7071)/8 \le 1e-5$ gives $h \le 0.01064$, and pi/$320 = 0.00982$ is the largest listed value that satisfies it.
tips: Error bound for linear interpolation: |E| <= $h^{2} M_{2}/8$ where M2 bounds |$f''$| on the interval. The 8 comes from $\max\mid p(p-1)$|/$2 = 1/8$.
For $f = \sin x, f''$ = -$\sin x$, whose modulus is largest at the right end of $[0, pi/4]$, giving $M_{2} = \sin(pi/4) = 0.7071$.
Solve for h: $h^{2} \le 8(1e-5)/0.7071 = 1.131e-4$, so $h \le 0.01064$. Then test the options: pi/$320 = 0.00982$ passes, pi/$120 = 0.02618$ fails.
'Best possible' means the LARGEST admissible step, since a smaller h wastes computation - pi/520 also satisfies the bound but is unnecessarily fine.
solution: For linear interpolation on an interval of width h, the truncation error satisfies |E| <= $h^{2} M_{2}/8$, where M2 is a bound on |$f''$| over the interval.
Here $f(x) = \sin x$, so $f''(x)$ = -$\sin x$ and |$f''$| is largest at x = pi/4, giving $M_{2} = \sin(pi/4) = 0.7071$.
Hence $h \le 0.01064$.
Testing the options: pi/$520 = 0.00604$ (satisfies), pi/$320 = 0.00982$ (satisfies), pi/$120 = 0.02618$ (fails), pi/$92 = 0.03415$ (fails).
The best choice is the largest admissible step, pi/320, option (b).

stem: The roots of the least degree polynomial satisfied by $(0,1)$, $(1/2,3/2)$ and $(1,3)$ are:
shortcut: The slopes 1 and 3 differ, so the least-degree polynomial is a quadratic; fitting gives $y = 2x^{2} + 1$, whose roots x = +-$i/sqrt2$ are purely imaginary.
tips: Test linearity first by comparing slopes: $(3/2 - 1)/(1/2) = 1$ but $(3 - 3/2)/(1/2) = 3$. Different, so the degree is 2, not 1.
Use the point $(0,1)$ to fix the constant immediately: $c = 1$, leaving only two unknowns.
Solving $a + 2b = 2$ with $a + b = 2$ gives $b = 0$ - the absence of a linear term is what makes the roots purely imaginary.
$y = 2x^{2} + 1$ has no real roots since $2x^{2} + 1 \ge 1 > 0$; the roots are +-$i/\sqrt{2}$, complex with real part zero.
solution: Test whether the three points are collinear: the slope from $(0,1)$ to $(1/2, 3/2)$ is 1, while from $(1/2, 3/2)$ to $(1,3)$ it is 3. They differ, so no line fits and the least degree is 2.
Write y = ax^2 + bx + c. From $(0,1)$: $c = 1$.
Subtracting gives $b = 0$ and hence $a = 2$, so $y = 2x^{2} + 1$.
Setting $2x^{2} + 1 = 0$ gives $x^{2}$ = -$1/2$, so x = +- $i/\sqrt{2}$: complex conjugates with real part zero. Option (b) is correct.

stem: The bound on the truncation error of Lagrange linear interpolating polynomial $f(x)$ on $[a,b]$ is $\varepsilon$. What is the bound on the truncation error of Newton forward interpolating polynomial of $f(x)$ on $[a,b]$?
shortcut: Through the same two points there is only ONE interpolating polynomial, so the Lagrange and Newton forward forms are algebraically identical and share the same error bound, $\epsilon$.
tips: Uniqueness theorem: through n + 1 distinct points there passes exactly one polynomial of degree at most n. Lagrange and Newton are just different ALGEBRAIC ARRANGEMENTS of it.
Since the polynomial is the same, the remainder term $f''(\xi)(x-x_{0})(x-x_{1})/2!$ is the same, and so is its bound.
The two forms differ in computational convenience - Newton's allows incremental addition of points - not in accuracy.
Any option other than $\epsilon$ would imply that two representations of the same function differ in error, which is impossible.
solution: Through two distinct points there passes exactly one polynomial of degree at most 1, by the uniqueness of the interpolating polynomial.
Lagrange's linear form and Newton's forward linear form are therefore two algebraic representations of the SAME polynomial.

The truncation error of linear interpolation is $R(x) = f''(\xi)(x - x_{0})(x - x_{1})/2!$ for some xi in the interval, and this expression depends only on the function and the nodes, not on how the polynomial is written.
Hence the two forms have identical remainder terms and identical error bounds.
So the bound for the Newton forward form is also $\epsilon$.
Option (b) is correct.

topic: Numerical Integration - Trapezoidal, Simpson's 1/3 & 3/8, Weddle's Rule
subtopic: Numerical Integration - Trapezoidal, Simpson's 1/3 & 3/8, Weddle's Rule
stem: If the formula $$\int_{x_0}^{x_2} f(x)\,dx = \alpha f(x_0)+\beta f(x_0+h)+\gamma f(x_0+2h)$$ is exact for polynomial of as high order as possible for any $h>0$, then what are the values of $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ respectively?
shortcut: Three equally spaced nodes with maximum exactness is Simpson's one-third rule, whose weights are $h/3, 4h/3, h/3$.
tips: Recognise the pattern: a three-point rule on $[x_{0}, x_{0}+2h]$ with the highest possible order IS Simpson's $1/3$ rule - no derivation needed.
If you derive it: exactness for $f = 1$ gives $\alpha + \beta + \gamma = 2h$, and symmetry gives $\alpha = \gamma$, so exactness for $x^{2}$ completes the system.
The weights must sum to the interval length 2h: $h/3 + 4h/3 + h/3 = 6h/3 = 2h$. Only option (a) satisfies this AND the symmetry $\alpha = \gamma$.
Bonus fact: this rule is exact for cubics too, because the odd-degree error term cancels by symmetry.
solution: The three nodes $x_{0}, x_{0} + h, x_{0} + 2h$ are equally spaced across the interval of length 2h, and we require exactness for polynomials of the highest possible degree.
Exactness for $f = 1$: $\alpha + \beta + \gamma = 2h$.
Exactness for $f = x - x_{0}$ (odd about the midpoint): $0(\alpha) + h(\beta) + 2h(\gamma) = 2h^{2}$, i.e. $\beta + 2\gamma = 2h$.
Exactness for $f = (x - x_{0})^{2}$: $h^{2} \beta + 4h^{2} \gamma = 8h^{3}/3$, i.e. $\beta + 4 \gamma = 8h/3$.
Subtracting the second from the third: $2 \gamma = 2h/3$, so $\gamma = h/3$; then $\beta = 2h - 2h/3 = 4h/3$ and $\alpha = 2h - 4h/3 - h/3 = h/3$.
These are Simpson's one-third weights $h/3, 4h/3, h/3$, option (a).

stem: For $\displaystyle\int_0^1 f(x)\,dx$, where $f(x)$ is cubic polynomial, consider the following statements: I. Trapezoidal rule will give the exact value of the integral. II. Simpson's one-third rule will give the exact value of the integral. III. Simpson's three-eighths rule will give the exact value of the integral. Which of the statements given above are correct?
shortcut: Both Simpson's rules are exact up to degree 3, but the trapezoidal rule is exact only up to degree 1. So II and III hold and I fails.
tips: Degrees of exactness: trapezoidal 1, Simpson's $1/3 = 3$, Simpson's $3/8 = 3$, Weddle 5. Compare each with the integrand's degree 3.
Simpson's $1/3$ fits parabolas yet is exact for CUBICS because its odd-degree error term cancels by symmetry - a bonus degree worth remembering.
The trapezoidal error involves $f''$, which is generally non-zero for a cubic, so statement I must fail.
Simpson's $3/8$ fits cubics directly, so its exactness for a cubic needs no special argument.
solution: Statement I: the trapezoidal rule replaces the integrand by a straight line, and its error term involves $f''$. For a cubic $f''$ is not identically zero, so the rule is not exact. FALSE.

Statement II: Simpson's one-third rule has error term proportional to the FOURTH derivative, which vanishes for a cubic, so it integrates cubics exactly - a bonus degree beyond the parabola it fits. TRUE.
Statement III: Simpson's three-eighth rule is derived by fitting a cubic through four points, so it reproduces any cubic exactly; its error term also involves the fourth derivative. TRUE.
Only statements II and III are correct.
Hence option (b) is correct.

stem: Consider the following data with regard to depth ($y$) at a distance ($x$) of a river 40 m wide: | Distance from one side, $x$ | 0 | 10 | 20 | 30 | 40 | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | Depth, $y$ (metre) | 0 | 4 | 7 | 9 | 12 | What is the approximate area of cross-section of the river? (Use Simpson's one-third rule)
tips: Check n first: five ordinates give $n = 4$ subintervals, an even number, so Simpson's $1/3$ applies.
Weight pattern 1, 4, 2, 4, 1: the odd-indexed depths get 4 and the single interior even one gets 2.
Weighted sum: $0 + 16 + 14 + 36 + 12 = 78$, then multiply by $h/3 = 10/3$ to get 260.
Plausibility: the average depth is roughly 6.5 m over 40 m, giving about 260 square metres - the answer is exactly of that order, unlike options (a) and (b).
solution: The distances are 0, 10, 20, 30, 40 with $h = 10$, giving $n = 4$ subintervals - an even number, so Simpson's one-third rule applies.
Simpson's rule: Area = $(h/3)[y_{0} + 4y1 + 2y2 + 4y3 + y_{4}]$.
Hence the cross-sectional area is about 260 square metres, option (c).

stem: Consider the initial value problem $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=-8y;\ y(0)=1$. What is the largest interval for step size $h$ so that the forward Euler method to solve the initial value problem is absolutely stable?
shortcut: Forward Euler is absolutely stable when |$1 + \lambda h$| < 1. With $\lambda$ = -8 this gives -2 < -$8h < 0$, i.e. $0 < h < 1/4$.
tips: Stability condition: |$1 + \lambda h$| < 1, which for real negative $\lambda$ becomes $0 < h < 2$/|$\lambda$|.
Here |$\lambda$| = 8, so $h < 2/8 = 1/4$ - one division once the general rule is known.
The step must be positive, giving the open interval $(0, 1/4)$; $h = 1/4$ exactly puts the amplification factor at -1, the boundary of stability.
Contrast with backward Euler, which is unconditionally stable for this problem - no restriction on h at all.
solution: Applying forward Euler to $y' = \lambda y$ gives $y_{n+1} = (1 + \lambda h) y_{n}$, so $y_{n} = (1 + \lambda h)^{n}$.
The numerical solution decays, matching the true solution $e^{\lambda x}$ for $\lambda < 0$, precisely when |$1 + \lambda h$| < 1.
This means -$1 < 1 + \lambda h < 1$, i.e. -$2 < \lambda h < 0$.
Here $\lambda$ = -8, so -2 < -$8h < 0$, which gives $0 < h < 1/4$.
Equivalently $h < 2$/|$\lambda$| = $2/8 = 1/4$.
Hence the largest interval is $(0, 1/4)$, option (b).

stem: X follows Beta distribution of first kind Beta$(\alpha, \beta)$ with $\alpha > 1$ and $\beta > 1$. What is the mode?
shortcut: Differentiating the Beta kernel $x^{a-1}(1-x)^{b-1}$ and setting the derivative to zero gives the mode $(a-1)/(a+b-2)$, valid when both parameters exceed 1.
tips: Mode of Beta(a,b) = $(a-1)/(a+b-2)$; mean = $a/(a+b)$. The '-1' and '-2' pattern distinguishes the mode from the mean at a glance.
The condition $a > 1$ and $b > 1$ is exactly what makes the density unimodal with an interior maximum, so the formula applies.
Symmetry check: for $a = b$ the formula gives $1/2$, as it must for a symmetric Beta - option (d) fails this at once.
Boundary check: as a grows with b fixed the mode tends to 1, which the formula reproduces; option (b) is the MEAN, the standard near-miss.
solution: The Beta density of the first kind is $f(x) = x^{a-1}(1-x)^{b-1}/B(a,b)$ on $(0,1)$.
Take logarithms: $\log f = (a-1) \log x + (b-1) \log(1-x)$ + constant.
Differentiating and setting to zero: $(a-1)/x - (b-1)/(1-x) = 0$.
Cross-multiplying: $(a-1)(1-x) = (b-1)x$, so $a - 1 = x(a - 1 + b - 1) = x(a + b - 2)$.
Hence the mode is $x = (a-1)/(a+b-2)$, and since $a > 1$ and $b > 1$ this lies strictly inside $(0,1)$ and is a maximum.
Option (a) is correct.

stem: For Beta distribution of first kind Beta$(\alpha, \beta)$, consider the following statements: I. For $\alpha > 1, \beta > 1$; density has unique mode. II. For $\alpha+\beta=2$ such that $\alpha=\beta=1$, all points in $[0,2]$ are modes. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
shortcut: Statement I is true - with both parameters above 1 the Beta density is strictly concave in $\log$ scale and has a unique interior mode. Statement II fails because Beta(1,1) is Uniform on $[0,1]$, not $[0,2]$.
tips: Beta support is ALWAYS $[0,1]$, whatever the parameters - so any claim about $[0,2]$ is wrong by definition.
Beta(1,1) is exactly the Uniform(0,1) distribution: the density is the constant 1, so every point of $[0,1]$ is a mode.
For $a > 1$ and $b > 1$ the density vanishes at both endpoints and is positive inside, so a unique interior maximum must exist - statement I follows.
Watch the support in every Beta question; the first-kind Beta lives on $(0,1)$ and the second-kind Beta on $(0, \infty)$.
solution: Statement I: for $a > 1$ and $b > 1$ the Beta density $x^{a-1}(1-x)^{b-1}$ vanishes at both $x = 0$ and $x = 1$ and is positive in between, and $\log f$ is strictly concave, so there is exactly one interior maximum at $(a-1)/(a+b-2)$. TRUE.
Statement II: with $a = b = 1$ the density becomes $x^{0} (1-x)^{0}/B(1,1) = 1$ on $(0,1)$, which is the Uniform(0,1) distribution.
Every point of $[0,1]$ is then a mode, since the density is constant there.
However the statement asserts that all points of $[0,2]$ are modes, whereas the Beta distribution of the first kind has support $[0,1]$ only, and the density is zero outside it. FALSE.
Only statement I is correct.
Hence option (a) is correct.

stem: Let X be a continuous random variable with the following pdf: $$f(x) = \begin{cases} \frac{1}{8}, & 2 \le x \le 10 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$ What is the distribution of $Y = aX+b$, provided $a>0$?
shortcut: A constant density $1/8$ on $[2,10]$ is $U(2,10)$; a positive linear map sends the endpoints to 2a+b and 10a+b, so $Y \sim U(2a+b, 10a+b)$.
tips: A linear transformation of a uniform variable is uniform - only the endpoints move, and they move by the same map as the variable.
Since $a > 0$ the order of the endpoints is preserved; a negative a would swap them, which is why the sign condition is stated.
Check the density: the range widens by a factor a, so the height falls to $1/(8a)$ - consistent with $U(2a+b, 10a+b)$.
Option (a) uses the wrong endpoints (8 and 12 rather than 2 and 10) - read the support from the stem, not from the constant $1/8$.
solution: The density is the constant $1/8$ on $[2, 10]$, an interval of length 8, so X ~ Uniform(2, 10).
Let Y = aX + b with $a > 0, a$ strictly increasing linear map.
The endpoints map to 2a + b and 10a + b, and the order is preserved because a is positive.
For y between these values, $F_{Y}(y) = \operatorname{P}(X \le (y-b)/a) = [(y-b)/a - 2]/8$, which is linear in y - so Y has a constant density.
That density is $1/(8a)$ over an interval of length 8a, confirming Y ~ Uniform($2a + b, 10a + b$).
Option (b) is correct.

subtopic: Conditional Probability, Law of Total Probability, Bayes' Theorem
stem: A player rolls a fair dice and simultaneously tosses a fair coin. If "head" appears on the coin, the player wins twice the value on the dice; if "tail" appears, the player wins half the value on the dice. What is the player's expected win?
shortcut: $\operatorname{E}(D) = 3.5$. Head pays 2D and tail pays $D/2$, each with probability $1/2$, so the expected win is $(1/2)(2)(3.5) + (1/2)(0.5)(3.5) = 3.5 + 0.875 = 4.375$.
tips: Condition on the coin: the payoff is a MULTIPLE of the die value in each case, so $\operatorname{E}\!\left(\text{win}\right) = \operatorname{E}\!\left(\text{multiplier}\right) x \operatorname{E}(D)$ with the multiplier averaging $(2 + 0.5)/2 = 1.25$.
$1.25 \times 3.5 = 4.375 - a$ one-line route once the independence of coin and die is noticed.
$\operatorname{E}(D) = (1+2+...+6)/6 = 3.5$ for a fair die; keeping it as $7/2$ makes the arithmetic exact.
Note the payoffs are asymmetric: doubling gains more than halving loses, so the expected win must EXCEED 3.5 - but only modestly, which rules out options (a), (b) and (c).
solution: Let D be the value shown on the die, uniform on 1 to 6, so $\operatorname{E}(D) = (1+2+3+4+5+6)/6 = 3.5$.
The coin is fair and independent of the die: with probability $1/2$ the player wins 2D, and with probability $1/2$ he wins $D/2$.
By the law of total expectation, $\operatorname{E}\!\left(\text{win}\right) = (1/2)\operatorname{E}(2D) + (1/2)\operatorname{E}(D/2) = (1/2)(2)(3.5) + (1/2)(0.5)(3.5) = 3.5 + 0.875 = 4.375$.
Equivalently, the expected multiplier is $(2 + 0.5)/2 = 1.25$ and $1.25 \times 3.5 = 4.375$. Option (d) is correct.

subtopic: Conditional Probability, Law of Total Probability, Bayes' Theorem
stem: A miner is trapped in a mine containing 3 doors. The first door leads to a tunnel that takes him to safety after 3 hours. The second returns him to the mine after 5 hours. The third returns him to the mine after 7 hours. Assuming the miner is equally likely to choose any door, what is the expected time until he reaches safety?
shortcut: Condition on the first door: $E = (1/3)(3) + (1/3)(5 + E) + (1/3)(7 + E) = 5 + 2E/3$, so $E/3 = 5$ and $E = 15$ hours.
tips: Set up a self-referential equation: doors 2 and 3 return the miner to the SAME situation, so E reappears on the right-hand side.
Collect the constants first: $(3 + 5 + 7)/3 = 5$, and the E-terms give $2E/3$. The equation $E = 5 + 2E/3$ then solves in one step.
The memoryless structure is essential - after returning, the miner's expected remaining time is again E, with no memory of the failed attempts.
Intuition check: he escapes on the first try with probability $1/3$, so he expects 3 attempts averaging 5 hours each, giving 15.
solution: Let E be the expected time to reach safety from inside the mine.
Condition on which door the miner chooses first, each with probability $1/3$.
Door 1: he reaches safety after 3 hours, contributing $(1/3)(3)$.
Door 2: he wanders for 5 hours and returns to the mine, facing the same situation afresh, contributing $(1/3)(5 + E)$. Door 3 similarly contributes $(1/3)(7 + E)$.
Hence $E - (2/3)E = 5$, so $E/3 = 5$ and $E = 15$ hours, option (a).

stem: The distribution function of the standard Laplace distribution with pdf $f(x) = \frac{1}{2}e^{-|x|}, -\infty<x<\infty$ is:
shortcut: Integrating $(1/2)e^{x}$ up to $x \le 0$ gives $e^{x}/2$; for $x > 0$ add the remaining area to get $1 - e^{-x}/2$.
tips: Split at 0 because of the |x|: the density is $(1/2)e^{x}$ on the left and $(1/2)e^{-x}$ on the right.
$F(0)$ must equal $1/2$ by symmetry. Check each option at $x = 0$: only options (a) and (b) give $1/2$ from the left branch, and only (a) gives $1/2$ from the right.
Limits check: F(-$\infty$) = 0 and F(+$\infty$) = 1. Option (c) tends to 0 at +$\infty$ and option (d) is discontinuous - both invalid.
solution: The standard Laplace density is $f(x) = (1/2)e^{-\lvert x\rvert }$, i.e. $(1/2)e^{x}$ for $x \le 0$ and $(1/2)e^{-x}$ for $x > 0$.
For $x \le 0$: F(x) = the $\int_{-\infty}^{x} (1/2)e^{t}\,dt = (1/2)e^{x}$.
In particular $F(0) = 1/2$, as symmetry requires.
So $F(x) = e^{x}/2$ for $x \le 0$ and $1 - e^{-x}/2$ for $x > 0$, option (a).

stem: Let $X_1$ and $X_2$ have joint pdf $f(x_1,x_2) = \begin{cases} 2, & 0<x_1<x_2<1 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$. What is the marginal distribution of $X_1$?
shortcut: For fixed x1, the variable x2 ranges over $(x_{1}, 1)$, so $f_{1}(x_{1}) = 2(1 - x_{1})$ on $(0,1)$.
tips: Get the limits from the region: $0 < x_{1} < x_{2} < 1$ means x2 runs from x1 up to 1, a range of length 1 - x1.
Integrating the constant 2 over that range gives $2(1 - x_{1}) - a$ DECREASING density, since small x1 leaves more room for x2.
Validity check: the $\int 2(1-x_{1})$ over $(0,1)$ is $2(1 - 1/2) = 1$. Option (c) 2x1 also integrates to 1, so use the limits, not this test, to choose.
Contrast with 2022 Q49, where the same density gave $f_{Y}(y) = 2y$ for the OTHER variable - the two marginals are mirror images.
solution: The joint density is $f(x_{1}, x_{2}) = 2$ on the triangle $0 < x_{1} < x_{2} < 1$, whose area is $1/2$, so the total probability is $2(1/2) = 1$.
The marginal of X1 is obtained by integrating out x2 over the values it may take for that x1.
The constraint $x_{1} < x_{2} < 1$ means x2 ranges from x1 to 1.
Check: the $\int 2(1 - x_{1})$ over $(0,1) = 2[x_{1} - x_{1}^{2}/2]$ from 0 to $1 = 2(1/2) = 1, a$ valid density.
Option (b) is correct.

stem: Let $k>0$ be a constant such that pdf of X is $f(x) = \begin{cases} kx(1-x), & 0<x<1 \\ 0, & \text{elsewhere} \end{cases}$. What is $E(X)$?
shortcut: kx(1-x) on $(0,1)$ is the Beta(2,2) density $(k = 6)$, which is symmetric about $1/2$, so $\operatorname{E}(X) = 1/2$.
tips: Recognise the Beta kernel: $x^{a-1}(1-x)^{b-1}$ with $a = b = 2$, so the distribution is Beta(2,2) and $k = 1/B(2,2) = 6$.
Beta mean = $a/(a+b) = 2/4 = 1/2$ - no integration needed once the family is identified.
Symmetry shortcut: the density kx(1-x) is symmetric about $x = 1/2$, so the mean must be $1/2$ whatever k is.
The constant k never enters the answer, which is why the question can leave it unspecified - a hint that symmetry is the intended route.
solution: The density f(x) = kx(1-x) on $(0,1)$ has the form $x^{a-1}(1-x)^{b-1}$ with $a = b = 2$, so X ~ Beta(2,2).
Normalisation: the $\int x(1-x)$ over $(0,1)$ is $1/2 - 1/3 = 1/6$, so $k = 6$.
For Beta(a,b) the mean is $a/(a+b) = 2/(2+2) = 1/2$.
Alternatively, the density is symmetric about $x = 1/2$ (since $x(1-x)$ is unchanged by $x \to 1-x$), so the mean is $1/2$ by symmetry.
Direct check: $\operatorname{E}(X) = 6$ times the $\int x^{2}(1-x)\,dx = 6(1/3 - 1/4) = 6(1/12) = 1/2$.
Option (a) is correct.
