subtopic: Languages, Compiler, Assembler, Interpreter; Low & High Level
stem: What is the main purpose of the linker in the compilation process?
options: To perform optimization of compiled code
To translate source code into machine code
To check syntax of the program
To combine object files and libraries into an executable program
shortcut: The linker's job is in its name - it links. It combines separately compiled object modules with library routines to produce a single executable. Answer (d).
tips: Pipeline order: preprocessor -> compiler -> assembler -> linker -> loader. Each option here names a different stage, so match the stage to the description.
Translation to machine code is the compiler/assembler's job (option b); syntax checking is the compiler front-end's job (option c); optimisation is the compiler's middle/back end (option a).
Static linking bakes library code into the executable; dynamic linking resolves it at load or run time via shared libraries (.so / .dll).
Undefined reference errors come from the linker, not the compiler - a useful diagnostic memory aid.
solution: After compilation each source file becomes an object file containing machine code with unresolved external references (calls to functions defined elsewhere or in libraries).

The linker takes these object files together with the required library modules, resolves all external symbol references, assigns final relative addresses, and merges everything into one executable file.
Option (a) describes the optimiser inside the compiler; option (b) describes the compiler/assembler; option (c) describes the compiler's syntax analysis phase.
Only option (d) states the linker's actual function.
Hence option (d) is correct.

topic: Data, Information, Database & DBMS; Frontend/Backend
subtopic: Data, Information, Database & DBMS; Frontend/Backend
stem: Which are characteristics of virtual reality? I. It is created using multimedia. II. It enables users to move and react in a computer-simulated environment. III. It stimulates senses like sight, hearing, and touch.
shortcut: All three statements are standard textbook properties of virtual reality - it is multimedia-based, interactive within a simulated environment, and multi-sensory. Answer (d).
tips: In UPSC computer-awareness sets, when every listed statement is a benign textbook property, 'all of the above' is usually right; look for a statement that is factually wrong before rejecting it.
VR is defined by three $I's$: Immersion, Interaction, Imagination - which map onto statements III, II and I respectively.
VR uses multimedia elements (3-D graphics, audio, animation, sometimes haptics) as its building blocks, so statement I is true by construction.
Contrast with augmented reality, which overlays computer-generated content on the real world rather than replacing it.
solution: Statement I: virtual reality environments are built from multimedia components - 3-D graphics, animation, sound, video and haptic feedback. True.
Statement II: the defining feature of VR is interactivity - the user moves within and reacts to a computer-simulated environment in real time. True.
Statement III: VR stimulates multiple senses - sight through head-mounted displays, hearing through spatial audio, and touch through haptic gloves or controllers. True.
All three statements are correct.
Hence option (d) is correct.

topic: Data, Information, Database & DBMS; Frontend/Backend
subtopic: Data, Information, Database & DBMS; Frontend/Backend
stem: Multimedia combines different media types. How many of the following are part of multimedia? I. Text II. Video III. Audio IV. Graphics and Images V. Animation
shortcut: The standard definition lists exactly five media types: text, graphics/images, audio, video and animation. All five listed items qualify. Answer (d).
tips: Mnemonic for the five elements of multimedia: TAGVA - Text, Audio, Graphics, Video, Animation.
'Multi' + 'media' means many media, so a definition question of this shape rarely excludes a genuine media type.
Distinguish video (captured motion of real scenes, frame sequences) from animation (synthetically generated motion) - both count separately.
Interactivity is often added as a sixth defining attribute of multimedia systems, but it is not itself a media type.
solution: Multimedia is defined as the integration of two or more media types in a single application.
The universally listed constituent media are: text, graphics and images, audio (sound), video, and animation.
Checking each listed item: I Text - yes; II Video - yes; III Audio - yes; IV Graphics and Images - yes; V Animation - yes.
All five are part of multimedia.
Hence option (d) is correct.

topic: Networks: LAN, WAN, Internet, Intranet
subtopic: Networks: LAN, WAN, Internet, Intranet
stem: In respect of the working of a router: I. It interconnects computer networks. II. It determines on which outgoing link an IP packet is forwarded. III. The destination address of the IP packet is examined and it is routed to the next router. Which are correct?
shortcut: All three describe exactly what a router does at the network layer: interconnect networks, choose the outgoing link, and forward on the destination IP address. Answer (d).
tips: Layer map: hub = physical (layer 1), switch/bridge = data link (layer 2), router = network (layer 3), gateway = up to application layer.
A router forwards on the destination IP address using its routing table (longest-prefix match); a switch forwards on the destination MAC address.
Routers separate broadcast domains, which is why they are the device that interconnects distinct networks - statement I.
Each hop re-examines the destination address and passes the packet to the next router - this hop-by-hop behaviour is statement III.
solution: Statement I: a router operates at the network layer and its primary purpose is to interconnect two or more distinct computer networks. True.
Statement II: on receiving a packet, the router consults its routing table and determines the outgoing interface (link) on which the packet should be forwarded. True.
Statement III: the forwarding decision is made by examining the destination IP address in the packet header, and the packet is passed to the next-hop router towards the destination. True.
All three statements are correct.
Hence option (d) is correct.

topic: Programming Basics: Algorithm, Flowchart, Control Structures, Arrays, Functions
subtopic: Programming Basics: Algorithm, Flowchart, Control Structures, Arrays, Functions
stem: In which construct is the same set of statements executed several times based on a specified condition?
shortcut: Repetition based on a condition is a loop. Among the options only Do-While is a loop; If-Then, If-Then-Else and Case are selection constructs. Answer (c).
tips: The three structured-programming control constructs are sequence, selection (if / case) and iteration (while / do-while / for).
Keywords in the stem give it away: 'executed several times' means iteration; 'based on a condition' means the loop is conditional rather than counted.
Do-While tests the condition after the body, so it runs at least once; While tests before, so it may run zero times.
Case Type (switch) is multi-way selection, not repetition - the most tempting distractor if you read only 'several'.
solution: The construct in which the same block of statements is executed repeatedly so long as a specified condition holds is called a loop or iteration construct.
If-Then (option a) executes a block at most once, depending on a condition - selection, not repetition.
If-Then-Else (option b) chooses between two blocks, each executed at most once - selection.
Do-While (option c) executes the body and then tests the condition, repeating while the condition remains true - this is repetition.
Case Type (option d) is multi-way selection, choosing one branch among many - not repetition.
Hence option (c) is correct.

topic: Memory: RAM, ROM, Cache; Units of Memory & Storage Capacity
subtopic: Memory: RAM, ROM, Cache; Units of Memory & Storage Capacity
stem: About virtual memory in a computer system: I. It provides large addressable space without worrying about physical memory size limits. II. It provides efficient sharing of main memory among users in a multiprogrammed OS. III. It provides a large secondary memory. Which are correct?
shortcut: Virtual memory enlarges the apparent address space and lets many processes share physical RAM - I and II. It does not create secondary memory; it merely uses the disk that already exists, so III is false. Answer (a).
tips: Virtual memory is an illusion of large main memory, not an enlargement of disk - statement III inverts cause and effect.
Two textbook benefits: (i) programs may be larger than physical RAM, (ii) more processes fit in memory simultaneously, raising multiprogramming and CPU utilisation.
Mechanisms: paging with a page table and MMU address translation, demand paging, page faults and replacement policies (FIFO, LRU, Optimal).
Thrashing is the failure mode - excessive page faults when the working set exceeds available frames.
solution: Virtual memory is a memory-management technique in which the logical address space presented to a program is decoupled from the physical main memory, with pages moved between RAM and a backing store on disk on demand.
Statement I: a process can use a large logical address space regardless of how much physical memory is installed - this is the defining benefit. True.
Statement II: because only the active pages of each process occupy frames, main memory is shared efficiently among many users in a multiprogrammed operating system. True.
Statement III: virtual memory does not provide or enlarge secondary memory. It consumes part of the existing secondary storage as a swap area to create the illusion of large main memory. False.
Only statements I and II are correct.
Hence option (a) is correct.

topic: Computer Security: Virus, Antivirus, Firewall, Spyware, Malware
subtopic: Computer Security: Virus, Antivirus, Firewall, Spyware, Malware
stem: A packet filter firewall can:
options: filter specific users from accessing network services.
block all IP packets from entering the networks.
check all IP packets and, if valid, allow entry or exit.
block any kind of viruses from entering the networks.
shortcut: A packet filter inspects each IP packet's header against rules and permits or denies it. Option (b) blocks everything (useless), (a) needs user identity which headers do not carry, and (d) needs payload/signature scanning. Only (c) survives.
tips: Packet filters work on header fields only: source and destination IP, source and destination port, protocol and flags. Anything requiring user identity or payload content is outside their scope.
Firewall hierarchy: packet filter (stateless, layer $3/4$) -> stateful inspection -> application/proxy gateway (layer 7) -> next-generation firewall with deep packet inspection.
Virus detection needs signature or heuristic scanning of the payload - that is antivirus or an application-layer gateway, not a packet filter, so (d) is wrong.
Beware absolutes: an option saying a device blocks 'all' or 'any kind of' something is usually a distractor.
solution: A packet filtering firewall examines the header of every IP packet crossing the boundary and compares it against an ordered access control list.
Based on the match it either allows the packet through (in or out) or drops it - exactly what option (c) states.

Option (a) is wrong: filtering by individual user requires authentication information, which is not present in the IP or TCP header; that is the role of an application-level or identity-aware firewall.
Option (b) is wrong: blocking all IP packets would disconnect the network entirely and defeats the purpose of a firewall, which is selective control.
Option (d) is wrong: viruses live in packet payloads and require content scanning; a header-based packet filter cannot detect them.
Hence option (c) is correct.

topic: Networks: LAN, WAN, Internet, Intranet
subtopic: Networks: LAN, WAN, Internet, Intranet
stem: Wi-Fi is often used as a synonym for which IEEE technology?
shortcut: Wi-Fi = IEEE 802.11. Direct recall, option (d).
tips: Memorise the IEEE 802 family: 802.3 Ethernet, 802.5 Token Ring, 802.11 Wireless LAN $(Wi-Fi), 802.15$ Bluetooth/WPAN, 802.16 WiMAX.
802.1 covers bridging and network management, 802.9 was integrated voice/data (isoEthernet, now withdrawn) - both are pure distractors here.
Wi-Fi generations: $802.11b/a/g/n (Wi-Fi 4)/ac (Wi-Fi 5)/ax (Wi-Fi 6)$/be $(Wi-Fi 7)$.
'Wi-Fi' is a trademark of the Wi-Fi Alliance certifying interoperable 802.11 equipment; it is not itself a standard number.
solution: The IEEE 802 committee standardises local and metropolitan area networks, with each working group numbered 802.x.
Working group 802.11 defines wireless local area networking - the media access control and physical layer specifications for WLANs.
Products certified as interoperable with 802.11 are branded Wi-Fi by the Wi-Fi Alliance, so the two terms are used synonymously.
802.1 is bridging/network management, 802.5 is Token Ring, 802.9 was integrated services (isoEthernet) - none relate to Wi-Fi.
Hence option (d) is correct.

topic: Computer Organisation: CPU, ALU, Control & Memory Units, I/O Units
subtopic: Computer Organisation: CPU, ALU, Control & Memory Units, I/O Units
stem: AND and OR operations are part of which unit of the CPU?
shortcut: AND and OR are logical, not arithmetic, operations - so they belong to the logic unit of the ALU. Option (b).
tips: The ALU has two functional halves: the arithmetic unit (add, subtract, multiply, divide, increment) and the logic unit (AND, OR, NOT, XOR, shifts, comparisons).
The control unit fetches, decodes and sequences instructions; it does not perform data operations.
Main memory stores data and instructions; it performs no operations at all.
Comparison instructions are also logic-unit work, since they are implemented by subtraction followed by flag testing.
solution: The CPU consists of the arithmetic and logic unit (ALU), the control unit, and registers, with main memory external to it.

Within the ALU, the arithmetic unit performs addition, subtraction, multiplication and division, while the logic unit performs Boolean operations such as AND, OR, NOT and XOR, along with shifts and comparisons.
AND and OR are Boolean operations, hence they are carried out by the logic unit.
The control unit (option c) only decodes instructions and generates control signals; the main memory unit (option d) only stores data.
Hence option (b) is correct.

topic: Random Vectors: Joint, Marginal & Conditional Distributions
subtopic: Random Vectors: Joint, Marginal & Conditional Distributions
sharedStem: > **Shared data for Q1–Q3.** X and Y have discrete joint distribution > $$P(X=x,Y=y) = \begin{cases} c|x+y| & \text{for } x,y \in \{-2,-1,0,1,2\} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$
stem: What is $\mathrm{Var}(X)$ equal to?
shortcut: Row sums of |x+y| for x = -2,-1,0,1,2 are 10, 7, 6, 7, 10, total 40, so $c = 1/40$ and $\operatorname{P}(X) = (0.25, 0.175, 0.15, 0.175, 0.25)$. Symmetry gives $\operatorname{E}(X) = 0$, so $\operatorname{Var}(X) = \operatorname{E}(X^{2}) = 2(4)(0.25) + 2(1)(0.175) = 2 + 0.35 = 2.35$.
tips: Get c first: the number of pairs summing to s is 5 - |s| for |s| <= 4, so sum |x+y| = $2(4 \cdot 1 + 3 \cdot 2 + 2 \cdot 3 + 1 \cdot 4) = 40$ and $c = 1/40$.
The marginal row sums 10, 7, 6, 7, 10 are symmetric about $x = 0$, which forces $\operatorname{E}(X) = 0$ and turns the variance into a pure $\operatorname{E}(X^{2})$ computation.
Only x = +/-2 and x = +/-1 contribute to $\operatorname{E}(X^{2})$; $x = 0$ contributes nothing, so it is a two-term sum.
The same marginal serves for Y by symmetry, so $\operatorname{Var}(Y) = 2.35$ as well - handy if a companion question asks for it.
solution: Normalising constant: sum over x, y in {-2,-1,0,1,2} of |x + y|. The number of pairs with $x + y = s$ is 5 - |s|, so the total is $4(1) + 3(2) + 2(3) + 1(4) + 0(5) + 1(4) + 2(3) + 3(2) + 4(1) = 40$. Hence $c = 1/40$.
Marginal of X: $\operatorname{P}(X = x) = (1/40) * \sum \mid x + y$|.
$\operatorname{Var}(X) = \operatorname{E}(X^{2}) - [\operatorname{E}(X)]^{2} = 2.35 - 0 = 2.35$.
Hence option (c) is correct.

topic: Random Vectors: Joint, Marginal & Conditional Distributions
subtopic: Random Vectors: Joint, Marginal & Conditional Distributions
sharedStem: > **Shared data for Q1–Q3.** X and Y have discrete joint distribution > $$P(X=x,Y=y) = \begin{cases} c|x+y| & \text{for } x,y \in \{-2,-1,0,1,2\} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$
stem: What is $E(Y \mid X=1)$ equal to?
shortcut: Along the row $X = 1$ the weights |1+y| for y = -2,-1,0,1,2 are 1, 0, 1, 2, 3 with total 7. So $\operatorname{E}(Y\mid X=1) = [(-2)(1) + (-1)(0) + 0(1) + 1(2) + 2(3)]/7 = 6/7$.
tips: For a conditional expectation on a discrete grid, work with the unnormalised row weights and divide by the row total once at the end - the constant c cancels.
The row total 7 is exactly the marginal weight $\operatorname{P}(X = 1) = 7/40$ found in the previous part; reuse it rather than recomputing.
Note that |1 + y| = 0 at y = -1, so that term drops out entirely.
Sanity check the sign: the row weights are heavier on the positive y side (2 and 3 versus 1 and 0), so $\operatorname{E}(Y\mid X=1)$ must be positive, ruling out any negative answer.
solution: The joint weights along the row $X = 1$ are $\operatorname{P}(X = 1, Y = y)$ = |1 + y|/40.
Row total = $(1 + 0 + 1 + 2 + 3)/40 = 7/40 = \operatorname{P}(X = 1)$.
Conditional pmf: $\operatorname{P}(Y = y \mid X = 1)$ = |1 + y|/7, giving $1/7, 0, 1/7, 2/7, 3/7$ for y = -2, -1, 0, 1, 2.
Hence option (d) is correct.

topic: Random Vectors: Joint, Marginal & Conditional Distributions
subtopic: Random Vectors: Joint, Marginal & Conditional Distributions
sharedStem: > **Shared data for Q1–Q3.** X and Y have discrete joint distribution > $$P(X=x,Y=y) = \begin{cases} c|x+y| & \text{for } x,y \in \{-2,-1,0,1,2\} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$
stem: What is $P(|X-Y|\le 1)$ equal to?
shortcut: |x - y| <= 1 means the main diagonal plus the two adjacent diagonals. Weights: diagonal |2x| gives $4+2+0+2+4 = 12$; each off-diagonal gives $3+1+1+3 = 8$. Total $12 + 8 + 8 = 28$, so $P = 28/40 = 0.7$.
tips: Organise the 25 cells by diagonals: on $y = x$ the weight is |2x|, on $y = x+1$ it is |2x+1|, on $y = x-1$ it is |2x-1|. Each diagonal is then a four- or five-term sum.
The two off-diagonals give the same total by the symmetry of the weight in x and y - compute one and double it.
Always divide by 40, not by 25: the distribution is not uniform on the grid.
0.7 and 0.3 are complements, and $0.06 / 0.12$ are far too small to be a 13-cell event - a quick magnitude check rules them out.
solution: The event |X - Y| <= 1 covers the cells with $y = x, y = x + 1$ and $y = x - 1$, i.e. $5 + 4 + 4 = 13$ of the 25 cells.
Cells with $y = x$: weight |x + y| = |2x| = 4, 2, 0, 2, 4 for x = -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, total 12.
Cells with $y = x + 1 (x = -2, -1, 0, 1)$: weight |2x + 1| = 3, 1, 1, 3, total 8.
Cells with $y = x - 1 (x = -1, 0, 1, 2)$: weight |2x - 1| = 3, 1, 1, 3, total 8.
Total weight = $12 + 8 + 8 = 28$.
$\operatorname{P}(\lvert X - Y\rvert \le 1) = 28/40 = 0.7$.
Hence option (b) is correct.

topic: Standard Continuous Distributions
subtopic: Standard Continuous Distributions
sharedStem: > **Shared data for Q4–Q5.** Let $f_X(x)$ be the pdf of $N(0,1)$ and $\Phi(x)=\int_{-\infty}^x f_X(\theta)\,d\theta$.
stem: What is $\Phi(-100)$ equal to?
shortcut: The standard normal density is symmetric about 0, so $\Phi(-z) = 1 - \Phi(z)$ for every z. Put $z = 100$. Answer (b).
tips: Memorise the symmetry relation $\Phi(-z) + \Phi(z) = 1$; it is the single most-used property of the standard normal CDF.
A CDF can never be negative, so option (a) is impossible on sight.
Option (d) would give a negative number since $\Phi(100)$ is essentially 1; another instant rejection.
Numerically $\Phi(-100)$ is about $10^{-2174}$, i.e. effectively 0, consistent with $1 - \Phi(100)$.
solution: By definition $\Phi(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{x} f_{X}(\theta) d \theta$, where $f_{X}$ is the $N(0,1)$ density.
The density is symmetric: $f_{X}(-t) = f_{X}(t)$.
Substituting $\theta$ = -u in the integral for $\Phi(-z)$ gives $\Phi(-z) = \int_{z}^{\infty} f_{X}(u)\,du = 1 - \Phi(z)$.
Options (a) and (d) would be negative (since $\Phi(100)$ is essentially 1), which is impossible for a CDF; option (c) contradicts the symmetry relation.
Hence option (b) is correct.

topic: Standard Continuous Distributions
subtopic: Standard Continuous Distributions
sharedStem: > **Shared data for Q4–Q5.** Let $f_X(x)$ be the pdf of $N(0,1)$ and $\Phi(x)=\int_{-\infty}^x f_X(\theta)\,d\theta$.
stem: What is $\displaystyle\int_{-10}^{10}\int_{-y}^{y} f_X(x)\,dx\,dy$ equal to?
shortcut: The inner integral $g(y) = \int_{-y}^{y} f_{X} = \Phi(y) - \Phi(-y)$ is an odd function of y, and the outer range $[-10, 10]$ is symmetric about 0. An odd function integrated over a symmetric interval gives 0.
tips: Do the inner integral symbolically first - here it collapses to $2\Phi(y) - 1$, whose oddness is the whole point.
Check oddness explicitly: $g(-y) = \Phi(-y) - \Phi(y)$ = -g(y). Do not assume the inner integral is automatically non-negative just because $f_{X}$ is.
When $y < 0$ the limits -y to y run backwards, so the inner integral is negative - this is the step most candidates miss, which is why $1/2$ is the popular wrong answer.
General principle: $\int_{-a}^{a}$ an odd function is 0; $\int_{-a}^{a}$ an even function is 2 * integral from 0 to a.
solution: Let $g(y) = \int_{-y}^{y} f_{X}(x)\,dx = \Phi(y) - \Phi(-y)$.
Using $\Phi(-y) = 1 - \Phi(y)$, we get $g(y) = 2 \Phi(y) - 1$.
Then $g(-y) = 2 \Phi(-y) - 1 = 2(1 - \Phi(y)) - 1 = 1 - 2 \Phi(y)$ = -g(y), so g is an odd function of y.
The required double integral is $\int_{-10}^{10} g(y)\,dy$.
An odd integrable function integrated over an interval symmetric about the origin gives 0: the contribution from y in $(0, 10)$ exactly cancels that from y in $(-10, 0)$.
Therefore the value is 0.
Hence option (c) is correct.

topic: Random Vectors: Joint, Marginal & Conditional Distributions
subtopic: Random Vectors: Joint, Marginal & Conditional Distributions
sharedStem: > **Shared data for Q6–Q7.** The joint pdf of X and Y is > $$f(x,y) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{2(x+2y)}{3}, & 0<x<1,\ 0<y<1 \\ 0, & \text{elsewhere} \end{cases}$$
stem: What is $E[X \mid Y=0.5]$?
tips: The marginal at $y = 0.5$ evaluating to exactly 1 is the designed simplification - the conditional density is then just the joint density with y substituted.
Substitute $y = 0.5$ before integrating, not after; carrying a symbolic y through doubles the work.
Verify the conditional integrates to 1: $\int_{0}^{1} 2(x+1)/3\,dx = (2/3)(1/2 + 1) = 1$. A ten-second check that catches algebra slips.
Since the conditional density increases in $x, \operatorname{E}(X \mid Y = 0.5)$ must exceed $1/2$ - that alone eliminates options (a) and (b).
solution: Hence option (c) is correct.

topic: Random Vectors: Joint, Marginal & Conditional Distributions
subtopic: Random Vectors: Joint, Marginal & Conditional Distributions
sharedStem: > **Shared data for Q6–Q7.** The joint pdf of X and Y is > $$f(x,y) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{2(x+2y)}{3}, & 0<x<1,\ 0<y<1 \\ 0, & \text{elsewhere} \end{cases}$$
stem: What is the conditional variance of X given $Y=0.5$?
tips: Reuse the conditional density and the conditional mean from the previous part; only $\operatorname{E}(X^{2} \mid Y = 0.5)$ is new work.
Convert to the common denominator 162 immediately: $7/18 = 63/162$ and $25/81 = 50/162$, so the subtraction is a single step.

Sanity bound: X lies in $(0,1)$, so its conditional variance cannot exceed $1/4 = 40.5/162$; $13/162 = 0.080$ is comfortably inside, and even the uniform value $1/12 = 13.5/162$ is close, as expected for a gently sloping density.
The distractors $11/162, 5/54 = 15/162$ and $17/162$ all come from small slips in $\operatorname{E}(X^{2})$ or in squaring $5/9$ - keep fractions exact throughout.
solution: From the previous part, $f(x \mid Y = 0.5) = 2(x + 1)/3$ on $0 < x < 1$, with $\operatorname{E}(X \mid Y = 0.5) = 5/9$.
$\operatorname{Var}(X \mid Y = 0.5) = \operatorname{E}(X^{2} \mid Y = 0.5) - [\operatorname{E}(X \mid Y = 0.5)]^{2} = 7/18 - (5/9)^{2} = 7/18 - 25/81$.
Hence option (b) is correct.

topic: Random Vectors: Joint, Marginal & Conditional Distributions
subtopic: Random Vectors: Joint, Marginal & Conditional Distributions
sharedStem: > **Shared data for Q8–Q9.** The joint pdf of (X, Y) is > $$f(x,y) = \begin{cases} x^2+\dfrac{xy}{3}, & 0<x<1,\ 0<y<2 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$
stem: The conditional density of Y given X is:
shortcut: Integrate out y over $(0,2)$: $f_{X}(x) = 2x^{2} + 2x/3 = (2x/3)(3x + 1)$. Dividing the joint by this cancels the x, leaving $(3x + y)/[2(3x + 1)]$. Option (a).
tips: Conditional of Y given X means divide by the marginal of X, so integrate the joint over the y-range - keep track of which variable is being eliminated.
Factor the joint as $x(3x + y)/3$ before dividing; the common factor x then cancels visibly and the answer's shape becomes obvious.

Elimination test: for a valid conditional density of Y given X, integrating over $0 < y < 2$ must give 1. Option (a): $\int (3x+y)/[2(3x+1)]\,dy = (6x + 2)/[2(3x+1)] = 1$. It passes; the others do not.
The conditional pdf of Y given X must not have a stray free x that fails to normalise - options (b), (c), (d) all break the normalisation check.
solution: Check normalisation: $\int_{0}^{1} (2x^{2} + 2x/3)\,dx = 2/3 + 1/3 = 1$, as required.
Joint density factored: $f(x, y) = x^{2} + xy/3 = (x/3)(3x + y)$.
Hence option (a) is correct.

topic: Random Vectors: Joint, Marginal & Conditional Distributions
subtopic: Random Vectors: Joint, Marginal & Conditional Distributions
sharedStem: > **Shared data for Q8–Q9.** The joint pdf of (X, Y) is > $$f(x,y) = \begin{cases} x^2+\dfrac{xy}{3}, & 0<x<1,\ 0<y<2 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$
stem: The conditional density of X given Y is:
shortcut: $f_{Y}(y) = \int_{0}^{1} (x^{2} + xy/3)\,dx = 1/3 + y/6 = (2 + y)/6$. Dividing the joint by this gives $6(x^{2} + xy/3)/(2+y) = 2x(3x + y)/(2 + y)$. Option (c).
tips: Now integrate out x over $(0,1)$ - the opposite variable from the previous part; mixing the two up is the classic error.
Write the marginal as a single fraction $(2 + y)/6$ before dividing, so the factor 6 comes up cleanly in the numerator.
Normalisation check: $\int_{0}^{1} 2x(3x+y)/(2+y)\,dx = (2 + y)/(2 + y) = 1$. Option (c) passes; test the others the same way and they fail.
Compare with the previous answer: the conditional of Y given X kept x in the denominator's shape, whereas this one keeps y - a useful structural cross-check.
solution: Conditional density: $f(x \mid y) = f(x, y)/f_{Y}(y) = (x^{2} + xy/3) \cdot 6/(2 + y) = (6x^{2} + 2xy)/(2 + y) = 2x(3x + y)/(2 + y)$, for $0 < x < 1, 0 < y < 2$.
Hence option (c) is correct.

topic: Standard Discrete Distributions
subtopic: Standard Discrete Distributions
stem: X, Y, Z are independent. X and Y each have a geometric distribution with parameter 1/2, and Z has a negative binomial distribution with parameters 3 and p. $E(X+Y-Z)=0$ if and only if p equals:
issue: The answer depends on the counting convention. Using the standard Indian-textbook convention in which both the geometric and the negative binomial count FAILURES (geometric mean $q/p$, negative binomial mean rq/p), $\operatorname{E}(X) = \operatorname{E}(Y) = 1$ and $2 = 3(1-p)/p$ gives $p = 3/5$, option (d). If instead both are taken as counting TRIALS (means $1/p$ and $r/p$), then $4 = 3/p$ gives $p = 3/4$, option (b), which is why both values appear among the choices. Option (d) is keyed here on the failure-counting convention; a candidate should state the convention used.
shortcut: With the failure-counting convention, geometric($1/2$) has mean $q/p = 1$, so $\operatorname{E}(X + Y) = 2$, and NB(3, p) has mean $3q/p$. Set $3(1 - p)/p = 2$ to get $5p = 3, p = 3/5$.
tips: State your convention before computing: geometric as number of failures has mean $q/p$; as number of trials it has mean $1/p$. The same split applies to the negative binomial (rq/p versus $r/p$).
Whichever convention you adopt, use it for BOTH distributions - the geometric is the negative binomial with $r = 1$, so mixing conventions is internally inconsistent.

Expectation is linear whether or not the variables are independent, so $\operatorname{E}(X + Y - Z) = \operatorname{E}(X) + \operatorname{E}(Y) - \operatorname{E}(Z)$; the stated independence is needed only if a variance were asked.
The two consistent conventions produce exactly the two 'nice' options $3/5$ and $3/4$ - recognising that tells you which pair of distractors are decoys.
solution: Adopt the standard convention in which the geometric variable counts the number of failures before the first success: $\operatorname{P}(X = x) = q^{x} p, x = 0, 1, 2$, ..., with $\operatorname{E}(X) = q/p$.
With $p = 1/2$: $\operatorname{E}(X) = (1/2)/(1/2) = 1$, and likewise $\operatorname{E}(Y) = 1$, so $\operatorname{E}(X + Y) = 2$.

Under the matching convention, the negative binomial with parameters $r = 3$ and p counts the failures before the 3rd success: $\operatorname{P}(Z = z) = \binom{z + 2}{z} p^{3} q^{z}$, with $\operatorname{E}(Z) = 3q/p = 3(1 - p)/p$.
By linearity, $\operatorname{E}(X + Y - Z) = 0$ requires $\operatorname{E}(Z) = \operatorname{E}(X) + \operatorname{E}(Y) = 2$.
So $3(1 - p)/p = 2$, giving $3 - 3p = 2p$, hence $5p = 3$ and $p = 3/5$.
(Consistency check: with $p = 3/5, \operatorname{E}(Z) = 3(2/5)/(3/5) = 2$, matching $\operatorname{E}(X) + \operatorname{E}(Y) = 2$.)
Hence option (d) is correct under the failure-counting convention; see the note above for the trials convention.

topic: Distributions of Functions of Random Variables
subtopic: Distributions of Functions of Random Variables
stem: If $X\sim N(0,1)$ and $Y\sim N(0,1)$ are independent, the distribution of $X/Y$ is:
shortcut: The ratio of two independent standard normals is the standard Cauchy - a memorised standard result. Answer (b).
tips: Memorise the family: X/Y is Cauchy(0,1); $X^{2}/Y^{2}$ is $F(1,1)$; $X^{2} + Y^{2}$ is $\chi^{2}$ with 2 df; X/|Y| is also Cauchy.
Option (d) is the trap: $F(1,1)$ is the distribution of the ratio of SQUARES, not of the variables themselves.
The Cauchy has no mean and no variance, which is why the ratio of two well-behaved normals is famously pathological - a favourite examiner point.
Cauchy(0,1) has density $1/[pi(1 + z^{2})]$ on the whole real line; the location 0 and scale 1 follow from both normals having mean 0 and variance 1, so (c) with location 1 is wrong.
solution: Let $Z = X/Y$ with X, Y independent $N(0,1)$.
Using the transformation $Z = X/Y, W = Y$ with Jacobian |w|, the joint density of (Z, W) is |w| * $(1/(2pi)) \exp(-(z^{2} w^{2} + w^{2})/2)$.
Integrating out w: $f_{Z}(z) = (1/(2pi)) * \int \lvert w\rvert \exp(-w^{2}(1 + z^{2})/2)\,dw = (1/(2pi)) \cdot 2/(1 + z^{2}) = 1/[pi(1 + z^{2})]$.
This is exactly the standard Cauchy density, i.e. Cauchy with location 0 and scale 1.
$\chi^{2}$ with 2 df (option a) is the distribution of $X^{2} + Y^{2}$, not X/Y; $F(1,1)$ (option d) is the distribution of $X^{2}/Y^{2}$; Cauchy(1,1) (option c) has the wrong location parameter.
Hence option (b) is correct.

topic: Conditional Probability, Law of Total Probability, Bayes' Theorem
subtopic: Conditional Probability, Law of Total Probability, Bayes' Theorem
stem: Three identical urns contain white/black balls: urn 1 has 2 white, 3 black; urn 2 has 3 white, 5 black; urn 3 has 5 white, 2 black. An urn is chosen at random and a ball drawn. Given the ball is white, what is the probability the second urn was chosen?
shortcut: The prior $1/3$ cancels, so the posterior is just $3/8$ divided by $(2/5 + 3/8 + 5/7)$. Over LCD 280 these are 112, 105 and 200, total 417. Answer $105/417 = 35/139$.
tips: When all priors are equal they cancel in Bayes' formula - the posterior is simply the likelihood divided by the sum of the likelihoods.
Put the three white-ball probabilities over a common denominator (280 here) at once; the numerators 112, 105, 200 then make the arithmetic exact.
Always reduce: $105/417$ has common factor 3, giving $35/139$. The unreduced form is deliberately absent, and $112/417$ is the answer for urn 1 while $200/417$ is for urn 3.
Cross-check: the three posteriors $112/417, 105/417$ and $200/417$ must sum to 1 - they do.
solution: Let U1, U2, U3 be the events that urn 1, 2, 3 is chosen, each with prior probability $1/3$, and let W be the event that the drawn ball is white.
Likelihoods: $\operatorname{P}(W \mid U_{1}) = 2/5, \operatorname{P}(W \mid U_{2}) = 3/8, \operatorname{P}(W \mid U_{3}) = 5/7$.
Law of total probability: $\operatorname{P}(W) = (1/3)(2/5 + 3/8 + 5/7)$.
Over the common denominator 280: $2/5 = 112/280, 3/8 = 105/280, 5/7 = 200/280$, so the sum is $417/280$ and $\operatorname{P}(W) = 417/840$.
Reducing by 3: $105/417 = 35/139$ (approximately 0.2518).
Hence option (a) is correct.

topic: Bivariate Normal Distribution
subtopic: Bivariate Normal Distribution
stem: (X, Y) has a bivariate normal distribution with $\mu_x=5,\ \mu_y=8,\ \sigma_x^2=16,\ \sigma_y^2=9,\ \rho_{xy}=0.6$. What is the regression coefficient of Y on X?
shortcut: $b(Y on X) = \rho * \sigma_{y}/\sigma_{x} = 0.6 \cdot (3/4) = 0.45 = 9/20$. The means 5 and 8 are irrelevant.
tips: Take square roots first: $\sigma_{x} = 4$ and $\sigma_{y} = 3$ from the variances 16 and 9. Using the variances directly is the standard trap and would give $0.6 \cdot (9/16) = 27/80$.
Y on X puts $\sigma_{y}$ on top: $b_{yx} = \rho \sigma_{y}/\sigma_{x}$. X on Y flips it: $b_{xy} = \rho \sigma_{x}/\sigma_{y} = 0.6(4/3) = 0.8$.
Check: $b_{yx} \cdot b_{xy} = \rho^{2}$, so $0.45 \cdot 0.8 = 0.36 = 0.6^{2}$. A five-second confirmation.
The means $\mu_{x}$ and $\mu_{y}$ affect only the intercept of the regression line, never the slope - ignore them here.
solution: For a bivariate normal distribution, the regression of Y on X is linear: $\operatorname{E}(Y \mid X = x) = \mu_{y} + \rho (\sigma_{y}/\sigma_{x})(x - \mu_{x})$.
The regression coefficient of Y on X is therefore $b_{yx} = \rho * \sigma_{y} / \sigma_{x}$.
Given $\sigma_{x}^{2} = 16$ so $\sigma_{x} = 4$, and $\sigma_{y}^{2} = 9$ so $\sigma_{y} = 3$, with $\rho = 0.6$.
Check with the reverse coefficient: $b_{xy} = 0.6 \cdot (4/3) = 0.8$, and $b_{yx} \cdot b_{xy} = 0.45 \cdot 0.8 = 0.36 = \rho^{2}$, as required.
Hence option (b) is correct.

topic: Standard Continuous Distributions
subtopic: Standard Continuous Distributions
stem: X is a continuous random variable whose density is constant on $a\le x\le b$ and zero elsewhere. What is the standard deviation of X?
shortcut: Constant density on [a, b] means X is uniform, whose variance is $(b-a)^{2}/12$, so the SD is $(b-a)/(2 sqrt 3)$. Answer (b).
tips: 'Density constant on an interval and zero elsewhere' is the definition of the continuous uniform distribution - recognise the phrasing.
Uniform facts: mean $(a+b)/2$, variance $(b-a)^{2}/12$, and $\sqrt{12} = 2 sqrt 3$.
Options (c) and (d) are the mean and the half-range respectively - both are spread or location quantities, but neither is the SD.
A standard deviation must be translation invariant, i.e. it can depend only on b - a, not on a + b. That instantly kills options (a) and (c).
solution: If the density is constant on $a \le x \le b$ and zero elsewhere, then $f(x) = 1/(b - a)$ on [a, b], i.e. X follows the uniform distribution U(a, b).
Mean: $\operatorname{E}(X) = (a + b)/2$.
Standard deviation = $sqrt((b-a)^{2}/12) = (b - a)/\sqrt{12} = (b - a)/(2 sqrt 3)$.
Hence option (b) is correct.

topic: Mathematical Expectation & Conditional Expectation
subtopic: Mathematical Expectation & Conditional Expectation
stem: X has pmf $p(x)=x/15$, for $x=1,2,3,4,5$. What is $E(X \mid x>1)$?
shortcut: Drop $x = 1$ and renormalise. The 15 in the denominator cancels, so $\operatorname{E}(X \mid X > 1) = (2^{2} + 3^{2} + 4^{2} + 5^{2})/(2 + 3 + 4 + 5) = 54/14 = 27/7$.
tips: For a conditional expectation on a truncated support, take the ratio of unnormalised sums - the common denominator (15 here) cancels.
Numerator terms are x * p(x) proportional to $x \cdot x = x^{2}$; denominator terms are p(x) proportional to x. Recognising this turns the problem into sum of squares over sum.
Check the pmf is valid: $(1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5)/15 = 1$, so $p(x) = x/15$ is proper.
Bound check: conditioning on $X > 1$ must raise the mean above the unconditional $\operatorname{E}(X) = 55/15 = 11/3 = 3.67$; $27/7 = 3.857$ is above it, while $15/7$ and $15/14$ are far too small.
solution: The pmf is $p(x) = x/15$ for $x = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5$ (check: sum = $15/15 = 1$).
$\operatorname{E}(X \mid X > 1) = (54/15)/(14/15) = 54/14 = 27/7$ (approximately 3.857).
Hence option (a) is correct.

topic: Conditional Probability, Law of Total Probability, Bayes' Theorem
subtopic: Conditional Probability, Law of Total Probability, Bayes' Theorem
stem: X has distribution $f(x) = \begin{cases} \frac{1}{12}, & 0<x<12 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$. What is $P(5<X<7 \mid X>6)$?
shortcut: Intersect the events first: $(5, 7)$ intersect $(6, 12) = (6, 7)$, of length 1. Divide by the length of the conditioning event $(6, 12)$, which is 6. Answer $1/6$.
tips: For a uniform variable, conditional probability is just a ratio of interval lengths - no integration needed.
Always intersect before dividing: the numerator is P($5 < X < 7$ AND $X > 6$) = $\operatorname{P}(6 < X < 7)$, not $\operatorname{P}(5 < X < 7) = 2/12$.
The distractor $1/3$ comes from forgetting the intersection: $(2/12)/(6/12) = 1/3$. This is the single most common error on this item.
General identity: $\operatorname{P}(A \mid B) = \operatorname{P}\!\left(A\ \text{intersect B}\right)/\operatorname{P}(B)$, valid whenever $\operatorname{P}(B) > 0$.
solution: X is uniform on $(0, 12)$ with density $1/12$, so probabilities are proportional to interval lengths.
Conditioning event: $\operatorname{P}(X > 6) = (12 - 6)/12 = 6/12 = 1/2$.
Hence option (d) is correct.

topic: Standard Discrete Distributions
subtopic: Standard Discrete Distributions
stem: X has a binomial distribution with parameters n, p, and $q=1-p$. What is $P[X=0 \text{ or even}]$?
shortcut: Add the expansions of $(q + p)^{n}$ and $(q - p)^{n}$: odd terms cancel and even terms double. So the sum of even-index terms is $[1 + (q - p)^{n}]/2$. Answer (b).
tips: The even/odd splitting trick: sum of even terms = $[f(1) + f(-1)]/2$ and sum of odd terms = $[f(1) - f(-1)]/2$, applied to the pgf.
Here $f(s) = (q + ps)^{n}$, so $f(1) = 1$ and $f(-1) = (q - p)^{n}$. That is the entire derivation.
Sanity check with $n = 1$: $\operatorname{P}(X = 0) = q$, and the formula gives $[1 + (q - p)]/2 = (1 + q - p)/2 = (q + q)/2 = q$ since $p + q = 1$. Correct.
Options (a) and (d) can exceed 1 (take $p = 0$, giving 2 and 2 respectively), so they are impossible probabilities; option (c) is the odd-count probability.
solution: $\operatorname{P}(X = x) = \binom{n}{x} p^{x} q^{n-x}$. We want $\operatorname{P}\!\left(X\ \text{is even, including 0}\right)$ = sum over even x of $\binom{n}{x} p^{x} q^{n-x}$.
Consider the binomial expansions $(q + p)^{n} = \sum \binom{n}{x} p^{x} q^{n-x} = 1$, and $(q - p)^{n} = \sum \binom{n}{x} (-p)^{x} q^{n-x} = \sum (-1)^{x} \binom{n}{x} p^{x} q^{n-x}$.
Adding the two: the terms with odd x cancel and the terms with even x double.
So $(q + p)^{n} + (q - p)^{n} = 2$ * sum over even x of $\binom{n}{x} p^{x} q^{n-x}$.
Therefore $\operatorname{P}\!\left(X\ \text{even}\right) = [1 + (q - p)^{n}]/2$.

Verification at $n = 1$: $[1 + q - p]/2 = q = \operatorname{P}(X = 0)$, correct. (Correspondingly $\operatorname{P}\!\left(X\ \text{odd}\right) = [1 - (q - p)^{n}]/2$, which is option (c) - a deliberate distractor.)
Hence option (b) is correct.

topic: Characteristic Function, MGF & PGF; Inversion, Uniqueness, Continuity
subtopic: Characteristic Function, MGF & PGF; Inversion, Uniqueness, Continuity
stem: $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ are iid, $S_N=X_1+X_2+\cdots+X_N$ where N is a random variable independent of the $X_i$. If $M_{X_1}(t)=E(e^{tX_1})$, the MGF of $S_N$ is:
shortcut: Condition on N: $\operatorname{E}(e^{tS_N}) = \operatorname{E}[(M_{X}(t))^{N}] = \operatorname{E}[e^{N \log M_{X}(t)}] = M_{N}(\log M_{X}(t))$. Answer (b).
tips: The compounding rule: for a random sum, the outer MGF is evaluated at $\log$ of the inner MGF - $M_{S_N}(t) = M_{N}(\log M_{X}(t))$.
In pgf language it is cleaner still: $P_{S_N}(s) = P_{N}(P_{X}(s)) - a$ straight composition, with no logarithm.
Derivation in one line: $\operatorname{E}[a^{N}] = M_{N}(\log a)$ with $a = M_{X}(t)$, by writing $a^{N} = e^{N \log a}$.
Standard application: if N is Poisson($\lambda$) then $M_{S_N}(t) = \exp(\lambda[M_{X}(t) - 1])$, the compound Poisson MGF - a frequent follow-up question.
solution: By the law of total expectation, $M_{S_N}(t) = \operatorname{E}[e^{t S_N}] = \operatorname{E}[ \operatorname{E}(e^{t S_N} \mid N) ]$.
Given $N = n, S_{N}$ is the sum of n iid copies of $X_{1}$, so $\operatorname{E}(e^{t S_N} \mid N = n) = [M_{X_1}(t)]^{n}$ by independence.
Hence $M_{S_N}(t) = \operatorname{E}[ (M_{X_1}(t))^{N} ]$.
Write $a = M_{X_1}(t) > 0$. Then $a^{N} = e^{N \log a}$, so $\operatorname{E}[a^{N}] = \operatorname{E}[e^{N \log a}] = M_{N}(\log a)$.
Therefore $M_{S_N}(t) = M_{N}(\log M_{X_1}(t))$.
Check with N Poisson($\lambda$): $M_{N}(u) = \exp(\lambda(e^{u} - 1))$, so $M_{S_N}(t) = \exp(\lambda(M_{X_1}(t) - 1))$, the standard compound Poisson result.
Hence option (b) is correct.

topic: Random Vectors: Joint, Marginal & Conditional Distributions
subtopic: Random Vectors: Joint, Marginal & Conditional Distributions
stem: The joint pdf of X and Y is $f(x,y) = \begin{cases} \frac{21}{2}x^2y, & x^2\le y,\ 0<x<1 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$. What is $P(X\ge Y)$?
tips: Sketch the region first: $y = x^{2}$ is the lower boundary and $y = 1$ the upper; the line $y = x$ cuts it, and on $(0,1)$ we have $x^{2} \le x$, so the y-limits are $x^{2}$ to x.
Do the y-integral first (it is a plain power of y), leaving a single polynomial integral in x.
Verify the constant: integral over the full support gives $(21/4)(1/3 - 1/7) = (21/4)(4/21) = 1$, so $21/2$ is right and your limits are set up correctly.
Note 0.7 is the complement $\operatorname{P}(X < Y)$; read the inequality direction carefully before choosing.
solution: The density $f(x, y) = (21/2) x^{2} y$ is supported on {$0 < x < 1, x^{2} \le y \le 1$}.
For $\operatorname{P}(X \ge Y)$ we need $y \le x$, and combined with the support $y \ge x^{2}$ the y-range is $x^{2} \le y \le x$ (valid since $x^{2} \le x$ for $0 < x < 1$).
Hence option (b) is correct.

topic: Classical & Axiomatic Probability, Consequences
subtopic: Classical & Axiomatic Probability, Consequences
stem: X is chosen at random between 0 and 6, and Y at random between 0 and 9. What is the probability that $Z^2-XZ+Y=0$ has real roots?
shortcut: Real roots need discriminant $X^{2} - 4Y \ge 0$, i.e. $Y \le X^{2}/4$. Since $X^{2}/4 \le 9$ on $(0,6)$, the favourable area is $\int_{0}^{6} x^{2}/4\,dx = 18$, out of the total area $6 \cdot 9 = 54$. So $P = 18/54 = 1/3$.
tips: Geometric probability: with X and Y independent uniforms, the probability is (favourable area)/(total area) of the rectangle - no densities needed beyond the constant $1/54$.

Check whether the curve leaves the rectangle: $y = x^{2}/4$ reaches 9 exactly at $x = 6$, so the parabola stays inside and no truncation ($\min$ with 9) is needed. Getting this wrong is the usual pitfall.
The condition for real roots of $z^{2}$ - Xz + $Y = 0$ is $X^{2} \ge 4Y$; note the sign convention $b^{2} - 4$ac with $a = 1, b$ = -$X, c = Y$.
Area under a parabola: $\int_{0}^{6} x^{2}/4\,dx = 6^{3}/12 = 18$. Memorising $\int x^{2} = x^{3}/3$ makes this instant.
solution: X is uniform on $(0, 6)$ and Y is uniform on $(0, 9)$, independently, so (X, Y) is uniform on the rectangle of area $6 \cdot 9 = 54$, with joint density $1/54$.
The quadratic $Z^{2}$ - XZ + $Y = 0$ has real roots iff its discriminant is non-negative: $X^{2} - 4Y \ge 0$, i.e. $Y \le X^{2}/4$.
For $0 < x < 6$ the bound $x^{2}/4$ ranges from 0 up to $36/4 = 9$, which is exactly the top of the Y-range, so the parabola lies entirely within the rectangle and no truncation is needed.
$\operatorname{P}\!\left(\text{real roots}\right) = 18/54 = 1/3$.
Hence option (b) is correct.

topic: Random Vectors: Joint, Marginal & Conditional Distributions
subtopic: Random Vectors: Joint, Marginal & Conditional Distributions
stem: X and Y have joint pdf $f(x,y)=\frac{1}{3}(x+y);\ 0\le x\le1,\ 0\le y\le2$. What is $E[Y \mid X=\tfrac12]$? *(corrected from "X = 2" — see note above)*
tips: Integrate y over its full range 0 to 2 (not 0 to 1) when finding $f_{X}$ - mismatched limits are the commonest slip on rectangular but non-square supports.
$f_{X}(1/2) = (2/3)(1/2 + 1) = 1$ exactly, so the conditional density equals the joint density with $x = 1/2$ substituted - a designed simplification.
Check the conditional integrates to 1: $\int_{0}^{2} (0.5 + y)/3\,dy = (1 + 2)/3 = 1$.
Bound check: Y lies in $(0,2)$ and the conditional density increases in y, so the answer must exceed 1; $8/9$ is therefore impossible.
solution: Verify the joint density: $\int_{0}^{1} \int_{0}^{2} (x+y)/3\,dy\,dx = \int_{0}^{1} (2x + 2)/3\,dx = (1 + 2)/3 = 1$. Valid.
Conditional density: $f(y \mid X = 1/2) = [(1/2 + y)/3]/1 = (0.5 + y)/3$, for $0 \le y \le 2$.
Hence option (c) is correct.

topic: Correlation: Distribution of r, Partial, Multiple, Intraclass, Correlation Ratio
subtopic: Correlation: Distribution of r, Partial, Multiple, Intraclass, Correlation Ratio
stem: How many pairs of observations (n) must be in a sample so that an observed correlation coefficient of 0.6 gives a calculated t greater than 2.72?
tips: Test statistic for H0: $\rho = 0$ is $t = r \sqrt{n-2}/\sqrt{1 - r^2}$ with n - 2 degrees of freedom - memorise it exactly.
$r = 0.6$ gives the Pythagorean pair $0.6/0.8 = 0.75$, so the algebra stays in clean decimals.
Solve the inequality for n rather than testing each option: $n > 2 + (2.72/0.75)^{2} = 2 + 13.15 = 15.15$.
Since n must be a whole number, $n \ge 16$, which is exactly the statement $n > 15$; do not round 15.15 down to 15.
solution: To test the significance of an observed correlation coefficient, $t = r \sqrt{n - 2}/\sqrt{1 - r^2}$ with $(n - 2)$ degrees of freedom.
Therefore $t = 0.6 \sqrt{n - 2}/0.8 = 0.75 \sqrt{n - 2}$.
Since n is an integer, n must be at least 16, i.e. $n > 15$.
Hence option (d) is correct.

topic: Correlation: Distribution of r, Partial, Multiple, Intraclass, Correlation Ratio
subtopic: Correlation: Distribution of r, Partial, Multiple, Intraclass, Correlation Ratio
stem: $b_{13.2}$ is the regression coefficient of $X_1$ on $X_3$ (holding $X_2$), and $b_{31.2}$ is that of $X_3$ on $X_1$ (holding $X_2$). What is $b_{13.2}\times b_{31.2}$?
shortcut: Exactly as in the two-variable case, the product of the two reciprocal regression coefficients is the square of the corresponding correlation - here the partial correlation $r_{13.2}$. Answer (b).
tips: Read the subscripts: both coefficients involve variables 1 and 3 with 2 held constant, so the answer must carry the subscript 13.2.
Simple-case analogue: $b_{yx} \cdot b_{xy} = r^{2}$. The partial version simply carries the conditioning subscript through.
Explicit forms: $b_{13.2} = r_{13.2} * \sigma_{1.2}/\sigma_{3.2}$ and $b_{31.2} = r_{13.2} * \sigma_{3.2}/\sigma_{1.2}$; the partial standard deviations cancel on multiplication.
Note $r_{13.2} = r_{31.2}$ (partial correlation is symmetric in the two primary subscripts), which is why the single symbol suffices.
solution: The partial regression coefficient of $X_{1}$ on $X_{3}$ holding $X_{2}$ fixed is $b_{13.2} = r_{13.2} \cdot (\sigma_{1.2}/\sigma_{3.2})$, where $\sigma_{1.2}$ and $\sigma_{3.2}$ are the partial (residual) standard deviations.
Similarly $b_{31.2} = r_{13.2} \cdot (\sigma_{3.2}/\sigma_{1.2})$, using the symmetry $r_{31.2} = r_{13.2}$.
This is the exact analogue of $b_{yx} \cdot b_{xy} = r^{2}$ in simple linear regression.
Options (a) and (c) carry the wrong variable pair, and option (d) refers to an unspecified simple correlation.
Hence option (b) is correct.

topic: Sampling Distributions: Sample Mean, Sample Variance, t, Chi-square, F
subtopic: Sampling Distributions: Sample Mean, Sample Variance, t, Chi-square, F
stem: $(X_1,\ldots,X_n)$ is a random sample from $N(\mu,\sigma^2)$. What is the distribution of $\dfrac{ns^2}{\sigma^2}$, where $s^2=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\bar X)^2$?
shortcut: Since $s^{2}$ is defined with divisor $n, n s^{2}$ = sum of $(X_{i} - \bar{X})^{2}$, and that sum divided by $\sigma^{2}$ is $\chi^{2}$ with n - 1 df (one df lost to estimating the mean by $\bar{X}$). Answer (c).
tips: Track the divisor: with $s^{2} = (1/n)$ sum, the $\chi^{2}$ variable is $n s^{2}/\sigma^{2}$; with $S^{2} = (1/(n-1))$ sum, it is $(n-1)S^{2}/\sigma^{2}$. Both equal the same raw sum over $\sigma^{2}$ and both have n - 1 df.

One degree of freedom is always lost because $\bar{X}$ is estimated from the same data; if the true mean mu were used instead, sum $(X_{i} - \mu)^{2}/\sigma^{2}$ would have n df - that is the trap in option (a).
Fisher's lemma also gives independence of $\bar{X}$ and $s^{2}$ in the normal case, which is what makes the t-statistic work.
Consequence to remember: $\operatorname{E}(s^{2}) = (n-1)\sigma^{2}/n$, so $s^{2}$ with divisor n is biased downward, while $S^{2}$ with divisor n - 1 is unbiased.
solution: Decompose sum $(X_{i} - \mu)^{2}$ = sum $(X_{i} - \bar{X})^{2} + n(\bar{X} - \mu)^{2}$.

Dividing by $\sigma^{2}$: sum $(X_{i} - \mu)^{2}/\sigma^{2}$ is $\chi^{2}$ with n df, and $n(\bar{X} - \mu)^{2}/\sigma^{2}$ is $\chi^{2}$ with 1 df, the two terms on the right being independent (Fisher's lemma).
By the additivity of independent $\chi^{2}$ variables, sum $(X_{i} - \bar{X})^{2}/\sigma^{2} = n s^{2}/\sigma^{2}$ must be $\chi^{2}$ with n - 1 degrees of freedom.
Hence option (c) is correct.

topic: Correlation: Distribution of r, Partial, Multiple, Intraclass, Correlation Ratio
subtopic: Correlation: Distribution of r, Partial, Multiple, Intraclass, Correlation Ratio
stem: If $r(2x,y)=0.25$, what is $r\!\left(4x-3,\ \dfrac{7-4y}{8}\right)$?
shortcut: Correlation is unchanged by any linear change of scale and origin except that a negative multiplier flips the sign. 4x - 3 keeps the sign; $(7 - 4y)/8 = 7/8 - y/2$ reverses it. So the answer is -0.25.
tips: Rule: $r(a + bX, c + dY)$ = sign(bd) * r(X, Y). Only the signs of the multipliers matter; their magnitudes and the additive constants do not.
First simplify the given information: $r(2x, y) = 0.25$ means $r(x, y) = 0.25$, since $2 > 0$.
Rewrite $(7 - 4y)/8$ as $7/8 - (1/2)y$ to expose the multiplier -$1/2$ clearly; leaving it as a compound fraction is what makes candidates miss the sign.
The magnitude never changes, so options (b) and (d) with $1/8$ are wrong on principle - a scale change can never shrink a correlation.
solution: The correlation coefficient is invariant under a change of origin and positive change of scale, and reverses sign under a negative change of scale: $r(a + bX, c + dY)$ = sign(b)*sign(d)*r(X, Y).
Given $r(2x, y) = 0.25$. Since the multiplier 2 is positive, $r(x, y) = 0.25$.
First variable: 4x - 3 has multiplier $b = 4 > 0$, so the sign is preserved.
Second variable: $(7 - 4y)/8 = 7/8 - (1/2) y$ has multiplier d = -$1/2 < 0$, so the sign is reversed.
Hence option (c) is correct.

topic: Order Statistics - Minimum, Maximum, Range, Median
subtopic: Order Statistics - Minimum, Maximum, Range, Median
stem: Let $Y_1\le Y_2\le\cdots\le Y_6$ be order statistics from $F(x)=1-e^{-\lambda x}$, $\lambda=0.5$. What is the cdf of $Y_1$?
shortcut: The minimum of n iid exponentials with rate $\lambda$ is exponential with rate $n*\lambda$. Here $n = 6$ and $\lambda = 0.5$, so $Y_{1}$ is Exp(3) and its cdf is $1 - e^{-3y}$.
tips: Memorise: $\min$ of iid Exp($\lambda$) is Exp($n \lambda$) - the hazard rates simply add. This is the exponential's most exam-friendly property.
Derive it in one line if you forget: $\operatorname{P}(Y_{1} > y) = [\operatorname{P}(X > y)]^{n} = (e^{-\lambda y})^{n} = e^{-n \lambda y}$.
A cdf must increase from 0 to 1, so any option with a positive exponent $(e^{y/2}, e^{y/3}, e^{3y})$ is impossible - that alone leaves only (d).
By contrast the maximum has cdf $[1 - e^{-\lambda y}]^{n}$, which is NOT exponential - a common companion question.
solution: The parent distribution is $F(x) = 1 - e^{-\lambda x}$ with $\lambda = 0.5$, i.e. exponential with rate 0.5, and the sample size is $n = 6$.
$Y_{1}$ is the smallest order statistic, so $Y_{1} > y$ if and only if every one of the six observations exceeds y.
By independence, $\operatorname{P}(Y_{1} > y) = [1 - F(y)]^{6} = (e^{-0.5 y})^{6} = e^{-3y}$, for $y > 0$.
Therefore the cdf is $F_{Y_1}(y) = 1 - \operatorname{P}(Y_{1} > y) = 1 - e^{-3y}$, for $y > 0$.
So $Y_{1}$ is exponential with rate $n*\lambda = 6(0.5) = 3$.
Hence option (d) is correct.

topic: Correlation: Distribution of r, Partial, Multiple, Intraclass, Correlation Ratio
subtopic: Correlation: Distribution of r, Partial, Multiple, Intraclass, Correlation Ratio
stem: $R_{i.jk}$ is the multiple correlation coefficient, $r_{ij}$ the simple correlation coefficient, and $\sigma_i$ the standard deviation of $X_i$. Consider: I. $R_{1.23}^2 = \sigma_1^2\sigma_2^2(1-r_{12}^2)(1-r_{13})^2$ II. $R_{1.23}^2 \ge r_{12}^2$ III. $R_{1.23}^2 \ge r_{13.2}^2$ Which are correct?
shortcut: Statement I is dimensionally impossible - a squared correlation cannot carry $\sigma^{2}$ factors - so drop it. II and III are both standard consequences of $1 - R^{2}_{1.23} = (1 - r_{12}^{2})(1 - r^{2}_{13.2})$. Answer (b).
tips: Key identity: $1 - R^{2}_{1.23} = (1 - r_{12}^{2})(1 - r^{2}_{13.2})$. Almost every multiple-correlation inequality follows from it in one step.
Correlations are unit-free, so any formula for $R^{2}$ containing $\sigma_{1}^{2} \sigma_{2}^{2}$ must be wrong - reject statement I on sight.
Remember the ordering $0 \le R^{2}_{1.23} \le 1$ and $R_{1.23}$ >= |$r_{1j}$| for every j: adding a regressor can never reduce the multiple correlation.
solution: Statement I: $R^{2}_{1.23} = \sigma_{1}^{2} \sigma_{2}^{2} (1 - r_{12}^{2})(1 - r_{13})^{2}$. This is false. $R^{2}$ is a unit-free quantity lying in $[0,1]$, so it cannot involve the variances; the correct expression is $R^{2}_{1.23} = (r_{12}^{2} + r_{13}^{2} - 2 r_{12} r_{13} r_{23})/(1 - r_{23}^{2})$.
Statement II: $R^{2}_{1.23} - r_{12}^{2} = (a + b - ab) - a = b(1 - a) \ge 0$, since $0 \le a \le 1$ and $b \ge 0$. So $R^{2}_{1.23} \ge r_{12}^{2}$ is correct.
Statement III: $R^{2}_{1.23} - r^{2}_{13.2} = (a + b - ab) - b = a(1 - b) \ge 0$, since $0 \le b \le 1$ and $a \ge 0$. So $R^{2}_{1.23} \ge r^{2}_{13.2}$ is correct.
Only statements II and III hold.
Hence option (b) is correct.

topic: Measures of Location & Dispersion
subtopic: Measures of Location & Dispersion
stem: Sample 1 has 100 items, mean 15, sd 3. The whole group (250 items) has mean 15.6, sd $\sqrt{13.44}$. What is the variance of the second group?
tips: Two-step routine: combined mean first (to get the missing group mean), then the combined-variance formula. You cannot do the variance without the mean.
Combined variance formula: $N*\sigma^{2} = \sum n_{i}(\sigma_{i}^{2} + d_{i}^{2})$, where $d_{i}$ = mean_i - combined mean.
Compute the deviations $d_{1} = 15 - 15.6$ = -0.6 and $d_{2} = 16 - 15.6 = 0.4$ and note $n_{1} d_{1} + n_{2} d_{2}$ = -$60 + 60 = 0 - a$ free check that the group mean is right.
The question asks for the variance, not the standard deviation: 16, not 4. Option (c) is the SD trap.
solution: Combined variance formula: $N \sigma^{2} = n_{1}(\sigma_{1}^{2} + d_{1}^{2}) + n_{2}(\sigma_{2}^{2} + d_{2}^{2})$.
Hence option (a) is correct.

topic: Bivariate Normal Distribution
subtopic: Bivariate Normal Distribution
stem: $(X,Y)\sim BVN(\mu_1,\mu_2,\sigma_1^2,\sigma_2^2,\rho)$. If $\sigma_1^2=2,\ \sigma_2^2=3,\ \rho=0$, consider: I. $E(X)=E(Y)$ II. $E(XY)=2$ III. X and Y are independent Which is/are correct?
shortcut: The means $\mu_{1}$ and $\mu_{2}$ are never specified, so neither $\operatorname{E}(X) = \operatorname{E}(Y)$ nor $\operatorname{E}(XY) = 2$ can be asserted. But for the bivariate normal, $\rho = 0$ does imply independence. Only III. Answer (c).
tips: Zero correlation implies independence ONLY for the joint normal - this is the single most-tested exception in the whole topic.
Ask what the data actually determine: the question gives variances and $\rho$ but leaves $\mu_{1}, \mu_{2}$ as free symbols, so any statement about means is unverifiable.
With $\rho = 0, \operatorname{E}(XY) = \operatorname{E}(X)\operatorname{E}(Y) = \mu_{1} \mu_{2}$, not $\sigma_{1}^{2} = 2$. Statement II confuses the covariance with a variance.
Beware the counterexample direction too: uncorrelated normal MARGINALS need not be independent unless the JOINT distribution is bivariate normal, which is given here.
solution: The distribution is bivariate normal with parameters $\mu_{1}, \mu_{2}, \sigma_{1}^{2} = 2, \sigma_{2}^{2} = 3$ and $\rho = 0$. Note that $\mu_{1}$ and $\mu_{2}$ are not specified numerically.
Statement I: $\operatorname{E}(X) = \mu_{1}$ and $\operatorname{E}(Y) = \mu_{2}$. Nothing in the data forces $\mu_{1} = \mu_{2}$, so this cannot be asserted. Incorrect.

Statement II: $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y) = \rho \sigma_{1} \sigma_{2} = 0$, so $\operatorname{E}(XY) = \operatorname{E}(X)\operatorname{E}(Y) = \mu_{1} \mu_{2}$, which is unknown. There is no basis for the value 2 (that is $\sigma_{1}^{2}, a$ different quantity). Incorrect.

Statement III: for a bivariate normal density, setting $\rho = 0$ makes the exponent separate into a function of x alone plus a function of y alone, so $f(x,y) = f_{X}(x) f_{Y}(y)$. Hence X and Y are independent. Correct.
Only statement III holds.
Hence option (c) is correct.

topic: Regression - Linear & Polynomial
subtopic: Regression - Linear & Polynomial
stem: The joint pdf of X and Y is $f(x,y)=\dfrac{y}{(1+x)^4}e^{\frac{-y}{1+x}};\ x,y\ge0$. The regression of Y on X is:
shortcut: Given $X = x$, the density in y is proportional to $y e^{-y/(1+x)}, a \Gamma$ with shape 2 and scale $(1+x)$, whose mean is $2(1+x) = 2 + 2x$. That is linear in x.
tips: The regression of Y on X is the conditional mean $\operatorname{E}(Y \mid X = x)$ viewed as a function of x - identify the conditional family first, then quote its mean.
Recognise the kernel: $y^{k-1} e^{-y/\theta}$ is $\Gamma$(shape k, scale $\theta$) with mean $k*\theta$. Here $k = 2$ and $\theta = 1 + x$.
You do not even need the marginal of X: the y-dependence alone identifies the conditional family, and the normalising factor is forced.
For completeness $f_{X}(x) = 1/(1+x)^{2}$ on $x \ge 0 - a$ Pareto-type density; the exponential shape in y must not be confused with an exponential regression curve.
solution: Write $\theta = 1 + x$. The joint density is $f(x, y) = y e^{-y/\theta}/\theta^{4}$ for $x, y \ge 0$.

Marginal of X: $f_{X}(x) = \int_{0}^{\infty} y e^{-y/\theta}\,dy / \theta^{4}$. Using $\int_{0}^{\infty} y e^{-y/\theta}\,dy = \theta^{2}$ ($\Gamma$ function with shape 2), we get $f_{X}(x) = \theta^{2}/\theta^{4} = 1/\theta^{2} = 1/(1+x)^{2}$.
Check: $\int_{0}^{\infty}\,dx/(1+x)^{2} = 1$, so $f_{X}$ is a proper density.
Conditional density: $f(y \mid x) = f(x,y)/f_{X}(x) = [y e^{-y/\theta}/\theta^{4}] * \theta^{2} = y e^{-y/\theta}/\theta^{2}$.
This is the $\Gamma$ density with shape 2 and scale $\theta$, whose mean is $2 \theta$.
Therefore $\operatorname{E}(Y \mid X = x) = 2(1 + x) = 2 + 2x$, which is a straight line in x.
Hence the regression of Y on X is linear, and option (b) is correct.

topic: Tests of Significance & Small Sample Tests
subtopic: Tests of Significance & Small Sample Tests
stem: Normal populations $\pi_1,\pi_2$ have equal means, but the sd of $\pi_2$ is twice that of $\pi_1$ (sd $\sigma$). In samples of size 2000 from each, the difference of sample means is, in all probability:
shortcut: SE of the difference = $\sqrt{\sigma^{2}/2000 + 4 \sigma^{2}/2000} = \sigma \sqrt{5/2000} = \sigma/20 = 0.05 \sigma$. 'In all probability' means within $3 SE$, i.e. less than $0.15 \sigma$.
tips: Variances add for a difference of independent means: $\sigma_{1}^{2}/n_{1} + \sigma_{2}^{2}/n_{2}$, even though the means are subtracted.
The second sd is $2 \sigma$, so its variance is $4 \sigma^{2}$ - squaring the doubled sd is the step most often skipped.
$5/2000 = 1/400$, so the square root is exactly $1/20$ - the numbers are chosen to make the SE come out as $0.05 \sigma$.
Exam convention: 'in all probability' (or 'practically certain') means within 3 standard errors, covering about 99.7% of the sampling distribution; 'probable error' would instead be $0.6745 SE$.
solution: Let $\sigma_{1} = \sigma$ and $\sigma_{2} = 2 \sigma$, with $n_{1} = n_{2} = 2000$, and equal population means so E(xbar_1 - xbar_2) = 0.
Standard error = $\sigma/20 = 0.05 \sigma$.
By the central limit theorem the difference of sample means is approximately normal with mean 0 and $SE 0.05 \sigma$.
'In all probability' means within three standard errors: |xbar_1 - xbar_2| < $3(0.05 \sigma) = 0.15 \sigma$, an event of probability about 0.997.
Hence the difference is in all probability less than $0.15 \sigma$, and option (b) is correct.

topic: Tests of Significance & Small Sample Tests
subtopic: Tests of Significance & Small Sample Tests
stem: Mean height of 50 male students with above-average athletic participation: 68.2 in, sd 2.5 in. 50 students with no interest: mean 67.5 in, sd 2.8 in. For the observed difference to be significant at 5% (critical Z = 1.645), the sample size of each group must be increased by:
shortcut: Difference 0.7, and $SE = \sqrt{14.09/n}$. Need $0.7 \sqrt{n} / 3.7537 \ge 1.645$, so $\sqrt{n} \ge 8.821$ and $n \ge 77.8$, i.e. $n = 78$. The increase over 50 is at least 28.
tips: Keep the sample means and sds fixed and treat only n as unknown - that is the whole idea of a 'how much must n increase' question.
$\sigma_{1}^{2} + \sigma_{2}^{2} = 6.25 + 7.84 = 14.09$ with equal n, so $SE = \sqrt{14.09/n}$ and the test statistic is $0.7 \sqrt{n}/\sqrt{14.09}$.
Solve for n directly: $n \ge 14.09 (1.645/0.7)^{2} = 14.09 \cdot 5.5225 = 77.81$, so $n = 78$ (round UP, since a larger n only helps).

Read the question's final step: it asks for the INCREASE, $78 - 50 = 28$, not the new size 78. That is why both 78 and 28 appear as options, and 'at least' is right because more data only strengthens significance.
solution: Observed difference of means: $d = 68.2 - 67.5 = 0.7$ inches, held fixed as n changes.
With equal sample sizes n in each group, SE(xbar_1 - xbar_2) = $\sqrt{s_{1}^{2}/n + s_{2}^{2}/n} = sqrt((6.25 + 7.84)/n) = \sqrt{14.09/n}$.
Test statistic: $Z = 0.7 / \sqrt{14.09/n} = 0.7 \sqrt{n}/\sqrt{14.09} = 0.7 \sqrt{n}/3.7537$.
Significance at the 5% level (one-tailed, critical value 1.645) requires $0.7 \sqrt{n}/3.7537 \ge 1.645$.
Since n must be an integer, $n = 78$ at minimum.
Required increase in each group = $78 - 50 = 28$, and any larger increase also gives significance, so the increase must be at least 28.
Hence option (c) is correct.

topic: Sampling Distributions: Sample Mean, Sample Variance, t, Chi-square, F
subtopic: Sampling Distributions: Sample Mean, Sample Variance, t, Chi-square, F
stem: A normal population has mean 0.1, sd 2.1. For a random sample of size 900, what is $P(\bar x<0)$? [Given $P(0<Z<1.43)=0.4236$]
tips: $\sqrt{900} = 30$ exactly, so the standard error is a clean 0.07 - the numbers are chosen so that z lands on the tabulated 1.43.
The supplied value 0.4236 is $\operatorname{P}(0 < Z < 1.43), a$ CENTRAL area, so subtract it from 0.5 to get the tail; adding it to 0.5 gives the distractor 0.9236.
Draw the picture: 0 lies below the mean 0.1, so the required probability must be less than 0.5 - that alone eliminates options (c) and (d).
Standard error uses $\sigma/\sqrt{n}$, not $\sigma$; using 2.1 directly would give z = -0.048 and a probability near 0.48.
solution: The population is normal with $\mu = 0.1$ and $\sigma = 2.1$, and the sample size is $n = 900$.
The sampling distribution of $\bar{x}$ is normal with mean 0.1 and standard error $\sigma/\sqrt{n} = 2.1/30 = 0.07$.
$\operatorname{P}(\bar{x} < 0) = \operatorname{P}(Z < -1.43) = 0.5 - \operatorname{P}(0 < Z < 1.43) = 0.5 - 0.4236 = 0.0764$.
Hence option (a) is correct.

topic: Standard Errors & Large Sample Tests
subtopic: Standard Errors & Large Sample Tests
stem: Sampling without replacement: $V(\bar x)=\dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}\left(\dfrac{N-n}{N-1}\right)$. Under which condition(s) is the factor $\dfrac{N-n}{N-1}$ ignored? I. n is small compared to N II. $n=N$ III. Population is infinite
shortcut: The finite population correction tends to 1 when n is negligible relative to N, and when N is infinite. When $n = N$ it equals 0 - the opposite of ignorable. So I and III only, option (c).
tips: Evaluate the factor at the limits: $n/N \to 0$ gives $(N-n)/(N-1) \to 1$ (ignorable); $n = N$ gives $(N-N)/(N-1) = 0$ (a complete census, zero sampling variance).
Rule of thumb used in practice: drop the fpc when the sampling fraction $n/N$ is below about 5%.
$n = N$ means the whole population is surveyed, so V($\bar{x}$) = 0 exactly - the factor is doing its most important work there, not being ignored.
For an infinite population, sampling without replacement is equivalent to sampling with replacement, so V($\bar{x}$) = $\sigma^{2}/n$ with no correction.
solution: The finite population correction (fpc) is $(N - n)/(N - 1)$; it may be dropped only when it is (approximately) equal to 1.
Statement I: if n is small compared with N, then $(N - n)/(N - 1)$ is approximately $1 - n/N$, which is close to 1. The factor may be ignored. Correct.

Statement II: if $n = N$, then $(N - n)/(N - 1) = 0$, so V($\bar{x}$) = 0. The whole population has been enumerated, so there is no sampling error at all; the factor is emphatically not ignorable. Incorrect.
Statement III: for an infinite population, letting N tend to $\infty$ gives $(N - n)/(N - 1) \to 1$, so V($\bar{x}$) = $\sigma^{2}/n$ with no correction. Correct.
Only statements I and III are right.
Hence option (c) is correct.

topic: Sampling Distributions: Sample Mean, Sample Variance, t, Chi-square, F
subtopic: Sampling Distributions: Sample Mean, Sample Variance, t, Chi-square, F
stem: A random sample of size 5 is from a normal population with mean 2.5, variance 36. What is the probability that $S^2=\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\bar X)^2$ lies between 27 and 45? [Given $P(\chi_4^2\ge3)=0.55783$, $P(\chi_4^2\le5)=0.71270$]
tips: Transform the limits, not the statistic: divide each bound by 9, since $S^{2}/9$ is the $\chi^{2}$ variable. $27/9 = 3$ and $45/9 = 5$.
Degrees of freedom are $n - 1 = 4$, not $n = 5$; the mean 2.5 is irrelevant because $S^{2}$ uses deviations from $\bar{X}$.
Convert the given tail probability first: $\operatorname{P}(\chi^{2}_{4} \le 3) = 1 - 0.55783 = 0.44217$. Mixing an upper-tail value with a lower-tail value is the main trap here.
Final subtraction: $0.71270 - 0.44217 = 0.27053$. The distractor 0.15487 is 0.71270 - 0.55783, i.e. what you get by forgetting to complement.
solution: For a random sample of size $n = 5$ from a normal population with variance $\sigma^{2} = 36$, the quantity $(n - 1)S^{2}/\sigma^{2} = 4S^{2}/36 = S^{2}/9$ follows $a \chi^{2}$ distribution with $n - 1 = 4$ degrees of freedom.
Convert the bounds: $S^{2} = 27$ gives $27/9 = 3$, and $S^{2} = 45$ gives $45/9 = 5$.
So $\operatorname{P}(27 < S^{2} < 45) = \operatorname{P}(3 < \chi^{2}_{4} < 5) = \operatorname{P}(\chi^{2}_{4} \le 5) - \operatorname{P}(\chi^{2}_{4} \le 3)$.
From the data, $\operatorname{P}(\chi^{2}_{4} \le 5) = 0.71270$, and $\operatorname{P}(\chi^{2}_{4} \le 3) = 1 - \operatorname{P}(\chi^{2}_{4} \ge 3) = 1 - 0.55783 = 0.44217$.
Therefore the required probability = $0.71270 - 0.44217 = 0.27053$.
Hence option (c) is correct.

topic: Tests of Significance & Small Sample Tests
subtopic: Tests of Significance & Small Sample Tests
stem: The t-statistic for a sample is 3. If the sample variance is doubled, the new t-statistic becomes:
shortcut: t is inversely proportional to the sample standard deviation s. Doubling the variance multiplies s by sqrt 2, so t becomes $3/sqrt 2$.
tips: Write $t = (\bar{x} - \mu) \sqrt{n}/s$ and note that only s changes - the numerator, n and mu are untouched.
Doubling the VARIANCE multiplies the SD by sqrt 2, not by 2; option $(b) 3/2$ is the trap for those who halve instead.
Option (a) 6 comes from multiplying rather than dividing - always check the direction: more variability means a smaller (less significant) t.
General scaling rule: if $s^{2}$ is multiplied by k, then t is divided by sqrt(k).
solution: The one-sample t-statistic is $t = (\bar{x} - \mu)/(s/\sqrt{n}) = (\bar{x} - \mu) \sqrt{n}/s$, where $s^{2}$ is the sample variance.
Only the sample variance is altered; the sample mean, hypothesised mean and sample size are unchanged.
If the sample variance is doubled, the new sample standard deviation is $\sqrt{2 s^2} = s \sqrt{2}$.
Hence the new statistic is $t_{new} = (\bar{x} - \mu) \sqrt{n}/(s sqrt 2) = t/\sqrt{2}$.
With $t = 3$, the new value is $3/\sqrt{2}$, approximately 2.121.
Hence option (c) is correct.

topic: Non-parametric Tests
subtopic: Non-parametric Tests
stem: The Kruskal-Wallis test is exactly equivalent to one-way ANOVA when:
options: population distributions are identical and normal
all observations are replaced by their ranks
shortcut: Kruskal-Wallis IS the one-way ANOVA computed on ranks - the H statistic is a monotone function of the between-groups sum of squares of the ranks. So the equivalence holds exactly when observations are replaced by their ranks. Answer (d).
tips: Most classical non-parametric tests are the corresponding parametric test applied to ranks: Kruskal-Wallis to one-way ANOVA, Wilcoxon rank-sum to the two-sample t, Spearman's $\rho$ to Pearson's r, Friedman to two-way ANOVA.
Kruskal-Wallis is distribution-free, so normality (options a, b) is exactly what it does NOT require - those options invert the point of the test.
Equal sample sizes (option c) are convenient but neither necessary nor sufficient for the equivalence.
$H = (12/[N(N+1)])$ * sum $(R_{i}^{2}/n_{i}) - 3(N+1)$, which is the between-groups sum of squares of the ranks scaled by the known variance of the ranks; H is compared with $\chi^{2}$ on k - 1 df.
solution: The Kruskal-Wallis H test is the rank analogue of the one-way analysis of variance for comparing k independent samples.
Its statistic is $H = 12/[N(N+1)] * \sum (R_{i}^{2}/n_{i}) - 3(N + 1)$, where $R_{i}$ is the rank sum of the i-th group and N is the total sample size.

Because the ranks 1, 2, ..., N have a known total sum and known total sum of squares, the total sum of squares of the ranks is a constant. Consequently H is a strictly increasing function of the between-groups sum of squares of the ranks, which is exactly what one-way ANOVA's F is based on.
Therefore performing a one-way ANOVA on the ranks gives a test equivalent to Kruskal-Wallis: the two procedures coincide precisely when all observations are replaced by their ranks.
Options (a) and (b) are wrong because Kruskal-Wallis is a distribution-free test that does not assume normality; option (c) is wrong because equal sample sizes are not what creates the equivalence.
Hence option (d) is correct.

topic: Order Statistics - Minimum, Maximum, Range, Median
subtopic: Order Statistics - Minimum, Maximum, Range, Median
stem: If $X\sim U(0,1)$, what is $P(X_{(1)}>x)$?
shortcut: The minimum exceeds x precisely when every observation exceeds x. For $U(0,1), \operatorname{P}(X_{i} > x) = 1 - x$, so by independence $\operatorname{P}(X_{1} > x) = (1 - x)^{n}$.
tips: Golden rule of order statistics: 'minimum > x' means ALL exceed x, and 'maximum <= x' means ALL are at most x. Convert to these two forms first.
For the maximum the companion result is $\operatorname{P}(X_{n} \le x) = x^{n}$, which is option (d) - the standard swap-the-extreme distractor.
Check the endpoints: at $x = 0$ the probability must be 1 and at $x = 1$ it must be 0. $(1 - x)^{n}$ gives 1 and 0; $x^{n}$ gives 0 and 1, so it is the wrong extreme.
Differentiating gives the density of the minimum, $n(1-x)^{n-1}$, i.e. $X_{1}$ is Beta(1, n) - useful if a follow-up asks for its mean $1/(n+1)$.
solution: Let $X_{1}$, ..., $X_{n}$ be a random sample from $U(0,1)$ and let $X_{1} = \min(X_{1}, ..., X_{n})$.
The event {$X_{1} > x$} occurs if and only if every observation exceeds x.
For a single observation, $\operatorname{P}(X_{i} > x) = 1 - x$ for $0 \le x \le 1$.
By independence, $\operatorname{P}(X_{1} > x) = [\operatorname{P}(X_{1} > x)]^{n} = (1 - x)^{n}$.
(Endpoint check: at $x = 0$ this is 1 and at $x = 1$ it is 0, as a survival function must be.)
Hence option (b) is correct.

topic: Order Statistics - Minimum, Maximum, Range, Median
subtopic: Order Statistics - Minimum, Maximum, Range, Median
stem: For a sample of odd size n from $U(0,1)$, the mean and variance of the distribution of the median are respectively:
shortcut: For odd n the sample median is the $((n+1)/2)-th$ order statistic from $U(0,1)$, which is Beta(m, m) with $m = (n+1)/2$. Symmetry gives mean $1/2$, and the Beta variance $m^{2}/[(2m)^{2}(2m+1)] = 1/[4(n+2)] = 1/(4n+8)$.
tips: Order statistics from $U(0,1)$: $X_{k}$ ~ Beta($k, n - k + 1$), with mean $k/(n+1)$ and variance $k(n-k+1)/[(n+1)^{2} (n+2)]$.
For the median of an odd sample, $k = (n+1)/2$, so both Beta parameters are equal and the distribution is symmetric about $1/2$ - the mean follows without computation.
Plug into the variance formula directly: $k(n-k+1) = [(n+1)/2]^{2}$, so the variance is $[(n+1)/2]^{2}/[(n+1)^{2}(n+2)] = 1/[4(n+2)]$.
Sanity check at $n = 1$: the 'median' is the single observation $U(0,1)$ with variance $1/12$, and $1/(4 \cdot 1+8) = 1/12$. Correct.
solution: For a sample of odd size n from $U(0,1)$, the sample median is the k-th order statistic with $k = (n + 1)/2$.
The k-th order statistic of a uniform $(0,1)$ sample follows the Beta distribution with parameters k and $n - k + 1$.
Here $n - k + 1 = n - (n+1)/2 + 1 = (n + 1)/2 = k$, so the median follows Beta(k, k) with $k = (n+1)/2 - a$ distribution symmetric about $1/2$.
Variance of Beta(a, b) is ab/$[(a+b)^{2} (a + b + 1)]$. With $a = b = k$: variance = $k^{2}/[(2k)^{2} (2k + 1)] = 1/[4(2k + 1)]$.
Check at $n = 1$: variance = $1/12$, matching $\operatorname{Var}(U(0,1)) = 1/12$.
Hence option (b) is correct.

stem: What is the mean of the numbers $1\cdot n^2,\ 2\cdot(n-1)^2,\ 3\cdot(n-2)^2,\ \ldots,\ n\cdot1^2$?
shortcut: The k-th term is $k(n-k+1)^{2}$. Reversing the index turns the sum into sum of $(n+1-j)j^{2} = (n+1)$*sum $j^{2}$ - sum $j^{3} = n(n+1)^{2}(n+2)/12$. Dividing by n gives $(n+1)^{2}(n+2)/12$.
tips: Write the general term first: the k-th number is $k \cdot (n - k + 1)^{2}$, since the second factor counts down as the first counts up.
Substituting $j = n - k + 1$ converts the awkward product into $(n + 1 - j) j^{2}$, which splits into the standard sums of squares and cubes.
Standard sums: sum $j^{2} = n(n+1)(2n+1)/6$ and sum $j^{3} = [n(n+1)/2]^{2}$. Factor $n(n+1)^{2}$ out of both before combining.
Verify with $n = 2$: the numbers are $1 \cdot 4 = 4$ and $2 \cdot 1 = 2$, mean 3; the formula gives $(3^{2})(4)/12 = 36/12 = 3$. Correct - a ten-second check that also kills options (b), (c) and (d).
solution: The k-th number in the list is $a_{k} = k (n - k + 1)^{2}$, for $k = 1, 2$, ..., n. (Check: $k = 1$ gives $1 \cdot n^{2}$ and $k = n$ gives $n \cdot 1^{2}$.)
Substitute $j = n - k + 1$, so $k = n + 1 - j$ and j runs from n down to 1: $S = \sum_{j=1}^{n} (n + 1 - j) j^{2}$.
Verification at $n = 2$: numbers are 4 and 2 with mean 3; formula gives $9 \cdot 4/12 = 3$. Correct.
Hence option (a) is correct.

stem: If the interval of difference is h, what is $\Delta[\log f(x)]$?
shortcut: $\Delta \log f = \log f(x+h) - \log f(x) = \log[f(x+h)/f(x)]$, and $f(x+h) = f(x) + \Delta f(x)$, so the ratio is $1 + \Delta f(x)/f(x)$. Answer (c).
tips: Turn a difference of logarithms into the logarithm of a ratio - that single step solves the whole item.
Use $E f(x) = f(x) + \Delta f(x)$ to convert the shifted value into something expressed through $\Delta$.
Options (a) and (d) are dimensionally wrong: $E f(x)/f(x)$ is already the full ratio $f(x+h)/f(x)$, so adding 1 to it double-counts.
Sign check with a growing f: $\Delta f > 0$ forces $\Delta \log f > 0$, which rules out the minus sign in options (b) and (d).
solution: By definition, $\Delta[\log f(x)] = \log f(x + h) - \log f(x)$.
Combining the logarithms: $\Delta[\log f(x)] = \log[f(x + h)/f(x)]$.
Since $\Delta f(x) = f(x + h) - f(x)$, we have $f(x + h) = f(x) + \Delta f(x)$.
Therefore $f(x + h)/f(x) = 1 + \Delta f(x)/f(x)$.
Hence $\Delta[\log f(x)] = \log[1 + \Delta f(x)/f(x)]$.
Hence option (c) is correct.

stem: A cubic polynomial $f(x)$ has values: | x | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | |---|---|---|---|---| | f(x) | 1 | 0 | 1 | 10 | What is $f(4)$?
shortcut: Build the difference table: $f = 1, 0, 1, 10$ gives $\Delta$ = -1, 1, 9; $\Delta^{2} = 2, 8$; $\Delta^{3} = 6$. For a cubic $\Delta^{3}$ stays 6, so extend: $\Delta^{2} = 14, \Delta = 23, f(4) = 10 + 23 = 33$.
tips: For a polynomial of degree 3 the third differences are constant - that constant is the engine that extends the table.
Extend the table from the bottom-right upwards: new $\Delta^{3} = 6$, then add up each column in turn.
Check: $\Delta^{3} = 6 = 3! * a_{3}$, so the leading coefficient is 1, i.e. $f(x) = x^{3} - 3x^{2} + x + 1$. Then $f(4) = 64 - 48 + 4 + 1 = 33 - a$ clean independent verification.
Do not use Newton's forward formula with a fractional argument here; simple table extension is faster and error-free for an integer node.
solution: Construct the forward difference table for $f(0) = 1, f(1) = 0, f(2) = 1, f(3) = 10$.
First differences: -1, 1, 9.
Second differences: $1 - (-1) = 2$, and $9 - 1 = 8$.
Third difference: $8 - 2 = 6$.
Since f is a cubic, all third differences equal 6.
Extend the table: next $\Delta^{2} = 8 + 6 = 14$; next $\Delta = 9 + 14 = 23$; hence $f(4) = f(3) + 23 = 10 + 23 = 33$.
Verification: $\Delta^{3} = 6 = 3!$ times the leading coefficient, so $a_{3} = 1$, and fitting gives $f(x) = x^{3} - 3x^{2} + x + 1$, whence $f(4) = 64 - 48 + 4 + 1 = 33$.
Hence option (b) is correct.
